items.title: WireWeaver
items.text:
Crates for designing no_std APIs with a rich type system, no allocation and a dense bit-level wire format, plus a whole set of standard types and traits, all in Rust.

Get started Standard library Examples Features

Pages are marked by how deep they go: Basic, Advanced or Nomicon. See reading levels.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
• Wire Wire Format

    Dense zero-copy, no-alloc and no_std wire format. Dynamically sized user-defined types and vectors (on no_std as well). Bit level packing and more, real-world use cases.

  • RPC

    Define and call methods with any number of arguments and return type. Call using blocking, async or promise interface.

  • Streams

    Stream data of any type, observe property changes. Both to and from device.

  • Evolution

    Evolve data types and API while still allowing:

    • newer code to work with older devices
    • older code to work with newer devices

    The evolution checker tells whether a change is compatible.

  • USB, Ethernet, CAN and more

    Host and device drivers. Plus a framer that can put many small messages in one packet or a bigger message across multiple packets.

  • Standard library

    Numerical, SI, date & time, version and other types. GPIO, I2C, CAN, UART, SPI, logging, firmware update and other traits.

  • Reference and Owned types

    Automatically generate owned types for std usage from referenced ones. &'i [u8] becomes Vec<u8>, MyType<'i> MyTypeOwned, etc.

  • First class MCU support

    Geared towards bare-metal development with FLASH and RAM in mind. No allocation with full feature support.

  • Tooling

    CLI and GUI for debugging. Virtual devices. Introspection and tracing. Dynamic Python clients.

items.title: ShrinkWrap in C
items.text:
shrink_wrap/c/shrink_wrap.h and shrink_wrap/c/shrink_wrap.c are the ShrinkWrap reader and writer for C99: the same bytes as the Rust BufReader and BufWriter, for firmware that is not written in Rust. Copy the two files into the project, nothing else is needed: no malloc, nothing from libc beyond <stdint.h>, <stddef.h>, <stdbool.h>, <string.h> (memcpy, memset) and the freestanding <limits.h>.

This is the runtime only (SW-43). Code generated from an API (types, a device-side dispatcher, introspection) is planned on top of it (API-26), until then values are written and read field by field, in the order and with the calls the Rust code generated by #[derive_shrink_wrap] uses.

items.title: Writing
items.text:
#include "shrink_wrap.h"

sw_octet buf[64];
sw_writer wr;
size_t len;

sw_writer_init(&wr, buf, sizeof buf / sizeof buf[0]);
sw_write_bool(&wr, true);
sw_write_un8(&wr, 3, 5);        /* 3 bits */
sw_write_u16(&wr, 420);         /* aligns to the byte, Little Endian */
sw_write_str(&wr, "hi", 2);     /* the length goes to the back of the buffer */
if (sw_writer_finish(&wr, &len) != SW_OK) {
    /* too small a buffer: the error of the first write that failed */
}
/* send buf[0..len]: D0 A4 01 68 69 02 */

sw_writer_finish() encodes the lengths collected at the back of the buffer (reversed UNib32, see wire format internals) right after the data and returns the size. An Unsized value inside another value (every struct or enum that isn't final_structure, self_describing or sized) is framed with sw_unsized_begin() / sw_unsized_end(), as the Rust BufWriter::write does:

sw_unsized u;
sw_unsized_begin(&wr, &u);
/* the fields of the value */
sw_unsized_end(&wr, &u);

items.title: Reading
items.text:
sw_reader rd;
sw_reader_init(&rd, buf, len);
bool flag = sw_read_bool(&rd);
uint_least8_t three_bits = sw_read_un8(&rd, 3);
uint_least16_t num = sw_read_u16(&rd);
sw_bytes name = sw_read_str(&rd);   /* points into buf, name.len bytes, no NUL */
if (sw_reader_error(&rd) != SW_OK) {
    /* malformed or truncated: flag, num and name are 0 / empty from the failing read on */
}

An Unsized value is read through a reader split off for its size, so fields added by a newer version are skipped and missing ones read as out of bounds:

sw_reader v = sw_reader_split_unsized(&rd);
/* read the fields from v */
sw_reader_join(&rd, &v);            /* v's error, if any, is rd's now */

items.title: Errors
items.text:
There are no Results: the first error is kept in the reader or writer, as the Rust _latch reads do (SW-41). A call that fails moves nothing, and while an error is kept no call moves, reads give 0 (an empty sw_bytes) and writes write nothing. So a run of calls needs one check at the end, and nothing read after an error can steer the code (a discriminant is 0, a flag false), but don't use a value as a loop bound before checking. sw_reader_take_error() / sw_writer_take_error() clear it, sw_writer_reset() starts over.

The numbers of sw_error are those of the Rust shrink_wrap::Error.

Differences to the Rust crate, none of them on the wire: every failing call keeps its error (in Rust only the _latch reads do), a failing call moves nothing (a Rust read can align or consume bits before it fails), and a writer stops at its first error (the Rust _latch writes go on).

items.title: Targets with a 16-bit char (TI C2000)
items.text:
A buffer is an array of sw_octet (uint_least8_t) with one octet in the low 8 bits of each element, where CHAR_BIT is 16 too. Every access goes through two accessors that mask to 8 bits, values are kept in unsigned / uint32_t / uint64_t, and shifts don't rely on int being 32 bits. Data received packed two octets per word has to be unpacked into one octet per element first, and packed after writing. Also there:

  • float must be 32-bit IEEE 754, checked at compile time;
  • double must be 64 bits for sw_read_f64() / sw_write_f64(). Where it is 32 bits (C2000 with the old COFF ABI, AVR), define SW_NO_F64 and read the bits with sw_read_u64();
  • sw_write_str() takes the low 8 bits of each char.

Checked so far: builds without warnings with -std=c99 -pedantic -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion on the host, and for MSP430 (16-bit int and size_t), Cortex-M0 and RV32 with clang. Not tested on a C2000 compiler yet.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
shrink_wrap/c is also a Rust crate (shrink_wrap_c, not published) that builds the C with the cc crate and checks it against the Rust one in just test: golden vectors for every primitive, the length layouts and finish(), the errors and the latch (tests/golden.rs), and a proptest cross-check of random sequences of writes and reads, in both directions, on truncated and corrupted input too (tests/cross.rs). just lint builds the C on its own with -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic.

Not ported: TailSize, Series, fill_*, and the code size tricks of the Rust writer (finish_no_lens, _latch writes).

items.title: Command line tool
items.text: ww is the WireWeaver command line tool. It finds connected devices and lists them with their API, prints a device's API as a resource tree using its introspection data (or an API crate's tree, from source), observes properties, asks any device what it is and what it counted, and tests the link.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Install from git with cargo (the binary ends up in ~/.cargo/bin):

cargo install --git https://github.com/vhrdtech/wire_weaver wire_weaver_cli

Or from a local checkout of the repository:

cargo install --path wire_weaver_cli

Re-run the same command with --force to update an existing installation.

Inside the repository it can also be run without installing, with cargo ww <args> (alias from .cargo/config.toml). just install-cli builds the current checkout in release mode and copies the binary into ~/.local/bin/ww, which is handy when testing changes to the tool itself.

Linux permissions

Listing devices works without any setup, but opening one (introspect, info, ...) needs read/write access to /dev/bus/usb/..., usually granted to your user with a udev rule. See USB.

items.title: Shell completions
items.text:
Completions are produced by ww itself, so they always match the installed version. Values of the device selection flags (--serial, --label, --api, --usb-path, ...) are completed from the devices connected right now, with the product and label of each shown as a hint. Register them once in the shell's startup file:

echo 'source <(COMPLETE=bash ww)' >> ~/.bashrc                  # bash
echo 'source <(COMPLETE=zsh ww)' >> ~/.zshrc                    # zsh
echo 'COMPLETE=fish ww | source' >> ~/.config/fish/config.fish  # fish

Elvish and PowerShell are supported as well (COMPLETE=elvish, COMPLETE=powershell). In bash, values containing spaces or quotes are inserted quoted, and values after @ or : complete too (--api blinky_api@<TAB>, --vid-pid c0de:<TAB>).

items.title: First steps
items.text:
Plug in a device and look at what is there:

$ ww list
LOCATION             PRODUCT             SERIAL                    API                 HASH              LABEL
usb 003-1 c0de:cafe  WireWeaver Generic  09000F000251313438333634  all_gpio_api@0.1.0  5ff989a95162d4d7

ww list reads the USB descriptors only, without opening the device. API is the API crate the firmware implements. With one device connected, every other command uses it; with several, pick one with a device selection flag such as --serial 0900.

Next, the device's API as a resource tree, from the introspection data it carries (-d hides doc comments):

$ ww introspect -d
trait AllGpioApi all_gpio_api@0.1.0
└─ 0 impl port[]: ww_gpio::Bank
   ├─ 0 impl pin[]: ww_gpio::Pin
   │  ├─ 0 fn set_output_level(level: Level)
   │  ├─ 1 fn toggle()
   ...

From there:

  • ww info: what the device is (firmware, board, ids, label, last reset), on any device implementing the device contract.
  • ww observe <path>: watch a trait level's observed properties change, no generated code needed. For calls and streams from a script, use Python.
  • ww usb-loopback: check the link itself, round trips and throughput, whatever the API.
  • ww api tree <path> and ww api scaffold <path>: the same tree from an API crate's source, and the server handlers to implement for it.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Command Needs a device What it does ww list no (not opened) Lists connected devices matching the device selection ww introspect yes Prints the device's resource tree from its introspection data ww api no From an API crate's source: resource tree, AST, server scaffold, snapshots (save, check, diff) ww observe yes Observes a trait level's +observe properties: values, rate, link bytes/s ww usb-loopback yes, any API Runs link loopback and throughput tests ww dfu yes, any API Firmware update steps through ww_dfu traits: ww dfu reboot ww counters yes, any API The device's cnt counters, decoded with its ELF: read, watch, TUI, reset ww info yes, any API What the device is: firmware, board, ids, label, last reset ww report yes, any API A bug report in one file: info, counters, stored log, crash, decoded with the ELF ww elf no The ELF directory: ww elf add a release archive, ww elf id ww settings no Decodes a ww_settings::Store flash dump ww bootsel a boot ROM RP2040 / RP2350 in BOOTSEL mode: list, flash, reboot, follow back ww config no Shows or saves the device selection in a project ww.toml

ww help <command> or ww <command> --help prints all options of a command; the command reference explains each one with examples.

items.title: Device selection
items.text:
Commands working with a device (introspect, observe, info, ...) connect to the only device matching the selection, and ww list shows all the devices it matches. With no selection, the only connected device reporting a WireWeaver API id is used; if several match, they are all printed and nothing is opened, run ww list to see them and narrow the selection.

Flag Env variable ww.toml key Matches -s, --serial WW_SERIAL serial Serial number containing the value -l, --label WW_LABEL label User label, whole -p, --product WW_PRODUCT product Product description containing the value --manufacturer WW_MANUFACTURER manufacturer Manufacturer containing the value --api WW_API api Implemented API: name[@req], e.g. blinky_api@^0.1 --vid-pid WW_VID_PID vid_pid USB VID:PID in hex, e.g. c0de:cafe --usb-path WW_USB_PATH usb_path USB bus and port chain as shown by ww list, e.g. 003-1.2 --timeout-ms WW_TIMEOUT_MS timeout_ms Request timeout in milliseconds, not a filter --link-setup-timeout-ms WW_LINK_SETUP_TIMEOUT_MS link_setup_timeout_ms How long to wait for the device to answer when connecting, in milliseconds, not a filter. Default: USB 1000, RTT 10000
  • All text matching ignores case.
  • The version requirement in --api uses Cargo's SemVer syntax; without it, any version matches.
  • --usb-path pins a physical port, so it keeps selecting the same device across re-enumeration, and tells apart identical devices without serial numbers.
  • The flags are global: they can be given before or after the subcommand (ww --serial 2100 list and ww list --serial 2100 are the same).

Settings of different kinds are combined, so for example api from ww.toml and --serial on the command line narrow the selection together. Each setting is taken from the first place that has it: command line flag > environment variable > ww.toml.

items.title: Project config: ww.toml
items.text:
Device selection that stays the same for a project goes into the [device] table of a ww.toml, using the keys from the table above:

# ww.toml
[device]
api = "blinky_api@^0.1"
serial = "4B333720"
timeout_ms = 2000

ww.toml is looked up in the current directory and then its parents, so one file at the project root covers the whole project. --config <path> (or WW_CONFIG) uses another file, --no-config ignores it. Unknown keys are reported as errors rather than ignored. ww config show prints the config file in use, then every setting with its resolved value and where it came from (flag, env variable or file), so it answers "why is this device (not) selected".

items.text:
• Command reference: every command and option
  • USB: how devices report their API id and user label, and how the host finds them
  • ww_self: introspection data format

items.title: Command reference
items.text: Every ww command with its options. Start with the command line tool page: installation, the first session with a device, and the device selection flags all commands share. ww help <command> or ww <command> --help prints the options of the installed version.

items.title: ww list
items.text:
Lists devices reporting a WireWeaver API id, without opening them: the information comes from USB string descriptors (see USB), so it works even while another application is connected to the device.

$ ww list
LOCATION             PRODUCT             SERIAL                    API                 HASH              LABEL
usb 003-1 c0de:cafe  WireWeaver Generic  09000F000251313438333634  all_gpio_api@0.1.0  5ff989a95162d4d7
  • LOCATION: transport, bus and port chain, VID:PID. The 003-1 part is what --usb-path expects.
  • API: name and version of the API crate the firmware implements, HASH: its signature.
  • LABEL: user label set by the firmware, if any.

Only devices matching the device selection are shown, so ww list is also the way to check what a set of filters (or a ww.toml) selects. When some of the filters come from ww.toml, a note saying so is printed to stderr.

Option Description -a, --all Also list USB devices not reporting a WireWeaver API id --plain One device per line with key=value fields, without table formatting 
$ ww list --plain
usb 003-1 c0de:cafe "Vhrd.Tech" "WireWeaver Generic" serial=09000F000251313438333634 api=all_gpio_api@0.1.0 hash=5ff989a95162d4d7

items.title: ww introspect
items.text:
Connects to the selected device, downloads its introspection data (see ww_self) and prints the API as a resource tree: resource ids, methods with their signatures, properties with their access mode, streams and sinks, nested traits, arrays of resources and doc comments. A summary follows: resource, trait and type counts, size of the full API bundle and of the introspection data the device sent, referenced crates and the API hash. Traits and types a device leaves out of its introspection data because they are known from snapshots are put back first, any that could not be put back are counted as not included.

The tree looks the same as the one printed by ww api tree from source. Here with docs hidden:

$ ww introspect -d
trait AllGpioApi all_gpio_api@0.1.0
└─ 0 impl port[]: ww_gpio::Bank
   ├─ 0 impl pin[]: ww_gpio::Pin
   │  ├─ 0 fn set_output_level(level: Level)
   │  ├─ 1 fn toggle()
   │  ├─ 2 fn output_level() -> Level
   │  ├─ 3 fn input_level() -> Level
   │  ├─ 7 stream event: IoPinEvent
   │  ├─ 8 fn set_mode(mode: Mode, initial: Option<Level>) -> Result<(), Error>
   │  ├─ 9 fn mode() -> Mode
   │  ├─ 10 rw property pull: Pull, write error: Error
   │  ├─ 11 rw property speed: Speed, write error: Error
   │  └─ 12 fn configure_events(enabled: IoPinEnabledEvents) -> Result<(), Error>
   ├─ 8 fn capabilities() -> BankCapabilities
   ├─ 9 rw property reference_voltage: Volt, write error: Error
   └─ 10 fn name() -> String

15 resources, 2 traits, 11 types, 4362 bytes full, 72 bytes sent
crates: all_gpio_api@0.1.0, ww_gpio@0.1.0, ww_si@0.1.0, ww_numeric@0.2.0
api hash: 6e87e4113afd0168

impl name[]: crate::Trait is a nested trait ([] marking an array of them), properties show their access (const, ro, rw, wo) and whether they are observable, stream is device-to-host and sink host-to-device. The values of const items outside of arrays of traits are read from the device and shown after their type, const property SERIAL: String = "E661A410" (byte vectors as hex, struct and enum names left out); --no-values skips the reads.

With -t, all types the API refers to are listed after the tree, by their index in the bundle: structs with their fields, enums with their variants and discriminants, and each type's size kind (unsized, final structure, self-describing, sized) and enum repr:

$ ww introspect -d -t
...
types
├─ 0 enum ww_gpio::Level sized, repr u1
│  ├─ 0 Low
│  └─ 1 High
├─ 1 enum ww_gpio::IoPinEvent sized, repr u2
│  ├─ 0 RisingEdge
│  ├─ 1 FallingEdge
│  └─ 2 Custom(u8)
...
Option Description -d, --skip-docs Do not print doc comments -t, --types Also print all types the API refers to --raw Print raw introspection data (Rust debug format) instead of the tree --raw-as-sent Same as --raw, but as the device sent it: traits and types known from snapshots are left out --no-values Do not read the values of const items

Fails with an error if the device did not provide introspection data.

items.title: ww api
items.text:
Works on API crate sources instead of a device: the crate is parsed the same way ww_codegen! does it, so no device and no build are needed.

ww api tree <path> prints the same resource tree as ww introspect, for the #[ww_trait] defined in the crate at <path>:

$ ww api tree examples/blinky_api
trait BlinkyApi blinky_api@0.1.0
├─ 0 fn led_on()
└─ 1 fn led_off()

ww api ast <path> prints the parsed API bundle in RON format, useful when debugging codegen or introspection.

Both take --name <Trait> to pick the trait when the crate defines more than one, and tree also takes -d/--skip-docs and -t/--types.

ww api scaffold <path> prints the server side of an API: a server struct, a stub for every handler with its exact signature (methods and property getters/setters answer Unimplemented, stream and on-changed handlers do nothing, no array index is valid) and the matching ww_codegen! call. The output compiles as is, so a new firmware answers every request right away and the stubs are filled in one by one. Handler signatures depend on the codegen options, so pass the same ones the ww_codegen! call uses:

Option Default Description --name <Trait> The trait, when the crate defines more than one --server <Struct> Server Name of the server struct --use-async Async handlers --handler-model <M> With --use-async: which handlers are async fn, the rest plain fn, see sync and async handlers --alloc Handlers for no_alloc = false, taking owned arguments (String instead of &str) --method-model <M> _=immediate As method_model in ww_codegen!, see methods --property-model <M> _=get_set As property_model, see properties --const-model <M> BOARD=fn and the like: const items fixed at boot or link time, see const items --medium <Type> () Medium type handlers get in their Context --omit <items> Optional items to leave out, e.g. i2c.pullups,reset -o, --output <file> stdout Write to a file; an existing file is not overwritten 
ww api scaffold examples/blinky_api --use-async -o firmware/src/server.rs

ww api save <path> saves every #[ww_trait]/#[ww_api_root] trait defined in the crate's src/lib.rs, and every #[derive_shrink_wrap] type and unit marker struct (pub struct Volt;) defined there, in a pub mod at any depth, or re-exported from a module with pub use (each known by its path and name, units::Volt) into <path>/api_snapshots/<crate>_<major>_<minor>_<patch>.ron, for example ww_stdlib/ww_gpio/api_snapshots/ww_gpio_0_1_0.ron. Commit the snapshot and never change it afterward. It is a regular API bundle in RON: the root is named after the crate and has one nested trait resource per trait, definitions from this crate are included, and traits and types from other crates are only referenced by crate version, path and name, and signature. Save a snapshot of each of those crates too.

A signature is a hash of the full definition with docs, including everything it refers to, calculated as if nothing was skipped (ww_self::signature). A definition restored from another crate's snapshot can then be checked to be exactly the one that was left out, which catches a crate changed without bumping its version. The client does the same when it compares its API with a device's: a skipped trait or type with the same crate version but a different signature makes the resources using it incompatible.

Snapshots of ww_global and the ww_stdlib crates are embedded into the wire_weaver_snapshots crate, used by codegen and by wire_weaver_client (and so by ww). A device leaves traits and types known from them out of its introspection data, referring to them by crate version, name and signature, which makes it much smaller (e.g. examples/all_gpio_api goes from 4363 to 72 bytes). A definition is only left out if it is exactly the one in the snapshot, e.g. an unpublished crate version that changed after its snapshot was saved stays in-line. The API hash is calculated over the data as sent. Generated clients embed their own API in the same form. A client puts the left out definitions back from its own snapshots after download or loading from cache, checking signatures; one it doesn't know (e.g. from a newer ww_stdlib crate) stays skipped, and resources using it are only checked by crate version and signature. In this repo, just save-snapshots saves the snapshots and copies them into wire_weaver_snapshots/api_snapshots/; a wire_weaver_core test fails if any of them is out of date.

$ ww api save ww_stdlib/ww_uart
saved ww_stdlib/ww_uart/api_snapshots/ww_uart_0_1_0.ron, 12 resources, 1 traits, 11 types (0 traits and 2 types not included)

Running it again does nothing if nothing changed. Any change is an error, including doc comments only: bump the crate version (see evolution rules, doc-only changes bump the compatible position, so that tools can tell that improved docs are available) and save a new snapshot. --force overwrites anyway, only use it for a version that was never published. A snapshot of a new version is only saved if the version is bumped enough since the previous snapshot, see below.

ww api check <path> is the evolution checker: it compares the crate with its latest snapshot and fails if the version is not bumped enough for what changed (breaking position for breaking changes, compatible position for anything else, doc comments included). ww api diff <path> compares the same versions and lists every change, doc comments included, see listing all changes.

Current limitations, same as for codegen: traits are only found in src/lib.rs, a dependency reached through another crate's re-export is only resolved for the ones wire_weaver re-exports (ww_version, shrink_wrap), and crates with a workspace-inherited version can't be loaded.

items.title: ww observe
items.text:
Observes a trait level's +observe properties (Observing properties) from introspection alone, no generated code needed (TOOL-11, the same dynamic client Python uses):

$ ww observe motor --rate 10
observing motor (3 properties): speed, current, position
budget: 20.0 kB/s
Ctrl+C to stop
{speed: 1500, current: 3, position: 1024}  rate 98.2/s  link 982/s

<path> is dotted/indexed (motor, bank[0]), empty for the API root. Without --rate every observable property is asked for on-change; with it, all of them periodically at that rate (milliseconds). Prints each update's present values, the measured update rate and the link bytes/s it costs, until Ctrl+C. See Observing properties for the host-side model this reuses.

--samples MS observes every sample of the level's +batched properties, in batches at most MS old (Every sample): one line per sample with its device time in seconds, the other properties as before.

$ ww observe foc --samples 5
  4294.966696 i_a: 1250 mA
  4294.966736 i_a: 1262 mA
  ..

items.title: ww explain
items.text:
Shows which bits of a buffer hold which value (TOOL-9): every field with its place in the buffer, its raw bits, its type and its decoded value, the lengths, enum discriminants, Option flags and padding in between, and a hex map coloured by field. Useful to check what a device really sends, to read a captured frame, or to learn the wire format on your own types.

$ ww explain --crate api 'sub_byte(I2cAddress::Ten(0x2A5), 100, -300)'
sub_byte arguments · 4 bytes

0000  d4 b9 2d 40 

bits             raw                  field                      type         value
0‥10                                  addr                       I2cAddress   Ten
0                1                      discriminant             u32          1
1‥10             1010 1001 01           0                        ub10         677  0x2a5
11‥17            1100 100             a                          ub7          100
18‥27            1011 0101 00         b                          ib10         -300  0x2d4

28 bits in values, 4 padding or unread

<what> is a type of the API (Config), or a resource path: a method's arguments (motor.set_speed, --return for its return value), a property's value, a stream's item. The bytes come in hex (0a1b2c, 0a 1b 2c, 0x0a,0x1b), from --file, or as a value written as a Rust expression, which is encoded first:

$ ww explain Config --value 'Config { mode: Mode::Fast, gains: [1.0, 2.5], name: "x", limit: None }'
$ ww explain 'motor.set_speed(1.5, Dir::Cw)'     # a call: its arguments
$ ww explain 'motor.limit = 3'                   # a property write

Literals take the type of their field: 5 is a u16, a ub3 or an f32 as the field says, and a value out of range is an error naming the field (argument a: 200 is out of range for ub7). Struct literals (Name { a: 1 }, ..Default::default() for the rest), enum variants (Mode::Fast or Fast), Some/None, Ok/Err, tuples, arrays ([0; 4], vec![..], b"bytes", 0xa102 for bytes), ranges and negative numbers work. The values ww prints (ww introspect, ww observe) are written the same way and can be pasted back; quantities go in q!(..): q!(3300 mV), q!(1.2e-4 N*m/(rad/s)) (* for ·, u for µ, a string for other symbols: q!("20 °C")), and a plain number is in the unit itself.

A whole message as it goes over the link, envelope and payload: ww explain request HEX for a request, ww explain event HEX for an event (--for PATH names the method or property it answers; a stream's data names its stream itself), and --request to see the request a call, a property write or a read is on the wire:

$ ww explain --crate api 'add(7, -2)' --request
Request Call add · 10 bytes

0000  01 01 00 07 00 00 00 fe  ff 01 

bits             raw                  field                      type         value
0‥79                                  ·                          Request      
0‥7              0000 0001              seq                      uvlq32       1
8‥15 ↩9l         0000 0001 ↩0001        path                     PathKind::Absolute [1]  (add)
16‥71                                   kind                     RequestKind  Call
16‥19            0000                     discriminant           nib          0
24‥71                                     args                   TailBytes    
24‥55            07000000                   a                    u32          7
56‥71            1111 1110 1111 1111        b                    i16          -2  0xfffe

72 bits in values, 8 padding or unread

The envelope (sequence number, path, request or event kind) is read with the ww_client_server types, the payload inside it by the resource the path names. A path through a global trait id is shown but its payload is not explained yet, nor are the multi requests and a level's property updates.

Front bits are counted from bit 7 of byte 0. Lengths and sizes are nibbles read from the back of the buffer (or of the unsized value they are in), shown as ↩ with the byte and its half: ↩97h is bits 7:4 of byte 97, ↩97l bits 3:0. The API comes from the device, or without one from the crate defining it (--crate PATH, --trait NAME when it has more than one) or a saved bundle (--bundle FILE, see ww api save). When the bytes don't decode, the tree shows how far it got and where it stopped.

ww explain FILE with a capture file (ww capture) prints the capture as ww monitor printed it live, with the same --layer, --bytes and --bits; the capture carries the device's API, so no device is needed. Replies are explained by the request their seq pairs them with.

items.title: ww monitor
items.text:
Prints what crosses the link as it happens, decoded (The link tap, TOOL-14), from the link setup on, until Ctrl+C or --duration S. --layer says how deep to look:

  • link (default): every ww_link message (data, link setup, pings) with the frames it came in, and the link events; data messages with their request or event title, replies with the request they answer and its time.
  • frame: every frame (USB packet, UDP datagram, RTT chunk) with its pieces as well.
  • api: only requests, replies and events, with their values; --bits adds each message's bit map and field table, as ww explain shows one.
$ ww monitor --layer api
   0.000000 L0 session Host Usb '3-1.2', U2 { checksum: Crc16IbmSdlc { full: false }, tail: None, stream: false }, frames up to 64 B
   0.000055 L0 connected
   0.000280 L0 link ready
   0.065600 L0 → Request Call add  a: 5, b: 100 #3
   0.065955 L0 ← Event Value add  105 (reply to #3 in 355.0 µs)

The time is seconds since the first record, L0 the link, → sent by the host and ← received. --bytes adds the bytes of every frame and message in hex. A frame line lists its pieces (Full Data0 12 B, Start Data0 6/12 B: 6 of a 12 byte message's bytes), a message line the frames it is in (in #3@58+6, #4@1+6: 6 bytes at offset 58 of frame 3, 6 at offset 1 of frame 4). Without a ww server, this is the command's own connection to the device: the link setup, the reads it makes to connect, its pings.

items.title: --monitor and --capture on any command
items.text:
The tap of ww monitor and ww capture is also a pair of global flags of every command that opens a device connection (info, observe, stream, introspect, dfu, counters, report, usb-loopback): they tap that command's own connection, so the traffic of a real call is seen without a ww server.

  • --monitor[=frame|link|api] (default link, the value needs =) prints to stderr, from the link setup on, as ww monitor does; the command's own output stays on stdout for scripts. --monitor-bytes and --monitor-bits are ww monitor's --bytes and --bits.
  • --capture FILE saves the same connection (frames included) to a new file, written as FILE.partial and renamed when the command ends, to read with ww explain FILE; it is refused when FILE exists (ww capture --append adds to one).
$ ww -l donguru-m1 --monitor=api info
...
   0.093976 L0 → Request Read  #3
   0.097889 L0 ← Event Value (reply to #3 in 3.91 ms)

Commands that don't connect (list, explain, api, udev, elf, config, settings) refuse the flags with an error, and so do ww monitor, ww capture and ww stats, which are the tap themselves.

items.title: ww stats
items.text:
Framer and link statistics of the same records, every --every S seconds (1 by default) for the time since the last print, until Ctrl+C or --duration S; --file FILE gives those of a whole capture instead:

$ ww stats --file link.wwtape
window 0.071 s, 5 blocks, 0 blocks lost, 0 records lost
link 0 tx:
  frames 7 (98.4/s), 138 bytes, fill 30.8%, 1.86 messages/frame
  overhead: heads 26 B, checksums and tails 2 B, unused 310 B
  messages 13, 1 split over 2 frames
  message to frame: mean 926.0 µs, max 2.44 ms
  link messages: Data0 9, Disconnect 1, GetDeviceInfo 1, LinkSetup 1, Nop 1
link 0 rx:
  frames 10 (140.6/s), 420 bytes, fill 65.6%, 1.20 messages/frame
  overhead: heads 25 B, checksums and tails 2 B, unused 220 B
  messages 12, 1 split over 5 frames
  link messages: Data0 9, DeviceInfo 1, LinkReady 1, Nop 1
link 0 api:
  Call add: 8 (112.5/s), reply mean 1.36 ms max 2.50 ms
  Call blob: 1 (14.1/s), reply mean 2.25 ms max 2.25 ms

Fill is the frame bytes used of what the frames could carry; trouble (dropped pieces, checksum failures, partial messages dropped, frame gaps, framer mismatches) gets its own line when there is any.

items.title: ww capture
items.text:
Saves what crosses the link into a file, until Ctrl+C or --duration S, with a spinner showing blocks and bytes:

$ ww capture -o link.wwtape --duration 10
captured 12 blocks, 48.2kB to link.wwtape
$ ww explain link.wwtape --layer api

The file is tape blocks back to back, each written as it comes. A new capture is written as FILE.partial and renamed to FILE when it ends; an existing FILE is refused unless --append adds to it. --sync says when the data is synced to the disk, which bounds what a crash or a power cut can lose: an interval (1s, the default, or 250ms), blocks:N (every N blocks) or none (only at the end). A failed write or sync ends the capture with the file as it is, never retried. The file carries the API bundles of the device and of the tap's own records. --layer link or api leaves the frames out (smaller files).

A capture is read up to its first damaged block (a crash's cut last block, a flipped byte, a block out of order), and where it was cut is said; zeros at the end (preallocated space) are the end. --resync on ww explain FILE and ww stats --file reads on past damage to the next block instead. A FILE.partial left by a crash reads the same way.

items.title: ww usb-loopback
items.text:
Checks the link to the selected device in three stages, each with a progress bar, then prints a summary table:

  1. loopback: one message at a time to the device and back, counting round trips per second, lost echoes (none within --echo-timeout-ms) and corrupted ones (each message carries data that checks itself).
  2. tx_speed: host → device, the device discards the messages. An echoed marker every 32 messages (at most 2 in flight) keeps the host from running ahead of a slow device.
  3. rx_speed: device → host, the device answers each request with 64 messages (at most 2 requests in flight); gaps in their numbering are lost.

The device's link layer answers (Loopback in ww_link), so this works with any device, whatever its API, without downloading its introspection. The command exits with an error when anything was lost or corrupted, or when the device stopped answering (3 timeouts in a row). The numbers above are defaults of the tuning options in the table below (--help lists them under "Test tuning"), e.g. for a slow transport or a device with small buffers.

Option Default Description --duration-sec <N> 10 How long to run each stage --packet-size <N> max Size of each link message (8 bytes of header and data), capped to what both sides accept --echo-timeout-ms <MS> 500 An echo (round trip, marker or device → host reply) missing for this long is lost --timeouts-in-a-row <N> 3 Give up after this many echo timeouts in a row --marker-every <N> 32 Host → device: messages between two echoed markers --markers-in-flight <N> 2 Host → device: markers in flight at most, the host waits for their echoes beyond that --rx-batch <N> 64 Device → host: messages the device sends for one request (at least 2) --batches-in-flight <N> 2 Device → host: requests in flight at most

Lost or corrupted packets usually point at the hardware rather than the software: a bad cable, a malfunctioning hub, a powered hub used without power, or power problems on an externally powered device.

items.title: ww dfu
items.text:
Firmware update steps through the ww_dfu traits. These work with any device that implements the trait somewhere in its API, whatever the API and its version: ww dfu connects without the user API check and calls the trait through a global trait path, which the device resolves itself. So a ww built today can still reboot a device whose firmware is years older.

$ ww dfu reboot --serial 4B333720
blinky_api@0.1.0 reboots into the updater
Command / option Default Description reboot ww_dfu::BootControl::reboot, then exits without waiting for the device reboot --into <TARGET> updater updater (bootloader with a transport or recovery app) or app (normal reset, applies a staged update)

A device without ww_dfu::BootControl, or with an incompatible version of ww_dfu, answers that it doesn't implement the trait. On an RP2350 whose updater is the boot ROM, ww bootsel flash --wait --follow then writes the new image and waits for the app to come back; a single command that follows any device through its updater is not done yet (CLT-21).

items.title: ww counters
items.text:
The cnt counters of any device implementing ww_counters::Counters anywhere in its API (a global trait, like ww dfu), decoded with the firmware's ELF found by the build id the device reports, and shown with the same views as cnt over a debug probe.

$ ww counters --serial 4B333720
Using ELF target/thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf/release/usb_io_fw
📍 RAM counters at 0x20000000, 64 B
INFO  boots         3
...
Command / option Default Description read yes All counters once watch [--interval MS] 100 All counters, then each change until q or Ctrl+C (reset / decrease marked) tui Terminal UI, a table per buffer; r / R reset RAM / backup counters reset [--bkp] Zero the RAM counters, with --bkp the backup ones too info Buffers, cnt format, build id, and the ELF that matches --elf PATH The ELF to use; refused if its build id differs from the device's --force Use the ELF anyway, or the newest under target/ when no ELF matches --format FORMAT text json (one document) or jsonl (one object per counter, watch events)

Without --elf, the ELF comes from WW_ELF_PATH, the ELF directory ~/.cache/ww/elf (filled by ww elf add or cnt elf add) or target/ of the cargo project in the current directory. See ww_counters.

items.title: ww info
items.text:
Firmware, board, ids, user label and last reset of any device, through the device contract traits (global trait paths, like ww dfu: whatever the device's API and version, no ELF needed).

$ ww info --serial 4B333720
API        usb_io_api@0.5.0
Firmware   b200_usb_io 0.5.0 (a1b2c3d-dirty, built 2026-10-03 18:20), release
Build id   28a4e144e867138da2cccccd14e3e6baa2c78fbc
Board      rePort rev B (strap 2), BOM std, serial RP-0042
Ids        chip e6613871235b1c2d (internal, primary)
Label      "bench 2" (kept over power cycles)
Last reset Panic, crash data 2 boots old, boot 3 since cleared, ran 2.5 s
Option Default Description --format FORMAT text json for scripts; each part says value, not_implemented or error

A part the device doesn't implement says so, the rest is still shown.

items.title: ww report
items.text:
ww info plus the counters, the device's stored defmt log and the last reset's fault and stack addresses named with the ELF, as one text a tester sends with a bug report. The ELF is found by the build id the device reports (where); a part whose ELF isn't found says so and names the places searched.

ww report --serial 4B333720 -o report.md
Option Default Description -o, --output F stdout Write the report to a file --elf PATH The ELF to use for everything; refused if its build id differs from the device's --force Use the ELF anyway --format FORMAT text json for scripts

Reading the log does not empty the device's store.

items.title: ww elf
items.text:
The ELF directory (~/.cache/ww/elf, or the ones in WW_ELF_PATH), where firmware ELFs are found by build id for ww counters, ww report and cnt.

ww elf add usb_io_fw-0.5.0-elf.tar.zst   # every ELF of a release, stored as <build id>.elf
ww elf add target/release/usb_io_fw      # one ELF
ww elf id target/release/usb_io_fw       # its build id, and whether it is in the directory

--dir DIR adds to another directory. A file without a build id is listed as skipped. See the release archive.

items.title: ww settings
items.text:
ww settings dump decodes a ww_settings::Store flash dump: no device needed, just the raw bytes of the store's flash range (read off the chip, from a .bin or a debug probe dump). The word and page size aren't in the dump itself, so they are given on the command line (completion suggests the sizes Store supports, with a chip example each):

$ ww settings dump settings.bin --word-size 8 --page-size 2048 --base 0x08078000
2 pages, word 8 bytes, page 2048 bytes, base 0x08078000
page 0 @ 0x08078000: page_seq 1
  0x08078010 +48     valid, stale key 0 seq 1 len 30
  ...
  0x080787f0 +16     erased
page 1 @ 0x08078800: page_seq 2 (current)
  0x08078810 +24     valid, stale key 1 seq 28 len 10
  ...
  0x08078b40 +48     valid, current key 0 seq 40 len 30
  0x08078b70 +24     valid, current key 1 seq 40 len 10
  0x08078b88 +1144   erased

current record per key:
  key 0 @ 0x08078b40 (page 1), seq 40, 30 bytes: 27272727...
  key 1 @ 0x08078b70 (page 1), seq 40, 10 bytes: d8d8d8d8...

Every item slot is shown, valid or not (cut: a write a power loss interrupted; garbage: neither a valid item nor erased), including on a page whose header is itself invalid, which a device's own Store never looks at. The "current record per key" section is cross-checked against a real Store run over the same bytes, so it is exactly what the device would read; a mismatch is a bug in the decoder, not a sign of a bad dump, and is reported as an error. --format json gives the same information as JSON instead.

items.title: ww bootsel
items.text:
RP2040 and RP2350 boot ROMs in BOOTSEL mode, over PICOBOOT: no WireWeaver on the device, no picotool or libusb on the host. Used to flash an RP2350 whose app rebooted itself into the boot ROM (ww_dfu::BootControl::reboot, see ww dfu), and to follow it back into the new firmware.

ww bootsel list                                   # boot ROMs in BOOTSEL mode with their serial numbers
ww bootsel info -s E661                           # chip id (RP2350)
ww bootsel flash app.uf2 -s E661                  # erase, write, verify, reboot into the new image
ww bootsel flash target/thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf/release/app -s E661  # an ELF works too, no objcopy needed
ww bootsel flash app.uf2 -s E661640843522C2F --wait 10 --follow
ww bootsel reboot -s E661 [--bootsel]             # reboot (RP2350), into BOOTSEL again with --bootsel
flash option Default Description --addr <ADDR> 0x10000000 Flash address of a raw binary (any file that isn't .uf2 or an ELF) --family <F> rp2350 UF2 family to take blocks of: rp2350, rp2040 or any --wait <SECONDS> Wait this long for the BOOTSEL device with the --serial to appear --follow After the reboot, wait for a WireWeaver device with the same serial and show it --no-reboot Don't reboot after writing

The file is a UF2 (by extension), an ELF (by its magic bytes, whatever the extension — target/.../release/app works straight from cargo build, no objcopy/elf2uf2), or otherwise a raw binary written at --addr. An ELF is taken by its PT_LOAD segments' physical (flash) address; a segment that isn't in flash (a RAM-only image) is an error.

--serial selects the device as for other commands; part of it is enough when only one matches, --wait and --follow need the full one. See following a reboot.

items.title: ww udev
items.text: Linux only. Meant to print a udev rule giving your user access to WireWeaver USB devices (ww udev | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/70-ww_device.rules), but not implemented yet: the command stops with a todo!() panic. Until then write the rule by hand, see USB.

items.title: ww config
items.text:
Manages the project config file:

ww config save --api blinky_api@^0.1 --serial 4B333720  # write flags into ww.toml (comments are kept)
ww config show                                         # resolved selection and where each setting comes from
ww config unset serial                                 # remove settings from ww.toml

ww config save writes into the --config file if given, otherwise into the ww.toml found in the current directory or its closest parent, otherwise creates ww.toml in the current directory. Only flags from the command line are saved, never environment variables, so a WW_* variable exported in a shell profile does not end up in project files.

items.title: Dev GUI tool
items.text:
wire_weaver_tool is an egui app (native, or in the browser through Trunk) for looking at what WireWeaver makes of an API definition: the parsed AST and the generated code side by side.

Out of date

The tool was last updated in June 2025 and does not build against the current wire_weaver_core (it uses modules that have since been reorganized, such as wire_weaver_core::ast). It lives outside the repository's Cargo workspace, so CI doesn't build it either. Status and plans: TOOL-6 in the feature tracker.

For the same jobs today:

  • ww api tree <path> and ww api ast <path> print an API crate's resource tree and parsed bundle, see ww api.
  • debug_to_file = "../../target/some_name.rs" in a ww_codegen! / ww_impl! call writes the generated code to a file.
  • ww introspect and the Python module show and call a connected device's API.

items.title: What it did
items.text:
• Load and parse a source file with type and API definitions, reload or reparse it
  • Show the internal AST and parser warnings and errors
  • Show the generated serdes code of each struct, enum and const
  • Show the generated server dispatcher and client code
  • A no_alloc switch to compare embedded and host code

items.title: Planned
items.text:
• Input and output widgets for the types (numbers with SI units as spinner, dial or slider, strings, colors, ...)
  • Documentation-like UI that can call a live server
  • Server mockup UI answering with user input, recorded answers or examples
  • Loading types and API from bytecode, and compiling sources to bytecode (through Rust FFI or a backend service)

items.title: WireWeaver features and roadmap
items.text: This file is the single source of truth for what WireWeaver supports, what is being worked on and what is planned, for humans and AI agents alike. It replaces the external task tracker.

items.title: How to use this file
items.text:
• Status of each item:
  • ✅ done
  • 🚧 in progress or partially done (the note says what is missing)
  • 📋 planned
  • 💡 idea, not committed to
  • ⛔ blocked (the note says on what)
  • 🔍 probably done or obsolete, needs a check before closing
  • 🧪 done and tested on the host, the check on hardware is still open (the note says what to check)
  • Target is the release an item is planned for: v0.5 is the next release (the workspace is at 0.5.0, crates.io has 0.4.0). v0.5.x is the next compatible release after it: v0.5.1 if nothing turns out to be breaking, otherwise the next minor. No tag means not scheduled. grep 'v0.5' FEATURES.md gives the release scope.
  • IDs (SW-3, CLT-12) are stable: never renumber or reuse one. New items take the next free number of their area, even when they are inserted in the middle of it. Use the ID in commit messages, CHANGELOG entries and code TODOs (// TODO(SRV-4): ...). When talking to people, name an ID with a short slug from its title (SW-3 string-and-vec), never bare.
  • Items are grouped by area. Each area lists what works first (✅), then open items ordered by target.
  • When finishing work, update the item in the same change: mark it ✅, move it up to the done items of its area and add a pointer (docs page, crate, test or example). Don't delete done items. Move items that turn out to be obsolete to Dropped and superseded with a one-line reason.
  • This file is also rendered as the docs site's "Feature tracker" page (docs/features.md includes it), so indent nested lists and paragraphs inside an item by 4 spaces, as Python-Markdown requires. The "Features" page (docs/features_today.md) is generated from it and from tests/features_page/entries.md, which has a short line, a reading level and a docs link per item: an item that becomes done or in progress gets a line there, then run just features-page; just test fails until both are done.
  • New ideas go into the matching area as 💡. Small code-level gaps stay as TODO comments in the source; only those that limit users or block a feature get an item here.

items.title: Wire format (shrink_wrap, SW)
items.text:
• ✅ SW-1 Structs, plain enums and data enums, discriminant type selection with ww_repr.
  • ✅ SW-2 Option and Result, also inside Vec, as one-bit flags.
  • ✅ SW-3 String and Vec<T>, with special handling of Vec<u8>.
  • ✅ SW-4 Fixed size arrays, tuples and the unit type ().
  • ✅ SW-5 Bit-aligned integers: nibbles and u1..u32 (un); un8/un16 are forwarded to un32 for smaller flash.
  • ✅ SW-6 Variable length numbers: UNib32, UVlq32, and UVlq32Backfill for values known only after the rest is serialized.
  • ✅ SW-7 Borrowed and owned types: Sized and Unsized traits, RefStr/RefVec, borrowed types by default and Owned variants generated automatically.
  • ✅ SW-8 Evolvable by default: every struct and enum is Unsized; final_structure, self_describing and sized are opt-ins.
  • ✅ SW-9 TailBytes / TailBytesOwned: bytes that take up the rest of the buffer, written without a size; only valid as the last item. Generated API code puts them in place of byte slices, e.g. for return values and property values.
  • ✅ SW-10 EitherAnyVec: zero-copy, no-alloc array of Either elements of any types, with the L/R flags packed in groups of 8 instead of padding each element. Packs e.g. a list of Results tightly; used for multi-read and multi-call results (only multi-read exists so far).
  • ✅ SW-55 OptionAnyVec: zero-copy, no-alloc array of Option slots of any types (numbers, structs, lists, strings, a nested OptionAnyVec for a child level), only the present values written, in slot order without padding between them. A presence header up front in the smallest of four modes (all, dense bits, two-level bits, index list), self-delimiting so that readers with fewer or more slots than the writer read it (slots are only appended); a malformed header is an error. Writer takes the present set up front (SetBits over a bitset, any increasing iterator), OptionAnyVecWriter / in-place OptionAnyVecBuilder. For a trait level's properties in one update (API-38). See docs/serdes/special_types.md#optionanyvec-sparse-slots-of-any-types, docs/serdes/showcase.md.
  • ✅ SW-68 Word-wide bit writer and reader, the same bytes: BitWriter with a 32-bit accumulator flushed a word at a time, BitSink::put_block for packed blocks, write_un* / write_bool / UNib32 and the reader's read_un* / UNib32 through one 4-byte window and one bounds check per call. The FOC observe poll on an STM32H725 75.5 k cycles instead of 99.9 k at opt-level = 3 (121.5 k against 172.2 k at "z"), a FOC level batch from the store 36.8 k instead of 58.9 k; reads of UN numbers and UNib32 take 0.4-0.6x the instructions on a Cortex-M4F; about 1.5 KB more flash at "z". See docs/articles/series.md#the-bit-writer-and-reader-a-word-at-a-time, examples_mcu/mcu_qemu/src/bit_io.rs (qemu-bit-io, qemu-m4f-bit-io, stm32h725ig-bit-io-cycles).
  • ✅ SW-64 Series written straight from a SeriesStore, column by column, the same bytes as the item walk: SeriesStore::columnar / write_store (leaves, Option, arrays, tuples, derived structs and enums, by hand for NumericValue) and series::write_store_series, used by ww_stream's batchers on their own. Needs one variant per enum and Option over the rows (a prefix change falls back to the walk). One FOC level batch (21 x Series<T> + clock, n = 32, DeltaPacked): 74.9 k instructions on a Cortex-M3 instead of 143.5 k, 100 k cycles on an STM32H725 instead of 312 k (60 k against 125 k at opt-level = 3). See docs/serdes/series.md#from-the-store-column-by-column, shrink_wrap/shrink_wrap/src/series/store_write_tests.rs, examples_mcu/mcu_qemu (qemu-store-columns).
  • ✅ SW-63 Fast and small Series encoding on MCUs, the same bytes: about 6x fewer instructions per item on a Cortex-M3/M4F (Series<Timed<Ampere>>, n = 32: 341 with a fixed codec, 969 with SMALLEST; 25 200 cycles per batch of 32 on an STM32H725), and codec policies fixed at compile time (SeriesPolicy, FixedCodecs, DeltaPacked, the no_std default of ww_stream's batcher) that link only their own codecs: 15 KB of encoder flash on a Cortex-M3 instead of 91 KB (25 KB with a run-time CodecPolicy). See docs/serdes/series.md#cpu-and-flash-on-an-mcu, examples_mcu/mcu_qemu, examples_mcu/qemu_icount.
  • ✅ SW-62 SeriesStore and series size bounds: room for N items of a series type as a struct of arrays (empty_store, set, get), derived for structs (field stores) and enums (discriminants and every data variant's fields), by hand for ww_numeric::NumericValue (a variant byte and one payload as wide as the widest variant enabled): Timed<Ampere> takes 12 bytes per item with number types up to 32 bits, against 24 as items. SeriesColumns::MAX_ITEM_BITS / MAX_FIXED_BITS and Series::max_bytes(n): the worst case of a batch under any codec policy, None for strings and opaque fields. series(no_store) leaves the derived store out. Piece 1 of API-41. See docs/serdes/series.md#collecting-items-on-a-device-seriesstore, shrink_wrap/shrink_wrap/src/series/store_tests.rs, ww_stdlib/ww_si/tests/store.rs.
  • ✅ SW-61 RefVecBuilder<T>: a list written in place, element by element (push, extend, push_with for a nested builder or an element written by hand), finish writes the count; same bytes as RefVec::Slice, as the whole buffer, a struct field or an element of another list. A failed push undoes its element, with_max_len for MaxLen<RefVec<..>, N>, RefVecBuilderOwned for BufWriterOwned. A byte list also has extend_from_slice and write_bytes_with (a byte blob written by other means), which replace RefVecU8Builder. See docs/serdes/special_types.md#refvecbuilder-lists-written-in-place, shrink_wrap/shrink_wrap/tests/ref_vec_builder.rs.
  • ✅ SW-59 Tuple and unit structs in the derive: struct Celsius(f32);, struct Pair<'i>(u8, &'i str);, struct Marker; in every layout and size assumption, same bytes as the struct with the fields named; positional names _0, _1, ... in consts, C names and errors. #[flag] needs named fields. The API model has them as unnamed fields, dynamic clients and Python (a tuple, a single field its value, a unit None) read and write them. A unit struct is evolvable (it records its length inside a parent); with sized, final_structure, self_describing or fixed_layout it is a compile error, as it could never change. See docs/types.md, shrink_wrap/shrink_wrap/tests/tuple_structs.rs, tests/dynamic.
  • ✅ SW-58 validate = path derive directive: a function checking every struct value just read, so a derived type (and the API model it gives to dynamic clients) can still reject out-of-range data; used by ww_date_time::Year.
  • ✅ SW-57 ArrayString<N> / ArrayVec<T, N>: owned, no-alloc string/list types backed by a fixed-size array, same bytes on the wire as &str/String and Vec<T>, for an owned no-alloc field (a value_on_changed field of a string/list property in a no_alloc server, a settings value); Error::MaxLenExceeded rather than a cut value, for serializing, deserializing, push_str/push and TryFrom<&str> alike. docs/serdes/special_types.md#arraystring-arrayvec-owned-values-without-an-allocator.
  • ✅ SW-11 Alloc writer BufWriterOwned, SerializeShrinkWrap for &[u8], String as UFS.
  • ✅ SW-12 In-place builders used by the server codegen (event and error builders), and the manual patch-the-discriminant-later pattern (docs/serdes/showcase.md).
  • ✅ SW-13 Binary format documented in docs/serdes/wire_format.md, worked tricks in docs/serdes/showcase.md.
  • ✅ SW-14 Usable standalone as a dense data storage format (examples/minimal_shrink_wrap, examples/compare_wire_formats).
  • ✅ SW-34 Smaller code on small CPUs: BufReader / BufWriter reads and writes that keep an error instead of returning it (read_u8_latch, write_u32_latch, .., latched()), used by #[derive_shrink_wrap] for plain fields with one check per type; Error without payloads; one shared integer read and write; no division in UNib32. 19 to 20 % less code for a derived request/reply codec on RV32IC and Cortex-M0, same wire format. Numbers, where the rest goes and what is left to do: docs/serdes/code_size.md (measured by TEST-17).
  • ✅ SW-36 No length FIFO code for types without lengths: SerializeShrinkWrap::PUSHES_LEN, computed by #[derive_shrink_wrap] from the fields (default true unless Sized), lets to_ww_bytes and BufWriter::finish_for::<T>() end with finish_no_lens() at compile time, so the FIFO encoder is not linked: about 510 bytes less per such encoder on RV32IC (a struct of plain fields 1476 → 964). For types with lengths encode_len_fifo / write_nib are smaller (vec_ser 1378 → 1142). Same wire format (shrink_wrap/tests/pushes_len.rs, docs/serdes/code_size.md steps 4 and 5).
  • ✅ SW-37 RefVec of plain numbers without the decode pass: a list of u8..u128, i8..i128, f32 or f64 finds its end with one bounds check instead of reading every element (4096 bytes: 10 µs → 6 ns on a host), same result, errors and reader state as the pass, same wire format (shrink_wrap/tests/ref_vec_skip.rs, just fuzz-shrink-wrap-ref-vec). Costs 50 to 140 bytes of code in a decoder with such a list. Other Sized types keep the pass on purpose (stride is not size_bits, elements are validated there): docs/serdes/code_size.md.
  • ✅ SW-38 Latched reads of U1..U64 / I2..I64 fields: read like the integers of SW-34, with one error check per type (through a hidden DeserializeShrinkWrap::des_shrink_wrap_latch); a bit-packed struct decodes in 40 bytes less on RV32IC (886 → 846), 88 on RV32I. Same wire format, results and errors as reading field by field (shrink_wrap/tests/latched_reads.rs, just fuzz-shrink-wrap-latched). Nibble, u64 and varints are not latched: one such field costs more than it saves (docs/serdes/code_size.md).
  • ✅ SW-41 First error in types that mix latched and other fields: an error kept by a _latch read stops the reader (reads with a Result return it, no read moves), so a derived decoder with lists or nested types next to plain fields returns the first error again, as before SW-34. 20 bytes on a request/reply decoder (RV32IC), four forms measured (docs/serdes/code_size.md, shrink_wrap/tests/latched_errors.rs).
  • ✅ SW-43 C99 runtime (first step of API-26): shrink_wrap/c/shrink_wrap.{h,c}, the BufReader / BufWriter of the Rust crate for C: bits, nibbles, un8..un64, LE integers, floats, UNib32, UVlq32 / UVlq64, bytes and strings as borrowed views, split, lengths at the back and finish, Unsized values. No malloc, the first error kept as in SW-41 (a failing call moves nothing), octets through accessors so 16-bit char (TI C2000) works. Checked against the Rust crate with golden vectors and a proptest cross-check in both directions, also on truncated and corrupted input (shrink_wrap/c/tests, part of just test; just lint builds the C with -std=c99 -pedantic -Werror). How to use it: docs/c.md. TailSize, the series types and the _latch / finish_no_lens code size tricks are not ported.
  • ✅ SW-44 Fixed-layout fast path: #[derive_shrink_wrap] sees when a type's encoding is a fixed little-endian byte layout (a sized or final_structure struct, a sized or self_describing enum with a u8 / u16 / u32 ww_repr; fields only u8..u64, i8..i64, f32, f64 and arrays of them) and generates an offset const per field, ENCODED_LEN, and from_fixed / to_fixed that load and store at those offsets on the slice, no BufReader / BufWriter, nothing generic. The fixed_layout directive makes it a requirement (and allows nested fixed-layout types): a bool, Option, list, string, varint or bit-packed field is a compile error naming the field. Same bytes as ser_shrink_wrap (shrink_wrap/tests/fixed_layout.rs, 2000 random values per type). FixedLayout::write_c prints the matching C reader (offset defines and static inline loads) from the same derive, fixed_layout::write_c_header a whole header: the first generated C of API-26. Code size on Cortex-M0 for a header of eight integers: decode 484 → 276 bytes, encode 888 → 462 (docs/serdes/code_size.md). First user: chunky_mcu_updater's plan format (P2625 PROTO-3); it serves the busgen idea of P2401 #9oct-1433 for types without dynamic fields. Open: arrays of nested types, a C writer, 16-bit char targets in the C reader.
  • ✅ SW-45 Bit fields and a variable last field in the fixed-layout fast path: bool, U1..U32, I2..I32 and Nibble get compile-time bit offsets (most significant bit first, a Nibble on a 4-bit boundary, a byte field after them starting a fresh byte, as BufWriter packs them) and are read and written with shifts and masks, in Rust and in the C reader (sw_fixed_bits, sw_fixed_sbits). Option<T>, Result<T, E> and enums of unequal variants are allowed as the last field (one rule for all variable-length fields); their flags are bit fields, also where #[flag] moves them. MIN_LEN and fixed_len() next to ENCODED_LEN (the longest, the buffer to have ready). A nested type cannot share a byte with bits of its parent: a compile error says so. Every refusal says why and what to use instead. Byte-equal to ser_shrink_wrap on mixed bit runs, a run at the end, options, results, relocated flags and enum variants with both (shrink_wrap/tests/fixed_layout.rs); the generated C is built and run with every warning an error (just lint-c). A bit-packed sample on Cortex-M0: decode 652 → 276 bytes, encode 1034 → 560.
  • ✅ SW-46 Fixed head, sequential tail (head_tail): an opt-in wire format of its own for types with lists, strings and options anywhere. The head holds every fixed-width field at a constant offset (numbers, arrays, bit fields as in SW-45) plus a u16 count per list or string, the flag bit of each Option / Result and the head of each nested type; the tail holds the variable parts in field order. An enum is its tag, then its variant's head and tail. Generated by #[derive_shrink_wrap(head_tail)]: offset consts, HEAD_LEN, from_head_tail / to_head_tail / head_tail_len, the HeadTail trait (also implemented for every fixed-layout type) and a C reader (head readers plus a <name>_tail() walker, shrink_wrap::head_tail::write_c_header), built and run by just lint-c. Non-generic, size first: no BufReader / BufWriter, no length FIFO, no reversed lengths; the tail is a cursor (head_tail::Tail) that takes lengths it already knows. Lists are head_tail::List<'i, T> (items numbers or fixed-layout types of one length, read when iterated). No sw serdes and no owned version: one type, one format. Tests: exact bytes, round trips, every truncation, 200 000 random buffers, UTF-8, counts over u16 (shrink_wrap/tests/head_tail.rs). busgen's request and reply enums (size bench busgen_ht): 4626 bytes on Cortex-M0 and 6004 on RV32IC, against 4408 / 5762 hand-written and 6652 / 8210 derived (P2401 #9oct-1433). Open: head_tail types as ww API arguments (they have no sw serdes), lists of variable-length items, a C writer, u8 counts for short lists (MaxLen).
  • ✅ SW-52 head_tail views and variant writers: Type::view(buf) gives a TypeView<'_> without making the value: the lengths checked and the tail walked once, the head's fields read by accessors at their offsets when called (the same code as from_head_tail, one field at a time), lists, strings, options and nested views kept from the walk; an enum's view is an enum of its variants' views (a tuple variant of one nested type holds its view). Every enum variant gets Enum::write_<variant>(buf, fields..): the bytes of to_head_tail for that variant without making the value (the same write_ht code). HeadTail::View / view_ht, head_tail::view. Tests: values back from every accessor, writers byte-equal to to_head_tail, every truncation, 200 000 random buffers agreeing with from_head_tail. Size bench busgen_view: 4988 bytes on RV32IC and 3894 on Cortex-M0, 13 % and 12 % below the hand-written codec; busgen's firmware 5608 / 5090 bytes (UART / I2C image, fpga_tools BUS-12). View types are always pub (the View of a public trait). Open: lazy views of nested fixed-layout types (read when the view is made), a writer for structs.
  • ✅ SW-53 Numbers through fixed_layout::Le, out of line on RISC-V: generated fixed-layout and head_tail code reads and writes multi-byte numbers with Le::ld / Le::st on the bytes at the field (fixed_layout::at), one function per type on RISC-V (no unaligned loads), inline elsewhere (on Cortex-M0 the byte loads are smaller than the calls, measured). Under LTO ld passes its pointer through black_box: argument promotion would otherwise move the load into every caller. Bit-field bytes cleared once per head. busgen_ht on RV32IC 6004 → 5658; a type read or written in one place grows (fixed_ser 498 → 612, docs/serdes/code_size.md).
  • ✅ SW-54 #[cfg] on head_tail enum variants: passed to everything generated for the variant (consts, arms, view, writer, C text); a variant compiled out keeps its tag and reads as an unknown one. busgen's firmware builds only its bitstream family's requests with it.
  • ✅ SW-39 Byte-wise memcpy, measured, advice for very small targets: a firmware's own memcpy (and __aeabi_memcpy on Arm) of 22 bytes instead of the word-wise one of compiler_builtins: 324 bytes less on RV32IC, 304 on Cortex-M0, for every image that moves a value, at the price of speed and of replacing memcpy for the whole firmware. Code and downsides in docs/serdes/code_size.md ("Build settings"), measured with just size-bench --fw-features byte_memcpy. Nothing in shrink_wrap depends on it.
  • ✅ SW-40 Bit reads stay out of the lengths in the last byte: read_un8..read_un64 (and U1..U64, I2..I64) no longer read into the length nibble the last byte shares with the forward data, and a length is no longer read from bits the forward side has read; both are OutOfBounds.. errors. Malformed input only, every message the writers produce decodes as before. Checked against a bit-level model in every reader state of 1 to 3 byte buffers (buf_reader.rs bounds_every_state_every_read) and by round trips of random messages (shrink_wrap/tests/rev_nibble_bounds.rs).
  • ✅ SW-35 Exact ElementSize of enums: a sized / self_describing enum reports the discriminant plus one variant (ElementSize::one_of) instead of the sum of all variants without the discriminant; sized with variants of different sizes is a compile error; user types inside arrays, tuples, ranges and options are counted. Same wire format (shrink_wrap/tests/enum_size.rs, docs/serdes/size_assumptions.md). Unblocks reading RefVec<Sized T> in place.
  • ✅ SW-33 UVlq64: byte-based variable length u64, same big endian VLQ encoding as UVlq32, 1 to 10 bytes, uvlq64 field type in #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)], BufReader::read_uvlq64/BufWriter/BufWriterOwned::write_uvlq64 (shrink_wrap/src/vlq64.rs, docs/types.md, docs/serdes/showcase.md). No UVlq64Backfill (not asked for).
  • ✅ SW-19 Bounded lists and strings MaxLen<T, N>: a RefVec, Vec, &str or String with at most N elements, same bytes as T (a bound can be added, raised or removed without a new wire form), checked on serialize and deserialize (Error::MaxLenExceeded, never truncated). Works in derived types and in every API position (arguments, returns, properties, stream and sink items), visible in introspection (ww_self::Type::MaxLen), honoured by the dynamic client and Python; raising a bound is compatible, lowering or adding one breaking (ww api check). SerializeShrinkWrap::MAX_SIZE: Option<MaxSize>, the worst-case size of a type whose every part is bounded, feeds API-18. docs/types.md, docs/evolution/rules.md, shrink_wrap/tests/max_len.rs, tests/bounded, examples_mcu/mcu_qemu (qemu-bounded).
  • ✅ SW-15 Handle end of buffer when reading evolved fields: a field with #[default = ..] reads as its default only when it starts at the end of the data and runs out of it (Error::is_read_eob); a truncated or malformed value is an error. The flag of an evolved Option / Result falls back with it, #[default] works on any type and its value is used (an Option was always None). Same in the ww_self dynamic decoder. Padding bits of the old data's last byte read as 0, so bit-sized fields default to their zero value. Decided: no implicit defaults for Vec/String/Option fields without #[default], the attribute is what marks a field as added later (and what ww api check looks for). docs/serdes/derive.md#evolving-types, shrink_wrap/tests/evolution.rs.
  • ✅ SW-16 FutureVersion enum variant: an enum ending with #[future_version] Unknown(u32) reads an unknown discriminant into it instead of failing with EnumFutureVersionOrMalformedData, and writes it back; an Unsized enum skips the newer variant's fields with its size slot, sized / self_describing ones only survive new unit variants. No wire number of its own, no change to ELEMENT_SIZE, left out of the API model. The ww_self dynamic decoder reads an unknown variant of an Unsized enum as <unknown N>. Added by default since SW-47. docs/serdes/derive.md#enum-variants-from-a-newer-version, shrink_wrap/tests/evolution.rs.
  • ✅ SW-48 Bit-sized fields and variant payloads: U1..U64 / I2..I64 (u7, ub10, i2.. in the API model) as struct fields, enum variant payloads and #[ww_trait] method arguments, returns and properties, packed bit after bit with a sub-byte discriminant: enum I2cAddress { Seven(U7), Ten(U10) } with ww_repr = u1, self_describing takes 8 or 11 bits instead of 16 or 24 with u8 / u16. Server and client codegen (it panicked on such a method argument), I16 (was missing), From / TryFrom to and from the backing integer. The dynamic client and Python already handled them, now tested byte for byte against derived types; the C runtime has the bit reads. Same wire format (shrink_wrap/tests/sub_byte.rs, tests/dynamic, tests/methods, docs/serdes/showcase.md#bit-sized-fields-and-variant-payloads-a-7-or-10-bit-i2c-address).
  • ✅ SW-47 #[future_version] variant by default: the derive adds Unknown(u32) to every Unsized enum with a free discriminant; no_future_version opts out (framework enums whose readers must fail: ww_self model, MultiIndex), future_version = Name renames it, final_structure / self_describing / sized enums only get it when written. A Rust API change of every such enum (exhaustive matches need the arm), not of the wire or the API model. docs/serdes/derive.md#enum-variants-from-a-newer-version, shrink_wrap/tests/evolution.rs.
  • 📋 SW-66 128-bit numbers in the C runtime — shrink_wrap/c reads and writes up to 64-bit numbers; u128 / i128 (two u64 halves in C) are missing. Conformance cases int.u128.max, int.i128.min.
  • 📋 SW-67 no_future_version and #[series(opaque)] have no conformance case — found by the coverage guard (TEST-25): no case turns off the Unknown(u32) catch-all (SW-47) and then feeds an out-of-range discriminant (needs hand-written reject bytes, no valid Rust value produces them), and no Series<T> (SW-60) case has a field marked #[series(opaque)], so its own column form is untested.
  • 📋 SW-17 Const / magic type · v0.5 — a simple type with a generic parameter that serializes a constant value or byte string and checks it on deserialization, failing on a mismatch. For example the magic field in ww_self (a plain u32 today).
  • ✅ SW-18 Size-of-enclosing-type field TailSize<N>: a field the derive macro fills in with the size of the rest of the value once it is serialized (a UVlq32 right-justified in N bytes, 1 to 5), in any position, nested types each with their own. Readers bound the value by it (a longer buffer stops at the right byte, a truncated one errors, newer trailing fields are skipped) or skip it without parsing. Fields before it must be Sized or SelfDescribing, checked at compile time. docs/serdes/special_types.md, showcase.
  • ✅ SW-60 Series<T>: columnar compressed sequences of any derive type — a list of T (structs, enums with data, Option, nested) written column by column, one column per leaf field: numbers as a numeric column whose predictor (raw, delta, delta of delta) and coder (SW-31 prefix code, bit-packed blocks of 8, constant, plain) the writer picks per column, floats plain or SW-32 XOR, enum tags, bools, Option presence and strings as runs (a value and one entry per change); a column restarts where an earlier enum field (a ww_si prefix) changes. 3 to 8 times smaller than a plain Vec<T> of ADC samples, self-contained per batch: the column codecs (numeric, 128-bit, float, runs, codec choice by counting bits or a fixed CodecPolicy, no alloc, malformed input an error), the Series<'i, T> / SeriesOwned<T> types and the SeriesColumns trait with impls for the primitives, Option, tuples, arrays, strings and bytes (one-pass validating skim, parallel item iteration, evolvable structs both ways, the design's examples and size tables as golden bytes), fuzz targets shrink-wrap-series-columns and shrink-wrap-series-type; the opt-in series directive of #[derive_shrink_wrap] for structs (also generic, DER-14) and enums, #[series(opaque)] fields, compile errors naming the field for what v1 doesn't take, on ww_si quantities and ww_numeric::NumericValue (shrink_wrap/tests/series_derive.rs, ww_stdlib/ww_si/tests/series.rs); docs (docs/serdes/series.md, the layout in docs/serdes/wire_format.md#seriest, worked bytes in docs/serdes/showcase.md#compressed-columns-seriest). Series<T> is usable today in any property, method or stream item; a dynamic (non-generated) decoder and batching a stream or property into Series<Timed<T>> automatically build on it as their own items (CLT-29, API-41), not blocking this one.
  • 📋 SW-42 MAX_SIZE on owned types · v0.5.x — SerializeShrinkWrapOwned has no worst-case size yet, only the borrowed trait has (SW-19); host code sizing a buffer for an owned value uses the borrowed type's.
  • 📋 SW-20 Sub-type numbers · v0.5.x — numbers restricted to a range, like 10..=25, or a set with gaps, like 0..=8, 12, 16; checked on serialization and deserialization, possibly using fewer bits on the wire (docs/types.md, "Subtypes").
  • 📋 SW-21 Multi-dimensional arrays (2D, 3D).
  • 🚧 SW-22 Fuzz shrink_wrap — fuzz/ has one shrink_wrap target, shrink-wrap-tail-size (TailSize types round-tripped, random bytes into their readers); shrink-wrap-ref-vec (SW-37) came with its feature, shrink-wrap-option-any-vec with SW-55 and DER-13 (sparse structs), shrink-wrap-series-columns and shrink-wrap-series-type with SW-60, shrink-wrap-nesting with the nesting depth limit (recursive types at random limits). Round-trip every built-in type and the derive's features.
  • 🔍 SW-23 Tuple enum variants evolution — check that tuple variants evolve as docs/evolution/rules.md says (fields can be appended) and add a test.
  • 💡 SW-65 Aligned plain Series columns — numbers byte-aligned and little-endian at their width (numeric escape 11 11, float codec 0010, an AlignedPlain policy), copied from a SeriesStore: 34 k cycles per FOC level batch on an STM32H725 at opt-level = 3 against 60 k for column-wise DeltaPacked (SW-64), for 2.3x the bytes. Built and measured on branch s/18oct2026-memcpy-fast-sw65, not landed; may come back after observe cells and a u32 payload in NumericValueStore.
  • 💡 SW-24 ZigZag encoding for signed variable length numbers — consider ZigZag (as in protobuf) so that small negative values stay short, e.g. signed counterparts of UNib32/UVlq32.
  • 💡 SW-25 In-place builder for server handlers · v0.5.x — a new step-by-step / partial builder (e.g. for a RefVec) might be useful with the new Context in server handlers, to write replies and events straight into the buffer. It might not work out.
  • 💡 SW-26 Map support — HashMap/BTreeMap, probably as a Vec of (K, V).
  • 💡 SW-27 In-place editing of serialized data.
  • 💡 SW-28 Compression wrappers — the time-series part is done as Series<T> (SW-60, with the SW-31 delta and SW-32 XOR codes); in-place dictionary compression as Compression<T> (strings?) stays an idea.
  • 💡 SW-29 Flatten support — apply a type's layout across struct/enum boundaries.
  • 💡 SW-30 derive_shrink_wrap on a whole module at once. For definitions in separate files with own syntax, see standalone definition files.
  • 💡 SW-56 Tri-state slots in OptionAnyVec — absent / value / error per slot, e.g. a property update that says why one value is missing. The header has room for it: mode nibbles 4..=15 are reserved (a reader fails on them today), so 2-valued vecs don't pay for it.
  • ✅ DER-1 #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] attribute with clear syntax, no hidden magic and good error messages (docs/serdes/derive.md); replaced #[derive(ShrinkWrap)].
  • ✅ DER-2 Discriminant checks: discriminants must fit ww_repr, implicit ones are numbered like in Rust.
  • ✅ DER-3 #[default = ..] for evolved fields and #[flag] relocation.
  • ✅ DER-4 TailBytes must be last: rejected anywhere but as the last field of a struct or enum variant, and nested in Option, Vec, tuples or arrays (check_tail_bytes_position), like UVlq32Backfill must be first.
  • ✅ DER-10 Generic arguments on user field types: Foo<u8>, Wrapper<'i, T> are emitted as written, Wrapper<'i, T> maps to WrapperOwned<T> in the owned variant (docs/serdes/derive.md, type mapping; test shrink_wrap/tests/generic_external.rs).
  • ✅ DER-14 Generics on derived types: structs and enums with type parameters (struct Timed<T> { t: Second, value: T }, enum Reading<'i, T>), const parameters of any type (struct Buf<const N: usize> { data: [u8; N] }, MaxLen<&'i str, N>, const STRICT: bool), defaults and where clauses, also with a lifetime (Tagged<'i, T> / TaggedOwned<T>); each impl bounds the type parameters by its trait (serdes, owned serdes, SeriesColumns) on top of the bounds and where clause as written, the size of T and N is part of the type's. series, display, validate and discriminants take generics, fixed_layout, head_tail and sparse reject them (docs/serdes/derive_reference.md#generics; tests shrink_wrap/tests/generic_items.rs, series_derive.rs; ww_si::Timed<T>). In APIs and the API model: API-43.
  • ✅ DER-15 PhantomData fields: PhantomData<T> is zero bits (Sized { size_bits: 0 }, like ()) borrowed and owned, and a SeriesColumns with no columns, for any T; the derive leaves a type parameter used only inside PhantomData<..> without the serdes / SeriesColumns bounds of DER-14, so struct Quantity<U> { value: i32, _unit: PhantomData<U> } works with a bare unit marker and writes the same bytes as without the field (docs/serdes/derive_reference.md#generics; test shrink_wrap/tests/phantom_data.rs). For ww_si units.
