Config and Sleep), recover, tx_abort, tx_events (marker, measured queue time), bus_errors, protocol_status, bus_load, detect_timing, set_filters, set_layout, rx_buffer, tx_buffer (once or cyclic), transceiver (standby / silent / sleep, wiring faults), terminator, test_pins. CanGroup (interface[]: Can, enable / disable, optional clock source and frequency, performance) for controllers sharing clock, power and message RAM; CanTimeTriggered (TTCAN); CanXl behind the xl feature. Errors on CommonError + OutOfFilters, OutOfMemory, BusOff; defmt no longer pulls std. Docs docs/std_library/ww_can_bus.md, tests tests/io_can (full and minimal node), tests/io_can_group (group, TTCAN, XL).
  • ✅ STD-42 ww_tape · v0.5 — tape blocks, the generic unit of track records for live feeds and log files (ww_tape, docs/transport/tap.md#tape-blocks): a 32 B header, varint records (track, time delta, length, item), CRC-32C, never padded; describe blocks with the producer, TrackDefs (stable key, API, resource path, sticky) and API bundles; TapeWriter writes them with database-style durability (.partial then rename, file and directory synced, a SyncPolicy, a failed write or sync fatal, never retried), FileBlocks reads the longest valid prefix (or skips damage, Recovery::Resync); tests cut and flip every byte, fuzz target tape-reader. Blocks of a later version or an unknown kind are skipped by length, Describe is evolvable. Open: splitting into several files by size or time, preallocation (zeros at the end already read as the end). Nothing in it knows a producer: the link tap (TR-14) writes it; it is also eventfull's own file format (CORE-19).
  • 🧪 STD-32 ww_settings settings store · v0.5 — a device's settings in its own NOR flash: #[derive(Settings)] on a plain struct (#[setting(slot = N, default = ..)], #[settings(retired(..))]), stored as a record of the fields not at their default, each a byte blob in an OptionAnyVec, so firmware versions skip and keep each other's slots; Settings<G, N> with write-on-change, a debounce and a durable persist, factory reset per group (Key); served through value_on_changed properties. Its own Store over an embedded-storage-async NorFlash (per-key seq in every item, page headers with crc, current records copied off a page before it is erased, loads never write, maintain() to erase ahead): power-cut safe at every word written and byte erased in any erase order, which sequential-storage 8 isn't. Docs docs/api/settings.md (pages, erase stalls on G0 / F4 / H7, big-sector options) and docs/evolution/rules.md#settings-stored-on-a-device, tests ww_settings/tests (just test-power-cut). Hardware check open: real power cuts on a G0B1 (TEST-21), dump decoder (TOOL-12), demo (EX).
  • 🧪 STD-35 Slave data paths in ww_i2c and ww_spi · v0.5.x — an #[optional(slave)] group in I2c and in Spi: opening the counted slave_events / slave_frames stream with a config starts slave mode (closing stops it) and reports every transfer (bytes both ways, register pointer or address, fill bytes, stretch time); the answers come from a register map the host fills and reads back (slave_map_write / slave_map_read, applied between two transfers) or from the slave_answers credit sink, one answer per read or frame. A host that is too slow: I2C I2cSlaveUnderrun (Fill, Stretch { max } with ReadWaiting sent at once, Nack while empty), SPI the idle byte or the last answer again, flagged underrun. Limits of clock stretching (SMBus 25 ms, masters without it) in the crate docs and docs/std_library/ww_i2c.md#slave-mode. I2cMode::Slave, SpiRole::Slave and the slave capability flags are gone. API, snapshots, docs, the device-side engine (SRV-26, ww_bus_slave) and an end-to-end test of both slaves done: tests/io_i2c / tests/io_spi drive I2cSlave / SpiSlave byte by byte as a simulated master (test-only slave_bus / slave_pump methods, a fake clock) through the real host and device event loops: register maps with page wrap and host updates between transactions, the answer queues, stretching to the deadline and past it, Nack, repeat_last, cleared answers and dropped events. Open: a check on real silicon, with the first user, the rePort (usb_io_fw IF-5, v1.0 launch, Roman 16 Oct 2026).
  • 🚧 STD-6 ww_gpio_hl — usable, some APIs are still missing.
  • 🔍 STD-7 Interrupt left enabled in ww_gpio_hl · v0.5 — the falling edge helper documents that it leaves interrupts enabled; decide whether that is the intended fix or a bug.
  • 🚧 STD-8 Prototypes, to be completed later: ww_i2c, ww_uart, ww_memory (was ww_ll: one word type per trait, optional watches, errors on CommonError, docs page), Known gaps are TODOs in their sources (e.g. SMBus and 7-bit addresses in ww_i2c; ww_can_bus is done in STD-29). ww_log (was ww_log_bare_metal) left for STD-26.
  • 💡 STD-9 Stubs, for later: ww_spi (ww_board_info, ww_firmware_info, ww_user_info and ww_uid moved to STD-24).
  • 🚧 STD-12 ww_dfu firmware update API — traits UpdateNode, BootControl, Inventory, Stage, StageBulk: each node (app, bootloader, recovery app) implements what it needs; A/B live, in place from a stored plan, in place live; step by step or bulk. Carries the octet records of the chunky protocol spec (P2625). End to end test tests/dfu. Guide with the eight update scenarios (2C-APP-STEP Swap Shuttle .. 1L-UPD-BULK Pit-stop Freight), each tested end to end over USB (simulated), WebSocket or UDP with reboots and power cuts, its exchange recorded as a golden transcript the docs include (docs/std_library/ww_dfu.md, tests/dfu_scenarios, just dfu-transcripts). StageBulk::plan is a credit sink (API-28 credit-sinks). Every variable-size field is bounded (SW-19: MAX_PIECE_LEN, MAX_HEADER_LEN, MAX_CHUNKS_PAGE, MAX_PRODUCT_LEN), so every method has a known largest request and reply. Profile::AB(SlotSwitch::{Copy, Remap}) / InPlace. Next: a chunky implementation (chunky NET-1).
  • 🚧 STD-13 IO trait family · v0.5 — ww_gpio, ww_uart (optional Uart::monitor), ww_i2c (+ I2cWatch, I2cMonitor, 10-bit addresses), ww_spi (optional Spi::monitor), ww_adc (STD-18), ww_pwm (STD-19), ww_onewire (STD-20), ww_timebase (STD-17), ww_logic_analyzer / ww_signal_generator (STD-21, STD-22); ww_si values and timestamps (STD-23): frequencies Hertz, baud rates Baud. Family overview in docs/std_library/io_family.md; every crate filled in with full rustdoc, a mock-server test pair tests/io_<x> and a docs page docs/std_library/ww_<x>.md; examples_mcu GPIO and UART boards follow. A bus or bank is configured with one configure(XConfig) answering what was actually set, the IO level inside it (io_level: Option<Volt>, capabilities io_levels / io_level_min / io_level_max). Every crate's error enum starts with #[common] Common(CommonError) (STD-16) and keeps only what is specific (Nack, NoPresence, NoSuchChannel, ...), methods list their variants with #[errors(..)] (API-32). Streams with a configuration are counted stream functions (API-31: AdcStream::samples, LogicStream::data, Pin::event, PwmCaptureChannel::capture, Spi::monitor, I2cMonitor::records, Uart::monitor), Uart::rx and I2cWatch::changes are counted: positions, device losses and the time of the first unit in the event head; UART chunks end on line idle (UartConfig::idle_chars, one back-to-back burst each) and carry the time of their last byte when the device measures it (RxChunk::end). Clients take one ? per call (CLT-24 CallError), Unsized enums read newer variants as Unknown(u32) (SW-47). Review round 1 (15 Oct 2026) done. Open: *_hl crates are STD-14.
  • 🚧 STD-21 ww_logic_analyzer · v0.5.x — LogicAnalyzer (triggered capture into RAM), LogicStream; Raw and per-channel Transitions encodings (edges as a Series<u32>), staged pattern triggers and protocol stages (UART byte, I2C address, SPI first byte). Skeleton written, docs page docs/std_library/ww_logic_analyzer.md; mock-server test pair still open (STD-13).
  • 🚧 STD-22 ww_signal_generator · v0.5.x — PatternGenerator (digital, replays analyzer captures through a credit sink), WaveformGenerator (DAC channels). Skeleton written, docs page docs/std_library/ww_signal_generator.md; mock-server test pair still open (STD-13).
  • ⛔ STD-31 Observable ww_gpio pin level · v0.5.x — property!(ro+observe level: Level) on Pin at one of its reserved indices 4..=6, so a host sees input changes without opening the event stream of every pin (slow inputs, a dashboard). Blocked on API-29 array-index-bounds: Pin sits in Bank::pin[] (and banks usually in an array too), and levels under a resource array can't be observed until their bound is known (SRV-18).
  • 🚧 STD-34 ww_recorder · v0.5.x — control a recorder over WireWeaver: Recorder (status, card facts, two-step prepare/format with a token, recordings, markers, sync, settings with the flush thresholds, counters, optional refresh_usb) and Track[] (info, enable, durability, compression, counters). For the SD card log store of P2628 (repo logring), usable by any recorder. API crate, snapshot and docs page docs/std_library/ww_recorder.md done, the scaffold compiles; the first server is the logring's (rePort integration).
  • 🚧 STD-39 ww_block · v0.5.x — a block device over WireWeaver (SD card, eMMC, flash): BlockDevice with geometry (block size and count, blocks per call, erase unit, erased value), free read and device-side crc (CRC-32, ww_block::crc32), claim / release of a write lease that stops the card's own user, write with a CRC and erase under it, and the optional bulk group: the write_runs credit sink acknowledged on the counted written stream, and the counted read_runs stream. Who may claim is the firmware's choice per link (Common(Refused)). Tier T1 of P2628 (logring's PC LinkMedium, S2 prepare on the PC). API crate, snapshot, docs page docs/std_library/ww_block.md and the round trip tests/block_sd done, the scaffold compiles; the first server is the logring's.
  • 🚧 STD-40 ww_sd · v0.5.x — raw SD card access over WireWeaver: SdCard with capabilities, state, the detect stream, raw registers (CID, CSD, OCR, RCA, SCR, SD Status), reinit with a per-step InitReport, and command: one raw command with an optional data phase, answering response bytes, CardStatus bits, the Outcome and timing. Commands are Free, need the ww_block lease, or are Restricted (CMD42, CMD27) unless the firmware builds with raw-sd-unrestricted (ww_sd::check_access). Tier T0 of P2628. API crate, snapshot, docs page docs/std_library/ww_sd.md and the round trip tests/block_sd done, the scaffold compiles; a device needs a raw-command hook in its SD driver (not checked yet for embassy-stm32's Sdmmc).
  • 💡 STD-33 ww_settings single-sector mode — a store in one sector with a RAM copy, for a part with exactly one sector to spare; a power cut during its erase loses every group (the window is the whole erase, 1 to 4 s on a 128 KiB sector, see docs/api/settings.md#parts-with-big-sectors). Only if a device needs it.
  • 💡 STD-10 Device state machine trait like CANopen.
  • 💡 STD-11 Register description registry — WireWeaver for describing device registers.
  • 💡 STD-41 Frame splitters for byte streams — a no_std, sans-IO splitter (bytes in, frames out with their time and status: CRC good or bad, truncated, overrun), the same code on the device and the host. Kernels: idle gap (today's RxChunk), delimiter (\n, \r\n, any byte), fixed length, length field, sync byte + length + checksum, COBS, SLIP, Modbus RTU, NMEA; picked by the host when it opens the stream (Uart::frames(cfg)), no new firmware. Frames of a bounded length are what a batched stream can take, where a raw byte stream can't (no size bound); with API-51, each frame XOR'd with the last one of the same key (Modbus address, NMEA sentence, CAN ID).
  • 💡 STD-44 SPI slave data-ready line — a GPIO the slave asserts while an answer is queued (or the register map changed), as most SPI slave protocols with a computed answer have (ESP32 handshake, nRF IRQ); the master reads only when it is set, so the answer queue needs no polling. Part of SpiSlaveConfig, the pin named by the board.
  • 💡 STD-45 Live registers in a slave's register map — address ranges of the I2C or SPI register map whose reads the host answers (I2C stretching meanwhile) or that change on read (clear-on-read status, FIFO data registers), so a chip with a few such registers can be emulated without moving it all to the answer queue.
  • 💡 STD-46 More I2C slave addressing — a second address or an address mask (one emulator answering for several chips, a 24C16's block bits), general call, SMBus PEC and SMBALERT#/ARA. RP2350's controller has one address only, so this is per-device capability.
  • 🚧 STD-47 ww_pin_diag pin tests · v0.5.x — PinDiag { const POINTS; set(point, PointState); read(point); release_all() }: raw access to a board's digital points (MCU pins, shift register and expander outputs) for bring-up, verification and production tests; the firmware keeps its board's rules and answers NotCapable, Common(InUse) or Refused { rule }. Done: crate, docs page docs/std_library/ww_pin_diag.md, test pair tests/pin_diag (mock board: short, external pull-up, input-only pin, interlocked outputs, held pin), snapshot. Missing: ww pins test (quick short test on any device) and plan files, a device implementing it (rePort).
  • 🚧 STD-48 ww_interned strings as ids · v0.5.x — Interned { Id(UNib32), Text(&str) } for names and reasons; ids resolved on the host from the firmware's ELF by build id. Done: the type, Display (#17 for an unresolved id). Missing: an accessor for defmt::Str's index (upstream), the host lookup in the ELF directory.

items.text:
• ✅ TEST-1 CI on GitHub Actions: fmt, sort, typos, clippy, rustdoc, nextest, doctests, semver-checks, MCU builds.
  • ✅ TEST-2 Integration tests against the real host event loop over in_process, one crate per API feature.
  • ✅ TEST-3 Device side end-to-end tests with real framers on both ends.
  • ✅ TEST-4 Timeout tests for methods, properties and streams (async, blocking, promise).
  • ✅ TEST-5 Method tests: calls, unimplemented, deferred replies, deferred not answered.
  • ✅ TEST-6 Property tests: multi-req and single-req servers, user errors.
  • ✅ TEST-7 Stream tests: byte buffers, basic and user types, open/close, sideband both ways, sinks, arrays of streams.
  • ✅ TEST-8 Framer fuzzing (fuzz/).
  • ✅ TEST-23 Wire-format conformance matrix: one corpus of cases (tests/conformance/corpus.json: a type, a value in the form Python uses, the golden bytes), run through every consumer of the wire format: the Rust derive (owned types, borrowed round trips), the ww_self dynamic client and Python (from the API model of tests/conformance_api), and C (the runtime for single values, the generated fixed_layout and head_tail readers compiled and run). 105 cases: numbers and varints, bit-sized fields and nibbles, relocated flags, Option / Result, enums with sub-byte, nibble and explicit discriminants, unknown and compiled-out variants, lists, strings, ArrayString / ArrayVec, MaxLen bounds both ways, nested, recursive, generic, sparse, sized and final structs, PhantomData, validate, TailBytes / TailSize, fixed layout, head_tail, Series, evolution both ways. A case a consumer can't express carries a gap mark naming the item that fixes it (shown in docs/serdes/conformance_matrix.md); a missing or stale mark fails. Part of just test and CI. It replaces an IR for the two layout engines (API-25 dropped). Found and fixed: fixed_layout types in APIs (the crate walker rejected them), unknown enum variants in Python; filed: INT-9, INT-10, TOOL-13, SW-66. See docs/serdes/conformance.md.
  • ✅ TEST-24 Frozen golden bytes guard: a case's bytes, direction and bytes_from don't change, and a case doesn't disappear, once they are in the corpus at the merge base with main (git merge-base HEAD origin/master, falling back to local master) — a hand edit or a reset to "?" re-sealed silently before this, CONFORMANCE=update on its own only refuses to overwrite a filled-in case. "wire_change": "EVO-n / reason" on a case is the escape for a deliberate wire break (needs the matching EVO-n item and a **Breaking:** CHANGELOG entry), shown in the matrix report. Depends only on the repo's own git: without git, or without the corpus at the merge base (a shallow clone, or the corpus being new), the guard says so and passes rather than failing a check it can't run; CI's test and coverage jobs fetch full history so it actually runs there. tests/conformance/src/frozen.rs, tests/matrix.rs::frozen_bytes. See docs/serdes/conformance.md.
  • ✅ TEST-25 Coverage guard: every ww_self::Type variant reachable from some case's type (an exhaustive match, so a new variant fails to compile here until handled) and every wire-relevant shrink_wrap_derive directive used by a type in tests/conformance_api is exercised by at least one case; a kind unlisted and unused fails, a kind listed (TYPE_GAPS / DIRECTIVE_GAPS) but now used fails too. Found two variants a prepared bundle never carries (filed INT-11) and two directives with no case yet (filed SW-67). tests/conformance/src/coverage.rs, tests/matrix.rs::coverage. See docs/serdes/conformance.md.

Found on the way: a 1 s flush stall after a resume (fixed), and a lost wrapped write in the firmware's pipes.
  • 🚧 TEST-9 Remaining test coverage · v0.5:

  • 🚧 TEST-10 Binary size tracking · v0.5 — flash and RAM per feature for a set of examples, in CI. Consider compile-time construction so that only final bytes remain.

Seen before the TR-12 changes too. The recorder needs one order for events of the host and the simulated device that happen at the same time. Found 15 Oct 2026.

  • reset loop: every boot loads and checks all keys against what earlier boots committed, then a SysTick reset at a random time cuts the stores. 3000 boots on the B153A (J-Link, 15 Oct 2026): 655 stores, resets during 28 programs, 453 erases and 1537 reads, every committed value loaded, none corrupted. src/bin/reset_cut.rs showed why no word ever failed its ECC check: on G0 a system reset waits for the flash operation (73 page erases cut 1-20 ms into their ~22 ms all left the page fully erased, programs only stop between double words).

The device can't keep its counters across a power cut: a host program reads the loaded and committed sequence numbers and the ECC count over SWD (Donguru CMSIS-DAP, session ended before each cut so SBU/CC don't back-feed the board) and checks every boot loads at least what was committed before the cut.

items.title: Dropped and superseded
items.text:
• API-25 Refactor codegen to use an IR — decided against (18 Oct 2026). There are two wire-layout engines by design: shrink_wrap_derive keeps its own AST, as ww_self's own types are encoded with #[derive_shrink_wrap] and the derive can't depend on ww_self (a bootstrapping cycle); the dynamic path (ww_self to the dynamic client, Python, the CLI and GUI) computes the layout again from the introspection model, and generated C (API-26) is one more consumer of that model. Instead of an IR, the conformance matrix (TEST-23), one corpus of cases run through every consumer, is the contract that keeps them byte-identical; ww_self is the shared model for everything outside the derive. Fallback if drift ever bites: a dependency-free crate holding only the layout rules (bit offsets, flags, nibble alignment), called by both shrink_wrap_derive and ww_self, breaks no cycle.
  • STD-30 ww_gpio port access — dropped (Roman, 20 Oct 2026), Bank::read_inputs / write_outputs, PinLevel and the simultaneous_* capabilities removed before ww_gpio 0.1.0 was published. ww_gpio stays simple and low speed, one pin per call (IO family D9): many pins in one round trip are per-pin calls in one multi request (CLT-15, docs/std_library/ww_gpio.md#several-pins); several pins at one instant or with precise timing (bit-banged parallel buses, a strobe with its data lines) belong to the signal generator (STD-22) and the logic analyzer (STD-21). The extra methods only cost flash on every GPIO server.
  • SW-31 Delta / DeltaOfDelta, SW-32 XorFloat, SW-50 compressed sequences in APIs — superseded by Series<T> (SW-60): its numeric columns use the SW-31 prefix code with the delta or delta of delta predictor, its float columns the SW-32 XOR code, plus packed, constant and plain and the smallest picked per column, in every API position and in dynamic clients and Python (CLT-29); the types were removed (18 Oct 2026).
  • API-15 Return streams from functions — superseded by API-31 stream functions: #[stream(T)] fn name(args) opens a stream with typed arguments and result.
  • Document things (old notes) — superseded by docs/serdes/shrink_wrap.md and docs/evolution/rules.md; the notes described an earlier format (field ids, vlu16n_rev). Remaining ideas moved to their areas.
  • LEB numbers — superseded by UNib32 and UVlq32 (ULeb128 is still in the derive AST, unimplemented).
  • Field ids — decided against for now: fields are identified by position, which works well, and ids would add confusion together with flag relocation. The id leftovers in shrink_wrap_derive/src/transform/ can go.
  • Option and Result taking two id numbers — dropped with field ids; flags are separate fields.
  • Put length in front into a specified field — done as UVlq32Backfill.
  • CLI common blocks AST generation and excluding common blocks from the AST — done as API snapshots.
  • Compatibility check using AST signatures on connect — done.
  • Introspect as a trait, removed from ww_client_server — won't do.
  • WebUSB descriptors — only some browsers support WebUSB and it needs separate host support; NCM is more appealing, especially with pre-programmed unique IPs.

items.title: Features
items.text:
WireWeaver lets you describe a device's API once, as a Rust trait with your own data types, and generates both ends from it: the server on the device, no_std and without an allocator, and the client on the PC. Calls, property reads and streams go over USB, RTT, UDP or WebSocket in shrink_wrap, a dense bit-packed format that also works on its own. Newer firmware keeps working with older hosts and the other way round.

This page goes through what works today, area by area, in the order you are likely to meet them. Each area starts with what it is for, then lists its features by reading level: Basic is what most projects use, Advanced is for when the defaults are not enough, Nomicon is about internals and code size. Features that work only in part are marked. What is planned, and the details of every item, are in the feature tracker.

items.title: Wire format
items.text:
shrink_wrap turns your Rust structs and enums into compact bytes and back, without an allocator and without copying. Every message between host and device is made of it, and it works on its own as a dense storage format.

Basic

  • Structs and enums: Your own structs, plain enums and enums that carry data, on the wire.
  • One derive attribute: #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] with a few clear options and error messages that say what is wrong.
  • Option and Result: Stored as a single flag bit, also inside lists.
  • Strings and lists: String and Vec<T>, Vec<u8> as plain bytes.
  • Arrays and tuples: Fixed-size arrays, tuples and ().
  • Tuple and unit structs: struct Celsius(f32); works like a named struct, with the same bytes; struct Marker; keeps room to grow fields later.
  • Integers of any width: u1 to u32 and nibbles, packed bit after bit, so a 3-bit field takes 3 bits.
  • Variable-length numbers: UNib32 and UVlq32, where small values take a nibble or a byte.
  • Zero-copy reads: Strings and lists are read in place from the received buffer; an owned twin of each type is generated for values you keep.
  • Evolvable by default: Add fields later with #[default = ..], and old and new code still read each other's data.
  • Enum variants from a newer version: An older reader takes an unknown variant as Unknown(u32) instead of failing.
  • Bounded lists and strings: MaxLen<T, N> holds at most N elements, checked both ways, with a worst-case size known at compile time.
  • Usable on its own: A dense format for storing many small objects, no API needed.

Advanced

  • Owned values without an allocator: ArrayString<N> and ArrayVec<T, N> on fixed arrays, same bytes as String and Vec.
  • Bit-sized fields and payloads: U7, U10, I2 and friends in structs, enum variants and method arguments, e.g. a 7- or 10-bit I2C address in 8 or 11 bits.
  • 64-bit variable-length numbers: UVlq64, 1 to 10 bytes.
  • Columnar series: Series<T>: a list of numbers, timestamps, floats or any struct written field by field, with deltas and bit packing per field, several times smaller than a Vec<T> of samples.
  • Sparse structs: A struct of optional fields stored as an OptionAnyVec, for "only what changed" updates.
  • Checks on read: validate = path rejects out-of-range values as they are read.
  • Display from doc comments: Error enums print their doc lines, no hand-written Display.
  • #[cfg] on enum variants: Compile a variant out; it keeps its number on the wire.
  • Checked discriminants: Variant numbers must fit the chosen ww_repr, implicit ones count like in Rust.
  • Generic field types: Wrapper<'i, T> and types from macro_rules work as fields.
  • Generic types: Structs and enums with type and const parameters (Timed<T>, Buf<const N: usize>) and where clauses derive like any other type.
  • PhantomData fields: A zero-bit PhantomData<U> field carries a unit marker type (Quantity<Volt>) that needs no impls of its own.
  • Growing writer: BufWriterOwned for hosts, when the size isn't known up front.
  • Writing in place: Builders that write a value straight into the output buffer, and patching a field after the rest is written.
  • Fixed layouts: Types with a fixed byte layout get fields at constant offsets, read and written without a parser, and a matching C header.
  • Fixed head, sequential tail: head_tail, a format of its own for small firmware, with views that read fields on demand and a writer per enum variant.
  • shrink_wrap in C: A C99 reader and writer of the same format, no malloc.

Nomicon

  • Format documented bit by bit: How every type is laid out, and why.
  • Small code on small CPUs: About 20 % less code on Cortex-M0 and RISC-V for the same bytes on the wire.
  • Number access tuned per CPU: Multi-byte numbers through one function on RISC-V, inline on Arm, whichever is smaller.
  • Byte-wise memcpy: Measured savings and downsides of a tiny memcpy for very small targets.
  • Exact sizes of enums: sized enums report the discriminant plus one variant; variants of different sizes are a compile error.
  • Strict bit reads: Malformed data near the end of a buffer is an error, never a misread.
  • Bytes to the end: TailBytes takes the rest of the buffer, written without a length; only allowed last.
  • Size of the rest of a value: TailSize<N>, filled in after writing, so a reader can skip a value or bound it.
  • Lists written in place: RefVecBuilder writes a list into the buffer one element at a time, from a loop or an iterator, with no slice and the same bytes.
  • Series stores and size bounds: A batch of samples kept as one array per field until it is written as a Series, in half the RAM of the samples, and the most bytes the batch can take.
  • Fast, small Series encoding on MCUs: About 340 instructions per sample on a Cortex-M3, and codecs fixed at compile time that link only themselves: 15 KB of flash instead of 91 KB.
  • Series straight from the store: A batch written column by column from the arrays it was collected in, the same bytes in half the instructions.
  • Word-wide bit writer and reader: Bits written and read a word at a time, the same bytes: the observe poll of a 21-value FOC level in three quarters of the cycles on an STM32H725.
  • Sparse slots: OptionAnyVec, a list of optional values of any types where only the present ones take space.
  • Lists of either-or values: EitherAnyVec holds one of two types per element, the flags packed by eight, e.g. a list of results.

Details and what is planned: Wire format in the feature tracker.

items.title: API
items.text:
You describe what a device offers as a Rust trait: methods to call, properties to read and write, streams of data in either direction. WireWeaver generates the device's server and the host's client from it.

Basic

  • Methods, properties, streams and sinks: All in one trait, with traits nested inside to group them.
  • Sync or async: Async and sync servers; async, blocking and promise-style clients, from the same trait.
  • Results and errors: Methods return a value, answer later or say "not implemented"; your own error types for methods and properties.
  • Request context: Every handler knows who asked and can send events or answer later.
  • Arrays of resources: led[] or motor[], one definition for many instances, with the valid indices asked from the device.
  • Shared traits: impl Gpio, impl Uart from the standard library, so common tools work with your device.
  • Constants: const NAME: T; items, read once per connection and cached.
  • Generic types: Timed<Ampere>, Window<4> and your own generic structs and enums anywhere in an API, also in the dynamic client and Python.
  • Type aliases: type Volt = Quantity<VoltUnit> and generic aliases anywhere in an API; tools show what they name.
  • Types in modules: API types can live in any pub mod or be re-exported under another name; generated code finds them.
  • Self-referential types: Trees and expressions (RefBox, a list of the type itself) anywhere in an API, also in the dynamic client and Python.

Advanced

  • Optional items: Leave out what a board doesn't have, with no flash spent, and clients know before they call.
  • Error lists: Which errors each method can return, shown in docs and tools and checked in tests.
  • Stream functions: Open a stream with typed arguments and a result, like a method call.
  • Observing properties: Ask a device to send changes on change or periodically, within a byte budget.
  • Observing every sample: A fast property's every sample, each at its time, in compressed batches; typed and dynamic clients, the CLI and Python.
  • One clock per observed level: The samples of a level's properties share one time column per update: about a third fewer bytes and half the encoding CPU.
  • Observe cells: Sample a level from an interrupt in place, value by value into a ring of atomics: a quarter of the cycles and a tenth of the stack of sample() at opt-level z, the same wire.
  • A cheaper observe poll: The poll that sends a level's samples spends its time on the codec: half the cycles at opt-level 3, a third at z, the same bytes.
  • Batched streams: A stream opts into sending samples many per event as a compressed Series instead of one at a time, for plain, counted and reliable streams; typed and dynamic clients, the CLI and Python.
  • Size analysis: Worst-case request and reply sizes as constants, checked at compile time; properties and streams are next. in progress
  • API docs in rustdoc: #[ww_trait] also leaves a plain Rust trait, so methods, properties and streams show up on docs.rs. in progress
  • Code generation from build.rs: gen_server / gen_client as an alternative to the macros.
  • Generated C: The C runtime is there; generated C for an API's types and server is next. in progress

Nomicon

  • Builders for events and errors: Written straight into the output buffer.
  • Dispatch on index slices: Requests are routed by match on their path, the base of multi requests.
  • Names and paths that don't collide: Generated names carry the whole trait chain; type paths come from Cargo.
  • Counted and reliable streams: Exact counts of lost items; acknowledgements, resends and resume after a reconnect. in progress
  • Credit sinks: Flow control for data sent to a device, so its buffer never overflows, and lossy links resume where they stopped.
  • Resend and resume inside a batch: A resend or a resume from the middle of a multi-unit item gets only the units you don't have.
  • Credit sinks without a size limit: Sessions of any length, positions at most 4 bytes on the wire.
  • Credit sinks that resume: A sink (UART tx, a DFU plan) continues after a reconnect or a host restart, on the same acknowledgements as reliable streams. hardware check open
  • Reconnect: Commander::reconnect() connects again after disconnect().keep_streams() and resumes streams, sinks and observers. in progress
  • Resume checked on hardware: A UART sink on a real board put 1 MB on the line exactly once through link drops and a host restart.
  • Trait paths: Call a shared trait wherever it sits in a device's API. in progress

Details and what is planned: API model and codegen, Documentation, Examples, Testing, CI and performance in the feature tracker.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
The server is the code on the device that answers requests. It is generated from the trait, needs neither std nor an allocator and does no IO itself, so it runs on any MCU and RTOS over the transport you choose.

Basic

  • no_std, no allocator: The generated server works on the smallest MCUs and does no IO itself.
  • Your event loop: An async Server with wait() / handle() inside your own loop, or a blocking one.
  • Media: USB (embassy), RTT, WebSocket and UDP, the last two also on embassy-net.
  • Device descriptors: Serial number, API name, version and a user label, visible before connecting.

Advanced

  • Deferred replies everywhere: Answer a call later, also on nested trait levels.
  • Errors that say where: A device's error names the site that raised it, by a number that is the same in every firmware.
  • Sync handlers in an async server: Handlers that never wait are plain fns, only the ones that await are async: less flash.
  • Observed properties: The device sends property changes within the budget each host asked for.
  • Event-driven observe: The device sleeps until an observed property is due, and wakes at once when one changes.
  • ECC-safe STM32 flash: Reads a flash word broken by a power cut as zeros instead of crashing. hardware check open
  • I2C and SPI slave engine: Register map, answer queue, clock stretching and events of a slave, wired to your peripheral's interrupts.

Nomicon

  • Split send and receive: Independent TX and RX paths for every transport; handlers called straight from the receive loop.
  • Stream stores: Data a host hasn't acknowledged yet, kept in RAM or in a power-cut safe log on SD card or flash.
  • Logs that survive a crash: A store in RAM that outlives a reset, for what happened just before a fault.
  • Smaller observe code: A firmware carries the observe logic once, not once per trait level: about 15 KiB less flash on a big API.

Details and what is planned: Server / device side in the feature tracker.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
On the PC, a generated Rust client calls a device like a local library. A dynamic client does the same for any device from the description the device sends of itself; the ww tool and Python are built on it.

Basic

  • Rust client: Async, blocking or promise-style calls on a typed client.
  • One ? per call: Device errors and link errors in one Result.
  • Transports: USB, RTT through a debug probe, WebSocket, UDP, and in-process for tests.
  • Picking a device: By serial number, label or path, with clear errors when none is found.
  • Compatibility check on connect: The client compares its API with the device's and tells what doesn't match.

Advanced

  • Dynamic client: Talk to an API known only at runtime.
  • Cached API descriptions: A device's description is downloaded once, then found by its hash.
  • Multi requests: Read many properties or call a method on many array elements in one request.
  • Observing properties: Typed subscriptions and a cache of the latest values, shared by everyone watching.
  • Series without generated code: ww, Python and any dynamic client read and write a Series<T> from introspection alone, Python reads it as numpy columns.
  • Quantities without generated code: ww and Python show a ww_si value with its unit (3300 mV), Python as a quantity object with to_si().
  • Link setup timeout: Connecting over a slow link (a debug probe) waits seconds, a fast one fails quickly, and you can set the time.
  • Calls that work on any device: Shared traits called whatever a device's own API version. in progress
  • Following a reboot: Stay with a device while it reboots into its updater (RP2040 / RP2350 boot ROM so far). in progress

Nomicon

  • Sans-IO event loop: One event loop core, independent of the transport, with separate send and receive flows.
  • Stream positions and resume: Gaps reported exactly, streams resumed after a reconnect. in progress

Details and what is planned: Client / host side in the feature tracker.

items.title: Transports
items.text:
How the bytes get from one end to the other. Small messages are packed into one packet and big ones split, and a link layer checks on connect that both ends speak the same protocol.

Basic

  • USB, RTT, WebSocket, UDP: And in-process, also as simulated USB for tests.
  • USB network adapter: The device shows up as a USB network card with its own DHCP server, for WebSocket or UDP without drivers.

Advanced

  • Framer: Packs messages into packets with 1 byte of overhead, CRC and recovery from lost frames.
  • Link layer: Link setup, device info and protocol version exchange.
  • Link tap: Every frame, message and link event of a link recorded and decoded: which packet a request went out in, what a lost packet took with it.
  • USB throughput on small MCUs: Measured and tuned on an STM32G0 so far. in progress

Details and what is planned: Transports and protocols in the feature tracker.

items.title: Introspection
items.text:
A device can send a description of its own API, so tools and scripts work with it without its source code.

Basic

  • Devices describe themselves: The API model, sent by the device on request.

Advanced

  • Bit-sized numbers in the model: U7, I12, nibbles and the like, read and written by the dynamic client and Python.
  • Moved flag bits: Relocated #[flag] fields in the model and in dynamic values.

Nomicon

  • Bundles: The model with the crate versions and signatures of what it leaves out.

Details and what is planned: Introspection in the feature tracker.

items.title: Evolution
items.text:
Devices and hosts are updated at different times. These keep old hosts working with new firmware and the other way round, and tell you before a release when a change would break that.

Basic

  • Evolution rules: What you can change in types and APIs, and which version to bump.
  • Evolution checker: ww api check and ww api diff say whether a change is compatible.

Advanced

  • API identity: Every API and type has a signature; shared traits are referred to by hash.
  • API snapshots: Descriptions of the standard library are left out of what a device sends and filled in by the host.
  • Definitions from another revision: A device built from an unpublished revision still connects, with a warning.

Details and what is planned: Evolution, versioning and compatibility in the feature tracker.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
A command line tool, a Python module and a GUI to work with devices and APIs without writing a client.

Basic

  • ww command line tool: List devices, show a device's API as a tree, with shell completions.
  • Python: Any device from Python, its API taken from the device itself.
  • Server scaffold: ww api scaffold prints a stub for every handler a server needs.
  • Device info and reports: ww info for any device; ww report adds counters, logs and crash data in one file.

Advanced

  • API bundles: ww api save, check and diff.
  • Watching properties: ww observe and Python print updates as they arrive, with rates.
  • Explaining bytes: ww explain shows every field of a buffer with its bits, from hex or a value written in Rust. in progress
  • Link test: ww usb-loopback measures round trips, losses and speed both ways.
  • Watching the link: ww monitor, ww stats, ww capture and ww explain FILE: the link decoded live, counted, saved and read back; --monitor and --capture do it for any command's own connection.
  • Settings from a flash dump: ww settings dump decodes a settings store without the device.
  • Values from text: Typed values written as text and turned into bytes at runtime.
  • Dev GUI: Shows the parsed API and the generated code side by side; a UI for any device is prototyped. in progress

Details and what is planned: Tooling: CLI, GUI, Python, Client / host side in the feature tracker.

items.title: Standard library
items.text:
Ready-made traits and types for what many devices have: units, time, GPIO and buses, logs, firmware info, updates. They are shared, so a tool that knows one of them works with every device that implements it.

Basic

  • Device contract: What every device answers: firmware, board, ids, user label and last reset.
  • Common errors: CommonError (Busy, Timeout, InvalidArgument, ...) shared by all APIs.
  • Units and numbers: ww_si quantities like volts, hertz and seconds, ww_numeric values.
  • Units checked by the compiler: One generic quantity type with the unit in the type: Volt * Ampere is a Watt, Volt + Ampere doesn't build, 3300 mV prints itself.
  • Units known at run time: A value whose unit is only known on the device, a configurable sensor channel, carries its unit and is shown like a typed one.
  • Date and time: ww_date_time.
  • IO family: GPIO, UART, I2C, SPI, ADC, PWM, 1-Wire and more, all in one style. in progress
  • GPIO: Pins and banks: levels, modes, pulls and edge events.
  • CAN bus: From a simple bridge to a bus debugger.
  • Logs: defmt logs over a reliable stream, including what was logged before the host connected. hardware check open
  • Indicators: LEDs off, essential or normal, and a blink to find a unit on the bench.
  • Firmware updates: ww_dfu for A/B, in-place and bootloader updates, tested with reboots and power cuts. in progress
  • 1-Wire: Transactions and ROM search.
  • More buses: ww_i2c, ww_uart, ww_memory and the ww_gpio_hl helpers, usable with gaps. in progress

Advanced

  • Quantities without wide integers: On a small MCU, comparing and converting quantities with 32-bit numbers takes only 32-bit code: no 64- or 128-bit arithmetic is linked.
  • ADC: Single reads, sample streams and triggered captures.
  • PWM: Outputs and input capture.
  • Device time: A clock with sync to a shared time source.
  • I2C and SPI slave: The device stands in for a chip on another master's bus: a register map the host fills, or answers the host sends, with every transfer reported back. hardware check open
  • Logic analyzer: Triggered captures, transitions compressed. in progress
  • Pin tests: Shorts, pulls and floating pins on any board through one trait, the board's safety rules kept in its firmware. in progress
  • Interned strings: Names and reasons sent as a small id, the text read from the firmware's ELF on the host. in progress
  • Signal generator: Replays captures, drives DAC channels. in progress
  • Counters: A device's cnt counters, named on the host from its firmware file.
  • Recorder control: Status, format, recordings, markers and settings of a logger that writes to an SD card. in progress
  • Block device: Read, check and write an SD card or flash by block over the link, writes under a lease. in progress
  • Raw SD card: Registers, init report and raw commands with timing, for bring-up and card checks. in progress
  • Age of a crash record: How many boots ago the saved crash happened.
  • Settings store: A device's settings in its own flash, power-cut safe, readable by older and newer firmware. hardware check open
  • Versions: ww_version.

Nomicon

  • Request and event model: ww_client_server, the messages every call is made of.
  • Tape blocks: ww_tape: the generic blocks of track records that live feeds and log files (link captures) are made of.

Details and what is planned: Tooling: CLI, GUI, Python in the feature tracker.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Working projects to start from: host programs, firmware for a few boards, and the crate layout to copy.

Basic

  • Project layout: An <name>_api crate with the trait and types, next to the code that serves and calls it.
  • Host examples: Blinky, all GPIOs, UART, and blinky from Python.
  • Firmware examples: STM32 Nucleo boards, RP2040 / RP2350 and QEMU, over USB, RTT, WebSocket and UDP.
  • Serialization only: shrink_wrap without an API, and a comparison with other formats.

Advanced

  • UDP over a USB network adapter: An RP2 board and its host side.
  • Motor controller demo: 52 observed properties at three rates on a simulated motor, in the motor_sim repo.
  • Counters in firmware: cnt counters in every probe-connected board example.
  • Settings demo: Settings that survive a reboot, on the host and on two Nucleo boards.

Details and what is planned: Examples in the feature tracker.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
How WireWeaver is kept working: every change runs through CI, against the real client and server code.

Advanced

  • Continuous integration: Formatting, lints, docs, tests, semver checks and firmware builds on every change.
  • Integration tests: Every API feature tested through the real host event loop and device server.
  • Fuzzing: The framer and shrink_wrap's readers fed random input; more targets to come. in progress
  • Test coverage: A few remaining cases. in progress

Nomicon

  • Conformance matrix: One corpus of golden bytes every wire-format implementation must match: derive, dynamic client, Python, C; guarded against a sealed case changing and against a wire kind going untested.
  • Code size bench: Firmware images per case for RISC-V and Cortex-M, measured on every change.
  • Binary size tracking: Flash and RAM per feature in CI. in progress
  • Power cuts on STM32: A flash store reset thousands of times mid-write on real hardware. in progress

Details and what is planned: Testing, CI and performance, Wire format in the feature tracker.

items.title: Reading levels
items.text:
Pages carry a small badge above their title: how deep the page goes. Read the Basic pages first and stop when you have what you need. The deeper levels are there for when you hit a limit, need the last bit of size or speed, or want to know why something works the way it does.

  • Basic

    What you need to use WireWeaver: what a feature is for, the common case, a working example. Enough to define types, put them on the wire and read them back. Start here.

  • Advanced

    Every option and when to pick it: compact layouts, special types, the full list of macro directives, worked byte-level examples. For when the defaults are not enough. Assumes the Basic pages.

  • Nomicon

    The internals, as in the Rustonomicon: exact bit layouts, how the reader and writer work inside, measurements and the reasons behind design decisions. For writing your own serializer, a reader in another language, or changing WireWeaver itself.

A level says how much a page assumes, not how important it is: a Nomicon page can be the one you need for a bootloader that has to fit in 2 KB.

For writers

The badge comes from the page's front matter, level: basic, level: advanced or level: nomicon, and is drawn by overrides/partials/level.html. A page without it has no badge. In the navigation, a section lists its Basic pages first and groups the Advanced and Nomicon pages after them.

For writers: bit layouts

A Nomicon or Advanced page that shows how bits are laid out uses a bits fence: one field per line, its kind, its bits (groups of 0 and 1), then its label. The site draws every bit in its byte, coloured by kind, with each byte's hex below and a table of the fields with their bit offsets. A bytes line checks the fields: the build fails when they don't make those bytes (MSB first, as shrink_wrap writes them). Take the bytes from a real run (a test or a scratch example, see AGENTS.md), never from the bits by hand.

```bits
head  0100              n = 4
run   0001 0            `v.prefix` run: `Milli`, end
value 0000110011100100  3300
width 00010             block width 2
delta 10 00 11          +1 0 -2 (zigzag 2 0 3)
pad   00                padding
bytes 42 11 ..
```

Kinds: head (counts, field counts, codec headers), run (tag runs), value (full values), delta (residuals and other coded data), width (block widths), pad (padding). The label starts at the first word that isn't only 0 and 1 and may have code. The column layout is a worked one. The fence is docs_ext/ww_docs_ext/bits.py (tests next to it, in just test), its colours .ww-bits in docs/stylesheets/vhrd.css.

items.title: Python
items.text:
The wire_weaver Python module talks to any WireWeaver device without generated code. The API tree (traits, methods, properties, streams) is built at runtime from the introspection data the device sends, or from the API crate source. Values are converted to and from plain Python objects and serialized exactly as the generated Rust clients do it, the module is a thin wrapper around the dynamic client in wire_weaver_client.

It is meant for debugging, quick tests and scripts: connect, look at what the device offers, call it. For a typed Python package wrapping one specific API, see the blinky_py example instead (Examples), it wraps the generated Rust client.

Both transports are built in: USB and RTT over a debug probe (probe-rs). Everything is pure Rust, the wheel needs no system libraries.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
The module is built with maturin, from a checkout of the repository (a Rust toolchain is needed):

cd wire_weaver_py
uvx maturin build --release        # wheel in target/wheels/, `uv pip install` it anywhere
uvx maturin develop --release      # or install into the active virtual environment

--no-default-features leaves RTT out for a smaller wheel.

Linux permissions

Listing devices works without any setup, but opening one needs read/write access to /dev/bus/usb/..., usually granted to your user with a udev rule. See USB.

items.title: Interactive console
items.text:
From the repository root, just py builds the module into wire_weaver_py/.venv (only when Rust sources changed) and opens a Python prompt with ww imported and the device connected as dev, if exactly one is found or a filter is given:

just py                                        # the only connected USB device
just py --serial 0123 --timeout 5              # pick one: --serial, --label, --vid-pid c0de:cafe
just py --rtt STM32G0B1RETx --elf fw.elf       # over RTT, the ELF makes attaching fast
just py --api examples/blinky_api              # API from source: device without introspection, or offline
just py --help

Relative paths are resolved from the directory just was run in.

items.title: Connecting
items.text:
import wire_weaver as ww

print(ww.list_devices())                       # connected USB devices, one line each
dev = ww.connect(vid_pid=(0xc0de, 0xcafe), timeout=1.0)
dev.info                                       # API, link and protocol versions reported by the device
dev                                            # resource tree with signatures and docs
dev.disconnect()                               # or `with ww.connect(...) as dev:`

connect() takes keyword arguments only. A USB device is used unless rtt is given; all given filters must match:

Argument Selects vid_pid=(vid, pid) USB vendor and product ID serial, serial_contains USB serial number user_label user label reported by the device product_contains, manufacturer_contains USB product / manufacturer string implements_api=("my_api", ">=0.2") API crate name and a SemVer requirement rtt="STM32G0B1RETx" RTT over a debug probe, probe-rs chip name rtt_elf="fw.elf", rtt_speed_hz firmware ELF to take the RTT control block address from, probe speed timeout default request timeout in seconds api API from load_api(), for a device with introspection disabled

The introspection data is cached in ~/.wire_weaver/, so reconnecting to a device with the same API is quick. Definitions the device leaves out are put back from the snapshots, or from the definition cache for a device built from another revision of an unpublished crate, so its values decode without load_api. Without rtt_elf, RTT attaching scans the target RAM for the control block, see RTT.

items.title: Using the API
items.text:
Resources are attributes, their repr() shows the tree with signatures and the first doc line, and dir() lists them for tab completion. For the Dynamic trait from tests/dynamic_api:

>>> dev
Dynamic
  no_args()
  add(a: u32, b: i16) -> i64
  echo(value: Everything) -> Everything
  check(x: Option<u8>) -> Result<u8, CheckError>
  rw speed: u16
  rw everything: Everything
  rw flagged: Flagged
  channel[]: Channel
>>> dev.channel[0]
channel[0]: Channel
  rw gain: f32
  id() -> u32

dev.no_args()
dev.add(40, b=-2)                      # positional or keyword arguments
dev.speed.write(1500)                  # properties
dev.speed.read(timeout=5)              # timeout overrides the default for one request
dev.channel.valid_indices()            # arrays: indices the device accepts, e.g. [0, 1, 2]
dev.channel[1].gain.write(0.5)

with dev.samples as samples:           # stream from the device: open(), iterate or recv(), close()
    for s in samples:
        ...
dev.samples.recv(timeout=1)            # after open(): next item, TimeoutError if none
dev.samples.try_recv()                 # next item if one is already received, None otherwise

with dev.commands as sink:             # stream to the device (sink): open(), send(), close()
    sink.send({"Move": {"x": 1, "y": 2}})

Every resource also has doc (its doc comment), path (e.g. channel[2].gain) and, except traits, signature. Use dev["name"] for a resource named like one of the Device attributes (api, info, disconnect).

Blocking calls release the GIL, and waiting on a stream can be interrupted with Ctrl+C.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
• A method returning Result<T, E> returns T, or raises ww.RemoteError with E in its value attribute.
  • A request without a reply raises TimeoutError.
  • Connection, protocol and device errors raise ww.WireWeaverError (RemoteError is a subclass of it).
  • Values that don't fit the API types raise TypeError or ValueError before anything is sent, e.g. add() argument 'a': -1 is out of range for u32.

items.title: Values
items.text:
WireWeaver Python bool bool integers, UNib32, UVlq32/UVlq64, u4, nib int (range is checked) f32, f64 float (int accepted) String, &str str Vec<u8>, [u8; N] bytes (bytearray or a list of ints accepted) Vec<T>, [T; N] list (any iterable accepted) tuple tuple struct with named fields dict (dataclass, namedtuple or an object with attributes accepted) tuple struct tuple, a single field one is its value enum unit variant "Variant" enum variant with fields {"Variant": fields}, fields as for a struct Option<T> None or T, a missing Option field is None Result<T, E> {"Ok": T} or {"Err": E} Range, RangeInclusive (start, end) (range with step 1 accepted) Series<T> list of T (any iterable accepted); numpy columns with decode_columns (below)

A Series<T> (a method's return value, a property, a stream item) can also be read column by column: the decode_columns(data) of the method, property or stream gives a dict of field path to numpy array over all items (numpy is imported then, install it next to wire_weaver). Paths join field names with ., a variant's fields are under its name (status.Fault.code), tuple and array elements under their position (pair.0), a Series of plain numbers is under "". An enum also gives the variant of each item under its own path, an Option is transparent. Numbers and bools get their dtype, other leaves (strings, lists, #[series(opaque)] fields) are object arrays. A leaf some items don't have (in another variant, or None) is a masked array (numpy.ma). See Series<T>.

items.title: More
items.text:
• Counted and reliable streams: positions, gaps, resuming from a cursor
  • Observing a trait level's properties as a group
  • API from source, offline use: a device without introspection, encoding and decoding without a device
  • Not supported yet

items.title: Python: streams, observing, offline
items.text: More of the wire_weaver Python module, after the basics on the Python page: counted and reliable streams, observing a group of properties, and working with an API crate without a device.

items.title: Counted and reliable streams
items.text:
A stream marked counted or reliable in the API (its signature says so) gives every item a position, reports what was lost and where, and can be resumed from a saved cursor (Stream reliability):

s = dev.samples
s.open(rate=1000, ack="explicit")      # the stream function's arguments; returns its result, an Err raises RemoteError
                                       # open(cursor=saved) after a restart; ack="receive" is the default
while True:
    ev = s.recv_event(timeout=1)       # dict: kind "item", "gap", "resumed", "backfill_done", "disconnected", "closed"
    if ev["kind"] == "item":
        write(ev["pos"], ev["t"], ev["value"])  # t: device time in seconds, or None
        s.ack(ev["pos"] + ev["units"])          # explicit: the device may free it now
        save_cursor(s.cursor)                   # (session, pos), with the data
    elif ev["kind"] == "gap":
        print(f'{ev["units"]} lost at {ev["at"]} ({ev["cause"]})')  # device, link, store or host
s.stats                                # received, lost by cause, duplicates, queued ...

recv() and iterating return values only, gaps are counted in stats. A resumed reliable stream delivers the latest values at once (run "live") and the backlog beside them (run "backfill"), each in order.

items.title: Observing
items.text:
A trait level's +observe properties (Observing properties) can be watched as a group, from introspection alone (TOOL-11):

m = dev.motor
m.observable_properties()                          # {"speed": "u32", "current": "u32", "position": "u32"}
with m.observe({"speed": 10, "current": None}) as obs:  # speed periodically every 10ms, current on change
    for u in obs:
        print(u["values"], u["t"], u["missed"])     # {"speed": 1500, "current": 3}, seconds or None, due sends that missed budget
obs.budget                                          # bytes/s the device applies to the whole level

Every sample of +batched properties (Every sample) comes item by item, each with its own device time, or per batch as numpy columns:

with m.observe({"current": {"samples": 5}}) as obs:  # every sample, in batches at most 5 ms old
    u = obs.recv()
    u["samples"]["current"]                         # [(t, value), ...], oldest first; u["values"] has the newest
    b = obs.recv_batch()
    b["batches"]["current"]                         # {"t": array of seconds, "": array of the values}

{"samples": max_age_ms, "every": ms} takes the first sample in each every (decimated on the device). The columns are keyed as in decode_columns and a batched stream's recv_batch(): "" for a number, a key per field for a struct (value, ok, ..).

observe() without cfg asks for every observable property on-change (what ww observe <path> does without --rate). recv(timeout=...) / try_recv() are also available. One device subscription is shared per level (One subscription per level); dropping the last observer (garbage collection) unsubscribes.

items.title: API from source, offline use
items.text:
A device with introspection disabled needs its API from the crate source:

api = ww.load_api("path/to/my_api", "MyApi")   # trait name is needed if the crate has several
dev = ww.connect(api=api)

load_api() alone works without a device: browse the API the same way, and serialize values to see what goes over the wire, or decode captured bytes:

>>> api = ww.load_api("tests/dynamic_api", "Dynamic")
>>> api.add.encode_args(40, b=-2).hex()
'28000000feff'
>>> api.speed.encode(1500)
b'\xdc\x05'
>>> api.speed.decode(b"\xdc\x05")
1500
>>> api.check.decode_return(b"\x00\x00\x01")
{'Err': 'TooBig'}

Methods have encode_args() / decode_return(), properties encode() / decode(), streams decode() and sinks encode(). Calling a resource of an offline API raises WireWeaverError.

items.title: Not supported yet
items.text:
• f16, UN/IN and LEB128 numbers.
  • Typed (non-integer) array indices, property write errors (not decoded, same as generated clients).
  • Observing a level inside a resource array (Limits).
  • asyncio: calls block the calling thread (with the GIL released).

items.title: Built-in types
items.text: Every type on this page implements the ShrinkWrap traits: it can be a field of a #[derive_shrink_wrap] type, and (unless noted) an argument, return value, property or stream item of an API. Sizes below are for the value on its own; how values share bytes is on the ShrinkWrap page.

items.title: At a glance
items.text:
Type On the wire Alignment bool 1 bit bit U1..U64, I2..I64 exactly that many bits bit Nibble 4 bits nibble u8..u128, i8..i128 1 to 16 bytes, little-endian byte f32, f64 4 / 8 bytes, IEEE 754, little-endian byte UNib32 1 to 11 nibbles, small values short nibble UVlq32, UVlq64 1 to 5 / 1 to 10 bytes, small values short byte &str, String UTF-8 bytes, length at the back byte RefVec<'i, T>, Vec<T> the elements, count at the back byte MaxLen<T, N> same as T, at most N elements as T [T; N] the elements, no count as T Option<T>, Result<T, E> a 1-bit flag, then the value bit tuples (2 to 8), Range<T>, RangeInclusive<T>, () the parts one after another (() is nothing) as parts RefBox<'i, T>, Box<T> the value and its size byte structs and enums the fields; an enum's discriminant in 1 bit to 4 bytes as fields

The special types (TailSize, ArrayString / ArrayVec, compressed sequences, OptionAnyVec) are listed at the end.

items.title: Booleans and numbers
items.text:
bool takes one bit. Bit-sized values pack back to back; the next byte-sized value starts a fresh byte.

u8..u128, i8..i128 are written at full width, little-endian, starting on a byte: 0x1234u16 is 34 12. f32, f64 are their IEEE 754 bits, little-endian: 1.5f32 is 00 00 c0 3f.

U1..U64, I2..I64 (shrink_wrap::un, in the prelude; u7, ub8, i12... in an API) take exactly as many bits as their name says. In Rust each is backed by the smallest standard integer, with checked constructors (U7::new(x), U7::try_from(x)) and .value() / u8::from(..). A (U3, U7) of (5, 100) is 10 bits: b9 00. Note that u8 is byte-aligned, while U8 is bit-aligned. They work as struct fields, enum variant payloads and API arguments: an enum I2cAddress { Seven(U7), Ten(U10) } with ww_repr = u1 takes 8 or 11 bits (see the showcase).

Nibble (nib in an API) is 4 bits on a 4-bit boundary.

Variable-length numbers take fewer bytes for small values:

Type Encoding Range 300 is UNib32 3 bits per nibble, the top bit says "more follows" u32 cd 4 UVlq32 big-endian VLQ, 7 bits per byte, the top bit says "more follows" u32 82 2c UVlq64 the same as UVlq32, 1 to 10 bytes u64 82 2c UN, IN the bit width (3 to 6 bits), then that many bits u64, i64

UNib32 is what ShrinkWrap uses for lengths and for ww_repr = unib32 discriminants; values below 8 take one nibble (showcase). UVlq32Backfill is a UVlq32 always written as 5 bytes, so its value can be filled in after the rest is written.

items.title: Strings and lists
items.text:
&'i str (borrowed, zero-copy) and String (std) are UTF-8 bytes, with the length at the back of the buffer as a UNib32 (why at the back): "abc" on its own is 61 62 63 03. Invalid UTF-8 fails to read with Error::MalformedUtf8.

RefVec<'i, T> (borrowed, no allocator) and Vec<T> (std) are the elements one after another, with the count at the back. A RefVec read from a buffer points into it and decodes elements as you iterate; to write one, make it from a slice (RefVec::Slice { slice: &items }, or RefVec::new_bytes(&[1, 2, 3]) for bytes). The derive macro maps RefVec to Vec and &str to String for the owned type (type mapping). Without a slice, e.g. elements coming from a sensor loop, RefVecBuilder writes a list into the buffer one element at a time, with the same bytes.

[T; N] is N elements with no count. N can be a literal or any const expression ([f32; MAX_SERIES]).

To own a string or list without an allocator, use ArrayString<N> / ArrayVec<T, N>: the same bytes, stored in a fixed-size array.

items.title: Bounded lists and strings: MaxLen<T, N>
items.text:
MaxLen<T, N> wraps a list or a string (RefVec<'i, T>, Vec<T>, &'i str or String) and allows at most N elements (bytes for a string). It works everywhere a type can appear: struct and enum fields, method arguments and return types, properties, stream! and sink! items, and nested inside other lists (MaxLen<RefVec<'i, MaxLen<&'i str, 8>>, 4>).

pub const MAX_PIECE: usize = 256;

#[ww_trait]
trait Stage {
    fn write(offset: u32, last: bool, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_PIECE>);
    property!(rw label: MaxLen<&'i str, 32>);
}

In a #[ww_trait], N is an integer literal, {literal}, or the name of a const defined in the API crate's lib.rs. In a plain #[derive_shrink_wrap] type it is any const expression.

  • Checked both ways, never truncated. MaxLen::new refuses a value that is too long. Serializing one (e.g. after changing it through DerefMut) fails with Error::MaxLenExceeded, and so does deserializing one, before any element is read. A server answers an over-long argument with an error, a client refuses to send one.
  • Same bytes as the unbounded type. The bound only exists in the code on both ends. That keeps it evolvable: a bound can be added, raised, lowered or removed without a new wire format, and the evolution rules say which of those old peers accept.
  • Visible in introspection. ww_self describes it as Type::MaxLen { max_len, ty }, so the dynamic client and the Python module check the bound too (Python raises ValueError: ... at most N ...).

MaxLen bounds the length of one value. The number of resources in a resource array (stream!(adc[]: u16)) is a different thing, see arrays.

items.title: Worst-case size at compile time
items.text:
Every type has a SerializeShrinkWrap::MAX_SIZE: Option<MaxSize>:

  • Some when every part of it is bounded: numbers, arrays, Option / Result, structs and enums of them, and MaxLen lists and strings of bounded elements;
  • None as soon as anything can grow without a limit: a plain Vec, RefVec, String, RefBox, compressed sequences.

MaxSize::buffer_len_of(T::MAX_SIZE) is a buffer length any value of T always serializes into. It is an upper bound, not the exact worst case: every length is counted as at least four nibbles and every alignment as needed. Owned types don't have MAX_SIZE yet (SW-42).

A generated no_alloc server also gets, per method, <METHOD>_REQUEST_MAX_LEN and <METHOD>_RESPONSE_MAX_LEN: Option<usize>: the longest request message that calls it and the longest reply, None when an argument or the return type is unbounded. A firmware can check at compile time that its message buffer is big enough:

const MAX_MESSAGE_LEN: usize = 512;
const _: () = assert!(matches!(
    api_server::WRITE_REQUEST_MAX_LEN,
    Some(len) if len <= MAX_MESSAGE_LEN
));

items.title: Option and Result
items.text: Option<T> is a 1-bit flag (1 for Some), then the value: Some(5u8) is 80 05, None is one zero bit. Result<T, E> is the same with 1 for Ok and 0 for Err, followed by the T or the E. Both work inside lists, as fields and in every API position. Where the flag goes can be moved with #[flag] (showcase), and why a flag beats an enum tag is in the showcase too.

items.title: Tuples, ranges and ()
items.text: Tuples of 2 to 8 elements, Range<T> and RangeInclusive<T> are their parts one after another, as if they were a struct's fields. () takes no bytes, for a method that returns nothing.

items.title: Self-referential types: RefBox
items.text:
A type that contains itself (a tree, an expression) needs indirection. RefBox<'i, T> gives it without an allocator: read from a buffer it points into it and decodes on .read(); its owned counterpart is Box<T>. On the wire it is the value plus its size, so a reader can jump over it. See the showcase.

Such types work anywhere in an API (API-44), as arguments, return values, properties and stream items, also in the dynamic client, ww and Python:

#[ww_trait]
trait Calc {
    fn eval(expr: Expr<'i>) -> Option<i32>;
    property!(rw tree: Tree<'i>);
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone), ww_repr = u4)]
pub enum Expr<'i> {
    Add(RefBox<'i, Expr<'i>>, RefBox<'i, Expr<'i>>),
    Neg(RefBox<'i, Expr<'i>>),
    Lit(i32),
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone))]
pub struct Tree<'i> {
    pub label: &'i str,
    pub children: RefVec<'i, Tree<'i>>,
}

The API model has each such definition once, referring to itself. As in Rust, every cycle goes through a RefBox or a list. Types with parameters can't be part of a cycle (struct List<T> { next: Option<RefBox<'i, List<T>>> } is an error), a type without them can use itself as an argument (children: RefVec<'i, Timed<Tree<'i>>>). A value is as deep as its bytes say; decoding it is bounded: the reader stops at its depth limit, the dynamic client at about 70 levels, so a malformed or malicious value is an error, not a stack overflow on a host.

Recursive types in firmware

Generated server code reads arguments with the default limit of 128 levels, which a small MCU stack may not hold: a host can send a value that deep. Until the server takes a lower limit, keep recursive types out of the arguments of methods and properties a device serves, or give its task a stack large enough for 128 levels.

items.title: Structs and enums
items.text:
Your own types, with #[derive_shrink_wrap]:

  • Structs are their fields in order. By default a struct is evolvable: fields can be appended later. Tuple and unit structs work too, see below.
  • Enums, with or without data in their variants, are a discriminant followed by the variant's fields. The discriminant takes what ww_repr says: u1, u2, ... (bits), nib, u8 / u16 / u32 (bytes), or unib32 (variable length).

items.title: Tuple structs
items.text:
A tuple struct is written exactly like a struct with the same fields named: Celsius(21.5) is the f32 alone, 00 00 ac 41, and Rgb(1, 2, 3) is 01 02 03.

A unit struct (struct Marker;) has no data, but inside a parent it records its length like any evolvable struct, a nibble that is usually shared with a neighbour: (1, Marker, 2) is 01 02 00. That is what makes it useful in an API: fn arm() -> Armed can later become Armed { at: Timestamp }, and older code still reads it. On its own (a whole message) nothing follows it, so it takes no bytes at all. A unit struct with sized, final_structure, self_describing or fixed_layout would be zero bits that can never change, so the derive refuses it: leave the size assumption out, or give it reserved bits to grow into (e.g. a U4 field).

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq))]
pub struct Celsius(pub f32);

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, sized, derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq))]
pub struct Rgb(pub u8, pub u8, pub u8);

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq))]
pub struct Pair<'i>(pub u8, pub &'i str); // and PairOwned(u8, String)

Everything a named struct can do works the same way: size assumptions, fixed_layout, head_tail, sparse, validate, display (with {0}, {1}), and new fields with #[default = ..], only at the end. Where the fields need a name (layout constants such as Rgb::_2_OFFSET, C names, error messages) they are _0, _1, ... The one thing that needs names is #[flag], which pairs a relocated flag with its field by name: name the fields to use it. Dynamic clients see the fields unnamed, Python as a tuple (a single field as its value, a unit struct as None).

How much a nested struct or enum costs on top of its fields depends on its size assumption: an evolvable one adds its length (usually a nibble), a sized one nothing.

items.title: Generic types in an API
items.text:
A generic struct or enum is used in an API with its arguments, in every position: arguments, return values, properties, stream items, fields of other types (API-43).

#[ww_trait]
trait Sensor {
    fn swap(pair: Pair<u8, u16>) -> Pair<u16, u8>;
    fn sum(window: Window<4>) -> u32;
    property!(ro current: Timed<Ampere>);
    stream!(readings: Reading<i16>);
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq))]
pub struct Window<const N: usize> {
    pub samples: [u16; N],
}

Generated server and client code uses the types as written (Window<4>, ww_si::Timed<ww_si::Ampere>, a Tagged<'i, T> as TaggedOwned<String> on the owned side). The API model has each generic definition once, with its parameters, and each use as an instance with its arguments; ww_si::Timed<T> is known from the ww_si snapshot, so a device leaves its definition out of its introspection data like that of any known type. The dynamic client, ww and Python see the concrete types (Timed<Ampere>, Window<4>) and read and write the same bytes as the derived ones.

Arguments can be types, integer and bool literals, const items of the crate, a const parameter passed on (struct Outer<const N: usize> { window: Window<N> }), or left to the parameter's default. How a generic type may change is in the evolution rules.

items.title: Type aliases
items.text:
A type alias stands for what it names, in every API position (API-45):

#[ww_trait]
trait Supply {
    property!(ro voltage: Volt);
    property!(ro sampled: Timed<Volt>);
    fn last(n: u8) -> Reading<u32>;
}

pub mod units {
    pub struct Volt;
}
pub type Volt = Quantity<units::Volt>;
pub type Reading<T> = Pair<Window<2>, Option<T>>;

Aliases are found like structs and enums: in lib.rs, in modules, through use imports (renamed ones too, use units::Volt as V) and globs, also in other crates. A generic alias puts its arguments where its parameters are, a const parameter too (type Buf<const N: usize> = Window<N>). The API model has no entry for the alias itself: voltage is a Quantity<Volt> there (the marker units::Volt), and ww, the dynamic client and Python show it that way. A PhantomData<U> field is left out of a struct's definition (it takes no bits on the wire), so U is a parameter that no field uses.

items.title: Types in modules
items.text:
A type the API uses can live in any module of its crate. Each definition records the path other crates name it by: the shortest one through pub mods and pub use re-exports (API-46). In the example above, that is my_api::Volt for the alias and my_api::units::Volt for the marker; a type in a private module re-exported at the root with pub use ty::Ty; is my_api::Ty, and one re-exported under another name (pub use ty::Inner as Outer;) is my_api::Outer, also in ww and the dynamic client. A type that other crates can't reach at all is an error that names it. The <Name>Owned variant of a type with a lifetime is named next to it: re-export it along with the type (pub use ty::{Label, LabelOwned};, or a glob).

The path and the name are the definition's identity: units::Volt and a Volt at the crate root are two different types, in generated code, in API snapshots (ww api save takes the types of pub mods too, unit marker structs like pub struct Volt; included) and in introspection data.

items.title: Special types
items.text:
For particular jobs, on their own page:

Type For TailSize<N> a value that bounds itself inside a longer buffer (file headers, records) ArrayString<N>, ArrayVec<T, N> owned strings and lists without an allocator Series<T> of numbers compressed time series of integers, timestamps and floats OptionAnyVec, EitherAnyVec sparse sets of values of any types; a sparse struct is built on it TailBytes bytes that take up the rest of the buffer, no length; generated API code uses it for byte slices

These are for Rust types and generated code; an API definition (#[ww_trait]) doesn't name them. The compressed sequences are the exception: they work in every API position.

items.title: Library types
items.text: The standard library has many more types built from these: date and time, versions, numbers with units, SI quantities, and the types of its I/O traits.

items.title: Not supported yet
items.text:
• char and maps (HashMap, BTreeMap; for now a Vec of (K, V), SW-26).
  • Numbers restricted to a range or a set (SW-20), like u16 in 1..=512 or u8 in 0..=8, 12, 16, checked on both ends. Until then, a struct can check its fields with validate.
  • Units on numbers (f32 in amperes) as a hint for code generation and tools, not sent over the wire. The ww_si crate has typed SI quantities today.

items.title: Resources addressing
items.text:
Every resource (method, property, stream, sink or trait) is reached by its path: an array of indices from the API root, each a UNib32 (4 bits for 0..=7). [0, 1, 2] takes 2 bytes, its length included. As a user you never write these indices: they are assigned in declaration order, and generated code uses the names.

#[ww_api_root]
trait ApiRoot {
    fn turn_on();               // [0]
    fn turn_off();              // [1]
    ww_impl!(motor: Motor);     // [2, ..]
    ww_impl!(port[]: Port);     // [3, <index>, ..]
}

A nested trait adds one index for its own items, an array one more for the selected index; with several arrays on the way, each puts its index at its place in the path, and the server's handler gets them all as its index chain.

A path only means something for one API and version, so it needs the host to know the device's API. When that is not possible or not wanted (calling a reusable trait on any device, or on many devices at once), a request names the trait instead.

items.title: Global trait addressing (FullVersion)
items.text:
A request can call a reusable trait without knowing where it sits: put a device to sleep through its power management trait, or read the firmware version of any device with ww_firmware_info. Instead of an absolute path, it carries the trait's crate name and version (FullVersion). That takes 8 to 16 bytes or more, depending on the crate name, where a path takes a few: costly on a constrained link, or when many calls share one packet.

The request carries the trait's crate name and version (FullVersion), the trait's name in that crate (a crate can define several, ww_dfu has five) and the path from the trait's root. The server finds the trait wherever it sits in its API tree and continues from there. It answers ErrorKind::TraitNotFound when it doesn't implement the trait, only implements an incompatible version of its crate (major and, before 1.0, minor have to match), or only implements it under a resource array (ww_impl!(port[]: ww_gpio::Bank): a global path can't select an index). When a trait is implemented several times, the first one in the tree (depth first, in resource id order) answers.

Global paths don't depend on the user API or its version, which makes them the way to talk to a device whose API the host doesn't know: a host built against a new API version can still reboot a device running an old one into its updater (ww_dfu::BootControl) or read its info traits. On the host, connect with traits_only and call through a trait client:

// any device, whatever its API and version: the user API check of link setup is skipped
let device = DynClient::traits_only(|c| c.usb().serial_eq(serial)).connect().await?;
// a client generated with `client = "trait_client"` for ww_dfu::BootControl, see tests/cross_version
let mut boot = BootControl::new(device.global_attachment(ww_dfu::BOOT_CONTROL_FULL_GID, "BootControl"));
