boot.reboot(BootTarget::Updater).call().await?;

A traits_only connection refuses absolute paths (Error::AbsolutePathInTraitsOnly): without the device's API they could mean anything. ww dfu reboot in the CLI does exactly this.

items.title: Global trait addressing (CompactVersion)
items.text:
CompactVersion is the short form: a globally unique type id and the version numbers, all UNib32. Unique ids can't come from crate names, so they are assigned by hand and tracked in git, in the ww_global registry.

Servers don't serve compact trait paths yet (ErrorKind::TraitNotFound): compact ids of traits are not in the API model, and none is assigned so far (API-20).

items.title: API report
items.text: TODO: export a file describing all levels of API with IDs (DOC-5).

items.title: Arrays
items.text:
A property, stream, sink or trait can be an array of resources, written with [] after its name:

#[ww_trait]
trait Board {
    stream!(adc[]: u16);
    sink!(lanes[]: [u8]);
    property!(rw gain[]: f32);
    ww_impl!(port[]: ww_gpio::Bank);
}

Methods can't be arrays, put them in an array of traits instead. The length isn't part of the API: the device says which indices exist with a valid_indices_root_<name>() handler returning ValidIndices (a range or a list), and a request for another index is answered ErrorKind::BadIndex. Bounds in the API itself (adc[8], motor[1..=4]) are not supported yet. The length of a list or string inside a resource's type is bounded with MaxLen instead.

On the host, an array item takes its index first: device.port(0).pin(3).read_pull(), device.adc(2).call(). On the device, every handler of an item inside arrays, at any depth, gets the indices leading to it as one more argument, index_chain: [UNib32; N], after cx; ww api scaffold prints the exact signatures. The generated code stays flat: the whole API tree becomes plain function calls on the server struct, with no per-index state.

A whole array can be read, written or called in one request, see Multi requests.

items.title: Array of resources vs resource of array
items.text:
Here, led is itself an array: each index is a resource of its own, with its own path, read and written separately.

#[ww_trait]
trait ArrayOfResources {
    property!(rw led[]: bool);
}

Here led is one resource whose type is an array: all three values are read and written in one go.

#[ww_trait]
trait ResourceOfArrays {
    property!(rw led: [bool; 3]);
}

Both together:

#[ww_trait]
trait ArrayOfArrays {
    property!(rw rgb_led[]: [u8; 3]);
}

items.title: Batching streams and properties
items.text: Batching (API-41) lets a stream or a +observe property send many samples as one Series (SW-60) instead of one item per event: one header, one presence bit and one set of per-column overhead for the whole batch, not for every item. It's opt-in, per stream or per property, and the device owns the batch itself - there is no batch size in the API, only a host-picked latency (how long a batch may wait before it's sent).

items.title: How to batch a stream
items.text:
Add batched (or batched(untimed) for an item type that already carries its own position or time) next to a stream's other directives:

#[ww_trait]
trait Sensors {
    #[batched]
    stream!(readings: Sample);                            // plain, timed

    #[counted]
    #[batched]
    stream!(counted_readings: Sample);                    // counted, timed

    #[stream(Sample, reliable, batched)]
    fn calibrated(gain: i32) -> Result<(), Error>;         // reliable, timed

    #[stream(Frame, counted, batched(untimed))]
    fn frames();                                            // counted, untimed: Frame has no own time
}

batched goes next to reliable/counted in #[stream(..)]'s argument list, or as its own #[batched] attribute above a plain or #[counted] stream!. Sample/Frame need #[derive_shrink_wrap(.., series)] (see which T); a timed stream's item becomes ww_si::Timed<Sample> on the wire, so the API crate needs ww_si. A type without a series size bound (a string, a byte list, an opaque field) is a compile error on batched.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
The stream field's type becomes ww_stream::batch::Batched<Sink, Timed<Sample>, N> (or Batched<Sink, Frame, N> untimed), built as Batched::new(sink, policy) from the same Sink an unbatched stream would use - Plain, Counted, or Reliable<Store> (see Counted and reliable streams) - and a SeriesPolicy, ww_stream::batch::DEFAULT_POLICY usually. N is the batch size (DEFAULT_BATCH = 32), a compile-time constant of the server, not part of the API.

struct Server {
    readings_stream: Batched<Plain, Timed<Sample>, 32>,
    // ..
}

async fn stream_readings(&mut self) -> &mut Batched<Plain, Timed<Sample>, 32> {
    &mut self.readings_stream
}

// feeding it, anywhere in the device's own code - an ISR, a control loop tick
let ser = api_impl::stream_data_ser();
ser.readings_push(&mut self.readings_stream, sample, t);               // one item, its own time
ser.readings_push_many(&mut self.readings_stream, t0, dt, block);      // a regularly-sampled block at once
ser.frames_push(&mut self.frames_stream, frame);                       // untimed: no `t`

// event loop, next to `poll_properties`
let mut scratch = Box::new(ww_stream::batch::Scratch::<SB>::new());
server.poll_streams(&mut out, now_ms, &mut buf, 4096, &mut scratch).await?;

<name>_push/<name>_push_many are O(1) and interrupt-safe (a copy of the item's fields and two atomic operations, see Sealing below), returning a Seal - whether this push sealed a batch, and whether anything was lost. poll_streams takes one extra argument next to the buffer and message-length bound an unbatched server already passes: a Scratch<B>, shared by every batcher of the server, where a sealed batch's items are rebuilt before they're written as a Series (see the store). close_<name>/the stream closing should call .batcher.flush() to send a half-full batch rather than wait out max_age.

items.title: Host side
items.text: Opening a batched stream is like opening any other (client.readings().call(), etc.), plus .max_age(duration) to pick the latency: the device clamps it to its own bounds and answers with what it granted (StreamOpened::max_age_us on the wire). Items come one at a time exactly as from an unbatched stream - recv_event()/recv(), each with its own t (or none, untimed) and its own position, as if it had been sent on its own - or recv_batch() gives a whole batch at once (pos, items, oldest first). The dynamic client (DynStreamOpen, no generated code needed) and wire_weaver_py's recv_batch() (numpy columns, via decode_columns) give the same two ways; ww stream <path> --batches prints whole batches from the CLI instead of one line per item.

items.title: How to batch property samples
items.text: A ro+observe+batched property sends every sample it takes, not just its latest value, when a host observes it in Samples mode - this is API-39, documented in full at Observing properties: every sample (the device's <Level>Sampler, the host's samples(max_age), Python). It uses the same Batcher as a stream's, one per trait level with +batched properties: all of a level's +batched properties share one call, sample(t, <Level>Samples { .. }), so the batcher keeps rows (the time and every value) and a level batch is sent as one Series<T> per observed property plus one Series<Second> of times for all of them, the update's sample_times (API-49, a shared clock). The batches feed a level-wide Outbox instead of a stream's own store - the rest of this page (sealing, budget, cost) applies to it the same way.

items.title: Sealing
items.text:
A batch is sealed - handed from the filling side to the side that encodes it - for one of four reasons (ww_stream::batch::Cause): it reached N items (Full), one more item would pass the event's byte budget (Budget), it got as old as the host allows (Age), or the user code asked for it early (Flush, e.g. on close_<name>). Full/Budget are decided by the push itself (Producer::push); Age/Flush by the event loop's next poll/flush call.

Each Batcher holds two stores of N items: one filling, one spare. Sealing swaps them - the filling store becomes the sealed one, the spare (now empty) starts filling - behind one atomic word (a push is a fetch_or and a compare-exchange, no lock, safe to call from an interrupt; see the module's own doc comment, ww_stream/src/batch/mod.rs, for the exact bit layout). If the spare isn't back from being encoded yet when a batch would seal, its items are lost instead (Seal::Lost) and the store starts over; losses are counted (BatchStats::lost) and reported in the next batch's lost_before, which becomes a stream's missed (Stream delivery) or an observe level's missed.

items.title: Budget
items.text:
The event loop gives the batcher a byte budget per event (set_budget); the producer seals at the most items that estimate allows, so the batch it hands over always fits. Two estimates, the bigger one wins: the worst case (Series::max_bytes, from the type's size bounds - always safe, but usually far from what real data takes) before anything has been encoded, and after that, the last batch's measured bytes per item with a margin (aimed at 80% of the budget) - real data is almost always much smaller than the worst case, so this measured limit quickly lets through far more than N would need. A sealed batch that still turns out bigger than the room it's encoded into is split: the largest prefix that fits goes out, the rest waits for the next call, so nothing is lost or sent twice over a budget surprise.

For a stream, the budget is the event/message size; for observe, it's a level's byte budget, shared with every other property of the level - a sample taken is always encoded (so an MCU needs a floor on sample rate, see below), but a batch that then doesn't fit the level's Outbox is dropped, oldest first, and counted as missed.

items.title: The store
items.text:
A Batcher<T, N>'s two stores are T::Store<N> (SeriesStore, SW-62): a struct of arrays, one per leaf field, with no padding between items - usually less RAM than [T; N] twice over (SeriesStore's own page has the exact per-item sizes). Encoding writes a sealed batch column by column straight from the store's arrays (write_store_series, SW-64), and counts its bytes the same way when it has to (count_store_series), the same bits as the item walk. Rows where an enum or Option tag changes are read back out of the store into the shared Scratch<B> (scratch_bytes::<T>(N) sizes it for one batcher; a server with several batchers shares one Scratch big enough for its biggest) and written with the ordinary Series::with_policy. A T aligned to more than 16 bytes, or one whose Store<N> doesn't fit B, is a compile error, not a runtime one.

An observe level's Outbox<BYTES> (see Every sample) sits after the Batcher: each level batch is its time column followed by the column of each property observed in Samples mode (each entry with a header: slot, items, length), encoded once, column by column (the scratch holds one column, not a row). A batch whose worst case fits the free room is written right away; one whose worst case doesn't is written into the room there is all the same and measured only when it didn't fit (to drop older batches or split it), so a big outbox and a small one cost the same CPU while batches fit (API-52). They wait there, oldest first, for poll_properties to send each whole in one update as budget allows; when it's full, the oldest batches are dropped to make room, also counted as missed. A stream has no outbox - its encoded batch goes straight into the stream's own store (reliable) or the next event (plain/counted).

items.title: Cost: CPU and flash
items.text:
Pushing an item and polling for a seal are cheap and flat regardless of batch size - on a Cortex-M3 (examples_mcu/mcu_qemu, Timed<Ampere>, instructions counted under QEMU): a plain push about 62 instructions, the push that fills and seals a batch about 71, a poll that seals nothing about 108, one that seals a due batch about 159. No interrupt is masked either way (LDREX/STREX, not a critical section, except on thumbv6m cores without compare-exchange).

Encoding is where the cost scales with batch size - see Series: CPU and flash on an MCU for the measured table (per-item instructions and flash by codec, Cortex-M3/M4F/M7, after SW-63's rework of the column writers: a fixed codec at n = 32 costs about 341 instructions per item on a Cortex-M3, 2.4-6.9x less than before it, and DeltaPacked (the no_std default, delta-packed residuals and XOR floats, chosen at compile time) links only its own codecs - about 15 KB of flash on an M3 against 25 KB for a runtime CodecPolicy). The Batcher itself (rebuilding a batch into the scratch, giving the store back) is a small fraction of that: about 2 270 of the roughly 65 000 instructions a 32-item encode takes on a Cortex-M3 with the pre-SW-63 numbers, the rest being the Series encode proper.

items.title: Which rates fit an MCU
items.text:
Count samples per second as properties (or a stream's items) x rate. A timed stream encodes each item with its own time: about 341 instructions per item on a Cortex-M3/M4F with DeltaPacked, n = 32, about 790 cycles on an STM32H725. Observed properties share their level's time column (API-49), which halves that: measured on the motor demo's 21 FOC properties (I32 storage, n = 32, DeltaPacked), a level batch of 672 samples takes about 213 instructions per sample on a Cortex-M3/M4F (QEMU) and about 380 cycles per sample on the H725, against 395 and 786 with a time column per property, and 36 % fewer bytes (1 251 B against 1 965 B):

Observed (one level, shared clock) Samples/s Cortex-M3/M4F, instructions/s STM32H725 (M7, 540 MHz), cycles/s Fits 2 currents at 1 kHz 2 000 ~0.4 M ~0.8 M any Cortex-M, trivially 4 properties at 4 kHz 16 000 ~3.4 M ~6.1 M any Cortex-M, with room to spare 5 properties at 25 kHz ("FOC subset 5") 125 000 ~27 M ~48 M (9% of the core) a fast M4F, comfortably an M7 all 21 FOC properties at 25 kHz 525 000 ~112 M ~199 M (37% of the core) a fast M7 next to the control loop; no smaller part

So on a small MCU, observe or stream a handful of properties at a few kHz, or decimate (every_us for observe); the full FOC rate above takes a fast M7, else it is for the simulator and the host (motor demo). A device sampling faster than its CPU can encode needs a floor on the rate it accepts (every_us/sample-rate clamps), since every sample taken is encoded whether or not its batch later fits the budget.

items.title: Observe cells, measured
items.text:
A level on observe cells moves the copy of a row out of the interrupt: the setters store each value into a ring where it is computed, poll_properties copies the waiting rows into a staging batch. Measured on the motor demo's 21 FOC properties (examples_mcu: stm32h725ig-foc-observe-cycles, DWT cycles at 540 MHz with caches on; qemu-foc-observe and qemu-m4f-foc-observe, instructions under QEMU), a host observing all of them in Samples mode, a poll every 16 rows, observe_batch = 32, a ring of 32 rows:

STM32H725, cycles opt-level = "z": sample() z: cells opt-level = 3: sample() 3: cells a row, observed: mean (first, worst) 412 (576, 641) 354 (426, 545) 419 (545, 858) 328 (422, 598) a row, nobody observes 204 300 153 284 a poll that encodes a batch 107-122 k 116-133 k 65-76 k 72-83 k a poll with nothing to send (16 rows waiting) 5.1 k 15.3 k 3.1 k 10.1-10.3 k stack of a row 108 B 44 B 116 B 52 B

On the Cortex-M3 and M4F models a row takes 189 instructions on cells against 250 through sample() at opt-level = "z", 206 against 260 at 3. Both send the same 2 021 bytes for the 64 rows; the level's RAM is the same too (8 656 B either way). The total CPU is about the same, the cells' a bit more: what the interrupt saves, the event loop spends copying the ring (about 440 cycles a row at opt-level = 3 on the H725 with all 21 observed; the poll copies only the observed columns, 4.4 k cycles for 16 rows of 3). The polls are those after API-52, which halved the one that encodes (it was 133-185 k at 3, 349-509 k at "z"), and after SW-68's word-wide bit writer, which took another quarter off (78-107 k at 3, 131-180 k at "z" before it). Without observers the cells' setters still store (the sampler returns before copying): skip them with is_sampling(). Both builds keep the batches in a static built in place (ObserveBatches::init, see Observing).

items.title: The motor demo, measured
items.text:
The motor demo (motor_sim repo) has every Foc property and Control's 13 measured values +observe+batched. Measured through the real generated code (one level observed per session, at its own level budget so budget never throttles what's measured, CodecPolicy::SMALLEST as std uses, batch 32):

foc (21 properties) control (13 measured) today, periodic every sample, ww_si quantities, unbatched 3.73 MB/s 99.0 kB/s batched, Samples mode, n = 32, a time column per property (before API-49) 983 kB/s 25.8 kB/s batched, Samples mode, n = 32, one time column per level (API-49) 812 kB/s 19.0 kB/s gain over unbatched 4.6x 5.2x

(motor_demo observe --foc samples:20ms --control off --telemetry off --budget 100000000, and the same per level, 8 s each; the "before" row from the same tool built on the commit before API-49.) The shared clock saves 17 % on foc and 26 % on control here, less than the 36 % of the DeltaPacked bench in which rates fit: SMALLEST already wrote each property's regular clock as a nearly constant run, so what goes is mostly the per-column overhead and one Series head per property. On no_std, with DeltaPacked, a time column costs about as much as a value column, and sharing it is worth more. One batcher per level also seals the level's properties together: control sends 48 updates/s, one batch per 20 ms max age (its 1 kHz fills 20 rows in that time), where a batcher per property sealed out of step and sent 238.

The flip side: an unbatched ww_si quantity (prefix + storage tag + the integer) is bigger on the wire than a bare f32, and with no series to amortize it across, every value pays that cost alone - a single update of one quantity already costs more than the same f32 would. Quantities only pay off once they're batched into a Series; see Series: integer storage for the general case, and the gain above for what it looks like once they are.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text: Adding or removing batched/batched(untimed) on a stream, or switching between timed and untimed, changes its item type on the wire (one Series<Timed<T>> or Series<T> per event instead of one T) - a break of the API crate, same as any other item-type change; see evolution rules: API. Making a property +batched or not changes its observe slot (a Batched<T> instead of a T): a break too. The times of a level's samples travel in the PropertyUpdate event (sample_times), not in a slot, so adding resources to such a level follows the usual rules. The batch size (N) is the device's own and isn't in the API at all, so changing it is never a break.

items.title: I2C and SPI slave engine
items.text:
A device that implements the slave group of ww_i2c or ww_spi stands in for a chip on another master's bus. What it answers, when a host update takes effect, what happens when the host is too slow and what each event says is fixed by the API; the ww_bus_slave crate does all of it, so a firmware only wires its peripheral's interrupts to it. It is no_std, sans-IO and needs no allocator.

[dependencies]
ww_bus_slave = "0.5"

items.title: Two sides
items.text:
I2cSlave and SpiSlave are plain structs with &mut self methods of two kinds:

  • Interrupt side, called per byte from the peripheral's interrupt handler: an address matched, a byte came, a byte is wanted, a stop; CS edges for SPI.
  • Task side, called from the API handlers: configure when the slave_events / slave_frames stream opens, disable when it closes, map_write / map_read, push_answer for each item of the slave_answers sink (free_answer_slots is how many credits it may give), clear_answers, and peek_event / pop_event / take_dropped to move events into the counted stream.

The firmware decides how the two share the engine, usually a critical-section mutex in a static. new is a const fn, so the engine (map, queue and event ring, a few KB) is built in place in that static and never passes through the stack:

type Slave = ww_bus_slave::I2cSlave<256, 64, 4, 64, 8, 64>;
static SLAVE: Mutex<CriticalSectionRawMutex, RefCell<Slave>> = Mutex::new(RefCell::new(Slave::new()));

The const parameters are the sizes: register map bytes, room for staged host updates (each takes 6 bytes more than its data), answer slots and their length, events and the bytes kept per event. They are what the device reports in I2cSlaveCapabilities / SpiSlaveCapabilities (map_len, queue_len), together with what the peripheral can do (the stretch limit, Nack, 10-bit addresses, the clock).

Times are u32 microseconds of the device clock, wrapping, the unit the events carry.

items.title: I2C
items.text:
Peripheral event Call Address matched (start or repeated start) address(read, now); it says whether to acknowledge Byte written by the master write(byte, now) Master reads a byte read(now): ReadByte::Byte(b) to send, or ReadByte::Stretch Repeated start reported on its own restart(now) Stop stop(now), then wake the task Bus error bus_error(now)

write and read see the direction themselves when a peripheral reports no address match (DW_apb_i2c on the RP2040/RP2350 reports bytes, RD_REQ and STOP_DET): a byte of the other direction ends the transfer going on as a repeated start.

  • Stretching. With I2cSlaveUnderrun::Stretch, read answers Stretch when no answer is queued and records I2cSlaveEvent::ReadWaiting for the task to send at once. The firmware leaves the TX register empty (DW_apb_i2c and STM32 hold SCL low on their own meanwhile), arms a timer for stretch_deadline(), and calls resume(now) when it fires and after each push_answer: it gives the byte to send once the answer is there or the limit passed.
  • Nack. acks_address() says whether the address should be acknowledged now. A peripheral that acknowledges by itself has its slave address enabled by it after configure, push_answer and stop.
  • A TX FIFO loaded ahead. Bytes read gave that the master didn't clock out (it NACKed earlier) are taken back with unsent(n) before stop, so the register pointer and the answer stay where the master left them.
  • Host updates of the map made during a transaction wait for its stop (map_write stages them; Busy when the staging room is full: try again once is_idle()), so a master never reads half of a multi-byte value.

items.title: SPI
items.text:
Peripheral event Call TX FIFO has room (also before CS goes active) miso(): the byte to load CS asserted cs_asserted(now) Byte received mosi(byte) RX FIFO overflowed overrun() CS released cs_released(now), then wake the task

SPI has no clock stretching, so a frame's answer has to be in the TX FIFO before the master clocks: the frame picks its answer at its first miso() call, usually right after the previous CS release. An answer queued after that goes to the next frame; a firmware that can empty its TX FIFO calls rewind() before CS and loads again, and the new answer goes out in this frame.

With the register map, the address arrives on MOSI while MISO already runs: a byte loaded before the address is complete goes out as idle, and the master's dummy bytes (SpiRegisters::dummy_bytes, before read data only) are the time the device has. With a FIFO d bytes deep, dummy_bytes >= d - 1 gives every data byte right; with fewer, the first data bytes come out as idle and the map data starts that many bytes in (the record shows what was sent). Host updates of the map wait for the CS release as on I2C; a Busy map_write is tried again after the next release, which empties the staging room. The engine takes 8-bit words only; configure answers Unsupported for others.

items.title: Cost per byte
items.text:
Instructions per hook call on a Cortex-M3 under QEMU (examples_mcu/mcu_qemu, bin qemu-bus-slave, counted with examples_mcu/qemu_icount), each including the bench loop and call, about 10 instructions:

Case opt-level = 3 opt-level = "z" I2C register map, master writes, per byte 69 66 I2C register map, master reads, per byte 58 59 I2C answer queue, master reads, per byte 76 82 I2C address + one byte + stop 194 218 SPI register map read frame, miso + mosi per byte 96 100 SPI answer queue frame, miso + mosi per byte 85 93 SPI CS asserted + one byte + CS released 232 240

At 150 MHz (RP2350) 100 instructions are under a microsecond: an I2C byte at 1 MHz takes 9 µs, so the engine is far from the limit there; for SPI, a FIFO and the dummy bytes are what keep up with a fast clock, not the per-byte cost alone. Instructions are not cycles: measure on the target for the exact time.

items.title: Counted and reliable streams
items.text:
A counted stream gives every item a position, so the host learns exactly what it missed; a reliable stream also keeps its items in a store on the device until the host acknowledges them, and sends them again after a loss or a reconnect. Both are declared in the API with #[counted] / #[reliable] (see Streams); what they guarantee and how is in Stream delivery. This page shows the device's and the host's code.

#[ww_trait]
trait Adc {
    /// Sample sets at `config.rate`; unit: sample set
    #[stream(SampleBlock<'i>, reliable)]
    fn samples(config: StreamConfig) -> Result<StreamActual, AdcError<'i>>;

    /// Bytes as they arrive on the line; unit: byte
    #[counted]
    stream!(rx: [u8]);
}

items.title: Device side
items.text: Besides the open and close handlers every stream has, a counted or reliable stream needs stream_<name>(), returning its state, and the server one new_stream_session() (see the handler table in Streams).

items.title: Counted streams
items.text:
A counted stream's state is a ww_stream::tx::Counted, usually a field of the server, handed to generated code by stream_<name>(). Generated code opens it (a new session, numbered by new_stream_session()), resumes it, closes it and answers a read on the stream with its StreamStatus. Producers send through it, naming the units of each item and the device time of its first unit, if any:

struct ServerState {
    rx_stream: Counted,
    sessions: u32,
}

impl ServerState {
    async fn rx(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        Ready(())
    }
    async fn close_rx(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) {}
    async fn stream_rx(&mut self) -> &mut Counted {
        &mut self.rx_stream
    }
    /// Put a boot counter into the high bits, so that a cursor from before a reboot never matches a new session.
    fn new_stream_session(&mut self) -> u32 {
        self.sessions = self.sessions.wrapping_add(1);
        self.sessions
    }
}

let ser = server_impl::stream_data_ser();
// sent right away; while no host has the stream open, the units are counted as lost instead
ser.rx_send(&mut state.rx_stream, &chunk, chunk.len() as u64, Some(t), &mut server.sink()).await?;
// the producer's own buffer overflowed: the next event reports it
state.rx_stream.lost(dropped_bytes);

stream_<name>() may return anything that dereferences to the state, e.g. a mutex guard when a producer task shares it. Counted streams work in sync servers too (<name>_send_blocking).

items.title: Reliable streams
items.text:
A reliable stream's state is a ww_stream::tx::Reliable<S> with a store S that keeps every event until the host acknowledges it: RamRing<N> in RAM, PersistentRamRing<N> across a soft reset, or LogStore on an SD card or flash (see Stream stores). Stores are async, so reliable streams need an async server (use_async = true, a compile error otherwise).

Producers push into the store and never wait for the link; the generated poll_streams sends what the stores have, called from the event loop between requests:

struct ServerState {
    samples_stream: Reliable<RamRing<{ 16 * 1024 }>>,
    sessions: u32,
}

impl ServerState {
    async fn stream_samples(&mut self) -> &mut Reliable<RamRing<{ 16 * 1024 }>> {
        &mut self.samples_stream
    }
    // samples(), close_samples() and new_stream_session() as above
}

// producer: `scratch` holds the serialized item on its way into the store
let pushed = server_impl::stream_data_ser()
    .samples_push(&mut state.samples_stream, &block, 256, Some(t), &mut scratch)
    .await?; // Pushed::Lost when the store was full: counted, reported to the host

// event loop
loop {
    if let Either::First(ready) = select(server.wait(), Timer::after_millis(5)).await
        && let Some(event) = server.handle(ready, state).await
        && matches!(event, LinkEvent::Down(_))
    {
        // stop sending, keep the data for the host's resume
        state.samples_stream.detach();
    }
    if server.is_up() {
        let now_ms = Instant::now().as_millis();
        // by priority, live before backlog, up to 2048 bytes of items; `buf` holds the biggest item
        _ = state.poll_streams(&mut server.sink(), now_ms, &mut buf, 2048).await;
    }
}

poll_streams(out, now_ms, buf, budget_bytes) is generated when the API has reliable streams. It also asks a host that went silent where it is, and the host's acknowledgements and resend requests reach the store through the dispatcher. Detaching on LinkEvent::Down is the firmware's job: a detached stream sends nothing and keeps its data for the host's resume.

A reliable stream only stores once it has a session: from the first open by a host, or from boot on when the firmware starts one itself, so that a logger keeps what it records before any host connects:

// at boot, before the event loop
let session = state.new_stream_session();
state.samples_stream.start_session(session).await?;
// or, with a store that survives reboots: continue the session it holds
state.samples_stream.continue_stored_session();

Reliable::new(store).priority(Priority::High) sets the stream's priority against other reliable streams, see Sending: producers, the event loop and priorities. examples_mcu/rp2/src/bin/usb_log.rs is a complete firmware with a reliable log stream.

items.title: Host side: PositionedStream<T>
items.text:
while let Ok(ev) = samples.recv_event().await {
    match ev {
        StreamEvent::Item { pos, units, t, run, value, .. } => { /* run: Live or Backfill */ }
        StreamEvent::Gap { at, units, cause, .. } => { /* cause: Device, Link, Store, Host */ }
        StreamEvent::Resumed { cursor, ended, .. } => { /* ended: the old session, when the device has a new one */ }
        StreamEvent::BackfillDone | StreamEvent::Disconnected | StreamEvent::Closed => {}
    }
}
  • recv() (_blocking, try_) returns values only; gaps are logged and counted in stats() (StreamStats: received, lost by cause, duplicates, late, out of order, resend requests, queued).
  • cursor() is where to resume from: everything before it was received (counted) or acknowledged (reliable). A recorder saves it with its data. session() is the device's session number.
  • .ack_mode(AckMode::Explicit) when opening: a reliable stream's data counts as received only once ack(pos) confirms it, e.g. after writing it to disk, so a crash in between loses nothing. By default (AckMode::OnReceive) it counts when user code takes it.
  • split() gives one handle per run, each in order: a dashboard reads the live one, a recorder both.
  • close(), or dropping the last handle, closes the stream on the device.

The receiver runs in the client's event loop, so a program that doesn't read still answers the device, and its memory stays bounded: a reliable stream holds at most its window (.window(bytes), 4 MiB by default) and the device keeps the rest in its store; a counted stream drops what goes beyond its queue and reports it as Gap { cause: Host }.

items.title: Resuming
items.text:
Counted and reliable streams also get <name>_resume(cursor) and <name>_status():

// after a restart: the backlog from the saved cursor, beside live data
let mut samples = device.samples_resume(saved_cursor).call().await?;
// open or not, session, positions, store use
let status = device.samples_status().read().await?;

A resume continues the session with the arguments it was opened with on the device, so it has no arguments and no result. A cursor of an older session (the device opened the stream again or lost its store) starts with the current session, and Resumed { ended: Some(old) } says so. Across a reconnect of the same program, disconnect().keep_streams() keeps the handles open (they see Disconnected, not the end), and Commander::resume_streams() on the next connection resumes each from its cursor: the same handle goes on with Resumed and whatever the device kept meanwhile.

The dynamic client opens streams with DynResource::positioned_stream (DynPositionedStream, values as ValueOwned), Python with open() on the stream (Python).

items.title: Credit sinks and sideband
items.text: A plain sink (Streams) sends what the host writes and hopes the device keeps up. A credit sink lets the device say how much it can take, and resends what a lossy link lost. Every stream and sink also has a sideband channel next to its data, for open and close and for the API's own signals.

items.title: Credit sinks
items.text:
A sink marked #[credit] gets flow control and acknowledgements built in, for bulk transfers into a device over slow or lossy links: a firmware update plan streamed into a single-bank MCU that stalls on every flash write, bytes for a UART bridge, frames for a CAN transmitter.

#[ww_trait]
trait Updater {
    /// Update plan: steps and data, tens to hundreds of KB, in pieces of up to 1 KiB
    #[credit]
    sink!(plan: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, 1024>);
}

The device grants the host credit in bytes: the bytes of the sink's items, one item being the serialized value of one write, as sent. The host sends an item only when all of it fits into the credit left, and never splits one. Out of credit, send() waits, send_blocking() blocks and try_send() returns Ok(false), so the host never outruns the device's receive buffer, however slow the device or fast the link.

Positions count units, which the host names for each item: one per value by default, the bytes of the payload on a byte sink ([u8], a UART's tx), or what send_units(value, units) says (at least one). So the device's position, its have, means something to user code on both sides: bytes on the line, samples, segments. Credit stays in bytes, positions in units.

The host names the session: every open is a StreamOpen with the host's session and position, a new random one at 0 for open() and the first send(), or one user code picks with open_session(session) (from a hash of the data, say). The device keeps a session it is in: an open of the same session (a repeated or late one, a reconnect) changes nothing and answers where it is; any other starts at 0.

items.title: Why bytes and not values
items.text:
What runs out on a device is RAM: the bytes of its receive buffer. Counting values (one slot per write) would make the device size every slot for the largest value, so a buffer that holds sixteen 1 KiB pieces would also hold only sixteen 20-byte ones. Counting bytes, the same buffer holds as many items as fit, however their sizes vary.

The price is one rule, since items are never split: the device must always be able to grant at least its largest item, or the host could never send it. Three things keep a transfer from getting stuck:

  • The buffer holds the largest item. The generated <SINK>_MAX_ITEM_BYTES: Option<u32> on the level's stream serializer (also stream_data_ser().<sink>_max_item_bytes(), a const fn) is the largest item, from the type's MAX_SIZE: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, N> gives N (bytes are sent as is), a type without an upper bound ([u8]) None. SinkCredit::sized_for(buffer_bytes, max_item) checks it, a compile error in a const; try_sized_for() returns an error for a size known at runtime. For an unbounded type the host checks: a value bigger than the device's buffer (the first credit of a session) fails send() with StreamError::ItemTooBig instead of waiting forever.
  • A re-grant lets the largest item in. The device re-grants once it freed threshold bytes (half the buffer by default); sized_for caps the threshold at buffer - largest item + 1, so a host waiting for room for a big item always gets it with the next grant. With an unbounded type, set the threshold that way yourself (with_threshold), or a waiting host only learns of the room from its next Query.
  • The device consumes without waiting for more. A device that collects data before writing it out (a flash page) has to write it once less room than the largest item is left: the host can't send the next item before that.

At the other end, a buffer is at most 64 MiB (ww_stream::sink::MAX_WINDOW): sized_for doesn't compile with a larger one, try_sized_for and set_capacity return SinkCreditError::BufferTooLarge. That keeps positions on the wire short and unambiguous (positions wrap at 256 MiB); a session itself has no size limit. The host also keeps at most MAX_WINDOW units in flight, and refuses an item of more.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
Generated server code does the bookkeeping; user code says how many bytes it can buffer and when it frees some. A credit sink has one more handler, credit_<name>(), returning its state, a ww_stream::sink::SinkCredit (so the firmware crate depends on ww_stream), usually a field of the server (arrays of sinks get the index chain and need one state per index):

const BUF: usize = 4096;
/// Some(1024), from the API's MaxLen bound
const LARGEST: Option<u32> = server_impl::stream_data_ser().plan_max_item_bytes();
/// a buffer smaller than the largest item would not compile
const PLAN_CREDIT: SinkCredit = SinkCredit::sized_for(BUF as u32, LARGEST);

struct Server {
    plan_credit: SinkCredit, // PLAN_CREDIT, re-granted every BUF / 2 bytes freed
    plan_buf: heapless::Vec<u8, BUF>,
}

impl Server {
    fn credit_plan(&mut self) -> &mut SinkCredit {
        &mut self.plan_credit
    }

    fn write_plan(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, data: &TailBytes<'_>) {
        // only called for writes in order, never more bytes than the credit granted
        self.plan_buf.extend_from_slice(data.0).unwrap();
        // the next item might not fit: write out now, the host can't send more before that
        if self.plan_buf.len() > BUF - LARGEST.unwrap() as usize {
            flash_write(&self.plan_buf); // stalls for a while
            self.plan_credit.free(self.plan_buf.len() as u32);
            self.plan_buf.clear();
        }
    }

    fn sideband_plan(
        &mut self,
        _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
        _sideband: StreamSideband,
    ) -> Option<StreamSideband> {
        None
    }
}

A handler of a typed sink gets the value, not its bytes: SinkCredit::last_item_len() is the size of the item it was called with, what to free() once that value is consumed; last_item_units() its units as the host named them.

  • On StreamOpen, generated code calls SinkCredit::open(cursor) (the host's session: kept if it is the one the device is in, else a new one at 0); for a new session it calls sideband_<name> with Open first, so user code sees where one logical write starts (it may change the capacity there; a resume of the same session doesn't call it). Then it answers with StreamOpened (where the device is, its buffer) and sends an Ack with the grant. An open without the host's session is refused.
  • On a write (SinkWrite, SinkWriteUnits), generated code checks its position, calls write_<name> for writes in order only, and after it returns sends an Ack with new credit if free() moved the limit far enough. A write after a lost one asks for a Resend (once per gap); a write while the device has no session (it rebooted, or the host closed) answers Close once, and the host opens its session again.
  • Query is answered by generated code, sideband_<name> doesn't see it; Close ends the session (SinkCredit::close()), then goes to sideband_<name> like any other sideband (it may free what is left there).
  • A read on the sink (<name>_status() on the host) returns its StreamStatus: open or not, the session, the position, bytes buffered and the capacity.
  • Data freed outside a handler (e.g. after a flash write in the event loop): if let Some(sb) = state.plan_credit.take_ack(), send it with stream_data_ser().plan_sideband_send_blocking(sb, out) (plan_sideband_send in an async server). If that is skipped, the host's next Query picks it up after its query interval.
  • SinkCredit::overruns() counts bytes the host sent beyond its credit (should stay 0; such writes still reach the handler).

items.title: Host side
items.text:
Sink<T> of a credit sink works like any other: send() opens a session if needed and waits for credit. Besides:

  • open() starts a new session and returns once the device answered; open_session(session) the same with the session named by user code.
  • send_units(value, units) (_blocking, try_send_units) sends a value that takes units positions; send_bytes() on a byte sink counts its bytes.
  • flush() / flush_blocking() / try_flush() waits until the device accepted everything sent so far, resending what was lost; close() flushes first, then sends Close.
  • credit_progress() returns (accepted, sent) units of the session (u64, a session has no size limit), e.g. for a progress bar.
  • A device that lost the session (it answers an open behind what it had acknowledged, after a reboot) fails the call with StreamError::SinkSessionLost { device_at, acked }: what was sent from device_at on is gone, user code decides what to do (a DFU plan starts over); the next value opens a new session. A link that went down without keep_streams fails the call with UnexpectedEvent(Disconnected) and ends the session on the host; to go on after a reconnect or a restart, see Resume.
  • set_credit_config(CreditConfig { query_interval, stall_timeout }) tunes it to the link: query_interval (1 s by default) longer than the link's round trip, stall_timeout (30 s by default) longer than the device's worst stall (a flash sector erase takes 1-2 s); with no progress for that long, send() fails with a timeout.

items.title: Resume
items.text:
A credit sink's session lives on the device until another session is opened (or the device reboots), so a transfer goes on after the link or the host program went away, from where the device is: nothing the device took is sent again, nothing is lost.

After a reconnect, with the program still running: disconnect with disconnect().keep_streams(), and connect again with Commander::reconnect() (the same transport and device selection, the same handles), which calls Commander::resume_streams() (it also resumes counted and reliable streams and observers). That registers every sink on the new connection and opens a credit sink's session again; the sink sends what the device didn't acknowledge, from the device's position, and goes on. While the link is down, send() and flush() wait for the resume (try_send() returns false); resume_streams() counts each session that goes on.

let mut tx = client.uart_tx().await?;
tx.send_bytes(&line).await?;
// .. the link goes
cmd.disconnect().keep_streams().await?;
// .. the device is back
cmd.reconnect().await?;
tx.send_bytes(&next_line).await?; // the device gets the rest of `line`, then `next_line`

After a restart of the host program, the program saves the sink's cursor with its own progress: Sink::cursor() is the session and the position up to which the device accepted everything. The new program continues with <sink>_resume(cursor) (Sink::resume(cursor) on a sink it has, _blocking variants), which returns the sink and the position where the device is: at or after the saved one, since the device may have accepted more before the old program went. User code continues its own data there, the byte at that offset on a byte sink:

// old program: from time to time, with what it sent
save(tx.cursor(), &state)?;
// new program
let (mut tx, at) = client.uart_tx_resume(saved_cursor).await?;
tx.send_bytes(&data[at as usize..]).await?;

A device that lost the session (it rebooted while the host was away) answers the open at 0: resume() and, after a reconnect, the sink's next call fail with StreamError::SinkSessionLost { device_at, acked }, and resume_streams() doesn't count the sink. What the device had is gone; user code decides (a DFU plan starts over with open(), see ww_dfu).

A resume opens the same session (StreamOpen with the cursor), so a device's sideband_<name> doesn't see an Open: for user code on the device, the logical write goes on. A late duplicate of an open (UDP) answers where the device is and changes nothing. What can't be told apart is described in ww_stream::sink.

The dynamic client and Python speak the same protocol for credit sinks (Python: sink.cursor, sink.resume(cursor), ww.SessionLost). How the credit is exchanged, and how writes lost on UDP are found and resent: Stream protocol.

items.title: Sideband
items.text:
Next to its data, every stream and sink has a sideband channel in both directions, StreamSideband values sent in order with the data. Generated code uses it for the protocol, user code may use the rest:

Sideband Used for Close the host closes a stream or sink (close_<name> on a stream, sideband_<name> on a sink); the device ends a stream Open the host opens a plain sink; a credit sink's handler gets it when a StreamOpen starts a new session FrameSync, SizeHint(n), User(n) free for the API's own meaning: frame boundaries in a byte stream, the size of what follows, application events Ack, Resend, Query counted and reliable streams and credit sinks, handled by generated code

From the host, plain streams and sinks pass a sideband to the device's sideband_<name>(cx, sideband): returning Some(sideband) sends it back as a sideband event on the same stream, None only acknowledges the request. Either way the host's request gets its answer. Counted and reliable streams take only Close and the protocol messages, other sideband is refused.

// host
stream.sideband(StreamSideband::User(UNib32(5))).await?;
match stream.recv_any().await? {
    TypedStreamEvent::Sideband(StreamSideband::User(n)) => { /* .. */ }
    _ => {}
}
// device
fn sideband_uart_rx(
    &mut self,
    _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
    sideband: StreamSideband,
) -> Option<StreamSideband> {
    Some(sideband) // echo
}

The device sends sideband events on its own with stream_data_ser().<name>_sideband_send(sideband, out) (_sideband_send_blocking, <name>_sideband(sideband, scratch)), for streams and sinks alike; a Close this way ends a stream on the host (recv_all_bytes() returns, a PositionedStream sees Closed):

// e.g. tell the host a sink's buffer is full
server_impl::stream_data_ser().uart_tx_sideband_send(StreamSideband::User(UNib32(1)), cx).await?;

On the host, a Stream returns sideband events from recv_any(), a Sink from recv_sideband() (_blocking, try_recv_sideband()); credit events of a credit sink are used up internally.

items.title: ECC-safe flash for stores
items.text: Stores in the MCU's own flash (settings, logs, a sequential-storage map) are written for power cuts: a record cut in the middle fails its CRC and is skipped, a half-erased page is erased again. On STM32 parts with flash ECC there is one more outcome of a power cut, and it stops a device from booting unless the flash driver handles it.

items.title: The problem
items.text:
Flash with ECC stores a few check bits next to every flash word: 8 bytes on STM32G0/G4/L4, 32 bytes on STM32H74x/H75x/H72x/H73x (16 on H7A3/B0). A power cut while a word is programmed, or while its page is erased, can leave data and check bits that don't match: an uncorrectable ECC error. Reading that word doesn't return data:

Family What a read of a broken word does Default outcome STM32G0 NMI with FLASH_ECCR.ECCD (bank 2: FLASH_ECCR2) set the default NMI handler hangs, a watchdog reset reads the same word again: boot loop STM32H7 bus error, FLASH_SR.DBECCERR set HardFault, same boot loop

embassy-stm32's flash read is a plain memcpy, and sequential-storage passes a read error up as Error::Storage without skipping or repairing anything. One cut write, and the device never gets past loading its settings.

items.title: EccSafeFlash
items.text:
ww_ecc_flash (crate in the mcu/ workspace) wraps any embedded-storage NorFlash, e.g. embassy-stm32's Flash<'_, Blocking>, and reads the flash itself, one ECC word at a time. A word that fails its ECC check reads as zeros. Stores already handle a word of zeros, because it is what they see after other cut writes:

  • an item header of zeros fails its CRC and is skipped word by word;
  • item data of zeros fails the item's CRC, the item is skipped;
  • a page marker of zeros counts as written, a legal outcome of a cut marker write.

Writes and erases go to the wrapped flash unchanged. EccSafeFlash implements the blocking (embedded-storage) and the async (embedded-storage-async) NorFlash traits, so it fits sequential-storage directly. It never implements MultiwriteNorFlash: programming a word twice is not allowed with ECC.

use embassy_stm32::flash::{FLASH_BASE, Flash};
use ww_ecc_flash::EccSafeFlash;

let flash = Flash::new_blocking(p.FLASH);
// SAFETY: offsets of embassy's `Flash` start at FLASH_BASE
let flash = unsafe { EccSafeFlash::new(flash, FLASH_BASE as u32) };
let mut map = MapStorage::<u8, _, _>::new(flash, const { MapConfig::new(0x7_0000..0x7_2000) }, Cache::new_uncached());

ww_ecc_flash::ecc_errors() counts the words read as zeros since boot, worth reporting in device diagnostics.

items.title: STM32G0: the NMI handler
items.text:
Enable feature stm32g0. The NMI handler has to give ww_ecc_flash the first look:

#[cortex_m_rt::exception]
unsafe fn NonMaskableInt() {
    if ww_ecc_flash::on_nmi() {
        return; // a word read through EccSafeFlash failed its ECC check, it reads as zeros
    }
    // any other NMI: the application's own handling
}

Or enable feature nmi-handler (implies stm32g0), which defines this handler and panics on any other NMI. on_nmi() only takes an ECC error at the address EccSafeFlash is reading at that moment (it compares the ADDR_ECC field with it); an ECC error in code, constants or another driver's read is left to the application.

items.title: STM32H7: no handler
items.text: Enable feature stm32h7. Each flash word is read with all exceptions masked (FAULTMASK) and SCB.CCR.BFHFNMIGN set, so the bus error is ignored; then DBECCERR of the word's bank is checked and cleared. With the D-cache on, the cache lines of the word are invalidated before the read. Keep the store region non-cacheable anyway (MPU): a bus error on a cache linefill may be reported imprecisely, and an imprecise bus error is not ignored.

items.title: Tested so far
items.text:
• STM32G0B1 (Donguru B153A), examples_mcu/ecc_flash_g0b1: a sequential-storage map on EccSafeFlash in bank 2, reset by SysTick at a random time while it stores, 3000 boots: every committed value loads, nothing corrupt.
  • What a reset does to a flash operation on G0 (src/bin/reset_cut.rs there): a system reset waits for it. Erases cut 1-20 ms into their ~22 ms still leave the page fully erased, programs stop between double words. So a reset never produces an ECC error on G0: only a real power cut does, and the zeros path is still to be run on hardware with one (TEST-21 in Features).
  • STM32H7: built, not run on hardware.

items.title: Running the hardware test
items.text:
The test runs on any STM32G0B1 board (it uses no pins). With probe-rs and the board's probe:

cd examples_mcu/ecc_flash_g0b1
PROBE_RS_PROBE=1366:0105 cargo run --release                 # the store test, ends with "TEST-21 PASSED"
PROBE_RS_PROBE=1366:0105 cargo run --release --bin reset_cut  # what a reset leaves of a program / erase

It erases and writes flash at 0x0807_0000..0x0807_2000 and 0x0807_4000..0x0807_4800, and replaces the firmware.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
A call to a device can fail in three different ways, and WireWeaver keeps them apart all the way to your code:

  • The device said no. The method ran and returned its own error: an I2C address wasn't acknowledged, a pin is in use. This is the E of a method returning Result<T, E>, a normal ShrinkWrap value.
  • The device can't do this at all. There is no implementation: the handler answered Unimplemented, or the device left an optional item out.
  • The call didn't go through. The link dropped, the request timed out, the device was disconnected.

This page explains how to declare errors in an API, how a device returns them, what a client gets, and how errors stay readable when the device and the host are built from different versions.

items.title: Declaring errors in an API
items.text:
A method that can fail returns Result<T, E>, where E is the error enum of its crate:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2c {
    /// Writes `data` to the device at `addr`.
    #[errors(Common, Nack, Arbitration, Timeout, BufferTooBig)]
    fn i2c_write(addr: u8, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_WRITE_LEN>) -> Result<(), I2cError<'i>>;
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone), display, ww_repr = unib32)]
pub enum I2cError<'i> {
    #[common]
    Common(CommonError<'i>),
    /// The address or a data byte was not acknowledged.
    Nack,
    /// Arbitration lost to another master.
    Arbitration,
    /// The bus stayed busy longer than the timeout.
    Timeout,
    /// The transfer is longer than the device can buffer ({max} bytes).
    BufferTooBig { max: u16 },
}

Use one error enum per crate (or per group of traits, when a crate's traits really fail for unrelated reasons). The same type is used on the wire, in the device's handlers and in the client, so device code can share helpers and ? them anywhere, and a driver crate converts it into its own error with a single #[from].

items.title: Which errors a method returns
items.text:
#[errors(..)] lists the variants a method can actually return. For a variant holding one enum, such as Common(CommonError), the entry names the variants of that one: Common(InUse, Refused); Common alone means any CommonError. The list is checked when the trait is parsed, so an unknown or repeated name is a compile error on that name.

The list doesn't change the type or the wire; it goes into the API model, and from there:

  • into the docs, as an # Errors section with each variant's doc line, both in the generated client and on the trait's rustdoc;
  • into introspection, so ww api tree and Python's help() show it;
  • into the evolution checker: a changed list is reported as a compatible change;
  • into a check on the client: when a device returns a variant outside the method's list, the generated and the dynamic client log a tracing warning, so a device that doesn't keep its contract is noticed early. wire_weaver_client::set_strict_error_lists(true) makes it a panic instead; the test harness (tests_common) turns that on.

A method without #[errors] may return any variant of its error enum.

Stream functions and properties take the same list, with the same outputs. On a stream function (#[stream(..)] fn, API-31) it is about the Err of its Result, which opening the stream answers; the client checks the open's result. Above a property! with an error type (property!(rw mode: Mode, ModeError)) it is about that type: a property has one error type for reading and writing, so one list covers both. The generated client checks writes (its reads return the error as raw bytes), the dynamic client reads and writes.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2cMonitor {
    #[errors(Common(InUse, Unsupported))]
    #[stream(I2cRecord<'i>, counted)]
    fn records(io_level: Option<Volt>) -> Result<(), I2cError<'i>>;

    #[errors(Common(Unsupported, Busy))]
    property!(rw speed_hz: u32, I2cError<'i>);
}

ww_error walks through the Common(..) nesting and real examples from ww_stdlib.

items.title: Messages from doc comments
items.text: With the display directive, the derive writes Display and std::error::Error (core::error::Error on no_std) from the first doc line of each variant, filling in {field} placeholders: BufferTooBig { max: 64 } reads "The transfer is longer than the device can buffer (64 bytes)": the trailing period of the doc line is left out, as Rust error messages go. Use #[display("...")] on a variant when the message should differ from its doc. On a device the code is unused and the linker drops it; hosts need no hand-written Display for any API error.

items.title: Common errors
items.text:
Some situations come up in almost every crate: the device doesn't support a mode, a resource is in use by something else, the device is busy. These are ww_error::CommonError (also in wire_weaver::prelude), nested as the first variant of a crate's error enum and marked #[common]:

Variant Meaning Unsupported the device knows this call but can't do what was asked (a mode, a range, a feature) InvalidArgument { arg, reason } argument number arg is invalid InUse { by } the resource is in use, by names the user Busy busy with another operation, try again later WrongState { reason } not possible in the current state NoPower { rail } the rail the operation needs has no power Refused { reason } refused, e.g. by a safety rule Timeout timed out Fault { code } a hardware fault

Strings are bounded and may be empty, so a device short on flash sends "".

On the device, #[common] gives the crate error a From<CommonError>, so a helper returning CommonError can be ?-ed into any crate's error:

fn check_level(&self) -> Result<(), CommonError<'static>> {
    if self.io_level.is_none() {
        return Err(CommonError::NoPower { rail: MaxLen::new_unchecked("VIO") });
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn write(&mut self, addr: u8, data: &[u8]) -> Result<(), I2cError<'static>> {
    self.check_level()?; // CommonError becomes I2cError::Common
    // ...
    Ok(())
}

async fn i2c_write(
    &mut self,
    _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>,
    addr: u8,
    data: MaxLen<RefVec<'_, u8>, MAX_WRITE_LEN>,
) -> RpcResult<Result<(), I2cError<'_>>> {
    Ready(self.write(addr, data.as_slice()))
}

On the host, e.common() (trait HasCommon, in the prelude) works on any crate's error, for example on call_error.device(), so generic code (a GUI, a _hl crate) handles the common cases without knowing the crate. Tools recognise CommonError by its type in the API model: ww api tree -t marks it, and in Python RemoteError.common holds the variant and its fields next to .value.

Keep a crate-specific variant when a caller should act on exactly that case: Nack for I2C, an UnsupportedSpeed that carries the supported range.

items.title: On the client: one ? per call
items.text:
For a method returning Result<T, E>, call(), blocking_call() and promises return Result<T, CallError<E>>:

pub enum CallError<E> {
    /// The device answered with its error: the `Err(e)` of the method.
    Device(E),
    /// The device has no implementation of this item.
    Unimplemented { resource: String },
    /// The call didn't go through: link, timeout, disconnect or another framework error.
    Client(wire_weaver_client::Error),
}

CallError<E> implements std::error::Error when E does, and its Display is the inner error's, so it fits anyhow and thiserror as is:

// a script
async fn script(dev: &Board) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    dev.i2c().i2c_write(0x50, data).call().await?;
    Ok(())
}

// a driver crate with its own error
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
enum SensorError {
    #[error(transparent)]
    I2c(#[from] CallError<I2cErrorOwned>),
    #[error("unexpected chip id {0:#x}")]
    ChipId(u8),
}

// handling one case: retry while an EEPROM is busy with a page write
loop {
    match dev.i2c().i2c_write(0x50, data.clone()).call().await {
        Err(CallError::Device(I2cErrorOwned::Nack)) => continue,
        other => break other?,
    }
}

Methods without a Result return Result<T, wire_weaver_client::Error>; is_unimplemented() on it answers the same "can the device do this at all" question. Python already flattens all of this: a call returns T or raises.

items.title: Unsupported is not Unimplemented
items.text:
Two answers look alike and mean different things:

  • CommonError::Unsupported comes from code that ran on the device: it knows the call, and this case isn't possible.
  • Unimplemented means there is no code for the item at all: the handler returned RpcResult::Unimplemented (GetResult / SetResult for properties), or the item is an optional one the device left out.

RpcResult, GetResult and SetResult let a handler leave an implementation out without todo!(), or answer later (Deferred), and the framework reports it properly. ww api scaffold generates every handler answering Unimplemented, so a new device builds and answers sensibly before anything is written. On the client this is CallError::Unimplemented, never confused with an error of the device.

items.title: Where on the device an error came from
items.text:
Errors of the framework itself (a path that doesn't exist, arguments that don't decode, an answer that doesn't fit) come back as ww_client_server::Error: an ErrorKind and an err_seq, the number of the site in the generated server that raised it (SRV-22). Together with the firmware build (its build id or git sha) and the request's path, which the host knows, they pinpoint one place. The host prints them as one line:

Remote device returned Unimplemented at item site 2 (handler)
Remote device returned BadPath at level site 40 (no such item)

The numbers are the same in every server, defined in ww_client_server::err_seq:

err_seq Range Sites 0..31 item the steps of a method, property, stream or sink, in step order and the same for every item: 0 request kind not taken, 1 decode, 2 handler (Unimplemented), 3 encode, 4 user error encode, 5 stream store, 6 stream resume, 7 data too long, 8 credit position (firmware before API-34, not reused), 9 deferred method in a multi request 32..35 deferred return <method>_ser_return_event of a deferred method 40..46 level a trait level's dispatch: 40 no such item, 41 item left out, 42 index not valid, 43 index expected, 44 a level doesn't take this request, 45 valid indices too big, 46 answer header too big 48..59 request before or around the path: 48 global trait not found, 49 path too deep, 50..53 multi requests, 54..58 observe requests, 59 introspection u32::MAX generic ww_device couldn't get any answer out of the server

The item kind, the request kind and the error kind tell apart what shares a number: a decode failure of a method's arguments and of a property's value are both 1, one comes with ArgsDesFailed on a call, the other with PropertyDesFailed on a write. Since the same step of every item is the same constant, the firmware's error arms are shared code (Donguru: 1.5 KiB less flash at opt-level = "z" than one number per site, 1.7 KiB at 3). Error::site() sorts a number into its range.

items.title: Devices and hosts of different versions
items.text:
An error enum grows: a later firmware may return a variant an older host has never heard of. Every Unsized enum (the default kind) therefore gets one more variant from the derive, Unknown(u32), which catches any discriminant the reader doesn't know instead of failing to decode the whole reply:

match e {
    CallError::Device(I2cErrorOwned::Nack) => { /* ... */ }
    CallError::Device(I2cErrorOwned::Unknown(n)) => warn!("device error {n} from a newer firmware"),
    // ...
}

The variant takes no number on the wire and isn't part of the API model, so adding it changes neither the bytes nor snapshots. The dynamic decoder and Python show such a value as <unknown N>.

Enum Gets Unknown(u32) Unsized with a free discriminant in its ww_repr yes, automatically final_structure, self_describing, sized only when written by hand every discriminant of the ww_repr already taken no marked no_future_version no, for sets that are complete by nature

When a variant of the enum is already called Unknown, name the catch-all with future_version = Other.

items.title: Optional items
items.text:
Not every device can do everything a trait describes. An API author marks such items #[optional], and a device that lacks them leaves them out at code generation, paying neither a dispatch entry nor a handler:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2c {
    /// Clocks SCL until SDA is released, then a stop.
    #[optional]
    fn i2c_wiggle_clock(count: u8) -> Result<I2cLinesState, I2cError<'i>>;
}

// a device without it
ww_codegen!(board_api::Board for Server, server = true, omit = ["i2c.i2c_wiggle_clock"]);

Called anyway, an omitted item answers Unimplemented, and a client with the device's introspection data fails the call locally, without a round trip. Optional items has the details: groups, omit_if, what clients see, measured code size, and when to make a trait of its own instead.

items.title: Folder structure
items.text:
An API is shared by the device and every host program that talks to it, so it lives in a crate of its own:

  • my_device_api: the API trait and its data types, nothing else. Used by the firmware and the host, so it must build for no_std, with an optional std feature for owned types (see examples/blinky_api).
  • Firmware: depends on the API crate and implements the server. WireWeaver generates the serdes and dispatch code, the firmware writes the handlers (see examples_mcu/).
  • Rust driver (my_device): depends on the API crate with std. WireWeaver generates the client; a hand-written, higher-level driver can sit on top of it (see examples/blinky).
  • Applications: CLIs, GUIs, test benches and scripts depend on the Rust driver. A typed Python package wraps the Rust driver with PyO3 (see examples/blinky_py); for quick scripts without generated code, the Python module and the ww CLI build the API at runtime from what the device sends.

The wire_weaver_template repository has this shape ready to copy.

items.title: The API crate's name and version
items.text:
The name of the API crate (from Cargo.toml) identifies the API worldwide (it goes into ww_version::FullVersion, the generated <ROOT_TRAIT>_FULL_GID constant), so publish it to crates.io for an open-source project, or pick a name unique enough for internal use.

Its version is checked on every connection: a host and a device with compatible versions talk, others are told apart before the first call, and your code can read the device's version to show a proper message when it meets an older or newer firmware. Normal SemVer rules apply, what counts as a breaking change is in the evolution rules. More in Versioning.

items.title: Sync and async handlers
items.text:
A server generated with use_async = true expects every user handler to be an async fn, and with use_async = false every handler to be a plain fn. Most handlers of a device never wait for anything (they read a field, set a pin, answer Unimplemented), and an async fn costs flash even when it never awaits: each call becomes a state of the dispatcher's future. On Donguru (Cortex-M0+), ~115 of ~130 handlers never await; making them plain fns saved 20.2 KiB of flash at opt-level = "z" (282 -> 262 KiB) and 12.6 KiB at 3.

handler_model lists the exceptions, so an async server can have sync handlers (SRV-21):

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        donguru_api :: DonguruApi for super::ServerState,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = true,
        // these await (flash writes, ADC reads, a VBUS cycle), all others are plain `fn`s
        handler_model = "device.settings.*|meter.reading|plug.vbus_cycle=async, _=sync",
    );
}
  • Each pattern is a regex matched against an item's whole dotted path in the API tree (device.settings.vbus_mode for the vbus_mode property of the settings trait under device); the first one that matches decides. . matches the dot between levels too, so device.settings.* takes everything under device.settings.
  • _ is the default for the items no pattern matches. Without _, they follow use_async; without handler_model, every handler does, as before.
  • A pattern can't contain ,, = or whitespace. A pattern that matches no method, property or stream is a compile error (a typo, or an item that was renamed), and so is async in a server with use_async = false.

The model is per item: every handler of an item is the same kind. For a property that is its getter, setter and changed_<name>, for a stream its open handler, close_<name>, sideband_<name> and the stream_<name>() state accessor, for a sink write_<name> and sideband_<name>. valid_indices_<..> and observe_state() are always plain fns.

items.title: What the generated server does with it
items.text:
• The dispatcher calls a sync handler without .await, and poll_properties reads a sync getter without it.
  • A trait level whose items are all sync, down to its leaves, gets a plain fn dispatcher (process_<level>), called without .await from the level above. Some items await on their own whatever their handlers are: a reliable stream (its store is async), a credit sink (it sends credit events), and the root level when it serves introspection.
  • process_request_bytes and poll_properties stay async fn in an async server.

A sync handler in an async server still gets cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut, ..>, but can't await a send on it: a handler that sends events (a deferred answer right away, a stream item) stays async.

items.title: A handler written the other way
items.text:
Every call goes through wire_weaver::handler::sync(..) or wire_weaver::handler::r#async(..), which compile to nothing but check the kind: a handler written as async fn where the model says sync is a compile error, not a future that is dropped without running, and the other way round.

error[E0277]: this handler is `async fn`, but `handler_model` (or `use_async = false`) makes it a plain `fn`
    = note: make the handler a plain `fn`, or list it as `async` in `ww_codegen!(.., handler_model = "..")`

The error points at the ww_codegen! call, and names the handler's output type; debug_to_file shows which call it is.

items.title: Scaffolding
items.text: ww api scaffold <api_crate> --use-async --handler-model "<model>" writes async fn or fn per item to match, and passes the model on to the ww_codegen! call it prints. To change an existing server, set handler_model, then let the compiler list the handlers that are now the wrong kind.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
A method is a call into the device: the host sends the arguments, the device runs a handler and answers with the return value.

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    fn led_on();
    fn set_brightness(value: f32);
    fn temperature() -> f32;
    fn user_type(state: State);
    fn user_ret_type() -> UserType<'i>;
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap]
#[ww_repr(unib32)]
pub enum State {
    Off,
    On,
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap]
#[owned = "std"]
pub struct UserType<'i> {
    a: u8,
    b: RefVec<'i, u8>,
    c: SomeOtherType<'i>
}

Any number of arguments are supported, of any ShrinkWrap type. Arguments evolve like struct fields, e.g. an Option<T> argument can be appended later (see evolution rules). A method that can fail returns Result<T, E>, see Errors.

items.title: Server side
items.text:
Server side is responsible for deserializing requests from clients and dispatching them to user-provided functions. On a high level, this is the process that takes place:

  1. Incoming byte array is deserialized into ww_client_server::Request.
  2. Resource path contained in the Request is used to reach appropriate resource (or BadPath error is sent back).
  3. Depending on the resource kind, appropriate actions are handled (Call, Read, Write, etc.).
  4. User defined request types are deserialized (method arguments, sink data, property set values).
  5. User provided action is called.
  6. User defined types are serialized (method return types, stream data, property get values).
  7. Response is serialized and sent back to client.

Generated code can be of two flavors - async and sync. The only difference is that each user action is await'ed in the async version.

Additionally, there is deferred mode that can be turned on for user-selected methods. It works with both sync and async versions and allows to immediately return from the user handler and send an answer later. For example move_motor(x: f32) -> Result<(), Error> method can take a long time to finish, without deferred, it would block all other API resources.

items.title: async
items.text:
On the server side, this is how generated server code is tied with user provided implementation:

use api::{State, UserType};

struct ServerState {
    // any user data required for the server to function (e.g, peripherals, channels)
}

impl ServerState {
    async fn led_on(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        /* do things */
        Ready(())
    }
    async fn temperature(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<f32> {
        Ready(20.0)
    }
    async fn user_type(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>, state: State) -> RpcResult<()> {
        Ready(())
    }
}

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        api :: MyDevice for super::ServerState,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = true,
    );
}

ww_codegen! implements async fn process_request_bytes(bytes, scratch, out, medium) -> Result<..> on ServerState, which deserializes a request, calls one of the handlers and serializes the reply into scratch. ww api scaffold <api_crate> prints all the handlers a server is expected to implement, with exact signatures.

items.title: sync
items.text: By setting use_async = false, a blocking implementation is generated: handlers are plain fns and take cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>. A sync server also runs on the async ww_device::Server: events sent by its handlers are queued and sent out after it returns (EventWriter::queued()), so they are limited by the event scratch buffer size.

items.title: Handler context
items.text:
Every handler (methods, get_/set_/changed_ of properties, sideband_/write_ of streams) gets cx: &mut wire_weaver::Context as the first argument:

  • cx.seq() - sequence number of the request, 0 if the client does not expect a reply.
  • cx.medium() - the medium the request came from. The type is set with ww_codegen!(.., medium = "crate::Medium") (() by default) and the value with Server::with_medium(..). A device with USB and CAN runs one server per medium, all handling requests with the same server state.
  • cx.reply_to() - medium and seq to answer a deferred call later, None if no reply is expected.
  • cx sends events: stream updates and property updates with the generated stream_data_ser().<name>_send(&value, cx).await (_send_blocking for sync servers), or any event with send_event(). Events sent from a handler go out before its reply.
#[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Medium { Usb, Can }

impl ServerState {
    async fn start_adc(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut, Medium>, rate: u32) -> RpcResult<()> {
        if cx.medium() == Medium::Can {
            self.adc_rate = rate.min(100);
        }
        // first sample right away, the rest from the event loop through server.sink()
        _ = server_impl::stream_data_ser().adc_send(&self.sample(), cx).await;
        Ready(())
    }
}

cx only reaches the medium the request came from. Events for other media are sent from the event loop through their servers' sink().

items.title: deferred
items.text: method_model = "move_motor=deferred, _=immediate" lets a method return Deferred and answer later. The handler keeps cx.reply_to(), and the reply is sent with the generated ServerState::move_motor_send_return(out, seq, output) (_send_return_blocking for sync), where out is another handler's cx or server.sink() of reply_to.medium. A deferred method on a nested level (ww_impl!(plug: Plug)) uses the prefixed name everywhere, like its handler: method_model = "plug_vbus_cycle=deferred, _=immediate" and ServerState::plug_vbus_cycle_send_return(..). On a resource array level the handler gets the index chain, the helper does not need it (seq identifies the call). A deferred call that is never answered times out on the client.

items.title: Handler names
items.text: To avoid shared data structures and allocation on no_std, all API levels are flattened into one: every handler is a method of the one server struct, and handlers of nested traits carry the trait item chain as a prefix (ww_impl!(plug: Plug) with fn vbus_cycle() is plug_vbus_cycle). Items in arrays get their index chain after cx, see Arrays.

items.title: Client side
items.text:
client = "..." in ww_codegen! generates a client struct with one function per method. It returns a PreparedCall, which is executed with call().await, blocking_call(), call_forget() (no reply) or call_promise(marker) (polled from immediate mode UI code).

A method without Result gives Result<T, wire_weaver_client::Error>. A method returning Result<T, E> gives Result<T, CallError<E>>, so one ? is enough:

pub enum CallError<E> {
    /// The device answered with its error: the `Err(e)` of the method.
    Device(E),
    /// The device has no implementation: its handler returned `Unimplemented`, or the device's API doesn't have
    /// the method (known locally from introspection, no round trip).
    Unimplemented { resource: String },
    /// The call didn't go through: link, timeout, disconnect, another framework error.
    Client(wire_weaver_client::Error),
}

// trait: fn move_motor(x: f32) -> Result<(), MotorError>;
client.move_motor(1.0).call().await?; // with anyhow, or a thiserror enum with #[from] CallError<MotorError>

match client.move_motor(1.0).call().await {
    Ok(()) => {}
    Err(CallError::Device(MotorError::EndStop)) => { /* the device said no */ }
    Err(CallError::Unimplemented { .. }) => { /* this device can't move motors */ }
    Err(e) => return Err(e.into()), // CallError::Client: link, timeout, ...
}

Display and source() of CallError are the inner error's, and it is std::error::Error when E is. Methods without Result tell an unimplemented method apart with wire_weaver_client::Error::is_unimplemented(). A property with a user error type (property!(rw mode: u8, ModeError)) gives the same CallError<ModeError> from write(). See Errors for declaring errors, common errors and errors of newer firmware.

items.title: Several calls in one request
items.text: Several methods can be called in one request/response pair, each answered on its own: (client.inc(), client.dec()).multi_call().await, or the same method across a whole array with call_array(..). This is shared machinery with properties and reads/writes - see Multi requests for the full picture (the server's multi_req = true option, MultiIndex, the generated/array/dynamic-client APIs, errors and limits).

items.title: Error lists
items.text:
#[errors(..)] on a method names the variants of its error enum it returns (API-32), Common(InUse, Refused) the variants of the enum a Common(CommonError) variant holds, Common all of them:

#[ww_trait]
trait Sensor {
    /// Reads one sample.
    #[errors(Common(Busy, InUse), Nack)]
    fn read() -> Result<u16, SensorError<'i>>;
}
