The list is checked when the trait is parsed (an unknown or repeated name is a compile error on that name), goes into the API model and from there into the generated client's docs (# Errors, each entry with its variant's doc line), ww api tree, Python's help() and ww api check (a changed list is a compatible change). The device and the wire don't see it: a device may still return any variant, the client logs a tracing warning when one is outside the list, and tests_common makes that a test failure (wire_weaver_client::set_strict_error_lists). Without #[errors] a method may return every variant. Stream functions and properties take the same list. More in Errors.

items.title: Multi requests
items.text: A multi request (CLT-15) answers several resources in one request/response pair instead of one round trip per resource: several different properties or methods at the same level, or the same property/method across a whole array. Each index is answered on its own, so one bad index never fails the others. Use them to cut round trips on a slow or high-latency link - reading a dashboard's worth of properties, writing several settings at once, backing up or restoring a whole array - not for a single resource, where a plain read/write/call is simpler and already one round trip.

items.title: Server side: multi_req = true
items.text:
A server only answers MultiRead, MultiCall and MultiWrite when it opts in:

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        my_device_api :: MyDevice for super::Server,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = false,
        multi_req = true,
    );
}

Without it, a server refuses the request. With it, the dispatcher gets one more arm that treats every index of MultiCall/MultiRead/MultiWrite as a Call/Read/Write of its own: an index that fails is answered with an error in its own slot and the rest go on, the request never panics on malformed input (an unknown path, a mode the server doesn't support, a path at the depth limit), and it is answered with EventKind::Value holding an EitherAnyVec of Either<Error, value>, one per index, in index order.

Cost. This is not free: every handler whose reply can end up inside a multi response gets an extra branch in its serialization path (write the value directly, or into the shared EitherAnyVec, decided at runtime by one bool), on top of the multi dispatcher itself. Flash use grows with the number of resources the server has, not just once for the feature - multi_req = true is an opt-in for this reason, not the default.

items.title: MultiIndex: which resources
items.text:
multi_idx: MultiIndex<'i> names the indices at the one path element where they diverge (see split_common on the client side for how that element is found):

Variant Meaning List(indices) exactly these indices, answered in the given order Range(a..b) a..b, ascending; a >= b is an empty list, not an error Mask32(bits) bit i set selects index i, so up to 32 indices in one request

in_each_array_id: Option<UNib32> is one more path element, the same for every index, right after the varying one - e.g. pin[] selected by multi_idx, then set_level inside each selected pin. The request's own path is the common prefix shared by every index (everything before the varying element).

items.title: The reply: an EitherAnyVec of results
items.text: The answer is shrink_wrap::either_any_vec::EitherAnyVec (SW-10), read with EitherAnyVecIter: the type of each slot (the error type, and the index's own value type) is known to both sides from the API model, not stored, and the element count is implied by multi_idx.len() rather than written - EitherAnyVec only stores one bit per element (whether it is Left/error or Right/value) plus the bytes of whatever each element actually is, packed with no padding between elements. It is the same low-level machinery OptionAnyVec is built on (sparse structs use that one), but for a vec where every slot is present and holds one of two types instead of an optional value of one type.

items.title: A byte-level example
items.text:
Three indices answered as Either<SimpleError, _>: the first fails (SimpleError::BadIndex), the second is a u8 (7), the third a u16 (0x1234) - the shape of a MultiRead reply where one index is out of range:

use either::Either;
use shrink_wrap::either_any_vec::EitherAnyVecWriter;
use shrink_wrap::prelude::*;

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u8)]
enum SimpleError {
    BadIndex,
}

let mut buf = [0u8; 16];
let mut wr = EitherAnyVecWriter::new(&mut buf).unwrap();
wr.write::<SimpleError, ()>(Either::Left(SimpleError::BadIndex)).unwrap();
wr.write::<SimpleError, u8>(Either::Right(7)).unwrap();
wr.write::<SimpleError, u16>(Either::Right(0x1234)).unwrap();
let bytes = wr.finish_and_take().unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, [0x60, 0x00, 0x07, 0x34, 0x12, 0x01]);

60: the L/R flag byte, one bit per element MSB-first (011 then padding - Left, Right, Right); 00 the BadIndex discriminant; 07 the u8; 34 12 the u16 (little-endian); the trailing 01 is the length (in bytes) of the one value that is Unsized (SimpleError, since it wasn't marked sized) - EitherAnyVec stores unsized elements' lengths in reverse order at the back, as OptionAnyVec does.

items.title: Several resources at the same level
items.text:
MultiRead<Out>, MultiCall<Out> and MultiWrite<Out> (wire_weaver_client::MultiRead/MultiCall/MultiWrite) are implemented for tuples of 2 to 8 of the generated PreparedRead/PreparedCall/PreparedWrite builders, at any depth - any resources that share a common path prefix and diverge at exactly one element, optionally followed by one more shared element (e.g. the same property across two array elements):

// N > 2, any depth, not just a root 2-tuple
let (x, y, mode) = (client.read_x(), client.read_y(), client.read_mode())
    .multi_read()
    .await
    .unwrap();

let (wx, wy, wcustom) = (
    client.write_x(1),
    client.write_y(2),
    client.write_custom(custom),
)
    .multi_write()
    .await
    .unwrap();
wx.unwrap();
wy.unwrap();
wcustom.unwrap();

Each item comes back as Result<T, ErrorOwned> in the same order the tuple was given. MultiArgs::Same/ Different - whether every index gets the same serialized argument/value or its own - is chosen automatically by comparing the serialized bytes of each item.

items.title: The same resource across a whole array
items.text:
read_array/call_array/write_array (+ _blocking, wire_weaver_client::multi) take a MultiIndexOwned selector and the existing generated per-index accessor as a closure, called once per index locally (no network traffic) just to find the common path:

use wire_weaver_client::multi::{read_array, write_array};
use ww_client_server::MultiIndexOwned;

// write different: one value per channel, in list order
let r = write_array(
    MultiIndexOwned::List(vec![UNib32(0), UNib32(1), UNib32(2), UNib32(3)]),
    |i| client.ch(i).write_level((i as u8 + 1) * 10),
)
.await
.unwrap();

// read range: same order back
let r = read_array(MultiIndexOwned::Range(UNib32(0)..UNib32(4)), |i| {
    client.ch(i).read_level()
})
.await
.unwrap();

A method with a custom #[errors(..)] result (CallError<E>) can't go into a tuple multi_call or call_array; call it on its own instead - see Errors.

items.title: The dynamic client
items.text:
DynResource::multi_read/multi_write/multi_call are the same three operations without generated code: child names the resource inside the array's trait (None for an array of a flat property/method, e.g. property!(led[]: bool)), and DynMultiArgs/DynMultiValue give Same (one value/argument list for every index) or Different (one per index, in multi_idx order):

let channel = root.child("channel").unwrap();
channel
    .multi_write(
        cmd,
        MultiIndexOwned::List(vec![UNib32(0), UNib32(1), UNib32(2)]),
        Some("gain"),
        DynMultiValue::Different(&[num(N::F32(0.1)), num(N::F32(0.2)), num(N::F32(0.3))]),
    )
    .await
    .unwrap();

items.title: Errors per index, and for the whole request
items.text:
Most problems land on the one index they belong to and leave the rest answered: an unknown path or index (BadIndex, BadPath), a property or method the device left out (Unimplemented), one entry of MultiArgs::Different that doesn't deserialize (ArgsDesFailed), a write whose value doesn't fit its property (PropertyDesFailed). A deferred method called inside a multi request answers OperationNotSupported in its slot instead of running (see Limits) - the rest of the request still goes through.

The whole request fails instead (no EitherAnyVec at all) only for something that isn't about one index: the path is deeper than the depth limit (BadPath), MultiArgs::Different/MultiArgs::Different itself doesn't deserialize as a list (ArgsDesFailed), or the answer doesn't fit the reply buffer (ResponseSerFailed) - which is also why a huge Range (e.g. 0..u32::MAX) fails outright rather than running for billions of indices.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• Depth: the request's own path plus the varying element plus an optional in_each_array_id must stay within MAX_DEPTH (16, hardcoded - API-12 would calculate it per API instead); a path one level over fails the whole request with BadPath.
  • Deferred methods are refused with OperationNotSupported inside a multi request, even one that defers although its method_model says immediate (deferred methods need a reply tied to one request's seq, which a shared multi-request slot can't carry).
  • A method with a custom error result (#[errors(..)], CallError<E>) can't go into a tuple multi_call on the client - call it on its own.
  • A trait level itself (not a leaf resource) inside a multi request answers OperationNotSupported, as does a server without multi_req = true for any multi request at all.

items.title: Observing properties
items.text: Observing (API-38) is how a host gets a device's fast-changing values without polling: it asks once, and the device sends updates on its own, at the rates the host picked, within a byte budget.

items.title: The concept
items.text:
The unit is a trait level - the root API, or one ww_impl! trait - not a single property. A host observes a whole level with one Observe request (RequestKind::Observe, ww_client_server::observe), picking a mode per +observe property, and from then on the device sends one EventKind::PropertyUpdate per level whenever anything in it is due, carrying whatever subset of its properties is actually due this time - not every observed property every time. That update is a sparse struct (OptionAnyVec): a presence header up front, then only the present values, so a property that isn't due this time costs roughly one bit, not a byte, let alone its own message. This is what makes observing cheaper than one StreamData event per value - see cost vs StreamData below.

#[ww_trait]
trait Motor {
    property!(ro+observe speed: f32);
    property!(ro+observe current: f32);
    property!(rw+observe mode: u8);
    property!(rw gain: f32); // not observable
}

Only properties declared ro+observe/rw+observe can be observed; see Properties for declaring them and the two ways a server can implement a property (get_set/value_on_changed), which also decide how its observed value is read.

items.title: Modes
items.text:
Per property, one of:

Mode Sent Off never OnChange { min_us } on a change, at most once every min_us Periodic { every_us } every every_us, on a fixed grid, changed or not OnChangeOrBeat { min_us, max_us } on a change (at most every min_us), and at least every max_us even without one Samples { every_us, max_age_us } every sample the device takes (or the first in each every_us), in batches at most max_age_us old; +batched properties only, see Every sample

A property that starts being observed is always sent once right away, so the host has a value to start from. Periods and min/max are in microseconds (UNib32), evolvable: a mode a device doesn't know (sent by a newer host) reads as Unknown(_) and is refused for that entry rather than guessed at.

items.title: Budget
items.text:
Each level gets a budget in bytes per second, granted by the device (a host may ask for one, or leave it to the device); all levels together are capped at ObserveLimits::total_budget - properties' share of the link, next to reserved streams (stream stores/reliable streams get what's left per turn). What the device grants and clamps:

  • a period or min/max below ObserveLimits::min_period_us is raised to it;
  • a level's budget is clamped to ObserveLimits::max_level_budget, and to what's left of total_budget;
  • an Observe request is validated entry by entry before anything changes: an unknown index, a property without +observe, a duplicate index or an unknown mode is refused on its own and listed in the answer (ObserveGranted::refused), the rest of the request still applies. A request that doesn't decode, or lists more than 16 refused entries, fails outright (ArgsDesFailed/BadIndex) and changes nothing; an answer that doesn't fit the reply buffer fails with ResponseSerFailed, also undone.

items.title: The device side
items.text:
Three things the user adds, for an API with any +observe properties: an ObserveState field, handed out by observe_state(), a poll_properties call in the event loop, and mark_changed_<name>() where the device changes a value by itself (a value_on_changed write calls it automatically). ww api scaffold prints the field and observe_state().

struct Server {
    observe: api_impl::ObserveState,
    // ..
}

impl Server {
    fn observe_state(&mut self) -> &mut api_impl::ObserveState {
        &mut self.observe
    }

    fn on_new_measurement(&mut self, current: f32) {
        self.current = current;
        self.mark_changed_current(); // sent to hosts observing it on change
    }
}

let mut server = Server {
    observe: api_impl::ObserveState::new(ww_stream::observe::ObserveLimits::DEFAULT),
    // ..
};

// event loop, between requests: when something is due, see "The server loop" below
let mut buf = [0u8; 256]; // as big as the biggest update the link carries
server.poll_properties(&mut ww_server.sink(), medium, now_us, &mut buf).await?;
server.poll_streams(&mut ww_server.sink(), now_ms, &mut stream_buf, 4096).await?; // stored streams after

ObserveState holds one ObserveTable<[Slot; N]> per trait level, sized at compile time (N = the level's property count) - the per-property deadlines, modes and the level's token bucket. The table's code is the same for every level (it works on ObserveTable<[Slot]>, SRV-23), and so is the loop of poll_properties (SRV-24): plan, choice, writing the update and its bookkeeping are ww_stream::observe's (plan_level, select, write, ser_update), one loop over the levels sends from one place, and what the generated code adds per property is reading its value (size and write arms, and the .await of an async getter). A firmware carries the algorithm once however many levels its API has. ww_stream::observe::ObserveLimits is what the device allows every observer: shortest period, default/max budget per level, the total budget, and whether to send timestamps.

  • Due: Periodic on its grid, never early; OnChange once marked changed and min elapsed since its last send; OnChangeOrBeat also once max passed without a send.
  • Values: get_set properties are read through their getter when sent; value_on_changed ones from their field directly. An unbounded value (e.g. a string) is measured before it is chosen: a sync getter is called for that and again to write it, an async one (handler_model, SRV-21) once, its value kept for both. A getter that fails skips that send.
  • Token bucket, earliest deadline first: each level has a bucket filled at its granted bytes/s, holding at most a tenth of a second of it (64 bytes at least). poll_properties sends at most one update per level per call: its due properties earliest deadline first, as many as fit the bucket and the buffer. A level short of budget holds: when the due properties don't all fit yet the bucket isn't full, nothing is sent this call - the level waits until they fit or the bucket fills, so it sends fewer, fuller updates (one header each) instead of one value per call with a header of its own (SRV-18; see the motor demo for measured numbers). What's left out keeps its deadline, so a property that slipped goes first next time and none starves.
  • Missed: a periodic property counts one missed send per whole period it fell behind; an on-change one counts once it was held back or left out for min or longer. Held back for less, it's only late - polling often doesn't inflate the count. The count travels in the next update's missed.
  • Timestamps: t is the device's microsecond clock as a wrapping u32 (Second { Micro, U32 }, 5 bytes on the wire), wrapping every ~71.6 minutes; the host unwraps it into a U64 per level, by the same rule as stream times (timestamps). Only sent when ObserveLimits::timestamps is set.
  • Limits: a level inside a resource array can't be observed yet (OperationNotSupported, the bound of its indices isn't known yet, API-29); nor can a +observe property that is itself an array or #[optional]. Observing stays set while the link is down; ObserveState::reset() (e.g. on a fresh connection) stops it all.

items.title: The server loop
items.text:
A device doesn't poll observed properties on a fixed tick (SRV-25): ObserveState::next_wake(now_us) says when poll_properties next has something to do, and the server task sleeps until then, or until a request comes or something outside the server changes. Nothing observed, or nothing that comes due without a change: None, no wake at all.

  • When: the periodic grid, last + min of a property marked changed, last + max of a beat, at once for a property just observed or one left out of the last update; a level short of budget no earlier than its bucket has the bytes its held update needs; a batch of samples when it is sealed or as old as the host allows.
  • Changes from outside the server state: ObserveSignal, generated next to ObserveState, is a static any task or interrupt marks a property changed through (SIGNAL.mark_changed_<name>(): a bit and a wake, lock-free). ObserveState::with_signal(&SIGNAL) lets poll_properties and next_wake take those changes; the server task waits on SIGNAL.wait(). SIGNAL.wake() wakes it for anything else (a deferred answer to send).
  • No lost wake: a mark sets its bit and a flag, then wakes the task; wait() registers the task, then takes the flag. A change that comes after the last next_wake and before the sleep makes the next wait() return at once. Changes made by handlers (self.mark_changed_<name>(), a value_on_changed write) need no signal: the server task is the one running, and its next next_wake sees them.
  • Samples: <Level>Sampler::with_wake(SIGNAL.as_wake()) and <Level>Writer::with_wake(..) (cells) wake the server task when a batch gets its first row (its age starts when a poll sees it) and when it is full or sealed. Without, the level's batches are only looked at when something else wakes the task.
static OBSERVE: api_impl::ObserveSignal = api_impl::ObserveSignal::new();

let observe = State::init(STATE.uninit(), ObserveLimits::DEFAULT, batches);
observe.with_signal(&OBSERVE);
let mut adc_writer = METER_CELLS.writer().unwrap().with_wake(OBSERVE.as_wake()); // to the ADC task

loop {
    let now_us = ww_server.now().as_micros();
    let next = state.observe.next_wake(now_us).map(Instant::from_micros);
    match select(ww_server.wait_until(next), OBSERVE.wait()).await {
        Either::First(ready) => {
            if let Some(event) = ww_server.handle(ready, &mut state).await { /* LinkEvent::Up / Down */ }
        }
        Either::Second(()) => {}
    }
    let now_us = ww_server.now().as_micros();
    if ww_server.is_up() && state.observe.next_wake(now_us).is_some_and(|at| at <= now_us) {
        state.poll_properties(&mut ww_server.sink(), medium, now_us, &mut buf, scratch).await?;
    }
}

// elsewhere, in another task or an interrupt
OBSERVE.mark_changed_plug_vbus();

ww_device::Server::wait_until(at) is wait() that also returns when at comes (Ready::is_due(), nothing for handle to do), on the server's own clock. Polling only at these times sends the same updates at the same times as polling every microsecond (ww_stream's next_wake_sends_what_polling_does); tests/observe checks that an event-driven device polls only on the grid and sends a change from another thread at once.

items.title: The host side
items.text:
Each trait level with +observe properties gets observe(cfg) on its generated client (the root client, or device.motor()); each +observe property also gets observe_<name>(mode). Both return a PreparedObserve, built further with .budget(bytes_per_s), then .subscribe()/.subscribe_blocking() to get an Observer:

use wire_weaver_client::observe::{on_change, on_change_or_beat, periodic};
use api_client::motor_api_motor::MotorObserve; // in the level's client module (`<api crate>_<trait>`)

let ms = Duration::from_millis(1);
let mut motor = device
    .observe(MotorObserve::default().speed(periodic(10 * ms)).current(on_change(ms)))
    .budget(20_000)
    .subscribe()
    .await?;
let granted = motor.granted().unwrap(); // Granted { modes: MotorObserve, budget, refused }
while let Ok(u) = motor.recv().await {  // Observed { value: MotorUpdate, t, missed, received }
    if let Some(speed) = u.value.speed { /* .. */ }
}
motor.with_latest(|l| l.speed.as_ref().map(|s| (s.value, s.received)));

let mut mode = device.observe_mode(on_change(ms)).subscribe().await?; // Observer of u8 values
mode.configure(MotorObserve::default().mode(periodic(100 * ms))).await?;
  • Types: <Trait>Update (the level's PropertyUpdate data, one Option per +observe property), <Trait>Observe (one Option<ObserveMode> per property, used both to ask and as Granted::modes), and <Trait>Latest (the latest-value cache: a Sample { value, received, t } per property).
  • One subscription per level: every observer of a level asks for its own settings; the host merges them (shortest min/period, biggest budget per property) into one Observe sent to the device, resent when an observer comes, calls configure(..), or goes - Off once the last one is gone. Every observer of a level sees every update of it; a property observer only the updates that carry its property. Settings apply to all observers of a level together, so one may get updates more often than it asked for.
  • Reconnects: observers outlive disconnect().keep_streams(); resume_streams() resubscribes every level on the next connection (the device may or may not still have the old state) and observers see Resumed. A link that's down for good ends them.
  • Old devices: a device whose API model predates ww_client_server 0.2 can't observe; .subscribe() fails with Error::Unsupported.
  • Limits: like the device side, a level inside a resource array has no observe() yet. Absolute paths only - a trait client (client = "trait_client") observes once it has a base path (attachment()).

items.title: Every sample (+batched)
items.text:
The modes above send a property's current value, at most once per update. A value that changes faster than updates can go - a motor current sampled in a 25 kHz control loop - loses everything in between. A +batched property (API-39) can also be observed in Samples mode: the device keeps every sample it takes and sends them as compressed Series columns in the level's update: a Series<T> in each property's slot, and one Series<Second> of the sample times for the whole update (sample_times, next to its t), since a level's samples are taken together.

#[ww_trait]
trait Foc {
    property!(ro+observe+batched i_a: Ampere);
    property!(ro+observe+batched i_b: Ampere);
    property!(ro+observe duty: f32); // observed as before
}

+batched comes after +observe (alone it is an error). The property's slot in <Trait>Update becomes a Batched<T>: One(T), one value as in the other modes, or Samples(..), a batch of samples. A host that doesn't ask for Samples gets One values from the getter, as for any +observe property.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
Next to the getter, the device feeds samples where it takes them. Codegen generates, per level with +batched properties, a <Level>Sampler with sample(t, <Trait>Samples { .. }): one value per +batched property of the level and their common time. It is O(1) and takes no lock: a gate per level (one atomic load) says whether a host wants this sample (any property of the level in Samples mode, and the sample on the level's grid), and the row, the time and every value, goes into the level's batch being filled. Encoding happens later, in poll_properties, one column at a time: the time once, then each property a host observes in Samples mode.

let mut server = Server {
    observe: api_impl::ObserveState::new(
        ObserveLimits::DEFAULT,
        api_impl::ObserveBatches::new(ww_stream::batch::DEFAULT_POLICY),
    ),
    // ..
};

// in the control loop, every tick
server.observe.samplers().root.sample(
    Second::micro(now_us),
    api_impl::FocSamples { i_a, i_b },
);

// event loop: encodes sealed batches, then sends updates while batches wait; the scratch holds one column of a
// batch: the biggest of `Second` and the `+batched` property types, `OBSERVE_BATCH` of them
const SB: usize = ww_stream::batch::scratch_bytes::<Second>(api_impl::OBSERVE_BATCH);
let mut scratch = Box::new(ww_stream::batch::Scratch::<SB>::new());
server.poll_properties(&mut ww_server.sink(), medium, now_us, &mut buf, &mut scratch).await?;

To sample from an interrupt or another thread, ObserveBatches::split() hands out the samplers (Send, moved into the interrupt) and the consumers, which the ObserveState takes instead (ObserveState::new(limits, consumers), the batches in a static). ww api scaffold writes the observe_batch argument and says how to build the state.

On a firmware, build the batches and the state where they stay: ObserveBatches::init and ObserveState::init write them into statics in place, every store, table and outbox where it lives, with a few dozen bytes of stack (8 B at opt-level = 3, 72 B at z for the motor demo's 21 FOC values on a Cortex-M4F). new returns them by value, and building them that way takes a stack frame of a few times their size (31.6 KB for the same level, more than a small MCU has). The server then keeps a &'static mut to the state:

type State = api_impl::ObserveState<api_impl::ObserveBatchConsumers<'static>>;
static BATCHES: StaticCell<api_impl::ObserveBatches> = StaticCell::new();
static STATE: StaticCell<State> = StaticCell::new();

let batches = api_impl::ObserveBatches::init(BATCHES.uninit(), ww_stream::batch::DEFAULT_POLICY);
let (samplers, consumers) = batches.split(); // samplers.root to the interrupt
let observe: &'static mut State = State::init(STATE.uninit(), ObserveLimits::DEFAULT, consumers);
  • Batches: each level with +batched properties has two stores of observe_batch = N rows (codegen argument, default 32), a row being one sample() call's time and values, kept column by column: the sampler fills one store while the event loop encodes the other. RAM is 2 x N x (the time and every value): for 21 FOC currents and voltages at N = 32 about 8.4 KB. A batch is sealed when it is full, when its worst case reaches what fits one update, or when it is as old as max_age_us. A burst of more than two batches between two poll_properties calls loses rows: a sample of each observed property per row, counted in the next update's missed.
  • Outbox: a sealed batch is encoded into the level's outbox (observe_outbox = N bytes, default 4096) as one unit, the time column and the column of each property in Samples mode, and sent from there whole, in one update, as budget allows, more than one update per call (at most MAX_UPDATES_PER_POLL). When the outbox is full or the budget can't keep up, the oldest batches go and count as missed.
  • Time: the samples of an update share its sample_times: every Samples slot has as many samples as it has times, sample i taken at time i. An update that carries only batches has no head t, one with One values or plain properties has it as before. Rows carry every value of the level, so a property switched into Samples also gets the rows not sent yet, each at its time; one switched out leaves the waiting batches.
  • Limits: Samples is refused for a property without +batched (ModeNotSupported); max_age_us is clamped to ObserveLimits::samples_max_age_us (1 ms to 10 s by default); every_us decimates on the device's grid (the first sample in each every_us), 0 is every sample, and is raised to ObserveLimits::samples_min_every_us (0, every sample, by default). The Samples entries of a level share one grid and one age, so they get the finest every_us and the shortest max_age_us any of them asked for: the grant says so, a host that asked for less gets more. Every sample taken is encoded, also when the budget then drops its batch, so on an MCU set that floor from the table below: without it any host can ask for more encoding than the CPU has. A property type that borrows (bytes, a string, a vector) can't be +batched.

items.title: Cells: sampling from an interrupt
items.text:
sample(t, FocSamples { .. }) takes the row as one value: the interrupt builds the whole <Trait>Samples on its stack and the sampler copies it into the batch. For a level sampled in an interrupt, ww_codegen!(.., observe_cells = "root_foc") (the level's field name in ObserveState, several separated by commas) puts it on observe cells instead: a ring of atomics the interrupt writes in place, each value where it is computed, and poll_properties reads. The API and the wire don't change, so this is the device's choice per level, and a host can't tell which one a device uses.

// ww_codegen!(motor_demo_api::MotorDemo for Device, server = true, .., observe_cells = "root_foc")
static FOC: api_impl::RootFocCells<32> = api_impl::RootFocCells::new(); // const fn, a ring of 32 rows
static BATCHES: StaticCell<api_impl::ObserveBatches<'static>> = StaticCell::new();
// the state borrows the batches in their static
type State = api_impl::ObserveState<&'static mut api_impl::ObserveBatches<'static>>;
static STATE: StaticCell<State> = StaticCell::new();

let batches = api_impl::ObserveBatches::init(
    BATCHES.uninit(),
    ww_stream::batch::DEFAULT_POLICY,
    FOC.reader().unwrap(),
);
let mut server = Server {
    observe: State::init(STATE.uninit(), ObserveLimits::DEFAULT, batches), // a `&'static mut State`
    // ..
};

// the interrupt keeps the writer (taken once)
let mut w = FOC.writer().unwrap();
// .. every PWM period, where the values are computed
w.i_a(Ampere::milli(ia));
w.i_b(Ampere::milli(ib));
// .. one setter per `+batched` property of the level
w.commit(Second::micro(now_us));
  • Writer: <Level>Cells::writer() hands out the one <Level>Writer (Send, not Sync, given back on drop). Each setter is a few relaxed stores into the row being written; commit(t) publishes the row when a host observes the level in Samples mode and t is on its grid (the gate sample() checks), between two release fences: no lock, no read-modify-write, nothing on the stack but the values. A debug build panics at commit when a setter of the row wasn't called; a release build pays nothing for that. With nobody observing, the setters still store: put them (or the expensive values) under if w.is_sampling() { .. }.
  • Reader: <Level>Cells::reader() goes to ObserveBatches::init or new (one per cells level, in the order of the levels), which then borrow the cells: ObserveBatches<'static> for a static, or ww_stream::batch::CellsReader::shared(arc) for cells in an Arc on std. Each poll_properties copies the rows committed since the last one into one staging batch, the time and the observed properties' columns only, then encodes and sends it as the sampler's batches are: the same columns, the same bytes. A property observed while rows are staged gets its column copied for them from the ring, so it has the batch's earlier samples as with sample(); if the interrupt wrote over those rows meanwhile, they go without it and the next batch has it.
  • Ring size: R rows (<Level>Cells<R>) hold what the interrupt commits between two poll_properties calls; R - 1 can wait. A row the writer writes over before it is read (the ring lapped) is dropped and counted in missed, never sent with values of two rows. RAM is R rows plus one batch of observe_batch rows, about what the sampler's two batches take (for the motor demo's 21 FOC values, R = observe_batch = 32: 8.6 KB).
  • Under backpressure: while a sealed batch waits for budget or room, the sampler fills its second batch and loses the rows past it; the cells keep up to R - 1 rows in the ring and send them later, so they lose fewer. When nothing waits, both send the same bytes.
  • Types: the property types need SeriesCells (#[derive_shrink_wrap(.., series(cells))], see Series); ww_si quantities, numbers and bool have it.
  • Cost: on an STM32H725 a row of the 21 FOC values takes 354 cycles at opt-level = "z" against 412 through sample(), 328 against 419 at opt-level = 3, and 44-52 B of stack against 108-116 B; the copy into the staging batch moves to poll_properties. See Batching: observe cells, measured.

ww api scaffold --observe-cells root_foc writes the static, the ObserveState type and the ww_codegen! argument.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
<Trait>Observe::samples(max_age) puts every +batched property of the level into Samples mode (observe::samples(max_age) / samples_every(every, max_age) for one property). A property observer gets one Observed per sample, each with its own device time, whether the device sent one value or a batch; a level observer gets BatchedOwned<T> slots and Observed::sample_times, unwrapped like t (BatchedOwned::into_samples pairs them, a count that doesn't match is an error), and <Trait>Latest keeps the newest sample. An update whose Samples slots don't match its sample_times is malformed: a warning, its samples left out. Observers of one level merge into Samples if any of them asks for it.

use wire_weaver_client::observe::samples;
let mut i_a = device.foc().observe_i_a(samples(Duration::from_millis(5))).subscribe().await?;
while let Ok(s) = i_a.recv().await {
    println!("{:?} {:?}", s.t, s.value); // every sample, oldest first
}

The dynamic client decodes the same slots from introspection (DynObserved::samples), ww observe --samples MS prints one line per sample, and Python gets them per update or as numpy columns (recv_batch()).

items.title: Which rates fit an MCU
items.text: sample() itself is a few loads and stores; the cost is encoding, and it scales with how many properties and how fast they're sampled - see Batching: which rates fit an MCU for the measured instructions/cycles-per-sample table (Cortex-M3/M4F/M7) and what it means for a real device. So on an MCU observe a few properties at a few kHz, or decimate (every_us); full-rate observing of a whole control loop is for the simulator and the host (motor demo), where it costs about 1 MB/s of link with integer storage.

items.title: Wire format
items.text:
EventKind::PropertyUpdate { path, t, missed, data } is one level's update. data is the <Trait>Update sparse struct: an OptionAnyVec presence header (the smallest of four modes - all, dense bits, two-level bits, or an index list, picked by the writer - see OptionAnyVec for the exact bit layout), then only the present properties' values in slot order, no padding between them. Slots are the level's resource indices, methods and streams included as gaps that are never present.

A +batched property's slot is a Batched<T>: a nibble tag, then T for One (tag 0), or for Samples (tag 1) padding to the next byte and a Series<T> to the end of the slot. The event's sample_times (after missed, an Option<Series<Second>>) is present whenever a Samples slot is, with one time per sample of each. In introspection such a property is batched: Some(SharedClock).

Slot order matters for size: a bool property takes one bit, but a byte-or-wider type aligns itself to a byte as always, so a bool between two f32s still costs a byte of padding around it. The sparse worked example shows this byte-for-byte (speed: Option<u16> and on: Option<bool> present: 17 c6 dc 05 4c 00 00 c0 3f 81) - group the sub-byte (bool) properties of a level together in the trait if the savings matter, so their bits share one byte instead of forcing alignment around them.

The event itself (ser_property_update_event) adds a small fixed header on top of the update's own bytes: with a device timestamp it's 10 bytes (sequence, result flag, the level's path, t as a u32), 4 bytes without t - see the motor demo's measured numbers for what this costs on a real update of many properties.

items.title: Cost vs StreamData
items.text: Sending the same values one at a time as StreamData events (stream_data_ser().<name>_send(..), see Before observe requests) costs a separate event header per value instead of one header per level per update. The motor demo measures this on a real controller with 52 observed properties: about 42% less bytes/s observing a level than sending the same values as StreamData, growing with how many properties share one update (a single current, a ww_si::Ampere of mA as I32, 5 bytes, already takes 9-10 bytes alone as StreamData; an update of 21 such values as one PropertyUpdate takes 117 bytes, 5.6 bytes per value). A level short of its budget that holds for fuller updates (see above) widens that gap further: the same page measures 2.7x more values per byte once updates stop being sent one value at a time.

items.title: Walk-through: the motor demo
items.text: The motor demo (code in motor_sim) observes a simulated FOC motor controller's ~50 properties across three trait levels (one per rate tier: 25 kHz, 1 kHz, 50 Hz), each tier as one observe subscription at whatever rate a host asks for, within a budget. It's the reference for everything on this page in a real API: declaring +observe properties by tier, wiring ObserveState/poll_properties/mark_changed_<name> on the device, observing tiers at chosen rates and a budget from the CLI, and the measured bytes/s numbers above.

items.title: From the CLI and Python
items.text:
Observing also works from introspection alone, no generated code needed (TOOL-11): DynResource's observable_properties() lists a level's +observe properties (resource index, name, type), and observe(cmd, entries)/observe_blocking(..) (entries: BTreeMap<u32, ObserveMode>) build a wire_weaver_client::DynObserver that decodes each update's sparse OptionAnyVec by resource index instead of a generated struct's fields - reusing the same Level<U>/Observer<U, T> machinery as the generated client unchanged: one device subscription per level, t unwrapped, reconnect/resume included. Each DynObserved carries values (present properties by name, in resource-index order), t, missed, received, and data_len (the update's raw byte length, e.g. for measuring link bytes/s).

ww observe <path> [--rate MS] uses it directly:

$ ww observe motor --rate 10
observing motor (3 properties): speed, current, position
budget: 20.0 kB/s
Ctrl+C to stop
{speed: 1500, current: 3, position: 1024}  rate 98.2/s  link 982/s

and wire_weaver_py's Node.observe(cfg) iterates the same updates as dicts:

m = dev.motor
m.observable_properties()                              # {"speed": "u32", "current": "u32", "position": "u32"}
with m.observe({"speed": 10, "current": None}) as obs:  # speed periodically every 10ms, current on change
    for u in obs:
        print(u["values"], u["t"], u["missed"])

Both ask for every observable property on-change without an explicit rate/cfg, and share one device subscription per level with any generated-client observers of the same level. +batched properties come sample by sample (DynObserved::samples, ww observe --samples MS, Python's {"name": {"samples": max_age_ms}}), see Every sample.

items.title: Optional items
items.text:
A method, property or stream of a trait can be marked optional. A device's server may then leave it out when it is built: no dispatch arm, no handler to write, no stub answering "not implemented". A client calling it gets Unimplemented, and a client with the device's introspection data knows it without asking. tests/traits has a worked example; Errors tells Unimplemented apart from a device's own errors.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2c {
    fn i2c_configure(config: I2cConfig) -> Result<I2cConfig, I2cError<'i>>;
    // ...
    /// Clocks SCL until SDA is released, then a stop.
    #[optional]
    fn i2c_wiggle_clock(count: u8) -> Result<I2cLinesState, I2cError<'i>>;
    /// Switchable pull-ups: both items or neither.
    #[optional(pullups)]
    fn i2c_set_pullups(enabled: bool) -> Result<(), I2cError<'i>>;
    #[optional(pullups)]
    property!(ro i2c_pullups: bool);
}

// a device without these: no handlers to write
ww_codegen!(nucleo_api::Nucleo for Server, server = true, omit = ["i2c.i2c_wiggle_clock", "i2c.pullups"]);

items.title: Marking items optional
items.text:
• #[optional] on a method, property or stream lets a device leave it out. #[optional(group)] names a set of items that go together: leaving the group out leaves out all of them.
  • Only marked items can be left out: the API author decides what is optional, the rest of the trait stays a contract every device keeps. Leaving out a required item is a compile error that lists the trait's optional items and groups.
  • An item keeps its resource index whether a device has it or not, so clients address it the same way everywhere.
  • The marker is part of the trait's signature: marking an item optional later changes the API model, and its snapshot has to be saved again.
  • #[optional] on ww_impl! (a whole trait) is rejected; mark the trait's items instead.

items.title: Leaving items out
items.text:
ww_codegen!(.., server = true, omit = [..]) takes paths "<trait item>.<..>.<item or group>" from the API root, without array indices: "periph.channel.run" leaves run out of every periph[i].channel[j]. Items of the API root itself are named directly (omit = ["reset"]). A group may not share a name with an item of the same trait (group format and method format): #[ww_trait] refuses it with an error naming both, rename the group. Naming an item twice (by name and through its group, or in omit and omit_if) is a compile error, as is an unknown name.

omit_if(<cfg>) = [..] ties optional items to the device crate's own Cargo features:

ww_codegen!(
    nucleo_api::Nucleo for Server,
    server = true,
    omit_if(not(feature = "pullups")) = ["i2c.pullups"]
);

The dispatch arm gets #[cfg(not(<cfg>))]; the handlers are the device crate's to cfg out. The introspection data (and with it the API hash) depends on which items are left out, so it is generated for each combination of the conditions, under #[cfg(all(..))]; at most 4 different conditions per ww_codegen!.

ww api scaffold --omit i2c.pullups,reset leaves the stubs of these items out and writes the same omit = [..] into the generated ww_codegen! call; the stubs of optional items it keeps carry a comment naming their path.

items.title: What a client sees
items.text:
• A call to an omitted item is answered ErrorKind::Unimplemented, the same answer as a handler returning Unimplemented. In a generated client that is CallError::Unimplemented (see Methods).
  • The device's introspection data lists the items it leaves out (ApiItemKind::Trait { omitted }, ApiBundle::root_omitted for the API root, ApiItem::optional for the marker). A client that has it fails a call to an omitted item locally with NotImplementedByDevice, without a round trip; the compatibility check doesn't count it as a mismatch, it is the device's choice.
  • The dynamic client (DynResource::is_omitted()) and Python fail such calls locally too. Python signatures end in (optional), or (left out by this device); ww api tree and ww introspect show #[optional] and (left out by this device).
  • A device without introspection data, and no cached copy on the client: the call goes out and is answered Unimplemented.

items.title: Cost
items.text:
The fallback arm of a trait level that leaves something out answers Unimplemented for an id below the trait's item count and BadPath above it: one comparison per level, no arm per omitted item. Levels that leave nothing out are generated as before.

Measured on thumbv7em-none-eabihf (opt-level = "s", LTO, introspection off) with a Board { ww_impl!(i2c: I2c); fn other(..) } API whose I2c has one required method and three optional items (two methods and an rw property):

Server .text Stub handlers answering Unimplemented (what the scaffold generates without omit) 7496 bytes The three items left out with omit 7204 bytes The three items not in the API at all 7192 bytes

Leaving an item out saves about 100 bytes (its arm, argument decoding and the stub); the comparison costs 12 bytes per level that leaves something out.

items.title: Optional item or its own trait
items.text:
Optional items are for one to three items within the trait's subject that some hardware lacks: a clock wiggle, pull-ups, a hardware CRC. Items with their own state, configuration or streams, a subject of their own (a bus monitor, ADC capture), anything a different set of devices implements, or four items and more make a trait of their own.

Optional is for what is known when the firmware is built. A capability that depends on what is found at run time (a board variant read from EEPROM) stays a capability the device reports, or a CommonError::Unsupported answer (see ww_error).

items.title: Getting started with APIs
items.text:
A WireWeaver API is a Rust trait describing what a device offers: methods to call, properties to read and write, streams of data from the device, sinks of data into it, and nested traits grouping them. From that one trait, ww_codegen! generates the device's server (request decoding and dispatch to your handlers, no_std and no allocation) and the host's client (a typed function per item, async, blocking or as a promise for GUIs). Data crossing the wire is any ShrinkWrap type.

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait BlinkyApi {
    fn led_on();
    fn led_off();
}

items.title: The project shape
items.text:
An API lives in its own small crate, shared by the firmware and the host:

Crate What it holds In this repo blinky_api the trait and its data types, no_std examples/blinky_api firmware implements the handlers, runs the server examples_mcu/rp2/src/bin/usb_blinky.rs blinky the generated client, used by apps and scripts examples/blinky

The API crate's name and version identify the API on the wire, see Folder structure. To start a new project, copy the wire_weaver_template repository.

items.title: A first API, end to end
items.text:
1. The API crate (examples/blinky_api/src/lib.rs):

#![no_std]

use wire_weaver::prelude::*;

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait BlinkyApi {
    fn led_on();
    fn led_off();
}

#[ww_api_root] marks the top-level trait of a device (#[ww_trait] the others). It generates nothing by itself: ww_codegen! reads the trait from its source file.

2. The device (from examples_mcu/rp2/src/bin/usb_blinky.rs) implements one handler per method:

struct ServerState {
    led: Output<'static>,
}

impl ServerState {
    async fn led_on(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        self.led.set_high();
        Ready(())
    }

    async fn led_off(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        self.led.set_low();
        Ready(())
    }
}

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        blinky_api :: BlinkyApi for super::ServerState,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = true,
    );
}

ww api scaffold blinky_api (CLI) prints the struct, a stub for every handler and the ww_codegen! call, so you never write handler signatures by hand. The generated server is sans-IO: a transport (USB, RTT, UDP, WebSocket, see Transport protocols) feeds it requests; the example uses wire_weaver_usb_embassy.

3. The host (examples/blinky) generates a client and calls the device:

pub struct Blinky {
    cmd: Commander,
}

impl WwClient for Blinky {
    fn default_config() -> ClientConfig {
        ClientConfig::new().usb_vid_pid(0xc0de, 0xcafe)
    }
    fn from_cmd(cmd: Commander) -> Self {
        Self { cmd }
    }
}

mod api_client {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(blinky_api :: BlinkyApi for crate::Blinky, client = "std_client");
}

// examples/blinky/examples/simple.rs
let device = Blinky::new().connect().await?;
device.led_on().call().await?;
device.led_off().call().await?;

.call().await is the async form; .blocking_call() and .call_promise(..) do the same without async. With no host code at all, ww introspect and Python talk to the device from the API it describes itself.

items.title: What an API can have
items.text:
#[ww_api_root]
trait MyDevice {
    /// Methods: any number of arguments, any return type, Result for errors.
    fn set_brightness(value: f32);
    fn temperature() -> f32;
    fn read() -> Result<u16, SensorError<'i>>;

    /// Properties: values the host reads, writes or observes.
    property!(rw speed: f32);
    property!(ro+observe current: f32);

    /// Streams out of the device, sinks into it.
    stream!(button: ButtonEvent);
    sink!(uart_tx: [u8]);

    /// Traits: groups of items, here an array of GPIO banks from the standard library.
    ww_impl!(gpio[]: ww_gpio::Bank);
}
Item Page fn Methods: handlers, async or blocking servers, deferred answers, the client property!, const Properties: get_set handlers or a plain field, reads, writes, consts stream!, sink! Streams: plain, counted and reliable streams, sinks ww_impl! Traits: grouping, reusable traits from crates, attachments Result<T, E> Errors: error enums, common errors, CallError on the client

Everything else builds on these: items can be arrays (gpio[]), optional for devices that lack them, observed without polling, and many can be answered in one multi request. The standard library has ready-made traits for GPIO, I2C, UART, firmware updates, logs and more.

The API and its types can evolve: newer hosts work with older devices and the other way round, as long as the evolution rules are followed.

items.title: Properties
items.text:
A property is a value of the device the host reads, writes or both: a setting, a measured state, a mode.

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    property!(ro button_pressed: bool);
    property!(rw speed: f32);
    property!(wo beep: u16);
    #[errors(TooBig, NotSet)]
    property!(rw mode: u8, ModeError);
    /// Known at compile time, never changes while the firmware runs.
    const LIMITS: Limits<'i>;
}
Access Declared as Read Write Observe read/write property!(rw name: T) ✓ ✓ with rw+observe read only property!(ro name: T) ✓ with ro+observe write only property!(wo name: T) ✓ const const NAME: T; ✓, once per connection

ro means read only for the host: the device changes the value whenever it likes, and may tell observers about it. +observe lets hosts observe it, see Observing changes. A const never changes while the firmware runs, see Const items.

Any type the SerDes system supports can be a property. A second type after the value's, property!(rw mode: u8, ModeError), is the property's error type: reads and writes may fail with it. #[errors(..)] above such a property lists the variants it returns, as on methods (see Errors). #[optional] / #[optional(group)] lets a device leave a property out (see Optional items), and a property can be an array, property!(rw gain[]: f32).

items.title: Device side
items.text:
A server implements each property in one of two ways, picked per property with the property_model argument of ww_codegen!: a comma separated list of regex=get_set|value_on_changed, the regex matching the property's name, _ for the rest; get_set is the default.

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        my_device_api :: MyDevice for super::Server,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = false,
        property_model = "speed=value_on_changed, _=get_set",
    );
}

ww api scaffold <api_crate> --property-model ".." prints the handlers and fields either way.

items.title: get_set: handlers
items.text:
User code provides get_<name> for reads and set_<name> for writes:

impl Server {
    fn get_button_pressed(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) -> GetResult<bool, ()> {
        Value(self.button.is_low())
    }

    fn set_beep(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, freq: u16) -> SetResult<()> {
        self.buzzer.start(freq);
        Set
    }

    fn get_mode(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) -> GetResult<u8, ModeError> {
        match self.mode {
            0 => GetError(ModeError::NotSet),
            mode => Value(mode),
        }
    }

    fn set_mode(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, mode: u8) -> SetResult<ModeError> {
        if mode > 10 {
            return SetError(ModeError::TooBig);
        }
        self.mode = mode;
        Set
    }
}
  • GetResult<T, E>: Value(v) answers the read with v; GetError(e) answers with the error; Unimplemented answers ErrorKind::Unimplemented.
  • SetResult<E>: Set acknowledges the write; SetError(e) answers with the error, the value is not applied unless the handler did so; Unimplemented answers ErrorKind::Unimplemented.
  • E is the property's error type, () without one. The error goes to the host serialized, as ErrorKind::UserBytes.

Both answer right away: a property has no deferred answer. Handlers get cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut, Medium> (impl EventOut and async fn for use_async = true), properties in arrays their index chain after it.

items.title: value_on_changed: a field
items.text:
Generated code reads and writes a field of the server struct named like the property, and calls changed_<name> after a write that changed the value (the type needs PartialEq; writing the same value calls nothing):

struct Server {
    speed: f32,
}

impl Server {
    fn changed_speed(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) {
        self.motor.set_speed(self.speed);
    }
}

Reads and writes can't fail with this model: a property whose writes have to be checked uses get_set. Properties of nested traits carry the trait item chain in their names (self.motor_speed, changed_motor_speed), as every handler does.

items.title: Observing changes
items.text:
A host can watch a trait level's +observe properties instead of polling them, one subset per update instead of a message per value - see Observing properties for the full picture (device side, host side, the wire format, cost vs plain streams). Declaring one is just the property flag:

#[ww_trait]
trait Motor {
    property!(ro+observe speed: f32);
    property!(ro+observe current: f32);
    property!(rw+observe mode: u8);
    property!(rw gain: f32); // not observable
}

items.title: Before observe requests
items.text: stream_data_ser().<name>_send(&value, out) (_send_blocking for sync servers) still sends one property's value as stream data on its own path. Generated clients receive it with observe_<name>() for properties without +observe (a plain Stream<T>, no request is sent to the device); for +observe properties observe_<name>(mode) is the observe request below. It is superseded by observe requests.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
Generated clients have read_<name>(), write_<name>(value) and observe_<name>() per property, as its access allows. Reads and writes are prepared first, then sent async, blocking or as a promise:

let speed = device.read_speed().read().await?;            // Result<f32, Error>
device.write_speed(1500.0).write().await?;                // waits for the device's acknowledgement
device.write_speed(1500.0).write_forget().await?;         // no answer asked for, nothing waited for
let pressed = device.read_button_pressed().blocking_read()?;
let mut read = device.read_speed().read_promise("speed"); // poll it from a GUI
  • A write to a property with an error type returns Result<(), CallError<E>>: CallError::Device(e) is the device's error, decoded, see Errors. Without one it returns Result<(), Error>.
  • A read returns Result<T, Error>; a device's error arrives as Error::RemoteError with ErrorKind::UserBytes, the error's bytes (E::from_ww_bytes).
  • ErrorKind::Unimplemented (CallError::Unimplemented { .. } for writes) is a handler returning Unimplemented, or a property the device left out.
  • .with_timeout(..) overrides the request timeout for one read or write.
  • Several resources in one request, when the server is generated with multi_req = true (a server without it refuses the request): each index answered on its own (Result<T, ErrorOwned> per item, in order) - see Multi requests for the generated, array and dynamic-client APIs.
  • With an #[errors(..)] list, the generated client warns when a write fails with a variant outside it (the dynamic client checks reads too).

The dynamic client and Python have the same per property: dev.speed.read(), dev.speed.write(1500) (Python).

items.title: Observing
items.text: The host side of observing changes (CLT-28): observe(cfg) per trait level, observe_<name>(mode) per property, .subscribe() returning an Observer with a latest-value cache, reconnect support and more - see Observing properties: the host side for the full API and a dynamic-client/CLI/Python equivalent that needs no generated code at all.

items.title: Const items
items.text:
A const item of a trait is a value that doesn't change while the firmware runs: a firmware name and version, a board record, chip ids, limits of an implementation.

#[ww_api_root]
trait Device {
    /// Known at compile time.
    const LIMITS: Limits<'i>;
    /// Read from the chip at boot.
    const SERIAL: &'i str;
    ww_impl!(board: ww_board_info::BoardInfo);
}

On the server, no handler is called for it. The value comes from the generated trait <RootTrait>Consts, which the server struct implements, in one of two forms, picked per item with the const_model argument of ww_codegen!:

  • const (the default): a Rust const, const LIMITS: Limits<'static> = ..;.
  • fn: a value fixed at boot or link time (OTP, a chip id register, the build id in flash), fn serial(&self) -> &str. Items in an array of traits get the index chain: fn channel_gain(&self, index_chain: [UNib32; 1]) -> u8.

Names carry the trait item chain prefix, as handler names do: BOARD of board: BoardInfo is BOARD_BOARD as a const and board_board as a fn. const_model is a comma separated list of regex=const|fn, the regex matching the whole name of the item as written in its trait (BOARD, not board_BOARD); _=fn changes the default.

impl api_impl::DeviceConsts for Server {
    const LIMITS: Limits<'static> = Limits { max_len: 64, names: RefVec::Slice { slice: &["a", "b"] } };

    fn serial(&self) -> &str {
        &self.serial
    }

    fn board_board(&self) -> BoardSummary<'_> {
        self.board.summary()
    }
}

mod api_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        device_api :: Device for super::Server,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = false,
        const_model = "SERIAL|BOARD=fn",
    );
}

ww api scaffold --const-model "SERIAL|BOARD=fn" <api_crate> prints this impl with a todo!() for every value. An #[optional] const left out with omit = [..] has no item in the trait. A trait without const items has no <RootTrait>Consts. A const can't fail, so it has no error type and no #[errors(..)].

Clients read a const from the device once per connection and keep the value: later reads of it (generated read_<NAME>(), async, blocking or as a promise, the dynamic client and Python) return it without a request. A new connection, or a disconnect() through the same Commander, reads it again; Commander::clear_const_cache() does too. Errors are not kept. ww introspect reads the consts that are not in an array of traits and shows their values in the tree (--no-values to skip them).

items.title: Settings store
items.text:
ww_settings (STD-32) keeps a device's settings in its own NOR flash: a plain struct with a default for every field, stored as a record of the fields that differ from their default. It survives a power cut at any point of a write or an erase. Old and new firmware read each other's records without losing anything, and the fields are served as ordinary rw properties.

use ww_settings::{Debounce, Key, Settings, Store};

#[derive(ww_settings::Settings, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
#[settings(retired(3))] // slots of removed fields, never used again
pub struct UserSettings {
    #[setting(slot = 0, default = ArrayString::new())]
    pub label: ArrayString<32>,
    #[setting(slot = 1, default = false)]
    pub plug_vbus_at_boot: bool,
    #[setting(slot = 2, default = ButtonAction::Toggle)]
    pub button_action: ButtonAction,
    #[setting(slot = 4, default = 100)]
    pub meter_window_ms: u16,
}

The derive writes Default (every field at its default) and ww_settings::SettingsGroup: the slot table with field names, the crate's version, and per field the code to compare it with its default, write it and read it.

  • Slots are 0..=255, unique, in any order. A slot belongs to its field for good: renaming the field is fine, giving the slot to another field is not. A removed field's slot goes into retired(..), and the derive refuses to reuse it.
  • Field types are owned values with ShrinkWrap serdes and PartialEq: numbers, bool, enums and structs with #[derive_shrink_wrap], arrays, and shrink_wrap::ArrayString<N> / ArrayVec<T, N> (SW-57) for text and lists without an allocator. The same types work for properties, so a field and the property that serves it share one type.
  • Defaults are expressions: default = 100, default = ButtonAction::Toggle, a const.

items.title: On the device
items.text:
// a range at the end of bank 2 of an STM32G0B1 (4 pages of 2 KiB), see "How many pages" below
let mut store: Store<_, 512> = Store::new(flash, 0x0807_8000..0x0808_0000)?;
let mut user: Settings<UserSettings, 128> = Settings::new(Key::USER, Debounce::default());
let report = user.load(&mut store).await?; // defaults for anything not stored
// apply them: here to the server's value_on_changed fields
server.button_action = user.get().button_action;

Settings<G, N> holds the value in RAM, the stored record (up to N bytes) and whether something changed since. Store<F, B, K> holds the flash, a buffer of B bytes and the location of the current record of up to K keys (groups). Each group has its own key: Key::USER (0) for what users change, Key::FACTORY (1) for calibration and production data, written through a debug API only.

Served as properties. The API declares the settings as plain rw properties; the server keeps them in value_on_changed fields (properties), and each changed_<name> handler hands the new value to the settings, which only changes RAM:

impl Server {
    fn changed_settings_button_action(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) {
        let v = self.settings_button_action;
        self.user.set(now_ms(), |s| s.button_action = v);
    }
}

Written when it settles. set starts a Debounce: the record is written once the value was left alone for quiet_ms (default 1 s), or max_ms (default 10 s) after the first change not stored yet, so a slider dragged for a minute is written every 10 s, not on every step. The device's loop writes it:

loop {
    let wake = user.due_at(); // None: nothing to write
    match select(server.wait(), timer_at(wake)).await {
        Either::First(ev) => server.handle(ev).await,
        Either::Second(()) => {
            user.persist_if_due(&mut store, now_ms()).await?;
        }
    }
}

A write happens only when the record changed: setting a value and setting it back before the write costs nothing, writing the same value again costs nothing.

Written before answering. Where an Ok must mean "survives a power cut", as ww_user_info promises for a device name, the handler calls persist right away (an async handler, or a deferred reply):

user.set(now_ms(), |s| s.label = name);
user.persist(&mut store).await?; // Ok: written

Factory reset. user.reset_to_defaults(now) and persist: every field of the group at its default, an empty record written. Other keys (Key::FACTORY) are not touched.

What load reports. LoadReport says whether a record was found, which version wrote it (writer) and the highest version whose data is in it (newest, above the running firmware's after a downgrade), and how many fields were read, how many slots belong to a newer firmware (kept on the next write) or to removed fields (dropped). A record in an unknown format (a newer ww_settings) is left alone: is_read_only(), every field at its default, persist refuses with Error::ReadOnly until a factory reset.

Dropping a write. A persist or maintain future dropped half way (a select! with a timeout) leaves the flash as a power cut at that point would; the store goes on from there.

items.title: What is stored
items.text:
A page holds a log of records, not one struct: each write appends a new record for its key, and the newest one wins. The record is the group's version and the fields that are not at their default, each as its own ShrinkWrap bytes:

record: | format: u8 = 1 | writer: 3 × UNib32 | newest: 3 × UNib32 | pad | slots: OptionAnyVec of byte blobs |

Every slot of the OptionAnyVec holds the field's bytes as a blob (a length and the bytes). That is what lets a firmware skip a slot it doesn't know, keep it when it writes the record again, and drop a retired one, which a plain sparse struct can't do (its values carry no length). The cost is a length nibble and byte alignment per stored field.

In flash each record is an item: a 12-byte header (length, key, a 32-bit sequence number per key, CRC-32) and the record, padded to the flash word. Sizes for a Donguru-like group (label, a bool, an enum, two u16, a UART configuration), measured with record::encode and Store::footprint:

Record Bytes G0 item / per 2 KiB page F4 item / per 16 KiB H7 item / per 128 KiB SPI NOR item / per 4 KiB nothing set 4 16 / 127 16 / 1023 32 / 4095 16 / 255 one bool set 8 24 / 84 20 / 818 32 / 4095 20 / 204 label "bench-3" 14 32 / 63 28 / 584 32 / 4095 26 / 157 all six set, 16-char label 39 56 / 36 52 / 314 64 / 2047 51 / 80

(G0: 8-byte words, F4: 4-byte, H7: 32-byte, SPI NOR: 1-byte; a page loses 8 to 32 bytes to its header.)

When it compacts. When a record doesn't fit the current page any more, the store moves on to the next page (which is always erased or erasable), writes its header, and copies into it the current records that sit on the page after that one, so that page holds none and can be erased. On the G0 above, with every field set, that is every 36th write; on the H7 every 2047th. Each page is erased once per round, so the pages wear evenly.

items.title: How many pages
items.text:
At least 2: the store always keeps the page after the current one free of current records, so it has a page to compact into, and with only one page there would be nowhere to put the current records while the page is erased. Store::new refuses fewer. The current records of all keys, plus the one being written, must fit into one page: otherwise a write fails with StoreError::Full and what is stored stays readable. Keep them under half a page, so a cut copy (which wastes its space until the page is erased) can't fill it.

More pages spread the erases: with p pages, n records per page and an endurance of E cycles (10 000 on the STM32 parts below), the flash lasts about p · n · E writes. On the G0 with 4 pages and every field set: 4 · 36 · 10 000 ≈ 1.4 million writes, plenty with the debounce. On the G0, 4 pages (8 KiB) at the end of bank 2 is the recommendation: 2 would work, 4 halve the wear and leave room for records to grow.

items.title: What an erase stalls
items.text:
A write programs a few words, an erase takes milliseconds to seconds, and on a single-bank part the CPU can't fetch code from flash while either runs: every interrupt, the USB stack and the executor stop until it is done (code and interrupt handlers in RAM keep running). From the datasheets:

Part Erase unit Erase, typ / max Program Banks STM32G0B1 (DS13560) 2 KiB page 25 / 40 ms 8 bytes: 56 / 90 µs 2 on the 512 KiB parts: no stall from the other bank STM32F405/407/411 (DS8626, DS10314), x32 16 / 64 / 128 KiB sectors 250/500 ms, 550/1100 ms, ½ s 4 bytes: 16 / 100 µs 1 (F42x/F43x: 2) STM32H743/753 (DS12110) 128 KiB sector x8: 2 / 4 s, x16: 1.8 / 3.6 s 32 bytes: 100 / 200 µs (x64) 2 STM32H723/725/730/733/735 (DS13313) 128 KiB sector, 8 of them as H743 as H743 1 STM32H7A3/7B3 (DS13195) 8 KiB sector max 2.2 ms 16 bytes: max 20 µs 2 W25Q128JV SPI NOR 4 KiB sector 45 / 400 ms 256 bytes: 0.4 / 3 ms separate chip: no stall

What that means on a single bank: USB keeps NAKing in hardware, so the host sees a pause, not a disconnect, but a request with a timeout shorter than the erase fails; the watchdog period has to be longer than the longest erase; anything with a deadline (a control loop, a UART without DMA) misses it. A G0 page erase (25 ms) is a hiccup; a 128 KiB sector (1 to 4 s) is not.

Store::maintain() moves the stall to a time the device picks: it erases the page the next compaction will move to, if it needs it, so the write that starts a new page doesn't erase. Store::erase_pending() says whether one is due. A device can call it when the host is idle, at boot, or answer a request with Busy meanwhile.

items.title: Parts with big sectors
items.text:
On an STM32F4 or H7 the store needs two whole sectors, and on a single-bank part each erase stops the CPU for one to four seconds. The options, best first:

  1. The other bank. On a dual-bank part (H743/753, H7A3/7B3, F42x/F43x with DB1M), put the store in the bank the code doesn't run from: erases don't stall anything. On the H743 that is 2 × 128 KiB of bank 2; on the H7A3 2 × 8 KiB; on an F42x in dual-bank mode bank 2 starts with 16 KiB sectors (12 to 15), the same as bank 1.

  2. The small sectors at the start of an F4. Sectors 0 to 3 are 16 KiB each. Sector 0 has to hold the vector table (the part boots from 0x0800_0000), so the store takes sectors 1 and 2 (or 1 to 3), and the code starts after them. With cortex-m-rt that is one symbol in memory.x:

    MEMORY
{
  FLASH : ORIGIN = 0x08000000, LENGTH = 1024K
  RAM   : ORIGIN = 0x20000000, LENGTH = 128K
}
/* sector 0: vector table; sectors 1-2 (0x0800_4000..0x0800_C000): ww_settings; code from sector 3 */
_stext = 0x0800C000;

    The vector table stays at 0x0800_0000 (no VTOR change); the rest of sector 0, about 15.5 KiB, stays empty (or holds a bootloader). An erase still stalls the CPU (250 / 500 ms for 16 KiB), use maintain(). Flashing a new firmware with probe-rs erases only the sectors the image covers, so the settings survive it; a chip erase doesn't. 3. External SPI / QSPI NOR. 4 KiB sectors, about 45 ms per erase that doesn't touch the CPU (the bus is separate), 100 000 cycles; any embedded-storage-async NorFlash driver works. Not on a QSPI flash the code runs from (XIP): that stalls like internal flash. 4. Two of the big sectors with maintain(). On a single-bank H723/H733 (8 sectors of 128 KiB) there is no way around a 2 s stall per erase; with 64-byte records it happens every ~2000 writes, and maintain() puts it where it hurts least. 5. One sector with a RAM copy (not supported). A store in a single sector has to erase the sector that holds the only copy of every record, then write them back from RAM. A power cut from the start of that erase until the last record is written back loses every group, user settings and factory data alike: the device boots on its defaults. That window is the whole erase plus the rewrite, 1 to 4 s on a 128 KiB sector, once per sector fill. The RAM copy survives a soft reset, not a power cut. ww_settings doesn't offer this mode (STD-33); a device with exactly one sector to spare is better served by external NOR.

items.title: Power cuts
items.text:
What the store guarantees, at any point of any write or erase:

  • load returns, for each key, either the record from before the interrupted write or the one being written, never anything else, and never an error.
  • After the cut, the next write works, and finishes what the interrupted one left (a half done compaction).
  • Loading never writes: a device that boots in a brown-out loop wears nothing.
  • Every flash word is written once between erases, and only words that read erased are written (STM32G0/H7 ECC flash refuses or corrupts a second write).

How: every item carries a sequence number per key and a CRC-32, so the current record of a key is the valid item with the highest number wherever it is; a cut write leaves an item that fails its CRC and is skipped. A page carries a sequence number in a header with its own CRC, which says which page is current. Before a page is erased, the current records on it are copied away, so a cut erase can leave only older records and copies behind, in whatever order the erase cleared the bytes. The layout is in the ww_settings::store module docs.

The tests cut the power at every word written and every byte erased of a run that goes several times around the pages, on G0-like (8-byte ECC words, 2 KiB pages), H7-like (32-byte ECC words) and F4-like (4-byte words, 16 KiB sectors) flash, with erases that clear the bytes front to back, back to front or all at once, and cut again while recovering (ww_settings/tests/power_cut.rs; just test-power-cut runs every step, just test a sample).

ECC flash needs an ECC-aware driver. On the G0 and H7 a word whose write was cut has an uncorrectable ECC error, and reading it raises an NMI (G0) or a bus fault (H7): a plain flash driver turns a power cut into a boot loop. The driver has to return such a word as zeros, which the store skips like any damaged item (SRV-19, mcu/ww_ecc_flash).

Why not sequential-storage. Its map was the first choice. Under the same tests it ends permanently Corrupted, or returns an older value, when an erase is cut while the end-of-page marker already reads erased but the start marker doesn't: it assumes the start marker clears first, which a sector erase doesn't promise.

items.title: Evolution
items.text: The rules for changing a settings struct between firmware versions are in evolution rules. In short: add fields at new slots (also in gaps), retire removed ones, never change a slot's type except by that type's own rules, and know that changing a default changes the value of every device that never set the field.

items.title: Stream protocol
items.text: How streams and sinks work on the wire and inside: the head of counted and reliable stream events, their acknowledgements, the same messages for credit sinks, and the ww_stream state machines generated code drives. For using streams, read Streams, Counted and reliable streams, Stream delivery and Credit sinks and sideband first. The wire types live in ww_client_server (its page).

items.title: Opening and closing
items.text: On the wire, opening is a RequestKind::StreamOpen { resume, args } request, answered with a ww_client_server::stream::StreamOpened (the session and positions, empty for a plain stream) followed by the function's result. Closing is a StreamSideband::Close request from the host, or a Close event from the device when the stream ends on its own.

items.title: Head on the wire
items.text:
A counted or reliable stream sends EventKind::StreamItem instead of StreamData:

// ww_client_server
pub enum EventKind<'i> {
    // ... Value, Written, StreamData, StreamSideband
    StreamItem { path: RefVec<'i, UNib32>, head: StreamHead, data: TailBytes<'i> },
}

// ww_client_server::stream
pub struct StreamHead {
    pub pos: u64,             // position of the event's first unit since the session started
    pub units: u64,           // units of the event's item
    pub lost: Option<u64>,    // units the device dropped right before this event; `pos` counts them
    pub t: Option<Second>,    // device time of the first unit
    pub ext: Option<HeadExt>, // rare markers: the clock epoch changed (a reboot)
}

The head is laid out by hand, so that its four flags share the first byte with the length of pos:

 byte 0:  L T X U n n n p      L, T, X, U: lost, t, ext, units follow (units only when not 1)
                               nnn: bytes of pos after this one (0..7), p: the top bit of pos
 then:    n bytes of pos (1 + 8n bits in all, big endian)
          units: UVlq64             if U
          lost:  UVlq64             if L
          t:     ww_si::Second      if T (starts on a byte, so its prefix and type tag share one byte)
          ext:   HeadExt            if X (Unsized: fields can be appended later)
pos below 2 512 128 Ki 32 Mi 8 Gi 2 Ti 512 Ti 2⁵⁷ Head bytes (one unit, no lost, t, ext) 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

units (when not 1) and lost add 1 byte each below 128, 2 below 16 Ki, and so on; t as Second { Micro, U32 } adds 5 bytes, as U64 9. A stream of single items pays nothing for units, a byte stream 1-2 bytes. A position of 2⁵⁷ or more is a serialization error.

Example, from the tests of ww_client_server::stream: pos = 2³³, units = 3, lost = 7 and a t of Second { Micro, U32(0x12345678) } is the 13-byte head da 02 00 00 00 00 03 07 23 78 56 34 12; with the event header and a one-element path, 17 bytes come before the item's data.

A StreamData event costs 3 to 5 bytes of header and path before its data, so a long-running counted stream with a timestamp pays about 15 bytes per event: 3 % of a 512-byte item, 1 % of 1.5 KiB. Send small items in chunks (an item of type MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Record>, N>, counted in records), not one event per record.

items.title: Acknowledgements and resends
items.text:
A reliable stream's receiver (the host) tells the sender (the device) what it has. Positions are in units, grants in bytes, since what runs out on the receiving side is memory:

Sideband Direction Meaning Ack { have, backfill, grant } receiver → sender received every unit before have (live run) and before backfill (backfill run, while there is one); the sender may have up to grant bytes of events in flight beyond them Resend { from, grant } receiver → sender units from from on are missing, in whichever run from falls: send again from there Query { sent, backfill } sender → receiver "I have sent up to here, where are you?", when out of credit or nothing was heard for a while; answered with Ack or Resend

All three carry the whole state, so losing one is harmless: the next one replaces it.

  • The device keeps every event in its store until an Ack passes it, sends while the bytes in flight before the next event are below the grant (so a grant smaller than an item can't stall the stream), and goes back on Resend (go-back-N). A Resend acknowledges nothing (with Explicit the host may have received more than its user code confirmed); the host sends an Ack right before it when its position moved. With no host, nothing is acknowledged: the store fills, then data is dropped and counted.
  • The host accepts events of each run in order only, drops duplicates, asks for a resend once per gap, and acknowledges every half window or 100 ms. The window is what the host queues for the stream (4 MiB by default): a host that doesn't read stops granting, the device stops sending and keeps the data in its store, so the host's memory stays bounded.
  • When data counts as received (AckMode): by default when user code takes an event; with Explicit, only when user code confirms it, for example after writing it to disk.
