  • Defaults: a resend is asked again after 500 ms, the device queries after 200 ms of silence, the first grant is 4 KiB.

items.title: Positions inside an event
items.text:
An event of several units (a block of samples, a batch) has positions inside it, and the host can stand at one of them: user code confirmed part of a batch (ack(pos) with Explicit, items saved one by one) and resumes from that cursor, or a Resend comes from such a position. The device never splits an event: it sends the event that holds the position, whole and with its own pos (a store reads "the event that holds pos, or the first one after it"). The host takes it without the units it has (Verdict::Accept { skip } of ww_stream::rx::Receiver): a typed PositionedStream gives it with pos and units of the new part, the value is the whole item. The same holds for ranges the host had before a resume (they may end inside an event). An event that is all had is a duplicate.

On USB the link doesn't lose, so Resend never happens and an Ack is a few bytes every half window: a reliable stream costs almost nothing more than a counted one there, and adds backfill and bounded host memory.

items.title: Credit sinks on the wire
items.text:
A credit sink is its own resource kind (ApiItemKind::FlowSink { ty, flow: FlowControl::Credit } in ww_self), so turning a plain sink into a credit sink is an API break: its writes change. It speaks the streams' protocol the other way round: the host is the sender, the device the receiver, with the same Ack, Resend and Query. The state machines are ww_stream::sink::SinkCredit (device) and ww_stream::sink::SinkTx (host, sans-IO), both driven by generated code and the host runtime.

Positions count units, named by the host: one per item by default, the bytes of the payload on a byte sink, or what user code says (send_units), at least one per item, so an empty item takes a position too. Grants count bytes of items as written, the serialized value of each write, since what runs out on the device is its buffer.

Each write is its own request kind: RequestKind::SinkWrite { pos: UVlq32, data: TailBytes } for an item of one unit, exactly as long as a plain Write of the same data in every request (a variant of its own costs nothing, a flag for the units would cost a byte whenever the discriminant ends a byte), and SinkWriteUnits { units: UVlq64, pos, data } otherwise. pos is the position of the item's first unit in the session, modulo 2^28 (see below): 1 byte for the first 128 units of a session, 2 up to 16 Ki, 3 up to 2 Mi, never more than 4. The sideband messages carry the rest:

Message Direction Meaning StreamOpen { resume: Some(StreamCursor { session, pos }) } host → device opens the host's session: a new one at 0, or its own again StreamOpened { session, live_from, capacity, .. } device → host the answer: where the device is in that session (a full u64 position) and its buffer in bytes Ack { have, backfill: None, grant } device → host every unit before have accepted in order; the host may have up to grant bytes in flight beyond them Query { sent, backfill: None } host → device "I have sent up to unit sent, where are you?", answered with Ack or Resend Resend { from, grant } device → host writes from unit from on were lost: send again from there (an item boundary), with up to grant bytes in flight Close both the host ends the session; from the device: it has no session for a write (rebooted, or closed), open again

All of them carry the whole state, so losing one is harmless: the next one, or the answer to the next query, replaces it. Positions in Ack, Query and Resend are UVlq64, holding values below 2^28 for sinks.

  1. The host names the session (random, never 0, or picked by user code) and opens it with its cursor. The device keeps a session it is in: the same session again (a reconnect, a repeated or late duplicate open on UDP) changes nothing and answers where it is; any other session starts at 0. It answers with StreamOpened, then an Ack with the grant. The host takes in sideband only after the answer, so an Ack before it is never mistaken for one of an earlier session.
  2. A device answering behind what the host had acknowledged in that session has lost it (a reboot): the host reports it (StreamError::SinkSessionLost) and user code decides. One answering ahead of what was sent is a host bug, except for a restarted host that opens with a saved cursor: it continues from where the device is.
  3. The host sends an item while the bytes in flight plus its length stay within the grant, and while at most MAX_WINDOW units are in flight, keeping a copy of everything not acknowledged for a resend.
  4. The device counts accepted units (have), accepted bytes and bytes it freed (consumed, e.g. written to flash); its byte limit is freed + capacity. When the limit has moved by at least threshold since the last grant, it sends a new Ack: a large threshold means few acknowledgements over a slow link, a small one keeps the link full.
  5. When the host is out of credit and nothing arrives for query_interval, it sends Query (and the open again when it wasn't answered). This recovers from a lost Ack or answer, from a device that freed less than threshold, and finds lost data at the end of a transfer. flush() sends Query and waits until have == sent.
  6. Close ends the session on the device; a later write there answers Close once, and the host opens its session again, nothing lost. A read on the sink returns its StreamStatus (open, session, position, bytes buffered, capacity).

On a lossy medium (UDP, LoRa, LTE-M) the device accepts a write only at pos == have: one before it is a duplicate from a resend and is dropped; one after it means something was lost, so it is dropped too and the device sends Resend, once per gap. A Query { sent } with sent > have means writes were lost after the last one that arrived; the device answers with Resend instead of Ack. On Resend the host goes back to from and sends everything again from its copy (go-back-N). Requests are processed in order, so when the device sees a Query, everything sent before it has arrived or is lost; an Ack never rewinds the host, the rest may still be in flight.

items.title: Positions wrap at 256 MiB
items.text:
Both sides count positions in u64, so a session has no size limit. On the wire a position is sent modulo 2^28 (ww_stream::sink::POS_MODULUS, wire_pos()), the most a UVlq32 holds in 4 bytes, and the receiver takes the full position nearest to the one it expects (extend_pos(): from 2^27 behind it to 2^27 ahead, serial number arithmetic as in TCP). A value of 2^28 or more is no position: the device drops such a write (SinkVerdict::Invalid), the host ignores such an event.

That reads every position right as long as it is less than 2^27 away from what the receiver expects. The bound keeps it so, in two parts: what the host has in flight never exceeds the device's buffer in bytes, at most ww_stream::sink::MAX_WINDOW (64 MiB, a quarter of the modulus), and never more than MAX_WINDOW units either, which the host enforces since it names the units; an item of more is refused. SinkCredit::new and sized_for refuse a larger buffer (a compile error in a const), try_sized_for and set_capacity return SinkCreditError::BufferTooLarge. One window on either side of the reference takes half the modulus; the other half is the margin for a late packet, a duplicate held back on UDP. Such a packet looks like a write from ahead (a gap, answered with a Resend) only when it arrives more than 64 Mi units late, and like the expected write only when exactly a multiple of 256 Mi units late: far beyond how long a datagram lives on a network. Ordered links (USB, RTT, WebSocket) never deliver a late packet at all.

The modulus is the same on every link and fixed by the protocol: nothing is announced at the open, there is nothing to configure.

items.title: Sending: producers, the event loop and priorities
items.text:
A ww_stream::tx::Reliable is one state: the producer pushes events into it, whether a host is there or not, and the event loop reads the next event out of it and sends it. Shared between tasks, it sits behind the firmware's async mutex, held for a push or a store read only, never while the link is busy, so a slow link never stalls a producer.

Generated code drives it: stream_data_ser().<name>_push(..) pushes, the server's poll_streams sends and the dispatcher feeds it the host's sideband (Reliable streams). Underneath, and for a device without generated code, it is:

use ww_stream::{store::RamRing, sched::Priority, tx::{Reliable, Pushed}, Run};

let mut samples: Reliable<RamRing<{ 256 * 1024 }>> = Reliable::new(RamRing::new()).priority(Priority::Low);

// producer: units and time given here, nothing in the item type
if samples.push(&block_bytes, sets, Some(t)).await? == Pushed::Lost { /* counted, reported to the host */ }
samples.lost(dropped_sets); // the producer's own ring overflowed: goes into the next event's `lost`

// event loop: what may go out now, the host's Ack / Resend, a Query when the host went silent
if let Some(ev) = samples.next_event(Run::Live, &mut buf).await? { /* send ev.head and ev.item */ }
samples.on_host_sideband(&sideband).await?;
if let Some(query) = samples.poll_query(now_ms) { /* send it */ }

ww_stream::tx::Counted is the same for counted streams, without a store: head(units, t) returns the head of the next event (None while no host has the stream open: the units count as lost), lost(units) counts drops, unsent(&head) turns an event that couldn't be sent into lost units.

With several streams, ww_stream::sched::Scheduler decides which one sends next: by priority class (High, Normal, Low, set by the device, not the API), the live run before the backfill run within a class, round-robin between streams of one class, up to a byte budget per turn so that requests are read in between. A device puts its log stream above a bulk ADC stream, a logger the other way round. Plain streams write directly and are not scheduled: data that needs a priority is counted or reliable.

On the host, ww_stream::rx::Receiver takes each event's head (on_item) and returns a Verdict: accept (with the gaps before it, each with its run, position, size and cause: Device, Link, Store or Host), duplicate, already had, late or out of order; poll(now_ms) returns the next Ack or Resend to send. It runs in the client's event loop behind every PositionedStream, see Counted and reliable streams on the host.

items.title: The ww_stream crate
items.text:
no_std, sans-IO: generated code (or a test) feeds the state machines what arrived and sends what they return, and passes the time in milliseconds where timing matters. The wire types live in ww_client_server::stream.

Module What Used by tx Counted, Reliable: sender state machines (runs, credit, go-back-N, sessions) device rx Receiver: in order per run, gaps by cause, duplicates, Ack timing host store StreamStore, RamRing device sched Scheduler: which stream sends next, by priority device counters StreamCnt (cnt instance counters with the cnt feature), TxStats device

The protocol is tested with a seeded simulation of a lossy, duplicating and reordering link with reconnects and resumes (ww_stream/src/tests/sim.rs, more seeds with SIM_SEEDS=20000).

items.title: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams
items.text:
A plain stream! sends each item once and forgets it: nothing tells the host that an item is missing, and nothing is kept for a host that is slow or gone. That is right for a latest-value stream (a motor controller's state at 1 kHz, where an old value is worthless), and wrong for measured data, logs and monitors, where the host must know exactly what it didn't get, or must get everything.

WireWeaver has three delivery kinds for device → host streams:

plain counted reliable Position in each event – yes yes Data the device dropped reported exactly – yes yes Link losses, duplicates, reordering detected – yes yes, and repaired Device timestamp per event – optional optional Acknowledged, resent on loss – – yes Kept while the host is slow or gone, sent when it is back – – while the device's store has room Latest values first after a reconnect, the backlog beside them – – yes Extra bytes per event 0 1-8, plus units, lost, t when present the same Device state none a few counters counters and a store

Item types carry none of this: positions, loss counts and the time of the first unit are in a small head the framework puts in front of every event, so a SampleBlock stays pure data (an item may add a time of its own, such as when a UART chunk's last byte arrived).

This page explains what counted and reliable streams guarantee. How to declare them is in Streams, the device's handlers and producers and the host's PositionedStream in Counted and reliable streams, the bytes on the wire and the acknowledgement protocol in Stream protocol.

items.title: Where stream data gets lost
items.text:
From a producer on the device to user code on the host:

 producer ──► device buffer ──► event loop ──► framer ──► medium ──► host transport ──► event loop ──► stream queue ──► user code
 (DMA, ISR)   (user's ring)     (ww_device)               (USB..)    (nusb, socket)     (client)      (per stream)
  • The producer's buffer overflows: a producer can't wait, so it drops data. That happens on every medium, when the stream's rate is above what the link moves, while the device's event loop is busy (a flash erase, a long handler), and while no host is connected.
  • The medium loses it, depending on the transport (below).
  • The link goes down: whatever was in buffers on the way is gone, and whatever the producer makes until the host is back.
  • The host's queue is full, when user code doesn't read.
Medium The medium itself Where losses happen USB bulk / interrupt CRC and retries in hardware, flow control by NAK: no loss the producer's buffer, unplug, device reset, USB suspend, host process exit RTT RAM rings, no corruption; a chunk that doesn't fit is retried, then the link goes down the producer's buffer (a probe polls at its own pace), detach UDP datagrams lost, duplicated, reordered; a message split across datagrams is dropped whole when a piece is lost any datagram, the producer's buffer, link down WebSocket TCP: no loss while connected, backpressure blocks the device the producer's buffer, what is in flight when the connection drops In-process none the producer's buffer

Counted streams make every one of these losses visible, with its size and place. Reliable streams also repair link losses and keep data on the device while it has room.

Choose by what a missing piece costs:

  • plain: the latest value is all that matters, and counting costs more than it tells;
  • counted: measured data, telemetry over UDP: gaps are acceptable, but must be shown where they are;
  • reliable: logs, monitors whose protocol decoders can't recover from a gap, data loggers that collect while no host is connected.

The kind is part of the API, visible in introspection (ApiItemKind::StreamFn { delivery, .. }), so it is chosen in the API crate. How much a reliable stream keeps, and where, is the device's choice: one device keeps 256 KB in RAM, another days of data on an SD card, behind the same API.

items.title: Positions and units
items.text:
A counted or reliable stream counts units from the start of its session, as a u64. What a unit is, the stream's documentation says, and the device says how many units each item has when it sends it:

Stream Unit An item of… …has units UART receive byte 37 bytes 37 I2C monitor transaction 12 transactions 12 ADC samples sample set (one sample of every channel) 1 536 bytes, 4 channels × 12 bit 256 a status stream item one value 1

Each event carries the position of its first unit (pos) and its number of units (units). The next event starts at pos + units + lost:

  • lost: units the device dropped right before this event (producer overflow, store full, no host). It explains a jump of pos exactly and says the gap is the device's.
  • A jump of pos that lost doesn't explain is a link loss (UDP): the host knows exactly how many units are missing, though not their content. A reliable stream gets them resent.
  • An event that starts before what the host expects is a duplicate or a late one: the host drops it and counts it.

The host never counts units of an item: it only compares positions, so units are whatever the device says (an ADC block's bytes don't tell its sample sets without the sample format). Counting units rather than items keeps every position exact: a protocol decoder can say "the frame starts at byte 4711 of this capture", and a gap of 60 000 bytes says how much is missing even when the device dropped raw bytes before they ever became items.

Positions are 64-bit because a store can be big: a 32 GB SD card holds 2³⁵ bytes of a byte stream within one session. On the wire a position costs only the bytes it needs (below), and it is never truncated, so the host never has to guess its high bits.

items.title: Sessions, cursors and resuming
items.text:
A session is one run of a stream with one meaning of its positions, numbered by the device (session: u32, for example a boot counter combined with an open counter). A cursor names a point in it:

pub struct StreamCursor { pub session: UVlq32, pub pos: UVlq64 }
  • A session starts when the host opens the stream, or when the device starts it by itself (a logger that samples from power-on). Positions start at 0.
  • It ends when the stream is opened again (the units may mean something else now), or when the device's store is erased. It does not end when the link goes down, nor, with a store that survives reboots, on a reboot.
  • Opening can carry a cursor: a resume. The device answers with StreamOpened { session, oldest, live_from, resume_from }:
    • same session, cursor still in the store: the backlog starts at the cursor, nothing is lost;
    • same session, cursor older than the store keeps: the backlog starts at the oldest event kept, the units before it are reported lost (cause Store);
    • another session: the old one has ended, the host starts with the new one.
  • Counted streams resume too. They keep nothing, but the device keeps counting while the host is away, so after a reconnect the first event's lost says exactly what the host missed.

A host that saves data also saves the cursor with it, and resumes from it after a restart: with explicit acknowledgements (below), nothing is lost even when the host crashes between receiving data and saving it.

Credit sinks, the other direction, have sessions and cursors too, with the roles swapped: the host sends, so the host names the session, and the device's position says how far it accepted. A sink continues after disconnect().keep_streams() and Commander::resume_streams() from where the device is, and a restarted host continues from a saved Sink::cursor() with <sink>_resume(cursor); a device that lost the session is reported (StreamError::SinkSessionLost). See credit sinks.

items.title: Latest values while backfilling
items.text:
A resumed reliable stream has two runs of positions, each delivered in order:

  • the live run starts at the newest event the device has (live_from), so a slow stream shows its latest value at once instead of after its next event, and goes on with everything new;
  • the backfill run goes from the resume point up to live_from.

The device sends live events first, and backfill events with whatever capacity the link has left. A data logger with six hours on its SD card shows its current readings on a dashboard as soon as the laptop connects, while the backlog arrives beside them; when the live data alone fills the link, the backlog waits in the store and nothing is lost. When the backfill run reaches live_from it ends, and the runs are one again.

Every event is sent once, and acknowledgements stay cumulative: one position per run. On the host each event says which run it belongs to, so a dashboard reads the live run, a recorder takes both and writes by position. While a backfill runs, acknowledged live events stay in the store until the backfill passes them.

items.title: Acknowledgements
items.text: A reliable stream's host acknowledges what it has, cumulatively per run, and grants the device a window of bytes in flight (4 MiB by default, what the host queues for the stream). A host that doesn't read stops granting: the device stops sending and keeps the data in its store, so the host's memory stays bounded. A gap (UDP) is asked for again from its first unit, and the device goes back and resends from there (go-back-N). Data counts as received when user code takes it, or with AckMode::Explicit only when user code confirms it, for example after writing it to disk. On USB the link doesn't lose, so an acknowledgement is a few bytes every half window. The messages and timeouts: Acknowledgements and resends.

items.title: Stores
items.text:
What a reliable stream keeps lives in a store, a ww_stream::store::StreamStore the device picks per stream: RamRing in RAM, PersistentRamRing in RAM that survives a soft reset, LogStore on an SD card or NOR flash that survives reboots and power cuts. When a store is full it drops the newest events (FullPolicy::DropNewest, the default) or the oldest (DropOldest); either way the units are counted and reported to the host as lost. See Stream stores.

Events are stored as they are sent, head included, so a resent event is bit-identical to the first send: its timestamp is the device's time when the data was made, never when it was sent. A reboot restarts the device's clock; the first event after one carries the new clock epoch in HeadExt::clock_epoch, so the host can tell the two timelines apart.

With several reliable streams, the device sends by priority class (High, Normal, Low, set by the firmware, not the API), live data before backlog within a class, see Sending.

items.title: Counting
items.text:
Every sending stream keeps TxStats (stats()): units sent and resent, lost by cause (producer, store full, no host), bytes acknowledged, resend requests, overruns. With the cnt feature it also counts into typed cnt instance counters, one set per stream, named by the firmware, so cnt tui shows per stream where data went:

use ww_stream::counters::StreamCnt;

static ADC_SAMPLES_CNT: cnt::Counters<StreamCnt> = cnt::counters!(StreamCnt, adc_samples);
let samples = Reliable::new(RamRing::<{ 256 * 1024 }>::new()).counters(&ADC_SAMPLES_CNT);

The host's receiver (ww_stream::rx::Receiver) keeps RxStats with the same causes: received, lost on the device, on the link and in the store, duplicates, late, out of order.

items.title: Timestamps
items.text:
t in the head is the device time of the event's first unit, a ww_si::Second in the storage the device's timer gives cheaply: Second { Micro, U32 } (5 bytes, wraps every 71.6 minutes, the host unwraps it) on most MCUs. A device uses one clock for every stream, so items of different streams line up.

The client unwraps every device time it gives out by one rule, for event heads, the items of batched streams and observe updates alike: a time in wrapping storage (U32 µs, U16 ms, ..) comes as a U64 in the same prefix that counts on across wraps, taking each time as the one closest to the previous with the same low bits (ww_si::Unwrapper without an anchor). That holds while consecutive times are less than half a wrap apart (35.8 minutes for U32 µs, 32.7 s for U16 ms); the device may change prefix and storage on the way. Each stream handle (each half of a split) and each observe level counts on its own, and the count starts over after a disconnect (the device may have rebooted) and at a new clock epoch in a head's ext. U64 and float times come as they are.

Three ways to timestamp, chosen per stream:

Granularity How Cost For Per anchor t in every N-th event (e.g. every 50 ms); the host interpolates by position and the configured rate ~5 B per anchor fixed-rate streams: ADC, logic analyzer Per event t in every event 5 B per event UART chunks (a chunk ends when the line goes idle, so t is its first byte), sensor readings Per item t per event, and each item's offset from it inside the item, in the head's unit, as a Series column (delta of delta) about 1.2 B per item for jittered ~100 µs gaps, 1.9 B for random 20-2020 µs gaps, 0.23 B for a regular rate monitors: I2C transactions, GPIO edges

Two examples:

  • An ADC at 500 kS/s, 12-bit packed, one channel (750 KB/s): in blocks of 1 024 samples (1.5 KiB), event header and head take 0.7 %, a t in every event 0.3 % more. Per-sample timestamps would take 15 % and tell nothing, the rate is fixed: use blocks of about 1 KiB and an anchor every 50 ms.
  • An I2C monitor at 1 MHz with about 20 000 transactions per second, in chunks of 32: 625 events per second of about 15 bytes of header, head and t (9.4 KB/s), plus per-transaction time at ~1.5 B each (30 KB/s), against ~10 bytes of data per transaction (200 KB/s).

items.title: With each transport
items.text:
Medium Counted Reliable USB, RTT, WebSocket, in-process device drops and link-down gaps exact nothing lost while the store has room; backfill after a reconnect, live first; bounded host memory UDP link losses, duplicates and reordering detected too go-back-N repairs them; acknowledgements carry the whole state, so losing one is harmless CAN, UART (planned transports) as UDP as UDP; keep events small, a message split across frames is lost whole

Resending is per stream, not in the link layer: a link that resends would hold latest-value streams back behind a lost datagram, couldn't keep data across a reconnect or a reboot, and wouldn't know about data the device dropped.

items.title: Stream stores
items.text:
A reliable stream (Stream delivery) keeps every event it sends until the host acknowledges it, so it can send it again after a loss and send the backlog after a reconnect. Where these events are kept is a store, a ww_stream::store::StreamStore the device picks for each stream: it is the S of the stream's ww_stream::tx::Reliable<S> state (Reliable streams). The API doesn't change with the store: the same stream can keep 256 KB in RAM on one device and 32 GB on an SD card on another.

Store Where Survives Feature RamRing<N> N bytes of RAM host reconnects always there PersistentRamRing<N> N bytes of .uninit RAM soft resets (fault → reset), not power cuts persistent-ram LogStore<M, BUF> SD card, NOR flash reboots and power cuts log-store (+ sdmmc / nor-flash)

All keep events as they go on the wire, head included, so a resent event is bit-identical: its timestamp is the device's time when the data was made, not when it was sent.

When a store is full, it does what its FullPolicy says:

  • DropNewest (default): the new event is refused (PushError::Full), the sender counts its units as lost and reports them in the next event's lost. What is kept stays contiguous.
  • DropOldest: the oldest events are forgotten to make room, a ring of the most recent data. Their units are counted in StoreState::dropped_units.

Either way the host learns exactly how much is missing and where.

items.title: RAM: RamRing
items.text:
use ww_stream::store::{FullPolicy, RamRing};

static SAMPLES: StaticCell<RamRing<{ 256 * 1024 }>> = StaticCell::new();
let store = SAMPLES.init(RamRing::new().with_policy(FullPolicy::DropOldest));

Each event takes its item, its encoded head and 21 bytes (RECORD_OVERHEAD).

items.title: RAM across a soft reset: PersistentRamRing
items.text:
A RamRing whose bytes sit in RAM the startup code leaves alone, so they are still there after a soft reset: a HardFault or panic handler that resets the chip (SCB::sys_reset) doesn't take the last logs before the crash with it. The next boot takes the events up again and the host gets them when it connects. A power cut loses them; RAM after a power-on holds garbage, which is never taken for events.

ww_stream = { version = "0.5", features = ["persistent-ram"] }

use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use ww_stream::store::{FullPolicy, PersistentRamRing, RamArea};
use ww_stream::tx::Reliable;

// cortex-m-rt leaves `.uninit.*` alone at boot
#[unsafe(link_section = ".uninit.ww_logs")]
static mut LOG_AREA: MaybeUninit<RamArea<4096>> = MaybeUninit::uninit();

// once, at boot
let area = unsafe { RamArea::from_uninit(&mut *core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(LOG_AREA)) };
let store = PersistentRamRing::attach(area).with_policy(FullPolicy::DropOldest);
// `store.recovery().formatted`: nothing was kept (a power-on), a new ring was started
let mut logs = Reliable::new(store);
// the ring from before the reset: continue its session and positions
logs.continue_stored_session();

Where the area goes is the firmware's business, and differs per chip: it must be RAM the startup code neither zeroes nor copies into (.bss, .data), nor a firmware's own RAM init (a loop zeroing a whole SRAM bank at boot takes the area with it). With cortex-m-rt, a .uninit.* section is enough. The same area must not be used for anything else, and only one store may be attached to it.

items.title: What it keeps
items.text: The same as a LogStore across a reboot: session, positions, the released position, dropped_units, and a new clock epoch per boot (clock_epoch(), 0 for a new ring), which the first event pushed after it carries in HeadExt::clock_epoch unless the sender set it already. state().persistent is true.

items.title: How it checks the RAM
items.text:
The area holds two 64-byte header slots and the ring. After every change (push, release, reset) the ring's header is written to the slot not written last, with a magic, the layout version, N, a sequence number and a CRC-32C; at boot, the good slot with the higher sequence number wins. A record goes into free room first, and old records a push drops to make room are forgotten by a slot written before the new record goes over them, so a reset at any byte leaves the state before or after the change, never a mix. Every record has its own CRC-32C, checked at boot too: if something wrote over the area before the reset, the ring is cut before the first bad record (recovery().truncated_bytes) and the stream continues after it.

The host tests (ww_stream/src/tests/persistent_ram.rs) carry the area's image over a simulated reset (RamArea::image(), load_image()), fault a push, release and reset after every byte written, and attach to random garbage, flipped header bits and records written over.

items.title: Sizing
items.text: Each event takes its item, its encoded head and 25 bytes (PERSISTENT_RECORD_OVERHEAD); the area is N bytes and 128 for the slots (RamArea::<N>::SIZE). Every change also writes a 64-byte slot; a push computes two CRCs (over the slot and over the record).

items.title: SD card or flash: LogStore
items.text:
LogStore is a log on a block device that keeps a stream's data across reboots and power cuts: a field logger keeps sampling to its SD card while no host is there, reboots, and the host still gets everything when it connects.

ww_stream = { version = "0.5", features = ["sdmmc"] }      # or "nor-flash"

use ww_stream::store::log::{LogConfig, LogStore, SdMedium};
use ww_stream::store::FullPolicy;
use ww_stream::tx::Reliable;

// blocks 2048.. of the card are the log's, the rest is free for a FAT partition
let medium = SdMedium::new(sd_card, 2048, num_blocks - 2048);
let config = LogConfig { segment_size: 64 * 1024, policy: FullPolicy::DropNewest };
// session 1 is used only when the card holds no log yet
let store: LogStore<_, 512> = LogStore::mount(medium, config, 1).await?;
let mut samples = Reliable::new(store);
// a log from before the reboot: continue its session and positions
samples.continue_stored_session();

On NOR flash, wrap an embedded-storage-async NorFlash (a QSPI chip, or a partition of the MCU's own flash) in NorMedium(flash); segments are then a multiple of the flash's erase size. Any other storage can implement LogMedium: its write and erase unit sizes, whether it needs erasing before a write, read, write and erase.

items.title: What it keeps
items.text:
• Positions and session: after a reboot state() gives back the session and next, the position the stream continues from, so the host sees one session across the reboot, not a new stream.
  • Released position: what the host acknowledged is freed. It is saved now and then, so after a reboot a few acknowledged events may be sent again; the host drops them as duplicates. Events not acknowledged are never lost.
  • Clock epochs: the device's clock restarts with a reboot, so each mount starts a new clock epoch (clock_epoch()), and the first event pushed after a mount carries it in HeadExt::clock_epoch, unless the sender set it already. The host maps each epoch to real time, or shows "before reboot N".

items.title: Power cuts
items.text:
A push writes its record before it returns. If the power fails during a push, at most that record is lost: on the next mount the store finds the end of the log and counts a record it finds cut short in recovery().torn_records. Positions continue after the last whole record; the cut one was never sent, so the host never saw it.

This holds for a power cut at any write or erase, which the tests check one by one on a simulated SD card and NOR flash (ww_stream/src/tests/log_store.rs). On an SD card it relies on a 512-byte block write either happening or not, as SD cards do; on NOR flash nothing is assumed about a cut write.

items.title: Sizing
items.text:
The log is a ring of segments of segment_size bytes, after two small superblock slots at the start:

  • A segment is the unit of room: it is freed once every event in it is acknowledged (or dropped), and the rest of a segment stays empty when the next event doesn't fit, and on every reboot (a new segment starts the new epoch). Make segments several times the biggest event.
  • Use many segments: a mount reads the superblock, at most a few segment headers and the last segment, and a read finds its segment by a binary search over the headers, so a big card mounts as fast as a small one. 64 KiB segments on a 32 GB card give half a million.
  • BUF is the size of the two buffers the store keeps, a multiple of the medium's write size: 512 for an SD card.

Each event takes its item, its encoded head (see StreamHead) and a 12-byte record header, rounded up to 4 bytes on an SD card or to the write size on NOR flash.

LogStore::mount returns LogError::Geometry when the medium holds a log with another segment size or medium size; LogStore::format starts a new, empty log on it.

items.title: Testing with a simulated medium
items.text: With the std feature, SimSd and SimNor are an SD card and a NOR flash in RAM. cut_power_at(n) makes the n-th write or erase the one the power fails in (it is torn, every later call fails), and image() / from_image() carry the content over a reboot, so a device's own power-cut tests run on the host.

items.title: Other stores
items.text:
Any storage can hold a reliable stream by implementing StreamStore (for a block device, implementing LogMedium for LogStore is usually less work):

pub trait StreamStore {
    type Error;
    /// Append an event, head and item bytes as they go on the wire.
    async fn push(&mut self, head: &StreamHead, item: &[u8]) -> Result<(), PushError<Self::Error>>;
    /// Copy the event at `pos`, or the first one after it, into `buf`.
    async fn read<'b>(&mut self, pos: u64, buf: &'b mut [u8]) -> Result<Option<StoredEvent<'b>>, Self::Error>;
    /// Events before `pos` are acknowledged and may go.
    async fn release(&mut self, pos: u64) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
    /// Session, oldest and newest kept positions, next position, bytes used and capacity, persistent or not.
    fn state(&self) -> StoreState;
    /// A new session: drop everything, positions from 0.
    async fn reset(&mut self, session: u32) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
}

A full store either refuses the push with PushError::Full (drop newest) or forgets its oldest events and moves state().oldest on, counting their units in dropped_units (drop oldest).

items.title: Streams
items.text:
A stream carries a sequence of values in one direction. Naming is from the device's point of view: a stream goes out of the device to the host (stream!), a sink goes into the device from the host (sink!).

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    stream!(button: ButtonEvent);
    stream!(uart_rx: [u8]);
    sink!(uart_tx: [u8]);
    sink!(leds: Vec<LedState>);
}

Any type the SerDes system supports works as a stream item. Items keep their boundaries: each value sent arrives as one value, in order, even when several are packed into one packet on the way. Sending [1, 2, 3], [4], [5, 6] on uart_rx gives the same three slices on the other end. A byte item ([u8], Vec<u8>, or MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, N> to bound it) is sent as is, without a length prefix.

Streams and sinks come in kinds that differ in what they promise about delivery:

Kind Declared as What is guaranteed plain stream stream!(name: T) nothing: items go out once, a lost one is gone unnoticed; the latest value wins counted stream #[counted] stream!(..), #[stream(T, counted)] fn .. every item has a position: the host learns exactly how much was lost, where and why reliable stream #[reliable] stream!(..), #[stream(T, reliable)] fn .. counted, acknowledged and resent; kept in a store on the device while the host is slow or gone plain sink sink!(name: T) nothing: writes are not acknowledged, the device keeps up or drops credit sink #[credit] sink!(name: T) flow control: the host never sends more than the device has room for, lost writes are resent

The kind is part of the API and visible in introspection, so it is chosen in the API crate. This page shows the common case, plain streams and sinks, and what every kind shares. The others have pages of their own: Counted and reliable streams (what they guarantee: Stream delivery) and Credit sinks and sideband.

items.title: Stream functions
items.text:
A stream is opened by calling it, like a method: the host sends its arguments, the device decides whether to start, and answers with a result. A stream that takes arguments or returns a result is declared as a stream function, a trait fn with a #[stream(ItemType)] or #[stream(ItemType, counted | reliable)] attribute:

#[ww_trait]
trait Adc {
    /// Sample sets at `config.rate`; unit: sample set
    #[errors(BadRate, Common(InUse))]
    #[stream(SampleBlock<'i>, reliable)]
    fn samples(config: StreamConfig) -> Result<StreamActual, AdcError<'i>>;

    /// Bytes as they arrive on the line; unit: byte
    #[counted]
    stream!(rx: [u8]);
}

stream!(name: T) is the short form of a stream function without arguments and result, #[counted] / #[reliable] above it choose its kind. The return type is either nothing or a Result<A, E>: Ok opens the stream and gives the host A (e.g. the rate the device actually picked), Err answers with the error and leaves the stream as it was. Calling an open stream again opens it again, a new session, e.g. with another configuration.

#[errors(..)] above a stream function lists the variants of E opening it returns, as on methods (see Errors); a stream! has no result, so no list. #[optional] / #[optional(group)] lets a device leave a stream or sink out (see Optional items). Counted streams document their unit (byte, sample set, transaction), the doc comments above do so with unit: ...

items.title: Device side
items.text:
ww api scaffold <api_crate> prints every handler and state field a server needs, with the right signatures for the ww_codegen! options (see ww api). For a stream named samples they are:

Handler Plain Counted Reliable Called fn samples(&mut self, cx, args..) -> RpcResult<R> ✓ ✓ ✓ the host opens the stream fn close_samples(&mut self, cx) ✓ ✓ ✓ the host closes it fn sideband_samples(&mut self, cx, sideband) -> Option<StreamSideband> ✓ other sideband from the host, see Sideband fn stream_samples(&mut self) -> &mut Counted / &mut Reliable<S> ✓ ✓ whenever generated code needs the stream's state fn new_stream_session(&mut self) -> u32 (one per server) ✓ ✓ a host opens a counted or reliable stream

All handlers get cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut, Medium> (impl BlockingEventOut for use_async = false); streams in arrays get their index chain after it. The open handler answers right away: Ready(..) with the result, Unimplemented refuses it; a deferred answer is not supported for an open. How counted and reliable streams keep their state and send is in Counted and reliable streams.

items.title: Plain streams
items.text:
The generated stream_data_ser() has, for every plain stream, <name>_send(&value, out) (async), <name>_send_blocking(&value, out), and <name>(&value, scratch) returning the serialized event. out is the cx of a handler, or server.sink() of the ww_device server anywhere in the event loop (in the snippets, server is the ww_device server and state the struct the API is implemented on):

impl ServerState {
    async fn button(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        self.button_open = true;
        Ready(())
    }

    async fn close_button(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) {
        self.button_open = false;
    }
}

// from a handler, goes out before its reply
server_impl::stream_data_ser().button_send(&event, cx).await?;
// from the event loop
if state.button_open {
    server_impl::stream_data_ser().uart_rx_send(&chunk, &mut server.sink()).await?;
}

Nothing stops the device from sending to a plain stream no host opened: the host drops events no handle waits for. Keeping track of whether a host listens is up to the open and close handlers.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
Generated clients have one function per stream. A stream function prepares the open; .call().await (or .blocking_call()) sends it and returns the stream handle, together with the function's result when it has one:

// stream!(button: ButtonEvent): a plain stream, Stream<ButtonEvent>
let mut button = device.button().call().await?;
// a counted stream, PositionedStream<TailBytesOwned>
let mut rx = device.rx().call().await?;
// a fallible stream function: Result<(StreamActual, PositionedStream<..>), AdcError> inside the call's Result
let (actual, mut samples) = device.samples(config).call().await??;

Before .call(), the prepared open takes .with_timeout(..), .queue_bytes(..) (how much the host queues before it drops, plain and counted streams), .window(..) and .ack_mode(..) (reliable streams). Only what the device sends after the open reaches the handle; events before it are not buffered.

items.title: Plain streams: Stream<T>
items.text:
• recv() returns the next value, recv_blocking() and try_recv() (None when nothing is there yet) the same without async. They skip Connected and fail on a sideband event or a disconnect.
  • recv_any() (recv_any_blocking()) returns every event: TypedStreamEvent::Data(value), Sideband(..), Connected, Disconnected, Dropped { events, bytes }.
  • A byte stream (Stream<TailBytesOwned>) has recv_all_bytes(), collecting everything until the device sends Close, with _blocking and _timeout variants.
  • close() closes the stream on the device. Dropping the handle doesn't.

The host queues at most ClientConfig::stream_queue_bytes (4 MiB by default) of a stream's items when user code doesn't read; what comes beyond is dropped, counted in dropped() and reported once as Dropped.

Counted and reliable streams return a PositionedStream<T> instead, with positions, gaps and resuming, see Counted and reliable streams.

items.title: Sinks
items.text:
A sink is written by the host, one value per write:

// host
let mut leds = device.leds().await?;            // Sink<Vec<LedState>>, `leds_blocking()` without async
leds.send(vec![LedState::On, LedState::Off]).await?;
let mut tx = device.uart_tx().await?;           // Sink<TailBytesOwned>
tx.send_bytes(b"hello").await?;

send() / send_blocking() take a borrowed value, send_owned() an owned type (FooOwned), send_bytes() the bytes of a byte sink; try_send() (try_send_owned(), try_send_bytes()) returns Ok(false) instead of waiting, for GUIs and promise-style code.

On the device, each write calls write_<name>(cx, value); a byte sink gets the bytes as &TailBytes<'_>, a byte sink with a MaxLen bound refuses a longer write before the handler sees it:

fn write_uart_tx(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, data: &TailBytes<'_>) {
    if self.tx_ring.push_slice(data.0).is_err() {
        self.tx_dropped += 1; // the device can't push back on a plain sink
    }
}

A plain sink's writes are sent without a request id: the device sends nothing back, and the host doesn't wait. A plain sink needs no opening, send() works right away; open() and close() send the Open and Close sideband, which reach the device's sideband_<name> handler, for devices that want to know.

items.title: Flow control
items.text:
What keeps a fast side from overrunning a slow one depends on the kind:

  • Plain streams: nothing. The device sends what it has, the host queues up to stream_queue_bytes per stream and drops beyond it.
  • Counted streams: nothing slows the device down either, but every loss, on the device, on the link or in the host's queue, is reported with its size and place.
  • Reliable streams: the host grants the device a window of bytes in flight and acknowledges what it received; a host that doesn't read stops granting, and the device keeps the data in its store (see Acknowledgements and resends).
  • Plain sinks: the host's writes go through the client's bounded command queue (ClientConfig::cmd_queue_size), so a program can't outrun its own link; nothing tells it whether the device keeps up. A device that can't has to drop, or tell the host with its own sideband events.
  • Credit sinks: the device grants room in bytes and the host never sends more, see Credit sinks.

items.title: Arrays of streams
items.text:
Streams and sinks can be arrays, and sit in arrays of traits:

#[ww_trait]
trait Board {
    #[counted]
    stream!(adc[]: [u8]);
    ww_impl!(port[]: Port);
}

#[ww_trait]
trait Port {
    stream!(event: PinEvent);
}

Each index is its own stream: the host opens device.adc(2).call() or device.port(0).event().call(), and every device handler gets the index chain after cx (index_chain: [UNib32; 1]), as does stream_adc(index_chain). valid_indices_root_adc() says which indices exist. On the device, send through the same chain: stream_data_ser().adc_send(2, &mut state.adc_streams[2], &chunk, units, t, out) for the array itself, stream_data_ser().port(0).event_send(&event, cx) inside an array of traits.

Reliable streams can't be in arrays yet: poll_streams refuses them with a compile error.

items.title: Properties as streams
items.text: An ro or rw property sends its changes as stream data on its own path: stream_data_ser().<property>_send(&value, out) on the device, observe_<property>() on the host, a plain Stream<T>. See Observing properties, superseded by +observe for properties that have it.

items.title: More on streams
items.text:
• Counted and reliable streams: device state, producers, PositionedStream, resuming.
  • Stream delivery: what counted and reliable streams guarantee, sessions, timestamps.
  • Stream stores: where a reliable stream keeps its data (RAM, SD card, flash).
  • Credit sinks and sideband: flow control into the device, the sideband channel.
  • Stream protocol: the bytes on the wire, acknowledgements, the ww_stream crate.
  • Batching: a plain, counted or reliable stream of a series type can opt into sending samples in Series batches instead of one item per event.

items.title: Trait attachments
items.text:
Host code written for a reusable trait (a ww_gpio::Bank, a ww_dfu::BootControl) shouldn't need to know which device it talks to, under which path the trait sits there, or how the device is connected. An attachment is what such code takes instead of a device.

Every generated client struct, at every level of the API tree (the root struct itself, or the struct returned for a nested / array trait, whether it implements a global trait or a project-local one), gets a .attachment() method for free. It returns a wire_weaver_client::Attachment: a self-contained handle bundling the underlying Commander (already pointing at that exact resource path on that exact device), plus the source crate name + version and trait name of whatever trait lives there. Because it carries this identity, an Attachment can be handed to code that has never heard of the concrete device or its top-level API trait, as long as that code knows what to do with the global trait underneath.

examples/all_gpio/examples/high_level.rs is the reference for this pattern end-to-end:

let device = AllGpio::new().connect_blocking()?;

// get a global trait "attachment" point
let attachment = device.port(0).attachment();
// init a high-level, hand-written driver with better ergonomics than generated code
let mut bank = BankBlocking::new(attachment)?;

let bank_name = bank.name()?;
let mut pins = bank.all_pins()?;
for pin in &mut pins {
    println!("{}{}: {:?}", bank_name, pin.index(), pin.mode()?);
}

device.port(0) only exists because all_gpio_api::AllGpioApi happens to declare ww_impl!(port[]: ww_gpio::Bank): it is all_gpio-specific generated code. .attachment() erases that specificity: BankBlocking::new never sees AllGpio or AllGpioApi, only something that claims to be a ww_gpio::Bank. It checks trait_name() and source_crate() on the attachment and returns Error::IncompatibleTrait if they don't match, so it will refuse an attachment that isn't really a ww_gpio::Bank, whatever device or resource path it actually came from - that runtime check is what makes it safe to accept an attachment from arbitrary device APIs.

The ww_gpio_hl crate (in ww_stdlib/ww_gpio_hl) is the reference for the driver side of this pattern - a higher-level API built on top of plain generated code:

  • src/ww.rs defines small wrapper structs (BankClient, GpioClient) and invokes ww_impl! against ww_gpio::Bank / ww_gpio::Pin directly, with client = "trait_client". That generated code only depends on ww_gpio, never on all_gpio_api or any other specific device API crate, so it is written and generated exactly once and reused by every device that happens to expose a compatible bank somewhere.
  • src/blocking.rs builds ergonomic, stateful types on top of that (BankBlocking, FlexBlocking, PushPullOutputBlocking, InputBlocking, OpenDrainOutputBlocking), each one constructed straight from an Attachment (BankBlocking::new, FlexBlocking::new_ignore_mode / new_get_mode). src/promise.rs does the same for immediate-mode UI use (BankPromise, FlexPromise); src/asynchronous.rs is the same idea for async, but is currently an empty stub.

Put together, a single ww_gpio_hl dependency can drive the GPIO bank of any device - regardless of what its top-level API trait is called - as long as it implements ww_gpio::Bank somewhere in its resource tree; reaching it takes exactly one .attachment() call on the device's own generated client.

items.title: Attaching without generated client code
items.text:
.attachment() is only available because the device's own API crate was run through ww_codegen!, which is what generates device.port(0) (and every other accessor) in the first place. When that generated code is available, it is the convenient way to obtain an attachment.

Without it, DynClient::global_attachment(gid, trait_name) gives an attachment that addresses the trait by its crate's name and version instead of a path: the device finds the trait wherever it sits in its tree. That needs no code generated for the device, works whatever its API version, and is how ww dfu reboot reaches any device's ww_dfu::BootControl (see global trait addressing). It can't reach a trait under a resource array (port[]), since a global path has no index.

Finding such a trait's absolute path from the device's introspection data (ww_self) and building a path attachment from it, for arrays, is not implemented yet.

items.title: Traits
items.text:
A trait is a block of an API: a set of methods, properties, streams and nested traits. The API root itself is one (#[ww_api_root]), and ww_impl!(name: Trait) puts another trait into it, once or as an array. A trait can come from the same file, to group related items, or from another crate, to reuse an API many devices share, such as a GPIO bank or a firmware updater from the standard library.

#[ww_api_root]
trait MyDevice {
    ww_impl!(motor: MotorControl);   // a trait from this crate
    ww_impl!(gpio[]: ww_gpio::Bank); // an array of a trait from another crate
}

WireWeaver traits are written in Rust syntax but not implemented like Rust traits: ww_codegen! reads the trait from its source file and generates the server's dispatch and the client's functions. What #[ww_trait] leaves in place is a Rust trait of the same name that only describes the API, so that cargo doc and docs.rs show it, see In rustdoc below.

items.title: Grouping items
items.text:
A trait defined in the same file as the API root groups related items:

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    ww_impl!(motor_control: MotorControl);
    ww_impl!(led_control: LedControl);
}

#[ww_trait]
trait MotorControl {
    fn turn_on();
    fn turn_off();
}

#[ww_trait]
trait LedControl {
    fn led_on();
    fn set_brightness(value: f32);
}

On the server, handlers of nested items carry the trait item's name as a prefix (motor_control_turn_on), and the generated client reaches them through it (device.motor_control().turn_on()). On the wire, each level adds one index to an item's path (Resources addressing), so there are 4 paths here:

  1. [0, 0] - turn_on
  2. [0, 1] - turn_off
  3. [1, 0] - led_on
  4. [1, 1] - set_brightness

When every byte counts, keep the tree shallow and put the most used items first: indices 0..=7 take 4 bits on the wire.

TODO: splitting into multiple files

items.title: Reusing traits from other crates
items.text:
A trait published in a crate is defined once and implemented by many devices: GPIO banks, I2C, UART, firmware updates, logs, counters, board and firmware info, memory access, CAN bus and more are in the standard library. A device API puts such a trait in with ww_impl! and the trait's path; the crate providing it (ww_gpio here) is a normal Cargo dependency of the API crate, see examples/all_gpio_api:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait AllGpioApi {
    ww_impl!(port[]: ww_gpio::Bank);
    // and device specific items next to the common ones
}

Host code written for ww_gpio::Bank then works with any device that has a bank somewhere in its API, whatever the device, the path or the transport: see Trait attachments. A host can also call a trait by its crate's name and version instead of its path, on a device whose API it doesn't know, for example to reboot any device into its updater: see global trait addressing.

items.title: In rustdoc
items.text:
#[ww_trait] and #[ww_api_root] turn the trait into a Rust trait of the same name and visibility, with every resource and its doc comment, so an API crate's documentation on docs.rs or from cargo doc shows the whole API. Methods keep their signature, the other resources become functions returning a marker from wire_weaver::api_doc:

pub trait Uart {
    fn rx<'i>() -> Stream<RxChunk<'i>>;               // stream!(rx: RxChunk<'i>);
    fn tx() -> Sink<[u8]>;                            // sink!(tx: [u8]);
    fn configure(config: UartConfig) -> Result<UartConfig, Error>;
}
pub trait Bank {
    fn pin(index: UNib32) -> impl Pin;                // ww_impl!(pin[]: Pin);
}
pub trait Pin {
    fn pull() -> Property<Pull, Error>;               // property!(rw pull: Pull, Error);
}

Access mode, array index, flow control and #[since] are added as the last paragraph of each resource's docs. reserved! doesn't show up. The trait is never implemented, handlers are generated by ww_codegen! (see server side), but it can be linked from docs ([Uart], [Uart::rx]).

Because it is a real trait, the compiler checks it in the API crate: every type must be valid Rust (RefVec<'i, &'i str>, not RefVec<'i, str>, lifetimes written out), and a trait used from another crate through ww_impl! must be pub.

More: Trait attachments, host code for a reusable trait on any device.

items.title: Versioning
items.text:
An API's version is its crate's version, and the same goes for every trait and type: a #[ww_trait] or a data type from another crate is identified by that crate's name and version. ww_version::FullVersion carries both; codegen puts the API root's into a <ROOT_TRAIT>_FULL_GID constant (BLINKY_API_FULL_GID), which the device reports when a host connects.

On connection, a generated client checks the device's API crate name and version against its own and refuses an incompatible device with Error::IncompatibleDeviceProtocol. Compatible means SemVer-compatible: the same major version from 1.0 on, the same major and minor before it (Version::is_protocol_compatible). Within that range the evolution rules keep old and new talking: added methods, appended fields, new enum variants. The dynamic client, the ww CLI and Python take the device's API from its introspection data, so they don't check.

Reusable traits are found by their crate's name and version too, whatever the device's own API is, see global trait addressing. The types are on the ww_version page.

items.title: Everything Series: from one line to the bit layout
items.text:
Roman Isaikin, 18 October 2026

A motor controller measures its phase current 25 000 times a second. Written one value after another, 32 of those readings with their timestamps take 321 bytes. As a Series, the same 32 readings take 34. Nothing is thrown away, nothing is rounded, the reader gets back exactly what the device measured: the bytes were redundancy all along.

This article is the whole story of Series<T> in WireWeaver, in three parts. Basic is what it is, the one line that uses it and what it saves, including batched streams and observing every sample. Advanced is every knob: codec policies, quantities and autoranging, how it compares with ALP and with raw globals, sealing, budgets, the shared clock, Python, what it costs on a microcontroller, and how far it goes at a power converter's 400 kHz to 2 MHz. Nomicon is how the bits are laid out and how the encoder got six times faster. Read until you have what you need; the numbers below were measured on the running code (the one worked out from the layout says so), and each part links to the reference pages for the details.

Basic

items.title: Basic: sequences that shrink
items.text: What a Series is, the line that uses it, what it saves, and how streams and observed properties batch into one.

items.title: Values over time
items.text:
Most of what a device sends is a sequence of values over time: currents, voltages, temperatures, counters, encoder positions, timestamps. Consecutive values are close to each other, a timestamp grows by the same step every time, and the unit or range of a reading almost never changes. A Vec<T> doesn't know any of that: it writes every item in full.

Series<'i, T> is a list of T that does know. It writes the list column by column instead of item by item: all the timestamps, then all the units, then all the values, each column compressed on its own with the code that fits it best. A timestamp ticking at a fixed rate can cost nothing per item; a unit that doesn't change costs about 5 bits for the whole batch; a slowly moving reading costs a few bits per item instead of 4 bytes.

It is still shrink_wrap: zero-copy reading, no_std and no allocation on the device, and it evolves the way T does (a field appended to T later is skipped by an older reader).

items.title: One line
items.text:
Mark the item type with series and write the slice:

use shrink_wrap::prelude::*;
use shrink_wrap::series::{Series, SeriesOwned};
use ww_si::{Ampere, Second, Timed};

let items: Vec<Timed<Ampere>> = /* 32 currents with their times */;
let bytes = Series::new(&items).to_ww_bytes_owned()?; // that's the line

let back: Vec<Timed<Ampere>> = Series::<Timed<Ampere>>::from_ww_bytes(&bytes)?.iter().collect();
let owned = SeriesOwned::<Timed<Ampere>>::from_ww_bytes_owned(&bytes)?; // std: straight into a Vec

ww_si quantities and Timed<T> already have series; your own types get it in their derive:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, series)]
struct IvSample { v: Volt, i: Ampere }

A Series goes anywhere a Vec would: a method argument or return value, a property, a stream item, a field of another struct.

#[ww_trait]
trait Sequences {
    /// Voltage history with device time
    fn history() -> Series<'i, Timed<Volt>>;
    property!(rw stamps: Series<'i, u64>);
}

Structs, enums with or without data, Option, all integers, floats, bool, tuples and arrays are in, nested to any depth, and so are strings and byte lists, written as runs; which T has the exact list and the few types that aren't yet. One limit for strings: a Series carries them anywhere a Vec would, but a batched stream or observed property needs a size bound per item, and observe cells a fixed-size cell per value, which a string doesn't have (see strings and byte lists below).

items.title: What it saves
items.text:
The 32 currents from the top of the page: a motor phase current in mA as I32, around 5 A on a slow sine with a few mA of noise, one sample every 40 µs:

32 × Timed<Ampere> bytes per sample Vec<Timed<Ampere>> 321 10.0 Series, current stored as f32 104 3.3 Series, current as I32 mA 34 1.1

On recorded test signals (IvSample above, a voltage and a current, 100 items):

100 items Vec<T> smallest plain form Series steady (±1 mV, ±2 µA) 902 B 802 B 104 B noisy (slow sine + noise) 902 B 802 B 251 B range switches (µA ↔ mA for 40 items) 902 B 802 B 110 B

3 to 8 times smaller is the rule of thumb: 7.7x on a steady signal, 3.2x on a noisy one. A single item costs one byte more than plain (the column headers are paid once), two items are already smaller, and most of the gain is there by 32 items per batch, which is why 32 is the default batch size everywhere below.

items.title: Quantities: integers with a prefix
items.text:
One piece of advice comes out of every measurement: store integers with a prefix, not floats. A steady f32 voltage (100 values) is 136 B; the same signal as millivolts in a U16 is 45 B (noisy: 277 B against 82 B). The prefix sets the resolution, and noise below the resolution costs nothing; an f32 pays for every mantissa bit the ADC's noise touches.

That is exactly what a ww_si quantity is: an SI prefix and a number, usually an integer (a firmware typically enables I32, U32 and F32 storage). Ampere::milli(4980) is 4 980 mA, and the unit itself takes no bits. In a Series the prefix and the storage type are runs that cost a few bits per batch when they don't change, and the integer column carries only the changes.

A device may also change the prefix on the fly: µA while a current is small, mA once it grows. This is autoranging, and it costs almost nothing: at a prefix change the column starts over with a full value instead of a meaningless delta across the jump, and goes on compressing in the new range. On the motor demo's currents, ranging between µA and mA switched 528 times a second and still came out a little smaller than staying in µA (details in the Advanced part).

items.title: Batched streams: one word
items.text:
You rarely build a Series by hand for a live signal. Mark a stream batched and the device collects items into batches for you:

#[ww_trait]
trait Sensors {
    #[batched]
    stream!(readings: Sample);
}

On the device, push items wherever they come from, an interrupt included; the push is O(1) and takes no lock:

let ser = api_impl::stream_data_ser();
ser.readings_push(&mut self.readings_stream, sample, t);          // one item with its time
ser.readings_push_many(&mut self.readings_stream, t0, dt, block); // a DMA block at once

On the host, items arrive one at a time, each with its own time, exactly as from a stream that isn't batched, or a whole batch at once with recv_batch(). The API has no batch size: the device owns it (32 by default), and the host picks only the latency, .max_age(duration), how long a batch may wait before it goes. Details: Batching streams and properties.

items.title: Observing every sample
items.text:
Observing a property sends its current value at the rate a host asks for. A value that changes faster than that, a current sampled in a 25 kHz control loop, loses everything in between. Add +batched and a host can ask for every sample:

#[ww_trait]
trait Foc {
    property!(ro+observe+batched i_a: Ampere);
    property!(ro+observe+batched i_b: Ampere);
}

The device hands over each new set of values once per control loop tick, and the host gets every one of them:

// device, in the control loop
server.observe.samplers().root.sample(Second::micro(now_us), api_impl::FocSamples { i_a, i_b });

// host
let mut i_a = device.foc().observe_i_a(samples(Duration::from_millis(5))).subscribe().await?;
while let Ok(s) = i_a.recv().await {
    println!("{:?} {:?}", s.t, s.value); // every sample, oldest first, each with its device time
}

A host may observe just a part of a level: here i_a alone, or 3 of the 21 values of the motor demo's FOC level. Only the properties in Samples mode get a column in the level's batch, are encoded and go on the wire. What doesn't shrink is the capture: the interrupt still hands over (or, with observe cells, writes) every value of the row. How much that is: a few properties of a level.

items.title: The motor demo, in numbers
items.text:
The motor demo is a simulated FOC motor controller with about 50 observable properties in three rate tiers. Its foc level has 21 values computed every 40 µs (25 kHz), control has 13 measured values at 1 kHz. Observing every single sample of a level, through the real generated code:

every sample foc (21 values, 25 kHz) control (13 values, 1 kHz) one update per sample, not batched 3.73 MB/s 99.0 kB/s batched, 32 samples per batch 812 kB/s 19.0 kB/s smaller by 4.6x 5.2x

The flip side: unbatched, a ww_si quantity is a little bigger than a bare f32 (it carries its prefix and storage type): the demo's foc level observed every millisecond went from 96 to 117 kB/s when it moved to quantities. Quantities pay off inside a Series, where a value costs its change from the previous one, not its width.

Advanced

items.title: Advanced: every knob, and what it costs
items.text: The choices behind a batch: which codecs, when it seals, how big it may get, what it costs a microcontroller, and when to leave batching off.

items.title: Codec policies: smallest, fixed, or fixed at compile time
items.text:
Each numeric column is written with a predictor (raw, delta, delta of delta) and a coder (prefix code, bit packed, constant, plain); floats are plain or XOR coded. Who picks them is the SeriesPolicy:

  • CodecPolicy::SMALLEST (the default of Series::new, and of everything on std) tries every combination per column and keeps the smallest.
  • CodecPolicy::fixed(numeric, float) uses one for every column, chosen at run time.
  • A type implementing FixedCodecs fixes the codecs at compile time and links only them. DeltaPacked (delta, packed residuals, XOR floats) is one, and the no_std default of a batcher. RawPlain is another.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct DeltaOfDeltaPacked;

impl FixedCodecs for DeltaOfDeltaPacked {
    const NUMERIC: NumericCodec = NumericCodec::new(Predictor::DeltaOfDelta, Coder::Packed);
    const FLOAT: FloatCodec = FloatCodec::Xor;
}

Series::with_policy(&items, DeltaOfDeltaPacked).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf)?;

All of them write the same bytes for the same codecs; the reader follows the column headers, whatever wrote them. What the choice costs, encoding 32 samples of a motor phase current (Series<Timed<Ampere>>) on a Cortex-M3:

policy instructions per item bytes encoder flash SMALLEST 969 50 25.4 KB fixed(delta, packed) 341 79 25.4 KB fixed(delta-of-delta, packed) 334 61 25.4 KB DeltaPacked 341 79 15.0 KB

So a fixed codec is about 3x cheaper in CPU than trying them all, for 1.2x to 1.7x the bytes. A run-time CodecPolicy value links every codec whatever its value; only a FixedCodecs type leaves the rest out. And RawPlain is not the CPU escape hatch it looks like: on an STM32H725 a level batch takes 567 k cycles with it against 529 k with DeltaPacked, for 2.8x the bytes; writing more bits costs more than predicting saves.

Where the fixed codecs lose most is a regular clock. SMALLEST writes it as delta + constant, zero bits per item; DeltaPacked has no constant coder and pays a packed residual per tick. The 32 currents from the Basic part are 34 B with SMALLEST and 65 B with DeltaPacked; without their times, 27 B and 30 B. That gap is what the shared clock of observe levels (below) takes away.

items.title: Quantities, autoranging and restarts
items.text:
A ww_si quantity is a final_structure struct { prefix: Prefix, value: NumericValue }, so a Series of quantities has three columns per quantity: the prefix, the storage type of the number (I32, U32, F32, ..), and the number itself, in one column per storage type that occurs.

Discrete leaves, enum tags like the prefix and the storage type, bool, Option presence and strings, are written as runs: the first value, then one entry per change. A value that never changes in a batch costs about 5 bits in all; a string costs its bytes once per change, which suits a status text, less a log line that changes every item. Measured on the motor demo, the prefix and storage runs of a quantity and its timestamp cost 3 B per series per update, 5 % of the bytes at 32 items: not worth a fixed-prefix wire form that would give up autoranging.

A numeric column restarts (a full value, fresh codec state) where an enum field declared earlier in the same struct changed. Ampere { prefix, value } restarts value when the prefix changes, so 480 µA followed by 120 mA is a full value, not a meaningless delta of -360 across two units. A switch costs a run entry, one full value instead of a residual and a packed block cut short: about 6 B, worked out from the layout.

What that means in practice was measured on the motor demo's simulated FOC level (21 values at 25 kHz, 7 of them currents, every sample, 32 per batch, an early prototype of batched observe with a time column per property and SMALLEST), with the 7 currents stored three ways:

currents bytes/s of the level prefix switches/s fixed mA 913.1 kB/s 0 fixed µA 1 126.7 kB/s 0 µA below 1 A, mA above (autoranging) 1 114.4 kB/s 528

Autoranging between µA and mA switched 528 times a second and came out 12.3 kB/s below a fixed µA range: the switches pay for themselves through the coarser range above 1 A. It still costs about what fixed µA costs, because 91 to 100 % of the current samples were below 1 A and were sent at µA resolution. Resolution decides the bytes, not switching: pick the prefix for the resolution you need, and let the device range freely where its measurement range does.

items.title: Compared with ALP
items.text:
ALP (Afroozeh, Kuffó, Boncz: ALP: Adaptive Lossless floating-Point Compression, SIGMOD 2024) is the state of the art for compressing doubles in analytical databases. It turns doubles that started out as decimals into integers: for each vector of 1 024 values it finds an exponent e and a factor f (by sampling, first per row group, then per vector) so that round(n × 10^e × 10^-f) decodes back to exactly n. Values that don't round-trip are stored as exceptions (64 bits plus a 16-bit position each), the integers are bit packed with a frame of reference, and doubles that aren't decimals go to a second scheme, ALPrd, which compresses their front bits.

A ww_si quantity does ALP's first step at the producer. The device already holds an integer (an ADC count scaled to mA, a time in µs), and the SI prefix is the decimal exponent, in steps of 10³ (with deci, centi, deca and hecto around the unit). So there is no search, no exceptions, it is lossless by construction, and the exponent may change per sample, where ALP keeps one per vector. What ALP has beyond that, a scale chosen from the data per block and at any power of ten, is what the planned common factor column mode would add: the predictor code 11 is kept free as an escape for it (see Ahead).

items.title: The store and the batcher
items.text:
A device collects items in a SeriesStore, which series derives next to the encoder: room for N items as a struct of arrays, one array per leaf field, no padding between them. Timed<Ampere> takes 12 bytes per item there, against 24 in a [Timed<Ampere>; 32].

A batched stream's or observe level's Batcher holds two such stores: the producer (an interrupt, the control loop) fills one while the event loop encodes the other, and sealing swaps them behind one atomic word, no lock. On a Cortex-M3 a push is about 62 instructions, the push that seals a batch 71, a poll that seals nothing 108. If the spare store isn't back from encoding when the next batch seals, that batch is lost and counted, it never blocks the producer. RAM for the motor demo's whole foc level at 32 samples: 8.4 KB. SeriesStore and the store have the per-type layouts.

When the batch is encoded, each column is written straight from its array in the store, one pass per column, with the same bytes as walking the items. A batch in which a prefix or another tag changes falls back to the item walk, so autoranging still works, at the walk's speed for that batch.

items.title: Observe cells: capture as cheap as a global
items.text:
sample(t, FocSamples { .. }) takes a level's row as one value: the interrupt builds all 21 values on its stack, and the sampler copies them into the batch. For a level sampled in a hot interrupt, a device can opt into observe cells instead, per level, in ww_codegen!: a ring of atomic cells the interrupt writes in place, each value where it is computed.

// ww_codegen!(motor_demo_api::MotorDemo for Device, server = true, .., observe_cells = "root_foc")
static FOC: api_impl::RootFocCells<32> = api_impl::RootFocCells::new(); // const fn, a ring of 32 rows

// the interrupt keeps the writer, handed out once
let mut w = FOC.writer().unwrap();
// .. every PWM period, where the values are computed
w.i_a(Ampere::milli(ia));
w.i_b(Ampere::milli(ib));
w.commit(Second::micro(now_us)); // publishes the row if a host wants it

Each setter is a few relaxed stores, typed by the API; commit publishes the row between two release fences. No lock, no read-modify-write, no unsafe in user code, and the writer can't be cloned, so there is one producer by construction. poll_properties copies the committed rows into one staging batch and encodes it as before. A row the interrupt overwrote before it was read is dropped and counted in missed, never sent half old, half new.

The API and the wire don't change: same columns, same bytes, a host can't tell which one a device uses. On the STM32H725 a row of the 21 FOC values takes 342 cycles at opt-level = 3 against 423 through sample(), and 357 against 1 400 at opt-level = "z"; its stack drops from 116-388 B to 44-52 B. RAM is the same, 8.6 KB for the FOC level with a ring of 32 rows. The copy moves to the event loop, so total CPU stays about the same; what changes is that the interrupt is short and predictable. Under backpressure cells even lose fewer samples: rows wait in the ring while a sealed batch waits for budget. Observing: cells has the setup, the Nomicon the numbers.

items.title: Sealing and budgets
items.text:
A batch is sealed for one of four reasons: it is full (N items), one more item could pass the event's byte budget, it got as old as the host allows, or the code flushed it (on closing a stream).

The budget needs to know how big a batch can get without writing it. Series::<T>::max_bytes(n) is the worst case under any policy, every column at its longest code and every run changing at every item, and it is far from real data: the 32 currents above are 34 B against a bound of 1 272 B (with every number type of NumericValue enabled). So the batcher starts from the bound and then seals by the last batch's measured bytes per item, aiming at 80 % of the budget. A batch that still turns out too big is split, the largest prefix that fits goes now and the rest next time: nothing lost, nothing sent twice. See sealing and budget.

items.title: One clock per observe level
items.text:
The batched properties of an observe level are sampled together, by one sample(t, ..) call, so they share their times. A level batch is one Series<T> per observed property plus one Series<Second> of times in the update's head (sample_times), not a time column per property. On the foc level's 21 properties at 32 samples with DeltaPacked, that is 1 251 B against 1 965 B (36 % less) and half the encode cycles. Through the real motor demo with SMALLEST, which already wrote each regular clock almost for free, it still saved 17 % (foc) and 26 % (control).

Two things follow. One batcher per level seals the level's properties together: control went from 238 updates/s, sealed out of step property by property, to 48. And a level's Samples entries share one grid and one age: they get the finest every_us and the shortest max_age_us any of them asked for, and the grant says so. A property that needs its own sample times belongs in its own trait level; levels are the rate tiers.

items.title: A few properties of a level
items.text:
Observing only some properties of a level is supported, and it is the usual case: a host asks for i_a, i_b and i_c in Samples mode and leaves the other 18 values of the FOC level alone. Only properties in Samples mode get a column in the level's batch, are encoded and sent. The others still cost CPU where the row is captured: sample() takes the whole row (FocSamples, all 21 values) and copies it into the batch store, and with observe cells the interrupt writes every cell. The poll copies only the observed columns out of the cells' ring. Measured on the STM32H725 at opt-level = 3, the FOC bench with the host observing all 21, then only i_a, i_b, i_c:

FOC level (21 values), H725 cycles all 21 observed 3 observed a row, sample() 408 386 a row, observe cells 333 316 a poll that drains 16 rows from the cells' ring 10 100 - 10 300 4 370 - 4 460 the poll that encodes a 32-row batch, sample() 100 200 24 500 - 24 900 the same with cells (it also drains 16 rows) 107 400 26 200 - 26 300 bytes sent for 64 rows 2 021 419

So the encode, the cells' drain and the bytes follow what is observed (4x fewer cycles and 5x fewer bytes here), the capture doesn't: a row costs the same whether a host watches 3 values or 21. At 25 kHz that makes 3 of the 21 FOC values about 6 % of the H725 (rows plus polls, sample() or cells alike), against 17 % for all 21 through sample() and 19 % with cells. A property a host starts to observe while a batch fills still gets that batch's earlier samples, as with sample(): the poll copies its column for the rows already staged from the ring (if the interrupt wrote over them meanwhile, the batch goes without it and the next one has it). To make the unobserved values free, put the ones that are rarely watched in a level of their own (a level is the unit a gate opens for), or skip computing them when nobody samples the level at all (if w.is_sampling()).

items.title: Without generated code: CLI, dynamic clients, Python
items.text:
A Series in an API is in its introspection data, so tools that only have that read and write it too. ww stream <path> --batches prints whole batches, ww observe --samples MS one line per sample.
