The dynamic client decodes items or columns, and it also writes a Series from a dynamic value with the same bytes the generated code gives (ValueOwned::ser_series_dyn, any policy). In Python a Series<T> is a list, so a host writes one as it would a list, and reads it as items or as numpy columns:

dev.stamps.write([1_700_000_000, 1_700_000_010, 1_700_000_020])  # property!(rw stamps: Series<'i, u64>)

cols = dev.readings.decode_columns(data)  # one numpy array per leaf field
with m.observe({"current": {"samples": 5}}) as obs:  # every sample, batches at most 5 ms old
    b = obs.recv_batch()
    b["batches"]["current"]               # {"t": array of seconds, "": array of the values}

Python: observing and values have the rest.

items.title: CPU and flash on a microcontroller
items.text:
Pushing is cheap and flat; encoding is where the CPU goes, and it scales with samples per second (properties × rate). Two kinds of numbers below, in different units:

  • Cortex-M3/M4F: instructions, counted under QEMU (examples_mcu/qemu_icount). QEMU has no timing model, so these are not cycles and give no time on their own.
  • STM32H725 (Cortex-M7 at 540 MHz, caches on): cycles, read from the core's DWT cycle counter on the real chip. Here one QEMU instruction took about 2 to 2.5 cycles, so a bigger number for the M7 doesn't mean more work.

With DeltaPacked at 32 samples per batch, a timed stream item is about 341 instructions on a Cortex-M3/M4F and about 790 cycles on the H725, 1.46 µs per item. An observe level's sample costs about half, thanks to the shared clock: 213 instructions on a Cortex-M3/M4F. How that scales:

observed (one level, shared clock) samples/s Cortex-M3/M4F, instructions/s fits, for the encode 2 currents at 1 kHz 2 000 ~0.4 M any Cortex-M, trivially 4 properties at 4 kHz 16 000 ~3.4 M any Cortex-M, room to spare 5 properties at 25 kHz 125 000 ~27 M a fast M4F, an M7 easily all 21 FOC values at 25 kHz 525 000 ~112 M a fast M7 only

On the H725, the whole FOC level (21 values at 25 kHz, one batch of 32 samples every 1.28 ms) depends as much on the compiler settings as on the codec. The batcher writes each column straight from its store; walking the items of the batch, as it did before, writes the same 1 251 bytes and is what a batch with a prefix change still does:

FOC level on the STM32H725 cycles per batch per sample share of 540 MHz item walk, opt-level = "z" 264 900 0.73 µs 38.3 % item walk, opt-level = 3 96 800 0.27 µs 14.0 % column-wise from the store, opt-level = "z" 53 200 0.15 µs 7.7 % column-wise from the store, opt-level = 3 36 800 0.10 µs 5.3 %

Before the word-wide bit writer (SW-68) the same batch took 98 500 and 58 900 cycles column-wise, 324 000 and 126 700 as an item walk. opt-level = "z" (smallest code) is the firmware examples' release profile, and it makes the encoder 1.4x (column-wise) to 2.7x (item walk) slower than opt-level = 3; at "z" the cycles also move by up to 15 % between builds as the code layout changes. Build firmware that encodes at 25 kHz at opt-level = 3. Setting it only for shrink_wrap, ww_si and ww_numeric doesn't help: the series code is generic and compiled in the firmware crate. The Nomicon has where the cycles go.

These tables count the encode, the Series writes of a batch. The whole poll_properties that sends it costs more: 75.5 k cycles for a 32-row FOC batch on the H725 at opt-level = 3 (a few properties, a batch with a current ramp, so more than the quiet one above), 13 % of the core at 25 kHz with the rows; 121.5 k at "z", 20 %. With the bit writer before SW-68 it was 99.9 k and 172.2 k (17 % and 27 %), and until API-52 191 k and 513 k (30 % and 77 %): whenever a batch's worst case didn't fit the outbox's free room, the poll measured it first by rebuilding each column of the batch into a scratch and walking it, and the outbox walked its entries for every lookup. Now a batch is written straight into the free room and measured only when it doesn't fit, a measure counts from the store's arrays, and the outbox keeps its offsets. In the profile of that poll on the Cortex-M4F model (74.8 k instructions; 104.8 k before SW-68, 207 k before API-52) the packed blocks and the delta code take 25.8 k (56.5 k before SW-68, when one put_bits per residual was 29.3 k alone), each column's framing and the scratch around it 11 k, memcpy 5.8 k; the rest is the update, its length and the outbox.

items.title: High rates: a few values at 400 kHz to 2 MHz
items.text:
A power converter switches at 400 kHz to 2 MHz and samples a few values once per period: inductor current, output and input voltage. Can those be observed at every period? Measured on the STM32H725 (540 MHz, caches on, opt-level = 3, DWT cycles), one observe level with its shared clock, observe cells as the capture, the column-wise DeltaPacked writer as the encode, 32 rows per batch, poll_properties every 16 rows; next to it a raw copy, the interrupt storing the time and the values into a ring of words and the event loop copying 32 rows out of it. The values are a synthetic buck stage (48 V to 12 V, 8 A, a load step to 12 A in the second batch, a few LSB of noise):

H725 cycles 3 values, 400 kHz 3 values, 1 MHz 2 values, 2 MHz capture: a cells row, warm (cold) 163 (456) 158 (178) 152 (313) capture: a raw row 57 58 52 a poll that drains 16 rows 3 770 3 650 3 144 the poll that drains 16 rows, encodes 32 19 945 19 498 17 316 a raw copy of 32 rows 369 382 295

Per rate, with the capture of every row and both polls of every batch:

per rate 3 values, 400 kHz 3 values, 1 MHz 2 values, 2 MHz one period 1 350 cycles 540 cycles 270 cycles capture, share of a period: cells / raw 12 % / 4.2 % 29 % / 11 % 56 % / 19 % CPU of the H725, Series 67 % 163 % 293 % CPU of the H725, raw copy 5.1 % 13 % 23 % bytes per row, Series / raw 5.5 / 16 5.3 / 16 3.9 / 12 on the wire, Series 2.2 MB/s 5.3 MB/s 7.8 MB/s on the wire, raw (no framing at all) 6.4 MB/s 16 MB/s 24 MB/s

What carries it: USB full speed (about 1 MB/s in practice) carries none of them. Ethernet (the H725 has a 10/100 MAC, 12.5 MB/s line rate) carries every Series row of the table and the raw copy at 400 kHz. USB high speed (480 Mbit/s, 60 MB/s line rate; on the H725 it needs an external ULPI PHY) carries all of them, raw included.

What limits first:

  • Series: the encode in the event loop. The capture fits at every rate (a cells row is 12 to 53 % of a period; at 2 MHz half the period is a lot for an interrupt that also runs the control loop). The polls don't: 3 values at 400 kHz take 67 % of the core, which leaves little for the converter, and 1 MHz and 2 MHz need 1.6x and 2.9x the core. Per row the polls cost about 4.5 times the capture.
  • Raw: the link. 4.5 to 19 % of the CPU, but 6.4 to 24 MB/s: Ethernet up to 400 kHz, USB HS above.
  • The Series bytes are 2.9x to 3.1x fewer than raw, which is what moves 1 and 2 MHz from USB HS to Ethernet, if the CPU were there.

Where a poll's cycles go, from its profile on the Cortex-M4F model (18 400 instructions for a 3-value batch, 22 900 before the word-wide bit writer of SW-68): the codec itself (delta, packed blocks, bit writer, runs) about 5 100, 9 300 before; each column's own framing (count, tag runs, the check that no tag changes) 2 000, the ring copy 1 800, the update's framing, the outbox and the poll's own code the rest. API-52 took 3 to 6 % off these polls (the FOC poll lost half, see above): this bench's 4 KB outbox always had room for a batch's worst case, so its batches were never measured. SW-68 took 13 to 15 % off them on the H725 (17 % at "z"), and what is left is about as much codec as framing around it: less framing per column would move it next. So today a device observes a few values at every period up to a few hundred kHz, and above that decimates (every_us, a grid in whole µs) or sends raw over a fast link.

Flash for the encoder is 15.0 KB on a Cortex-M3 with DeltaPacked (9.8 KB on an M4F), 25.4 KB (17.6 KB) with a run-time CodecPolicy. A firmware no longer carries 64-bit numbers for the protocol's own types: a NumericValue takes 8 bytes instead of 16, and the H725 firmware got 7.7 KB smaller in flash. Every sample taken is encoded, also when its batch is later dropped for lack of budget, so an MCU sets a floor on the rate it accepts (ObserveLimits::samples_min_every_us): otherwise any host can ask for more encoding than the CPU has.

items.title: When not to batch
items.text:
• Latest value is enough. If the host wants to see a value, not every sample of it, the plain observe modes (periodic, on change) are smaller and simpler. Batch what you would plot or analyze.
  • One value at a time. A batch of 1 costs a byte more than plain; a quantity sent alone costs more than an f32. Batching pays from two items on and most of it by 16 to 32.
  • Latency matters more than bytes. A batch waits up to its max age before it goes; an event that must arrive now is a plain stream item or a method's answer.
  • Strings, byte lists, opaque fields. A Series<T> carries them, as runs, in a method's answer or a property. A batched stream or an observed +batched property doesn't: the batcher needs the worst case of an item to keep a batch inside its byte budget, and a string has no bound, so batched on such a type is a compile error. Observe cells need a fixed-size cell per value, which a string doesn't have either. A fixed-size array ([u8; 16]) has both, at a column per byte. Planned for text and frames: see Ahead.
  • The CPU can't keep up. Check the table above; decimate (every_us) or observe fewer properties.

items.title: Compared with raw globals
items.text:
The usual way to get fast signals out of a controller is no protocol at all: copy the variables into a RAM buffer and send it as it is (a VESC-style sample buffer), or let the debugger read RAM while the core runs (TI-style RAM observe). How does a Series compare? Per FOC level batch (21 values and their time, 32 samples) on the STM32H725 at opt-level = 3, with 781 batches a second at 25 kHz:

one FOC level batch cycles bytes CPU at 25 kHz (of 540 MHz) link at 25 kHz raw copy of the 22 arrays (memcpy) 2 800 2 816 0.4 % 2.2 MB/s Series, column-wise DeltaPacked 36 800 1 251 5.3 % 0.98 MB/s the whole poll_properties, cells 83 300 - about 14 % with the rows -

The link decides first. USB full speed carries about 1 MB/s in practice: the raw copy at full rate doesn't fit it, the Series just does. Over USB high speed or Ethernet both fit, and raw wins on CPU by about 13x for the encode, and by about 30x counting the whole poll that sends the batch (the third row, a 32-row batch of the FOC bench, which carries a current ramp).

What that CPU buys:

  • Meaning on the wire. Types, names, units and prefixes come with the device's introspection data, so ww, Python and a dynamic client show 4980 mA without a hand-kept list of offsets and scale factors.
  • True time and counted losses. Every sample carries its device time, and a sample that couldn't be sent is counted in missed. A buffer read by the debugger can tear a row or skip samples without telling anyone.
  • Mixed rates. Each trait level is observed at its own rate and budget, a 25 kHz tier next to a 1 kHz one.
  • Autoranging. A value may change its prefix from sample to sample, at almost no cost.
  • An API that evolves. Fields and properties can be added without breaking older hosts or devices.
  • Tooling. ww observe --samples, and numpy columns in Python with recv_batch().

What it costs besides CPU:

  • RAM: the level's two batch stores (or a ring and one staging batch with cells), 8.4 to 8.6 KB for the FOC level at 32 samples, and its outbox (observe_outbox, 4 KB by default): about 12.5 KB.
  • Flash: the encoder itself is 15.0 KB on a Cortex-M3 with DeltaPacked and 9.8 KB on a Cortex-M4F (the observe and batcher code around it is not counted there, and the H725 build wasn't measured for flash).

The capture gap is closed by observe cells: the interrupt writes each value into its cell with a plain store, as it would write a global, and commits the row: 342 cycles and 52 B of stack for the 21 FOC values at opt-level = 3. What stays is the event loop's side: the encode, 5.3 % above, and the poll around it, about 14 % in all. There, less framing per column is next (see Ahead), and aligned plain (measured, kept on file) was 34 200 cycles per batch for 2 882 bytes when it was measured, before SW-68: now hardly cheaper than column-wise DeltaPacked for 2.3x the bytes.

Nomicon

items.title: Nomicon: the bits and the cycles
items.text: How a Series is laid out bit by bit, what each codec does, and where the encoder's cycles went.

items.title: The column layout
items.text:
A Series is a count, the columns, and padding to the next byte:

n:          UNib32 (nibble-aligned)     number of items; 0: nothing else follows
group(T):   the columns of T over all n items
padding:    zero bits to the next byte

The group of a type is written by its own rule, recursively: a struct is its fields' groups in declaration order (an evolvable one first writes its field count, or its bit length when nested, so an older reader can skip what it doesn't know); an enum is a tag run, then each variant's fields over only the items in that variant; Option is the same with two variants. Columns come depth first, which lets a reader find every column's start in one forward pass without a directory of offsets: the skim validates every code, records a cursor per column, and iter() then steps all columns in parallel, zero-copy, without allocating.

Four IvSamples, v = 3300, 3301, 3301, 3299 mV as U16 and i = 152 000, 152 002, 151 999, 152 001 µA as I32, are 14 bytes against 33 for the smallest plain form:

0100001042000100011100010100140011001133100100009001010001511001000191100010108a0000000000000001000410100011a31000000080000111001c10110000b0headerrunvalueresidualsblock widthpaddingbitbitsfield00100n = 440010IvSample field count = 280001 0v.prefix run: Milli, end130010 0v.value tag run: U16, end1801 01v.value U16 column: delta, packed22000011001110010033003800010block width 24310 00 11+1 0 -2 (zigzag 2 0 3)490010 0i.prefix run: Micro, end540110 0i.value tag run: I32, end5901 01i.value I32 column: delta, packed630000000000000010010100011100000015200095000011block width 3101100 101 100+2 -3 +2 (zigzag 4 5 4)11000padding

The first values and the 4.5 bytes of count, runs and headers are paid once per batch: that is why 4 items are 2.4x smaller and 100 items 7.7x. The full reference is Series<T> in the wire format.

items.title: Predictors
items.text:
A numeric column header is 4 bits: 2 for the predictor, 2 for the coder.

  • raw: every value as it is (zigzag for signed types).
  • delta: the segment's first value in full, then the zigzag of each difference to the previous value.
  • delta of delta: the zigzag of the change of that difference. A regular clock becomes all zeros, a ramp after a step too; on a flat noisy signal it amplifies the noise (a second difference), so it's no universal win.

A segment starts at the first item and at every restart; the predictor state starts over there. The fourth predictor code, 11, is reserved as an escape for later column modes, so a new mode never changes what an existing code means.

items.title: Coders
items.text:
• prefix: each residual in the variable-length delta code (0 for zero, 10 + 7 bits, 110 + 9, ...).
  • packed: blocks of 8 residuals, a width field (5 bits for 16-bit values, 6 for 32), then each residual at exactly that width. A block of zeros costs only its width field.
  • constant: the first residual once; every later one equals it. Delta + constant is t0 + period.
  • plain: every residual at full width.

Packing is where most of the gain over the older prefix code came from: a ±1 LSB delta costs 9 bits as a prefix code and 2 to 3 packed. Over 100 values, a steady voltage column is 659 bits with the prefix code and 359 packed. The prefix code still wins on flat data with rare jumps (235 against 433 bits), because a single jump widens a whole block of 8, which is why the writer can choose per column, and why columns restart at a range switch: 110 B with restarts against 118 B without on the range-switch signal.

items.title: XOR floats
items.text: A float column is plain, or the XOR code known from Gorilla: each value XORed with the previous one, then only the meaningful bits between the leading and trailing zeros, reusing the previous window when it fits. A repeated value is one bit. It does what it can, but a noisy float changes most of its mantissa every sample: on the motor demo, batching f32 values only went from 4.57 to 3.42 bytes per value, while the same values as I32 with a prefix went to 1.74. Integers with a prefix were about 60 % of the whole gain. The showcase walks through XOR-coded temperatures bit by bit.

items.title: How the encoder got 6x faster and 6x smaller
items.text:
The first encoder was correct and slow. Profiled under QEMU, a 32-item batch with fixed(delta, packed) took 63 359 instructions on a Cortex-M3, and they went to:

  • 27 %: restart checks building the tag arrays of every field, per item per column, also for fields that can't have a tag;
  • 24 %: the packed coder's look-ahead, which ran the predictor twice per item;
  • 20 %: nested walks over the items of each field;
  • 15 %: the bit writer, a read-modify-write per byte with 64-bit masks.

Flash had its own story: 16 copies of a ~4 KB column writer, one per leaf position and sink, each with all codecs and the trials. The fixes, each measured on its own: packed blocks buffered instead of looked ahead; restarts compare only fields that can carry a tag; enums write only the variants their tag run saw; the predictor works on left-aligned values in a u32 for leaves up to 32 bits; SMALLEST sizes the four coders of a predictor in one pass; the bit writer keeps the open byte in a register; column writers are small structs stepped per item, one copy per word size; and policies became types (FixedCodecs), so a firmware links only its codecs. The bytes are the same as before, down to the golden vectors.

Cortex-M3, instructions, n = 8 / 32 / 64 before after SMALLEST 53 873 / 213 233 / 428 825 8 894 / 31 014 / 60 813 fixed(delta, packed) 16 488 / 63 359 / 126 075 3 274 / 10 922 / 21 272 DeltaPacked (compile time) - 3 250 / 10 920 / 21 306 encoder flash before after, CodecPolicy after, DeltaPacked Cortex-M3 90 752 B 25 436 B 14 976 B Cortex-M4F 68 460 B 17 596 B 9 820 B

Per item at 32: 1 980 → 341 instructions with a fixed codec (5.8x), 6 663 → 969 with SMALLEST (6.9x); flash 6.1x (M3) and 7.0x (M4F) smaller.

items.title: On real silicon: the H725 cycle tables
items.text:
QEMU counts instructions; an STM32H725 (Cortex-M7 at 540 MHz, caches on) counts cycles with its DWT counter:

STM32H725, cycles, n = 8 / 32 / 64 before after SMALLEST 117 219 / 441 512 / 885 873 19 969 / 60 784 / 115 305 fixed(delta, packed) 27 706 / 104 027 / 205 922 8 732 / 26 664 / 50 792 fixed(delta-of-delta, packed) 30 153 / 110 380 / 216 670 8 759 / 26 406 / 49 943 DeltaPacked (compile time) - 8 293 / 25 241 / 47 929

A batch of 32 with DeltaPacked is 25 241 cycles, 47 µs. A cold first run is within 1 to 10 % of these warm numbers. All of these were built at opt-level = "z"; at opt-level = 3 the encoder was measured 2.4x faster. The M7 spends about 2 to 2.5 cycles per QEMU instruction on this code (three flash wait states, a call per value written, branchy code), more than the 1 to 1.5 first guessed, which is why the MCU table above quotes both.

items.title: Why the shared clock halves the CPU
items.text:
A Timed<T> item has a time column next to its value, and a time is itself a quantity: a prefix run, a storage tag run and a value column, the same three columns as the value. So the time is half of the columns an encoder walks per item, and sharing one time column across a level's properties removes nearly half the work. On the H725, one foc level batch (21 properties, 32 samples):

DeltaPacked, one level batch bytes cycles 21 × Series<Timed<T>> 1 965 528 538 21 × Series<T> + one Series<Second> 1 214 + 37 = 1 251 242 631 + 11 803 = 254 434 saved 36 % 52 %

Per sample that is 786 → 379 cycles, and the full 25 kHz FOC rate went from about 77 % of the H725 to 37 %. (Both measured in one build at opt-level = "z"; the same bench rebuilt later took 302 k cycles for the shared form with QEMU's instruction count unchanged: at "z" the M7's timing moves with the code layout, the work doesn't.) The bytes drop more than expected because DeltaPacked has no constant coder: each 40 µs step is a 7-bit residual, so each property's time column cost about 36 B per batch, 38 % of the update. One shared column is 37 B for the whole level. QEMU agrees: 46 % fewer instructions on both the M3 and the M4F.

items.title: Straight from the store
items.text:
Which part of that is the codec and which is walking items? Two experiments on the same FOC level batch answer it.

The first is a column-wise writer: instead of rebuilding each item from the batcher's struct-of-arrays store and walking the items once per column, it reads each column's array straight from the store, one pass per column. It writes the same bytes as the item walk (a property test over every policy checks it) whenever no enum or Option tag changes inside the batch; a batch with such a change, strings, or the odd-width UN/IN numbers still takes the walk. The second is aligned plain: values copied byte-aligned in their own width, no prediction, no bit packing, behind the predictor escape. Below both, an upper bound: the 22 payload arrays of the batch copied with memcpy.

one FOC level batch bytes H725 cycles, opt-level = 3 H725 cycles, "z" Cortex-M3 instructions DeltaPacked, item walk 1 251 125 300 302 200 143 463 DeltaPacked, column-wise 1 251 59 900 100 400 74 898 aligned plain, item walk 2 882 44 400 323 500 73 071 aligned plain, from the store 2 882 34 200 128 700 40 987 memcpy of the arrays, with framing 2 861 7 000 8 800 10 609 memcpy of the arrays, bare 2 816 2 800 2 900 3 911

The surprise is the third row: walking items with aligned columns is already 44 k cycles at opt-level = 3. So the item walk was not the main cost; the bit writer and the codec are. Column-wise, a column still costs about 3.3 k instructions on a Cortex-M3: about 1.2 k for the delta and block code, 1.2 k for writing bits (24 bits per push, one byte per loop), and 0.8 k for the column's own Series framing (count, two tag runs, the checks). The bit writer part is what SW-68 took down: a column is 1 601 instructions on the Cortex-M4F model now, against 2 510 before.

Aligned plain was measured and is not recommended. From the store it was 1.75x cheaper than column-wise DeltaPacked at opt-level = 3 (34 k against 60 k cycles; since SW-68 DeltaPacked is 37 k), but slower at "z" (129 k against 100 k; 53 k now), and it sends 2.3x the bytes: 2.25 MB/s for the FOC level at 25 kHz, more than a full-speed USB link carries. It wasn't a plain copy either: when it was measured, the store kept every NumericValue payload as a u64 (firmware carried 64-bit numbers for the protocol's own types, since dropped), so an I32 column was narrowed value by value, and the framing of 22 separate series, their tag runs and checks, already costs 5x the memcpy bound. And a new wire form is one that every older reader rejects. It stays an option for a device on USB HS or Ethernet that needs the last bit of CPU. The column-wise writer, in contrast, changes no byte on the wire: it is purely a faster way to write the same Series, and it is what the batcher uses.

items.title: Observe cells: the interrupt side
items.text:
The cells were measured against sample() on a no_std copy of the motor demo's 21 FOC properties: 64 real FOC ticks, a host observing all 21 in Samples mode, poll_properties every 16 rows. Both servers send the same 2 021 bytes in 2 updates for the 64 rows, with the same hash. Per row on the STM32H725, in cycles:

one FOC row (21 values) sample(), "z" cells, "z" sample(), 3 cells, 3 warm mean 1 400 357 423 342 cold (the first row) 1 725 412 976 486 worst 1 631 643 795 588 nobody observes 180 310 189 303 stack of a row 388 B 44 B 116 B 52 B

The Cortex-M4F model agrees in instructions: 189 against 1 122 at "z", 206 against 260 at 3. The cold row matters most, since a real 25 kHz interrupt mostly runs with cold caches: there cells take half the cycles at 3 and a quarter at "z".

Three details from the measurement:

  • Inlining decides "z". With plain #[inline] the setters called the cell writes out of line, and cells were no faster than sample() (2 055 against 2 022 cycles). The setters and the writes are #[inline(always)] now. sample()'s own copy into the store has the same problem at "z" (1 122 instructions against 260 at 3).
  • Nobody observing costs cells more. sample() returns before copying when no host wants the row; the setters store anyway: 310 against 180 cycles at "z", 303 against 189 at 3. Wrap them, or the expensive values, in if w.is_sampling() { .. }.
  • The work moves, it doesn't vanish. A poll copies the waiting rows from the ring, about 440 cycles a row at 3 with all 21 observed (10.1 k against 3.1 k cycles for 16 rows; only the observed columns are copied, 4.4 k for 3 of them), and the poll that encodes costs about 7 % more.

And what 64-bit payloads cost before they were dropped from firmware: the same row took 445 against 435 cycles at 3 and the level's samples 14.3 KB of RAM either way, against 8.6 KB with 32-bit payloads.

items.title: What a struct series costs: the restart check
items.text: The obvious alternative, the level batch as one Series<Timed<LevelRow>> with an Option<T> field per property, was measured and dropped. It is a little smaller (1 233 B against 1 251 B) but took about 2.0 M cycles on the H725 against 0.3 M. Inside a struct, a column restarts its predictor when a tag of an earlier field changes. With 21 tagged quantity fields that check is quadratic per item, and a decimated property's None rows would restart every later column's deltas. Restarts are the right rule for a quantity's own prefix; across unrelated properties they're pure cost, so a level is separate series per column.

items.title: The bit writer and reader, a word at a time
items.text:
After the column-wise writer, the bits themselves were the biggest cost left: in the FOC poll's profile on the Cortex-M4F model (104.8 k instructions), put_bits alone was 29.3 k and the packed blocks around it 27.2 k. SW-68 rewrote shrink_wrap's writers and readers to move a word at a time, with the same bytes (every golden vector, the conformance corpus and the fuzz round trips unchanged, no unsafe):

  • BitWriter (the Series sink) keeps a 32-bit accumulator in registers and stores four bytes when it fills, instead of a byte; the room left is cached, so a push is one compare, a shift and an or.
  • BitSink::put_block writes a packed block (its width field and all residuals) in one call: one bounds check for the block, the accumulator in locals for the loop. delta_packed_slice and the packed coder use it.
  • BufWriter::write_un*, write_bool (requests, replies, the non-Series paths) do one read-modify-write of a 4-byte big-endian window instead of a loop per byte, with one bounds check per call; only the last 3 bytes of a buffer take a cold byte-wise path.
  • UNib32 writes its nibbles as one run of bits, and BufReader::take_unib32 reads one in a single loop.
  • BufReader::read_un32 / read_un64 read through the same 4-byte window, one bounds check, and a failing read moves nothing.

Per operation, Cortex-M4F instructions (QEMU) and STM32H725 cycles (DWT, warm), before and after:

per case (ops) M4F 3 M4F "z" H725 3 H725 "z" write_un32, 1-24 bits (64) 6 306 → 4 100 6 179 → 4 952 5 936 → 3 809 6 264 → 5 141 write_un32, 25-32 bits (64) 8 178 → 5 386 7 470 → 6 073 6 875 → 5 175 6 936 → 6 113 write_bool (64) 1 836 → 1 259 3 592 → 3 664 1 110 → 730 3 916 → 3 841 write_unib32 (32) 5 385 → 3 703 13 645 → 4 966 4 652 → 3 744 13 137 → 4 762 bytes + rev len finish (16) 3 609 → 3 686 5 764 → 5 151 3 599 → 3 683 6 105 → 5 739 Series encode, DeltaPacked (32) 10 960 → 9 363 21 854 → 19 876 10 851 → 8 586 24 153 → 22 087 read_un32, 1-24 bits (64) 7 720 → 4 225 10 123 → 5 524 6 570 → 4 247 8 280 → 5 408 read_un32, 25-32 bits (64) 12 617 → 4 719 16 921 → 6 083 9 317 → 4 896 12 764 → 6 078 read_un64, 1-24 bits (64) 9 918 → 4 420 14 627 → 6 421 7 848 → 4 373 13 644 → 6 583 read_bool (64) 3 297 → 2 425 3 223 → 2 487 3 268 → 2 460 3 281 → 3 281 read_unib32 (32) 7 900 → 4 633 11 949 → 4 763 8 892 → 3 651 10 880 → 3 778 request decode, a call with args (1) 1 272 → 1 189 1 775 → 1 445 1 644 → 1 537 2 268 → 1 962 Series decode, DeltaPacked (32) 89 924 → 81 760 138 467 → 125 634 116 076 → 103 631 172 457 → 163 211

write_nib, read_nib and read_bytes are unchanged (a nibble is already one byte's read-modify-write). The 2-nibble length finish writes stays within 2 %. Series decode gains least: most of it is the series machinery (runs, predictors, the item builders), not reading bits.

What it does where it matters, the observe polls (warm, the poll that encodes):

before → after SW-68 M4F instr., 3 M4F instr., "z" H725 cycles, 3 H725 cycles, "z" FOC level from the store (21 + clock) - - 58 900 → 36 800 98 500 → 53 200 FOC poll, sample() 104 800 → 74 800 157 600 → 106 800 99 900 → 75 500 172 200 → 121 500 FOC poll, cells 115 300 → 85 300 170 400 → 119 600 107 600 → 83 300 182 100 → 132 900 high rate, 3 values at 400 kHz 22 900 → 18 400 35 500 → 27 400 23 500 → 19 900 42 000 → 35 100 one store column (M4F) 2 510 → 1 601 4 073 → 2 262 - -

The cost is flash at "z": the word paths and put_block are out of line there and take about 1.5 KB more, 2 % of the FOC bench (72.7 → 74.2 KB on the M4F, 84.9 → 86.5 KB on the H725); at opt-level = 3 the firmware got 0.2 to 0.4 KB smaller. What is left in the poll is about as much column framing as codec, the next thing to cut.

items.title: Ahead
items.text:
• More from cells. The snapshot modes (periodic, on change) could read a cells level's latest row instead of calling getters, and batched streams fed from an interrupt (ADC samples) could get the same cells.
  • Strings and frames in batches. Codecs across items (API-51, a "same" bit per string, a frame XOR'd with the last one) and dictionary compression for strings (SW-28) would make text cheaper per item; frame splitters for byte streams (STD-41: newline, idle gap, length field, CRC frames, COBS, Modbus RTU) would cut a UART or CAN byte stream into bounded frames, which a batched stream can take.
  • Less framing per column. With the poll's own bookkeeping gone (API-52), what is left around the codec is each column's framing: its count, its tag runs and the check that no tag changes, about 500 instructions a column on a Cortex-M4F; one framing for a whole level would make the high rates cheaper.
  • Room kept in the format. The reserved predictor escape is for a common factor per column, the values divided by it before the predictor, as ALP chooses its scale per block; the float codes have room for better float coders (Chimp, ALP). Diffs across batches would save the first values, about 8 B per batch, but only on reliable streams and with resync rules after a gap; not worth it at 32 items.

The feature tracker has the state of all of this: SW-60, SW-62, SW-63, SW-64, SW-68 for the type, the store, the fast encoder, the column-wise writer and the word-wide bit writer, API-41, API-39, API-49 and API-50 for batched streams, batched observe, the shared clock and observe cells.

items.title: Logo sources
items.text:
logos.py draws wire_weaver_logo.svg and shrink_wrap_logo.svg in docs/assets/, each with a -dark variant and a 2x PNG next to it (the READMEs on GitHub and crates.io embed the PNGs, the docs site the SVGs). Run just logos (or uv run docs/assets/src/logos.py); PNGs need rsvg-convert (librsvg).

The output is plain SVG: cubic Béziers, a mask for the clear rim where one conductor crosses over the other, and for ShrinkWrap a clip path and gradient mask for the pair's relief under the sleeve. No filters, no fonts: the wordmarks are JetBrains Mono Bold (fonts/, SIL Open Font License, see fonts/JetBrainsMono-OFL.txt) turned into outlines with fontTools. It is a Python script rather than Typst because Typst's SVG export has no masks or clip paths, which the weave and the relief need.

The geometry is the one of the original logos (kept as *_snake.svg): conductors 20 wide, 30 apart, crossing every 48 units, highlights 4.4 above the centre line, copper 10 wide with its tip 22 out from the insulation cut. The constants at the top of logos.py name them.

items.title: Evolution checker
items.text:
ww api check <path> compares the traits and types of a crate with the latest snapshot saved in <path>/api_snapshots/, and fails if the crate version is not bumped enough for what changed, following the evolution rules. The crate is parsed from source, same as for ww api save, so nothing has to be built.

$ ww api check ww_stdlib/ww_uart
ww_uart 0.1.0 (ww_stdlib/ww_uart/api_snapshots/ww_uart_0_1_0.ron) -> 0.1.1 (source): compatible changes
  compatible: Uart::flush added
version is bumped enough

To start, save a snapshot of each released version and commit it, then check before every release:

$ ww api save my_device_api     # once per released version, commit api_snapshots/
$ ww api check my_device_api    # after changing the crate and bumping its version

The snapshot used is the newest one of the same crate with a version not newer than the one in Cargo.toml, so it is the snapshot of the current version if it was already saved, and of the previous version otherwise. --against <file> compares with a specific snapshot instead. Nothing is checked if there is no snapshot yet.

<path> can also be a snapshot file, which is then compared with the previous snapshot in the same directory, e.g. to check snapshots that were saved with --force.

ww api save runs the same check before saving a snapshot of a new version, and refuses to save it if the version is not bumped enough (--force saves anyway). So in a crate that has snapshots of all of its published versions, every new snapshot is checked against the previous one.

items.title: Listing all changes
items.text:
ww api diff <path> compares the same versions as ww api check (and also takes --against or a snapshot file), and lists every difference, doc comments included, followed by the verdict. It never fails, and doesn't tell why a change is breaking, ww api check does:

$ ww api diff ww_stdlib/ww_uart
ww_uart 0.1.0 (ww_stdlib/ww_uart/api_snapshots/ww_uart_0_1_0.ron) -> 0.1.0 (source)
  ~ Uart::rx: docs
      /// Receive stream
    + /// of chunks
  ~ Uart::prevent_back_feed: docs
      /// Detect RX low for more than 1 byte interval and set TX low to avoid powering device in sleep mode through it.
    - /// Optional, check [Capabilities] if supported.
    + /// Check [Capabilities] if supported.
  + Uart::flush: fn flush()
  ~ RxFlags: field `parity_error`: docs
    + /// Parity error
  + RxFlags: field `framing_error`: framing_error: bool
breaking changes, version has to be 0.2.0 or later (run `ww api check` for details)

Each line is an added (+), removed (-) or changed (~) trait, resource, type, struct field, enum variant or dependency crate version. Changes are: a resource's signature (kind, arguments, return type, property access, stream direction, array or not), a resource's or variant's name, a type's kind, size kind or repr, a field's position, type or #[default] value, #[since] of any of them, and doc comments, shown as a line diff. Items are matched as described below, enum variants by discriminant, fields by name and unnamed ones by position. A renamed type is removed and added.

evolution::diff() in wire_weaver_client returns the same list, for use from other tools.

items.title: What is checked
items.text:
Changes are sorted into four kinds, and each kind requires a bump of a version position:

Change Examples Bump None exactly the same traits and types, doc comments included none Doc comments only a doc comment on a trait, resource, type, field or variant is changed compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after) Compatible new trait, new resource at the end of a trait, new field with #[default] at the end of an Unsized type, new field in unused padding bits of any type, new type, #[since] or #[default] value changed, max length raised or removed compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after) Breaking see below breaking position (minor before 1.0, major after)

Doc comments are not on the wire, but a released version's snapshot never changes, so they need a new version as well (see doc comments). A bigger bump than required is always fine.

Resources are matched by their id inside each trait (their position, as the device sees them), traits and types by name. A change is breaking if:

  • a trait, resource or type is removed, or a resource moved to another id (e.g. a new one inserted before it: add new resources at the end),
  • a resource, struct field or enum variant is renamed, or struct fields change between named and unnamed: this does not change the wire, but breaks Rust code using them,
  • a resource of the old version can't be used with the new one, in either direction (old client with a new device, and new client with an old device), compared the same way as a client checks its API against a device's: resource kind, number and types of arguments, return type, property access, stream direction, array or not,
  • a type can't be written by one version and read by the other: e.g. field type changed, field added without #[default] at the end of an Unsized type, field added in between old ones outside of unused padding bits (see below), field added at the end of a final_structure, self_describing or sized type, enum variant added or removed, ww_repr or size kind changed,
  • a max length is lowered or added (T -> MaxLen<T, N>): data the old version writes may no longer be read,
  • a trait or type from another crate is replaced by one from a wire-incompatible version of that crate (e.g. ww_si 0.1 -> 0.2), or one from the same crate version with a different definition.

It also warns about additions without #[since], or with a #[since] that is not the new version.

items.title: New fields in padding bits
items.text:
Padding inside a type, before a field aligned to a nibble or a byte, is always written as zero bits and skipped when reading. A new field of any type, Unsized or not, can take such bits, anywhere between the old fields, if:

  • none of the old fields moves and the size doesn't change: the new field only takes bits that were padding,
  • all zero bits are a valid value of it, as that is what it reads from old data: bool, numbers, arrays and non-Unsized structs of them, or an enum without data that has a variant with discriminant 0,
  • it's fixed size (not UNib32, Option, an enum with data, an Unsized type, ...).

Old fields are then matched by name. Where padding is depends on the bit offset the type starts at. An Unsized type always starts at a byte boundary, so its padding is always in the same place:

#[derive_shrink_wrap]
pub struct U {
    pub f: bool,
    // 7 bits of padding before `b`
    #[since = "0.1.1"]
    pub g: u7, // added in 0.1.1, reads as 0 from old data
    pub b: u8,
    pub s: String,
}

An Unsized type can gain fields with #[default] at the end as well, in the same version. Bits after its last field are not free though: lengths of variable size fields are written there.

final_structure, self_describing and sized types are packed tightly into their parent, so they can't grow at the end, and they can start at any bit inside the parent, so the checker requires that the new field fits for every start offset:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(sized)]
pub struct S {
    pub a: u8,
    pub f: bool,
    // 7 bits of padding before `b`, wherever S starts, as `a` is byte-aligned
    #[since = "0.1.1"]
    pub g: u3, // added in 0.1.1, reads as 0 from old data
    pub b: u8,
}

Without a, the padding before b is 7 bits if S starts at a byte boundary, but none if it starts at bit offset 7, so g can't be added. Padding after the last field is never free: whatever follows the type in its parent starts right there. Enum variants with data are not padded to the same size, so there are no free bits after a shorter variant either.

All of this was checked against real bytes: old and new versions read each other's data, with the new field reading as zero from old data. The client uses the same rules when comparing its API with a device's.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Snapshots of all published versions have to be kept in api_snapshots/, the checker can only see what is saved there. A crate without snapshots is not checked.
  • Only traits and types that ww api save finds are checked (see ww api).
  • Semantic changes that keep the same bytes, like changing units or the meaning of a value, can't be detected.
  • Padding bits are only reused when that works for every bit offset a type can start at, even if in all of its actual uses it's always at the same offset.

items.title: Crate layers and version bumps
items.text:
For changing WireWeaver itself or a ww_stdlib crate. An application only needs the evolution rules for its own API crate.

Every crate in the stack has its own versioning rules, because a change travels differently depending on where it is made: a shrink_wrap break cascades to every other crate, a framework crate is free to break its Rust API, and some framework code defines bytes on the wire although it lives in a "free to break" crate.

items.title: The layers
items.text:
Layer Crates Versioning 1. Wire format shrink_wrap, shrink_wrap_derive own version, changes rarely 2. Shared API & types ww_stdlib/*: base types (ww_numeric, ww_si, ww_date_time, ww_version) and traits (ww_gpio, ww_i2c, ww_client_server, ...); framework base types ww_global and ww_self (repo root) own version per crate, the version is the API identity 3. Framework wire_weaver, wire_weaver_core, wire_weaver_derive, wire_weaver_client, wire_weaver_cli, ww_device, ww_link, ww_framer, ... shared [workspace.package] version, free to break Rust API 4. User API my_device_api and friends (see folder structure) own version, the version is the API identity, checked on every connection

Everything above layer 1 implements ShrinkWrap's traits. Base type crates depend on shrink_wrap directly, trait crates and user API crates depend on wire_weaver, which re-exports shrink_wrap. Generated code refers to shrink_wrap::... through that re-export, so a single shrink_wrap version must be shared by the whole dependency graph of an application.

items.title: Checklist before breaking something
items.text:
1. Is it a wire change or only a Rust change? If unsure, serialize a few values before and after and compare the bytes (to_ww_bytes()), and run the evolution checker.
  2. Which layer is it in? Wire changes in shrink_wrap, ww_framer, ww_link, ww_client_server or server/client codegen affect every device - avoid them, and if unavoidable, batch them and mark them Wire format: in the changelog.
  3. For shrink_wrap (and base ww_stdlib types), list the reverse dependencies that need to be re-released.
  4. Bump the right position: patch for compatible additions in shrink_wrap and API crates before 1.0, minor for everything else before 1.0.
  5. Write the changelog entry, saying what users must change and whether deployed devices are affected.

items.title: Layer 1: shrink_wrap
items.text:
shrink_wrap is the foundation that every other crate and every user type is built on, so it is kept stable and changes to it are rare and deliberate.

Wire format changes - anything that changes the bytes produced for an existing type (alignment, length encoding, discriminant or flag layout, the meaning of an existing derive_shrink_wrap directive) breaks every device, every host and every stored blob at once, regardless of any API version. Post 1.0 this is not allowed at all. Before 1.0 it is allowed only with a strong reason, batched with other such changes, and listed under ### ⚠️ Breaking in the changelog starting with Wire format:, so that it can't be mistaken for a Rust-only break. The byte-level claims in the SerDes pages (wire format internals, showcase, ...) must be re-verified in the same change.

Rust API breaks (0.2 -> 0.3) do not touch the wire, but they still ripple through the whole ecosystem: to Cargo, shrink_wrap 0.2 and 0.3 are unrelated crates with unrelated SerializeShrinkWrap traits. A type from a ww_stdlib crate still built on 0.2 does not implement 0.3 traits, and can't be used inside a type or an API built on 0.3. So every ww_stdlib crate, the framework and every user API crate has to be re-released together. Therefore:

  • Prefer additive changes (new types, new methods, new directives, new features). They do not break anything and are released as a patch version (0.2.0 -> 0.2.1), so the rest of the ecosystem picks them up without re-releasing. This is the one exception to the "every change bumps minor" rule.
  • Collect breaking Rust API changes and release them together, rarely. When it happens, bump all ww_stdlib crates in the same release cycle.
  • shrink_wrap_derive is versioned together with shrink_wrap, as the generated code is tightly coupled to it.

items.title: Layer 2: ww_stdlib
items.text:
ww_stdlib crates are meant to be shared between unrelated projects, so their types end up inside many different APIs. Their versions travel on the wire (as FullVersion / CompactVersion with a ww_global id) for trait-based requests and introspection, so the version is not just Cargo metadata, it's a compatibility statement, same as for user API crates (layer 4):

  • Wire-compatible change (following the data type and API rules) -> bump the compatible position: patch before 1.0 (0.1.0 -> 0.1.1), minor after.
  • Wire-incompatible change -> bump the breaking position: minor before 1.0 (0.1.0 -> 0.2.0), major after. Every crate and user API that exposes the changed type or trait over the wire is then wire-incompatible too, and has to bump its own breaking position when it upgrades.
  • A Rust-only break (e.g. renaming a helper method, changing a std convenience impl) is still a Cargo breaking change and bumps the breaking position, even though the wire is unaffected. Avoid mixing such changes with releases that are supposed to be wire-compatible additions; prefer deprecating and adding.

Base type crates (ww_numeric, ww_si, ...) are used by other ww_stdlib crates as well, so their breaking changes cascade the same way shrink_wrap ones do, just over a smaller set of crates - check reverse dependencies in the root Cargo.toml before breaking one. ww_version and ww_global are special: FullVersion, CompactVersion and ApiHashPair are exchanged during link setup, before any version could be checked, so they are final_structure and must not change on the wire at all.

ww_client_server is the API model: it defines the request/event encoding that every generated server and client speaks. Its version is sent to the host in DeviceInfo::api_model_version, and a wire break there is a wire break for every user API, so it is treated with almost the same care as shrink_wrap - see API model.

items.title: Layer 3: framework
items.text:
The framework crates share one version and are free to break their Rust API: bump the minor version once per release cycle and describe what users must change in the changelog. A user API crate built against wire_weaver 0.5 keeps working with a host or firmware built against wire_weaver 0.6, as long as both still use the same shrink_wrap major version and the same wire protocol.

The exception is code that defines what goes on the wire:

  • ww_framer (frame layout, heads, checksums) and ww_link (message kinds, DeviceInfo, LinkSetup) - changing these breaks every device from every host. The link version is sent in DeviceInfo::dev_link_version but it is not checked yet, so a break there is not even detected cleanly. Only add new message kinds that old peers ignore; never change existing ones.
  • Server and client codegen in wire_weaver_core - how resources are indexed, how arguments and return values are wrapped. Changing it changes the wire for every user API without any user version changing, so it must stay byte-identical for the same API definition.
  • The settings record format and store layout of ww_settings (see settings stored on a device).

These are wire changes even though they live in "free to break" crates, so they follow the layer 1 rules: avoid, batch, and mark as Wire format: in the changelog.

items.title: Layer 4: user API
items.text: See your API's version in the evolution rules.

items.title: Evolution rules
items.text:
Two different things can break when a WireWeaver crate changes, and they are tracked separately:

  • Wire compatibility - whether bytes written by one side can still be read by the other. Firmware lives in the field for years, hosts are updated on their own schedule, and ShrinkWrap blobs may be stored on disk. A wire break means deployed devices stop talking to new hosts (or the other way around), which no cargo update can fix.
  • Rust (SemVer) compatibility - whether code still compiles against the new crate version. A break here is annoying, but it is found by the compiler and fixed by the developer, before anything ships.

A change can break one without the other: renaming a BufWriter method breaks Rust code but not a single byte on the wire; changing a field's u8 to u16 in an API type compiles fine and silently breaks the wire. The rules below say what you can change in your API crate without breaking either, and which version to bump when you do. For changing WireWeaver itself or a ww_stdlib crate, see crate layers and version bumps.

items.title: In short
items.text:
A device runs blinky_api 0.1.0. The next version adds a method and a field, and keeps everything else:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait BlinkyApi {
    fn led_on();
    fn led_off();
    #[since = "0.1.1"]
    fn led_toggle();
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap]
struct Status {
    on: bool,
    #[since = "0.1.1"]
    #[default = None]
    brightness: Option<u8>, // old data reads as None
}

Both are wire-compatible additions, so the crate goes from 0.1.0 to 0.1.1: an old device and a new host still connect, the host gets a clean error when it calls led_toggle on the old device, and reads None for the brightness it doesn't send. The rest of this page lists which changes are compatible like these. When in doubt, run the evolution checker, it compares your crate with its last release.

items.title: Your API's version
items.text:
Name and version of the user API crate are sent during link setup, and both device and host refuse to connect if they are not compatible (ww_version::Version::is_protocol_compatible):

  • Before 1.0: major and minor must match, so 0.2.0 and 0.2.7 connect, 0.2.0 and 0.3.0 don't.
  • After 1.0: major must match.

So the compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after) is for wire-compatible additions: new methods, properties, streams, new fields with defaults, etc. Mark them with #[since = "0.2.3"], so that a newer host can report a clean error when calling a resource that an older device doesn't have (see examples/blinky_api_evolved). Everything else bumps the breaking position.

The API crate's dependencies are part of this contract: upgrading a ww_stdlib crate or shrink_wrap to a wire-incompatible version, or the API model, is a breaking change of the user API too.

items.title: Doc comments
items.text: Doc comments on traits, resources and types are not part of the wire format, but they are shipped in introspection data and in crate snapshots, so a GUI or CLI can show them. A released version's snapshot never changes, so a doc-only change is still a new version: bump the compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after), same as for a wire-compatible addition. Devices with the old version keep connecting, and tools can tell that improved docs are available. ww api save refuses to overwrite a snapshot with changed docs, and the evolution checker requires the compatible bump.

items.title: Data types
items.text: WireWeaver considers two root types for evolution and evolution rule checks - struct and enum (plain and with data variants). Size of a type is marked as one of: Unsized, FinalStructure, SelfDescribing or Sized.

items.title: Unsized types
items.text:
By default, user defined struct or enum is Unsized. Both can contain variable-size types - vectors, strings or other structs and enums. Unsized types support all the evolution options. It is recommended to stick with unsized types, unless extreme space-saving is required.

When serializing, size of such objects is calculated and written to the resulting byte array. Which is the only overhead, giving all the nice backwards and forwards compatibility benefits.

  • New fields with #[default = ..] can be added to the end of structs and enum struct variants. Old data reads as the default (see derive), T can be anything:
    • Option<T> - #[default = None],
    • Vec<T>, String - #[default = Vec::new()], #[default = String::new()],
    • a bit-sized field (bool, nibble, Option / Result flag) can land in padding bits of the old data's last byte, which read as 0: give it its zero value as the default.
  • New enum variants can be added at the end. Readers of older versions fail on them unless the enum has a #[future_version] variant; with one, they get its discriminant. Every Unsized enum has one unless it says no_future_version (SW-47). In an Unsized enum new variants may carry data, in a sized or self_describing one only new unit variants can be read past by older readers. Adding or removing no_future_version changes the Rust type, not the wire: a Rust API break only.
  • New fixed size fields can be added in between old ones, into previously unused padding bits, without moving any other field (see the checker for exact conditions).
  • TODO: clarify: T -> struct containing T
  • Struct fields and enum variants can be renamed (but their position must NOT change).
  • A tuple struct (struct Pair(u8, u16);) follows the same rules by position: new fields with #[default = ..] only at the end. Naming the fields of a tuple struct, or the other way round, keeps every byte, but the API model then describes a different type (named instead of unnamed fields), which the checker reports as breaking. A unit struct (struct Marker;) can get fields with defaults later, named or not.

A TailSize<N> field (see wire format) is part of the layout like a Sized field: adding, removing or moving it, or changing N, breaks compatibility; fields after it evolve as usual, and old readers skip what newer writers append.

A Series<T> field is like a Vec<T> field: it can be appended with #[default = Default::default()] (old data reads as an empty series), but swapping it for a Vec<T>, or changing T other than as T's own rules allow, changes the bits and breaks compatibility.

items.title: Maximum lengths: MaxLen<T, N>
items.text:
A MaxLen<T, N> has the same bytes as T, so a bound never changes the wire, only which values the reader accepts (a longer one is an error, never truncated). Whether a change is compatible depends on what the old version writes:

  • Raising a bound or removing it (MaxLen<T, 64> -> MaxLen<T, 256> or T): compatible. Everything the old version writes is still read. The checker lists it as max length raised, because values the new version writes beyond the old bound are rejected by the old version (with an error): a new client sending a long piece to an old device gets an error reply, the same as any argument the device refuses.
  • Lowering a bound or adding one (T -> MaxLen<T, 64>, MaxLen<T, 256> -> MaxLen<T, 64>): breaking. Values the old version is allowed to write no longer fit, and nothing on the wire tells the old version so.
  • Changing T inside the bound follows the usual rules for T.

At connect time the client does not refuse a device whose bounds differ from its own: a longer value is rejected when it is sent, by whichever side has the smaller bound.

items.title: Compressed sequences: Series<T>
items.text: A Series has bytes of its own, so Vec<T> -> Series<T> or Series<u32> -> Series<u64> is breaking (ww api check reports it), unlike the borrowed / owned form (Series<'i, T> / SeriesOwned<T>), which is the same type. The codecs of its columns are not part of the type: each writer picks its own (CodecPolicy), every reader reads them all. A struct or enum T evolves inside a Series as it does on its own (see Series).

items.title: Sparse structs
items.text:
A sparse struct (DER-13) has a slot per field, all of them Option<T>:

  • New fields can be appended after the last slot, without #[default]: older data reads them as None, older readers ignore them.
  • A field can't be inserted before the last slot, also not into a gap left by #[slot = N]: a reader that doesn't know the slot can't step over a present value in it and fails with Error::OptionAnyVecUnknownSlot. Removing a field breaks too: data from an older writer can still have it present.
  • A field's slot and its T can't change (T evolves by its own rules); fields can be renamed.
  • Turning an ordinary struct into a sparse one or back changes every byte: breaking.

items.title: Generic types
items.text:
A generic struct or enum (Timed<T>, Window<const N: usize>, API-43) evolves like any other: its fields by the rules for its size assumption, its arguments by their own rules (Timed<Ampere> changes when Ampere does). Its parameters are compared by position and kind:

  • Renaming a parameter (Timed<T> -> Timed<V>) changes nothing.
  • Adding, removing or reordering parameters, turning a type parameter into a const one, or changing the type of a const parameter (usize -> u8) is breaking, also when a default keeps old code compiling: the uses on the wire carry one argument per parameter.
  • Making a fixed length a parameter ([u16; 4] -> [u16; N]) or back is breaking for the definition; uses that end up with the same length (Window<4>) have the same bytes.
  • A use with other arguments (Window<4> -> Window<8>, Pair<u8, u16> -> Pair<u8, u32>) is another type, as [u16; 4] -> [u16; 8] is.

items.title: FinalStructure, SelfDescribing and Sized types
items.text:
• Sized can become SelfDescribing and back (sized <-> self_describing): neither gets a size slot from its parent, the bytes are the same, and the checker reports it as compatible. A sized enum must have variants of one size (see derive).
  • New fixed size fields can be added in between old ones, into previously unused padding bits, without moving any other field (see the checker for exact conditions).
  • Struct fields and enum variants can be renamed (but their position must NOT change).

items.title: API
items.text:
Data types used in API are a part of SemVer guarantee and are subject to the rules above. Meaning that it's not allowed to break compatibility on any of the data types used directly or indirectly without also bumping the breaking position of the API version as well (minor before 1.0, major after, see your API's version).

  • Adding argument
  • T to struct of T in return position
  • T to Vec<T> in return position?

Streams (API-30, API-31, stream reliability): the delivery kind of a stream is part of the API. Turning a plain stream! into a #[counted] or #[reliable] one (or back, or one into the other), or giving a stream arguments or a result (#[stream(T)] fn name(args) -> Result<A, E>), changes its events and how it is opened, so it is a break of the API crate: bump its breaking version position, as for a plain sink becoming a #[credit] one. A plain #[stream(T)] fn name() without arguments and result is the same as stream!(name: T), the same bytes in introspection.

Batching a stream (API-41: batched / batched(untimed) in #[stream(..)], #[batched] next to stream!), or un-batching it, or switching between timed and untimed, changes its item type on the wire (one Series<Timed<T>> or Series<T> per event instead of one T): a break of the API crate too. The batch size is the device's (it is not in the API), so changing it is not a break.

Making a property +batched (API-39) or not changes its observe slot (a Batched<T> instead of a T): a break of the API crate. The times of the samples travel in the PropertyUpdate event, not in a slot, so adding resources to a level with +batched properties follows the usual rules.

items.title: API model
items.text:
API model (like ww_client_server) is part of the compatibility equation, it is not allowed to update the model version without breaking compatibility.

E.g., if user_device_api v0.1.0 depends on ww_client_server v0.4.0 and a new major version of ww_client_server comes out (v0.5.0), then user_device_api must be bumped to v0.2.0 to use the newer API model. This should only happen to add new features though, and if previous version is doing all that it is supposed to, there might not be a need to upgrade.

items.title: Settings stored on a device
items.text:
A settings store (ww_settings, STD-32) keeps a record per group in the device's flash, and the record outlives the firmware that wrote it: an update reads the old firmware's record, a downgrade the new one's. Each field has a slot, each stored field is a byte blob of its own, so every firmware can step over a slot it doesn't know. That makes the rules looser than for a sparse struct:

  • Adding a field: any slot that was never used, also one in a gap between older slots. Older records read it as its default. An older firmware keeps it unchanged when it writes its record.
  • Removing a field: put its slot into #[settings(retired(..))]; the derive then refuses to give it to another field. A record that still holds it is read without it, and the slot is dropped on the next write, so a downgrade to a firmware that still has the field finds it at its default.
  • Changing a field's type: only the way the type itself may evolve (a struct gets fields with #[default] appended, an enum gets variants). An older firmware reads what it knows of the newer value (a struct's first fields, an enum variant it doesn't know as Unknown(n)), and as long as it doesn't change the field, it writes the newer bytes back unchanged; if it changes the field, the parts it doesn't know are gone. Bytes it can't decode at all (an enum with no_future_version) are kept while the field stays at its default. Any other type change, or a change of what the value means (units, scale): a new slot, and the old one retired.
  • Changing a default: a stored record holds only the fields that differ from their default, so every device that never set the field takes the new default, and so does one that set it to exactly the old default. When that is wrong, the field needs a new slot.
  • Renaming a field is fine; the slot is what is stored. Moving a field to another group (another Key) is a new field there and a retired one here; copying the value over is the firmware's job on load.
  • The record format (ww_settings::record::FORMAT) and the store layout (the page and item headers in ww_settings::store) are defined by ww_settings itself: a change to either is a breaking change of ww_settings, as for ww_framer in layer 3. A firmware that finds a record in a format it doesn't know leaves it alone (is_read_only) instead of overwriting it.

items.title: Examples and Templates
items.text:
To start a new project, use the wire_weaver_template repository. The examples in this repository follow the same shape: an <name>_api crate with the trait and types (no_std), and a <name> crate with the host client using it (see folder structure).

New to WireWeaver: start with blinky_api and blinky (an API with two methods and its client), then blinky_evolved to see an old firmware keep working with a newer API. The rest show one feature each.

A firmware short of flash or RAM for code: linker relaxation on RISC-V saves about 10 %, and on very small targets a byte-wise memcpy about 320 bytes, with downsides, see code size on small CPUs.

A connected device can be inspected with the command line tool: ww list, then ww introspect.

items.title: Motor controller demo
items.text:
A VESC-like field oriented controller drives a simulated motor, and its ~50 variables are observed by a host, each at the rate it asks for, within a byte budget per trait level. It shows what observing many fast-changing properties costs on the link, and what it would cost as one StreamData event per value.

The demo lives in its own repo, motor_sim, next to the motor simulator it drives (it will grow into a full simulator with a GUI there, and those dependencies stay out of WireWeaver's workspace):

  • motor_demo_api: the API, 52 +observe properties in three trait levels, one per rate tier, their values ww_si quantities.
  • motor_demo: the controller, the device (in this process or on a UDP socket), the host side counting and the motor_demo CLI.
  • motor_sim: the motor, inverter, mechanics and sensors (a PMSM in dq, solved exactly per PWM period, with ADC noise, offsets and quantisation, an encoder and seeded faults).

It builds against a WireWeaver checkout next to it (../wire_weaver):

git clone https://github.com/vhrdtech/wire_weaver
git clone https://github.com/vhrdtech/motor_sim
cd motor_sim
cargo run --release -p motor_demo -- observe --compare        # a device in this process, 3 tiers, 1 s reports
cargo run --release -p motor_demo -- device --listen 127.0.0.1:9000
cargo run --release -p motor_demo -- observe --udp 127.0.0.1:9000 --prop i_q=every:1ms,speed_electrical,fault
cargo run --release -p motor_demo -- list                     # every property with the unit it is shown in
source <(COMPLETE=bash motor_demo)                             # completion of commands and property names

items.title: The API: one trait level per rate tier
items.text:
The VESC firmware (vedderb/bldc) computes its variables in three tiers, and so does this controller:

Level Rate Properties What foc 25 kHz, every PWM period 21 phase, αβ and dq currents, dq and αβ voltages, duties, the angle in use, the flux observer's and the encoder's angles, observer state, bus voltage, the true angle control 1 kHz 18 setpoints (mode, sensor_mode, duty, current, speed, all rw), PLL speed, current setpoints, filtered currents, input current, duty, torque, position, observer error, the true speed telemetry 50 Hz 13 time, charge and energy drawn and returned, tachometer, input voltage and power, averaged currents, fault, the real time factor sim 4 + 2 methods time_scale, load, motor, profile; inject(fault), reset() 
#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MotorDemo {
    ww_impl!(foc: Foc);
    ww_impl!(control: Control);
    ww_impl!(telemetry: Telemetry);
    ww_impl!(sim: Sim);
}

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Foc {
    /// Phase a current as measured (offset calibrated): `Milli` `I32`.
    property!(ro+observe i_a: Ampere);
    // ..
}

Each level is one observe subscription, so whatever is due in a level goes out in one PropertyUpdate, and a host asks for each tier at its own rate: foc at 1 kHz for a scope, control on change, telemetry at 10 Hz for a dashboard.

items.title: Values are ww_si quantities
items.text:
Every physical value is a ww_si quantity: Ampere, Volt, Radian, Weber, AngularVelocity, Degree, Torque, Coulomb, Joule, Watt, Second, and Ratio for duties, probabilities and the time scale. VESC's own units become SI: erpm is speed_electrical in rad/s (×60/2π back to erpm), Ah is charge_drawn in C (÷3600), Wh is energy_drawn in J (÷3600). The docs of each property give the prefix and storage the device sends it in, three number types in all:

Storage For Examples I32 at a fixed prefix every signed physical value currents and voltages in mA and mV, angles in µrad, speeds in mrad/s, flux in nWb, duties in millionths U32 totals that only grow time in ms, charge_drawn in C, energy_drawn in J F32 values that span decades time_scale, real_time_factor; setpoints the host writes

The prefix sets the resolution, so noise below it costs nothing: the device marks a value changed only when its quantity changed, which is why telemetry on change sends 311 values/s instead of the 520 it did with f32. Setters take whatever prefix and storage the host sends: the CLI writes F32 in the base unit. A firmware of this API compiles ww_si with only the i32, u32 and f32 number types. The host shows values in the old units (erpm, rpm, Ah, Wh, degrees), as VESC Tool does.

Next to f32, an I32 quantity is one byte more per value (the prefix and storage nibbles): the foc level at 1 kHz takes 117 kB/s instead of 96. Batched observe (a Series per property and the level's times once, API-39) is where the fixed prefix pays off: there the cost of a value is its change from the previous one, not its storage width.

items.title: The device
items.text:
The device's clock is simulated time, one PWM period (40 µs) per step; simulated time follows real time times sim.time_scale. Every step:

  1. the controller runs on the sensor readings (current offsets measured during the first 0.1 s, Clarke and Park, the Ortega flux observer and a PLL, d/q current PI loops with decoupling, space vector PWM; the speed loop and the filters every 25th step, the counters every 500th), the simulator steps with the duties it gives;
  2. every value of a tier that ran and changed is marked, mark_changed_<name>(), so change: observers get it, and every sample goes to the batches a samples: observer gets: foc writes its 21 values into its observe cells and commits the row, as a FOC interrupt would (observe cells, observe_cells = "root_foc"), control hands its row to sample(t, ControlSamples { .. }): both paths in one device, the same wire;
  3. poll_properties(out, (), now_us, buf) sends what is due, with now_us the simulated microseconds.

Messages are up to 4 KiB (MAX_MESSAGE_LEN) each way, the in-process and UDP buffers sized from it: room for the whole foc level batched, a Series of 32 values per property is about 1.3 kB.

ObserveLimits::min_period_us is one PWM period, so the 25 kHz tier can be observed at every step. Periods, the timestamps and the budgets are in device time: with time_scale 0.01, every:40us arrives at 250 Hz real, and the CLI converts --budget from real bytes per second. When a step can't keep up, the simulation falls behind instead of catching up in a burst later; telemetry.real_time_factor says how fast it really runs.

The controller's gains come from the motor parameters, as VESC's motor detection would set them: current loops with a 0.2 ms time constant, a 10 Hz speed loop. The PLL is faster than VESC's default (kp 2000, ki 30 000): the light hobby outrunner accelerates at ~60 000 rad/s² electrical, which made that one slip.

items.title: Measured
items.text:
On a laptop (Ryzen AI 9 HX 370), release build, the VESC outrunner with a propeller and the built-in speed steps running. Bytes are whole messages, serialized Events, rebuilt on the host from what arrived; the framing (USB packets, UDP datagrams) is shared by every message in a frame and left out on both sides. In-process and UDP give the same numbers. StreamData/s is the same values sent as one StreamData event each, as stream_data_ser() sends a property's change, without a timestamp.

$ motor_demo observe --compare
Observing sim time ×1; periods and budgets below are device (simulated) time, rates real time
  foc        21× every:10ms, budget 20.0 kB/s
  control    18× every:10ms, budget 20.0 kB/s
  telemetry  13× change:1ms, budget 20.0 kB/s
      t  level      updates/s  values/s     bytes/s   use  missed/s  StreamData/s  saving
   1.0s  foc              101      2118    11.8 kB/s   59%         0      20.4 kB/s     42%
   1.0s  control          101      1815     9.6 kB/s   48%         0      16.5 kB/s     42%
   1.0s  telemetry         51       311     2.2 kB/s   11%         0       2.9 kB/s     25%
Case Level Updates/s Values/s Bytes/s As StreamData Saving all 52, foc and control every 1 ms, telemetry every 20 ms, 200 kB/s each foc 1000 21 005 117.0 kB/s 202.1 kB/s 42 % control 1000 18 005 95.0 kB/s 164.0 kB/s 42 % telemetry 50 654 3.7 kB/s 5.9 kB/s 38 % foc every PWM period, time_scale 0.01 foc 250 5 247 29.2 kB/s 50.5 kB/s 42 %

Where the bytes go: a PropertyUpdate has a header of 10 bytes (sequence, result, the level's path, t as a u32 of microseconds; 4 bytes without t), then the update's presence header (a bit per slot, or a list of indices when few are present) and the values. A current in mA as I32 is 5 bytes, alone as StreamData 9 (10 for a resource index above 15). An update of 21 such values takes 117 bytes, 5.6 per value.

--time-scale 200 gives a real time factor of about 120 for the simulator and controller (one thread; ~140 with the f32 API, the conversion of every value to its quantity at 25 kHz costs the rest); above that, the device falls behind and says so.

items.title: A level short of budget
items.text:
--foc every:1ms --budget 30000 with 8 foc properties: 32 kB/s of values asked for, 30 kB/s granted, and poll_properties called every 40 µs. The scheduler used to send whatever fit the bucket at each call, so a level short of budget sent about one value per update, each with its own header. Now a level holds until all its due properties fit, or its bucket is full (ww_stream::observe, SRV-18):

Updates/s Values per update Bytes/s As StreamData Missed/s before 1432 1.4 31.5 kB/s 16.1 kB/s 7280 after 666 8 31.0 kB/s 44.0 kB/s 2668

The same bytes now carry 2.7 times the values. What doesn't fit is reported in missed: 8000 due per second, 5331 sent. A property held back counts as missed only once it really falls a period behind, so polling often doesn't inflate the count. Both rows were measured with the f32 API; with quantities (a byte more per value) the same case gives 565 updates/s of 8 values, 31.0 kB/s, 41.8 kB/s as StreamData and 3472 missed/s.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
cargo nextest run -p motor_demo in motor_sim:

  • tests/controller.rs: the controller against the simulator without WireWeaver: current, speed (both directions) and duty control, the observer tracking the angle and running sensorless, hybrid start from standstill, every motor preset, the counters against the simulator's energy.
  • tests/observe.rs: through the generated client, each tier at its rate, a budget below what is asked for, slow motion (the 25 kHz tier at 2.5 kHz real) and fast forward, UDP.

items.title: Code size on small CPUs
items.text:
How much code shrink_wrap costs on a CPU with a few kilobytes of memory, where the bytes go, what was changed because of it and what is left. Measured in October 2026 for a softcore firmware with 8 KB of RAM for code, data and stack (the QERV RISC-V of fpga_tools' busgen). Its request/reply codec was hand-written because the derived one did not fit; since fpga_tools 0.9.0 (BUS-12) the firmware runs on head_tail views and variant writers (SW-52, SW-53, SW-54), and no hand-written codec is left.

Summary:

  • The derived codec of that firmware went from 11.3 KB to 9.0 KB on RV32IC (15.1 → 12.5 KB on RV32I, 9.3 → 7.3 KB on Cortex-M0) with five changes that keep the wire format as it is. With sized / final_structure types and linker relaxation it is 7.3 KB. The same codec written by hand is 5.2 to 5.8 KB.
  • Half of what was saved came from one thing: plain fields are no longer checked for an error one by one.
  • An encoder whose types have no lists, strings or nested evolvable types does not link the code for lengths at all: a struct of eight fields is 964 bytes on RV32IC instead of 1476 (1934 before any of this).
  • No cargo feature was needed, and none is proposed: what a firmware does not call is not linked, and a feature that changes the wire format would be a trap (see Feature flags).
  • A build setting found on the way is worth more than any of the code changes on RISC-V: linker relaxation was off, -C target-feature=+relax saves 9 to 11 % for any firmware, hand-written ones too.

items.title: The bench
items.text:
just size-bench (the size_bench crate in shrink_wrap/size_bench) builds one bare firmware image per test case from shrink_wrap/size_bench/fw and prints .text + .rodata in bytes. just size-bench -c busgen -t rv32ic -s 30 prints the 30 largest symbols of an image instead.

The build profile is the one of the softcore firmware: nightly, build-std = ["core"], panic = "immediate-abort", opt-level = "z", fat LTO, one codegen unit, -Zlocation-detail=none -Zfmt-debug=none. Targets:

name target flags rv32i riscv32i-unknown-none-elf rv32ic riscv32i-unknown-none-elf -C target-feature=+c (what the softcore runs) rv32ic-relax riscv32i-unknown-none-elf -C target-feature=+c,+relax thumbv6m thumbv6m-none-eabi Cortex-M0, for comparison thumbv7em thumbv7em-none-eabihf Cortex-M4F / M7 (Thumb-2), for comparison with larger MCUs

Every case is a run(rx, tx) that decodes from one buffer and encodes into another. Inputs and outputs go through core::hint::black_box, so nothing is computed at compile time and every decoded field counts as used. The images are measured, not run.

case what it holds empty no shrink_wrap code: 38 bytes on RV32IC, the floor of every other case rw_de, rw_ser BufReader / BufWriter alone: a u8, a bool, a u16, a u32 (rw_ser ends with finish_no_lens() since step 4) struct_de, struct_ser a struct of eight integers and flags (Wave) enum_de, enum_ser an enum of five small variants vec_de, vec_ser a struct with a u16 and a RefVec<u16>, the list walked after decoding bits_de, bits_ser a bit-packed struct: U3, bool, U4, U12, I10, U20, U5, u8 (Sample, since SW-38) option_de, option_ser a struct of ten fields, two of them Option busgen_de the softcore firmware's receive side: Request (18 variants, lists of structs and of u16, nested structs, an Option<Wave>) decoded and acted on busgen_ser its transmit side: one of the nine Reply variants encoded busgen both: a request decoded, acted on, its reply encoded busgen_hand the same as busgen with a hand-written codec: bytes, little endian, a list is a count and its items, reading past the end gives zeros reply a method's reply as ww_codegen! server code encodes it: a Wave return value alone, then the ww_client_server::Event around its bytes, and the error event when that fails

The cases with derived types are built twice: evolvable (the default, every type Unsized) and final (sized where the fields allow it, else final_structure). The two differ only where a type is nested in another, so the small cases give the same number for both.

busgen_hand is the yardstick, not empty: the handler that acts on a request, the enum values it builds and the bench's own black_box calls are in both busgen and busgen_hand. What the two differ by is the codec.
