Directive For fixed_layout every field at a constant offset: headers, flash records, the smallest possible reader head_tail lists and strings in a format a tiny C or Rust reader walks front to back sparse a struct of many optional fields, where only the present ones are written

fixed_layout keeps the regular shrink_wrap bytes and adds a fast path; head_tail and sparse are encodings of their own.

items.title: fixed_layout: fields at fixed offsets
items.text:
shrink_wrap writes a value field after field. When no field's size depends on its value, every field starts at the same place in every value: a header, a record in flash, a descriptor that is signed as bytes. Reading a field is then a load at a constant offset, and the macro generates that next to the usual serdes code (SW-44, SW-45).

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, fixed_layout)]
struct Header {
    magic: [u8; 4],
    urgent: bool,
    retries: U3,
    count: u32,
    inner: Inner,         // another fixed_layout type
    extra: Option<Extra>, // last: present when its flag bit is set
}

let header = Header::from_fixed(&bytes)?; // what a tiny bootloader links: loads at constant offsets
let header = Header::from_ww_bytes(&bytes)?; // the same value through BufReader

What gets generated:

  • ENCODED_LEN: the longest encoding, the buffer to have ready. MIN_LEN: the shortest. fixed_len(): the length of this value. All three are the same unless the last field has a variable length (see below).
  • An offset const per field: COUNT_OFFSET in bytes, or for a bit field URGENT_BIT_OFFSET and URGENT_BITS, counted from the most significant bit of the first byte. For an enum TAG_LEN, and per variant <VARIANT>_TAG, <VARIANT>_LEN and <VARIANT>_<FIELD>_.. (unnamed fields by their index). An Option's flag is <FIELD>_FLAG. A tuple struct's fields are _0, _1, ...: _2_OFFSET, in C PX__2_OFFSET and px__2() for struct Px(u8, bool, u16).
  • from_fixed(&[u8]) and to_fixed(&mut [u8]): loads and stores (shifts and masks for bit fields) at those offsets, without a BufReader or BufWriter. The bytes are those of ser_shrink_wrap. A short buffer is an error, never a panic.
  • The FixedLayout trait, whose write_c prints the C reader of the type: a define per offset and a static inline reader per field (shrink_wrap::fixed_layout::write_c_header writes a whole header).

On a Cortex-M0, decoding a header of eight integers takes 276 bytes of code this way and 484 through BufReader; a bit-packed sample 276 instead of 652 (code size).

items.title: What has a fixed offset
items.text:
Field Rule u8..u64, i8..i64, f32, f64, arrays of them start on a byte, little-endian, as BufWriter writes them bool, U1..U32, I2..I32, Nibble packed most significant bit first; a Nibble starts on a 4-bit boundary; the next byte-aligned field starts a fresh byte another fixed_layout type starts on a byte; it can't share a byte with bit fields of the parent (a compile error asks for a byte-aligned field between them) Option<T>, Result<T, E>, an enum whose variants differ in length only as the last field: the fields before it keep their offsets, nothing after it could. The payload starts on a byte; the flag is an ordinary bit field, also where #[flag] moves it

Not: lists, strings, MaxLen, varints (UNib32 and friends), RefBox, TailSize, tuples, ranges, 128-bit numbers, bit fields wider than 32 bits, #[default] fields. A struct must be sized, final_structure or self_describing: an evolvable struct may grow, so it has no fixed layout. An enum must be sized or self_describing with a byte-aligned tag (ww_repr = u8, u16 or u32).

The rule for variable length is the same everywhere: an Option, a Result and an enum of unequal variants are each a value whose length depends on what it holds. As a whole type, or as the last field of one, that is fine: fixed_len() says how long this value is. Before another field it is not, because that field would move.

items.title: With and without the directive
items.text:
Types that qualify get the fast path without asking. The fixed_layout directive makes it a requirement:

  • a field that breaks it is a compile error that says why and what to use instead, for example "field count: a variable-length number takes more bytes for larger values, so the fields after it have no fixed offset. Use u32 / u64, or U1..U32 for fewer bits";
  • only with the directive may a field be another fixed-layout type (the macro can't look inside a type it doesn't see; the compiler checks that it implements FixedLayout);
  • on a struct it also picks the size assumption when none is given: sized, or self_describing when the last field is an Option or Result. A struct whose last field is an enum of unequal variants says self_describing itself.

items.title: head_tail: a fixed head and a sequential tail
items.text:
For types with lists, strings or options in the middle, where no fixed layout exists, head_tail picks a wire format of its own (SW-46), made for the smallest reader on a microcontroller:

  • the head has a length known at compile time and holds every fixed-width field at a constant offset, as fixed_layout places them, and for each variable field what is fixed about it: a u16 count for a list or string, the flag bit of an Option or Result, the head of a nested head_tail or fixed_layout type;
  • the tail follows the head and holds the variable parts in field order: list items, string bytes, option payloads, the tails of nested types.

An enum is its tag (ww_repr = u8, u16 or u32), then the head and tail of its variant. Reading the head is loads at constant offsets; the tail is read front to back by a cursor that only takes lengths it already knows (Tail). There are no lengths at the back, no BufReader, no per-type generic reader.

use shrink_wrap::head_tail::List;

#[derive_shrink_wrap(head_tail)]
struct Utx<'i> {
    ch: u8,
    fmt: UartFormat,        // a fixed_layout type: in the head
    glitch: Option<Wave>,   // flag bit in the head, the Wave in the tail
    perr: List<'i, u16>,    // count in the head, the items in the tail
    name: &'i str,          // the same
    defer: bool,            // a bit in the head, after all of them
}

let utx = Utx::from_head_tail(&bytes)?;
let n = utx.to_head_tail(&mut buf)?;
  • A list is a shrink_wrap::head_tail::List<'i, T>: List::new(&items) to write; read from the wire it keeps the bytes and reads an item when its iterator reaches it. Its items are numbers or fixed_layout types of one length.
  • Option / Result payloads are numbers, arrays of them, or head_tail / fixed_layout types.
  • Every fixed_layout type implements HeadTail (all head when it has one length, else all tail), so the types of a protocol mix freely.

It is one type with one format: a head_tail type has no SerializeShrinkWrap / DeserializeShrinkWrap (and no owned version), so it can't be a field of an ordinary shrink_wrap type or a WireWeaver API argument. write_c_ht prints the C reader: head defines and readers as for fixed_layout, and per type a <name>_tail_t and a <name>_tail() that walks the tail and points at each variable part (shrink_wrap::head_tail::write_c_header writes a whole header).

items.title: Views and writers
items.text:
For firmware that should not build the whole value first (SW-52):

  • Utx::view(&bytes)? checks the lengths and walks the tail once (counts and flags are the only fields it reads) and gives a UtxView<'_>: a reference to the head whose accessors (v.ch(), v.defer()) read each field at its offset when called, and the variable parts found on the way (v.perr() a List, v.glitch() an &Option<Wave>, a nested head_tail type its own view).
  • An enum's view is an enum of its variants' views: RequestView::Stop(v) with v.mask(); a tuple variant of one nested type holds that type's view (RequestView::Utx(UtxView)).
  • Each enum variant also gets a writer, Reply::write_run(&mut tx, run, started, mark, lead, mark_line)?, which writes the same bytes as to_head_tail of that variant without making the value.

Both come from the code of from_head_tail / to_head_tail and are tested against it byte for byte. View types are always pub (the View of the public HeadTail trait).

Enum variants may have a #[cfg] (SW-54): a variant compiled out keeps its tag, and a build without it reads that tag as an unknown one. One protocol enum can then serve firmware images that each handle a part of it.

On busgen's request and reply enums the codec takes 4590 bytes on a Cortex-M0 through values and 3894 through views and writers, a hand-written one 4408 and the derived shrink_wrap one 6652 (code size).

items.title: sparse: a struct of optional fields
items.text:
sparse (DER-13) encodes a struct whose fields are all Option<T> as an OptionAnyVec: a presence header, then only the present values. Each field is one slot, in declaration order; #[slot = N] places a field at slot N instead (slots increase, gaps are allowed).

It is made for updates that carry any subset of many values, such as the per trait level <Level>Update of an observe request, whose slots are the level's resource indices with methods and streams in between:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq, Default), sparse)]
struct MotorUpdate<'i> {
    speed: Option<u16>,    // slot 0
    name: Option<&'i str>, // slot 1
    #[slot = 5]
    current: Option<f32>,  // slot 5, slots 2..=4 are never present
    on: Option<bool>,      // slot 6
}

let update = MotorUpdate { speed: Some(1500), on: Some(true), ..Default::default() };
assert_eq!(update.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf)?, [0x17, 0x82, 0xdc, 0x05, 0x80]);

The bytes:

  • 1 7: the dense header mode, 7 slots, then a bit per slot, 1000001 and a padding bit (82);
  • dc 05 is speed, the 80 bit on.

With all four fields present it is 17 c6 dc 05 4c 00 00 c0 3f 81: the bits 1100011, speed, "L", 1.5f32, the on bit, and the length of "L" in the last nibble. One field present is three bytes (MotorUpdate { speed: Some(1500), .. } is 01 dc 05: the all mode, one slot), none is no bytes at all. The writer picks the header mode with the fewest bits for the present set (header modes).

A field may be any type, including another sparse struct: a child level is then one slot holding its own sparse struct, so one message carries any subset of a tree of levels. The borrowed and the owned type write the same bytes.

Rules, checked at compile time:

  • every field is an Option<T>; #[flag] and #[default = ..] don't apply (any field can be absent, a field added later reads as None from older data);
  • sparse is an encoding of its own: no final_structure, self_describing, sized, fixed_layout or head_tail with it, and no enums. The struct is Unsized;
  • #[slot = N] is an integer literal past the previous field's slot, below u32::MAX, and only on sparse fields.

Evolution: fields are only appended, after the last slot (see the rules). An older reader reads the fields it knows and ignores the rest, a newer reader reads the new fields as None. A reader whose struct has a gap where the data has a present value fails with Error::OptionAnyVecUnknownSlot: a gap is never filled later.

items.title: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type
items.text:
SW-60. Series<'i, T> is a list of T written column by column instead of item by item: one column per leaf field, each compressed on its own. For samples that change slowly (sensor readings, counters, timestamps) it is 3 to 8 times smaller than a plain Vec<T>, without giving up evolution, zero-copy reading, or no_std/no-alloc.

A Series is a type you reach for explicitly today, in a property, method argument/return or stream item, the same way you'd use Vec<T>; a Series of plain numbers is the compressed number sequence. A stream or property can also opt into batching many samples into one Series automatically instead of sending one item at a time (API-41, see Batching); nothing below needs that.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Which T
items.text:
Any #[derive_shrink_wrap(.., series)] struct or enum, nested to any depth, including generic ones (Timed<T>, DER-14): structs (named fields), unit-only enums and enums with data, Option, integers (u8..u64, i8..i64, U1..U64, I2..I64, 128-bit), f32/f64, bool, tuples, arrays, &str/String/bytes (as an opaque run), and any other type marked #[series(opaque)]. A field of a user type needs series on that type too; see series for the exact directive and what it doesn't take in this first version (recursive types like RefBox, Result, lists other than of u8, TailSize, sparse and tuple structs) — each is a compile error naming the field, not a silent fallback.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, series, final_structure)]
struct Volt { prefix: Prefix, value: NumericValue }

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, series)]
struct IvSample { v: Volt, i: Ampere }
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Why it's smaller
items.text:
A plain Vec<T> writes one T after another; a Series writes one column per leaf field, over all items, and picks the cheapest representation per column:

  • Discrete leaves (enum tags — so a ww_si prefix or a NumericValue storage tag, bool, Option presence, strings) are runs: the first value, then one entry per change. A value that never changes across a whole batch costs about 5 bits total, not a bit (or a byte) per item.
  • Numeric leaves are a numeric column: a predictor (raw, delta, delta of delta) and a coder (the SW-31 prefix code, a new block bit-packed coder, constant, or plain) picked per column, by trying each and keeping the smallest. A column restarts (a full value, fresh codec state) where an enum field declared earlier in the same struct changed — so a current reading that jumps from the µA range to the mA range gets a full value instead of a meaningless delta across the jump.
  • Floats are a float column, plain or the XOR code (Gorilla), but integers with a predictor compress markedly better than floats — see below.

A Series is self-contained: every batch carries its own first values and codec headers, so a lost batch never corrupts the next one, on any stream.

The full bit-level layout (column order, run and numeric column encoding, restarts, evolution) is in wire format internals; this page is about when and why to reach for it.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Sizes against Vec<T>
items.text:
IvSample { v: Volt, i: Ampere }, v as millivolts (U16), i as microamps (I32), 100 items per batch (100 ms at 1 kHz):

100 items Vec<T> (evolvable) Vec<T> (final_structure) Series steady (v ±1 mV, i ±2 µA) 902 B 802 B 104 B noisy (slow sine + noise σ≈8 mV / 300 µA) 902 B 802 B 251 B range switches (i jumps µA ↔ mA for items 30..70) 902 B 802 B 110 B exactly flat, a spike every 25 items 902 B 802 B 88 B

7.7x smaller on a steady signal, 3.2x on a noisy one, against the smallest plain form. With time added (Series<Timed<IvSample>>, t as microseconds since batch start) against a final_structure Vec of { t, v, i } (13 B/item plain): 113 B steady, 260 B noisy, regular 1 kHz; a regular clock costs nothing extra (constant delta), ±3 µs of jitter adds about 6 bits/item. Timed<T> is just another struct field, not a special case.

Bytes per item by batch size, steady signal (plain final_structure / Series):

n 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 bytes/item 9.0 / 10.0 8.5 / 6.0 8.3 / 3.5 8.1 / 2.1 8.1 / 1.6 8.0 / 1.2 8.0 / 1.1 8.0 / 1.0 8.0 / 0.9

A single item costs one byte more than plain (the column headers have to be paid once); from 2 items on Series is already smaller, and most of the gain is there by 32 items — the default batch size the planned API-41 batching is expected to use.

The showcase has the exact bytes of a 4-item batch, checked against the running code.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Integer storage beats floats
items.text:
A steady f32 voltage (100 values) is about 136 B with the XOR code; the same signal stored as U16 millivolts with a ww_si prefix is 45 B. Noisy: 277 B vs 82 B. The prefix sets the resolution, and noise below that resolution costs nothing — so a device sending ww_si quantities (which carry a prefix and an integer storage tag by construction) gets this for free, while a bare f32 pays for every bit of mantissa the ADC's noise floor touches.

This has a flip side: unbatched, a ww_si quantity (prefix + storage tag + the integer) is bigger than a bare f32 in a single plain update — measured on a motor control demo, moving one observe property from f32 to ww_si went from 96 to 117 kB/s. Quantities pay off once they're batched into a Series; sending one at a time gets you the worse of both.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Time: Timed<T>
items.text: ww_si::Timed<T> { t: Second, value: T } (DER-14 generic struct with series) is not a special case of Series — it gets a t column like any other field, and a regular sampling rate costs about nothing (delta + constant: t0 + period). Use Series<Timed<T>> wherever a batch needs its own timestamps; where a stream already carries time for the whole batch, a plain Series<T> works just as well.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Using it
items.text:
use shrink_wrap::series::{Series, SeriesOwned};

let items: Vec<IvSample> = /* ... */;
let bytes = Series::new(&items).to_ww_bytes_owned()?;       // picks the smallest codec per column
// or, on a small MCU: fixed codecs, chosen at compile time, only they are linked
// Series::with_policy(&items, DeltaPacked).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf)?;

let back: Vec<IvSample> = Series::<IvSample>::from_ww_bytes(&bytes)?.iter().collect();
let owned = SeriesOwned::<IvSample>::from_ww_bytes_owned(&bytes)?; // std, into a Vec<T>

Deserializing validates every column in one pass (SeriesColumns::skim) with no allocation; iter() then decodes items one at a time, stepping all columns in parallel, zero-copy for borrowed &str/&[u8] leaves. Malformed data is always an Error, never a panic; the number of items is capped at u16::MAX (a column can take zero bits per item — a constant run — so, unlike Vec<T>, the count can't be checked against the remaining bytes and has to be bounded instead).

Series<T> evolves exactly as T does (see evolution): an appended #[default = ..] field gets its own column at the end of the group, which an older reader skips and a newer reader reading older data fills from the default; a new enum variant an older reader doesn't know fails the same way a plain decode of that item would.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: CPU and flash on an MCU
items.text:
SW-63. How the codecs of the columns are picked is a SeriesPolicy: CodecPolicy::SMALLEST tries every codec per column and keeps the smallest, CodecPolicy::fixed(numeric, float) uses one for every column, both values chosen at run time, so both link every codec and the trials. A type with FixedCodecs fixes the codecs at compile time and links only them: DeltaPacked (delta and packed residuals, XOR floats) is one, and the no_std default of a ww_stream batcher. All of them write the same bytes for the same codecs.

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct DeltaOfDeltaPacked;

impl FixedCodecs for DeltaOfDeltaPacked {
    const NUMERIC: NumericCodec = NumericCodec::new(Predictor::DeltaOfDelta, Coder::Packed);
    const FLOAT: FloatCodec = FloatCodec::Xor;
}

Series::with_policy(&items, DeltaOfDeltaPacked).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf)?;

What a Series<Timed<Ampere>> costs (64 samples of a motor's phase current, examples_mcu/mcu_qemu and mcu_qemu_m4f, instructions counted in QEMU with examples_mcu/qemu_icount; flash is the bin's .text minus the same bin without a Series):

Cortex-M3 instructions per item, n = 8 / 32 / 64 bytes, n = 8 / 32 / 64 flash SMALLEST 1112 / 969 / 950 21 / 50 / 89 25.4 KB fixed(delta, packed) 409 / 341 / 332 27 / 79 / 153 25.4 KB fixed(delta-of-delta, packed) 411 / 334 / 321 28 / 61 / 100 25.4 KB DeltaPacked 406 / 341 / 333 27 / 79 / 153 15.0 KB

A Cortex-M4F takes about the same instructions; its flash is 17.6 KB with a CodecPolicy and 9.8 KB with DeltaPacked. On an STM32H725 (Cortex-M7 at 540 MHz, caches on, examples_mcu/usb_stm32h725ig's series_encode_cycles) a batch of 32 takes 25 200 cycles with DeltaPacked (47 µs, 790 cycles per item) and 60 800 with SMALLEST. A fixed codec is about 3x cheaper in CPU than SMALLEST, for 1.2x to 1.7x the bytes on this signal (a ramp after a step: delta of delta is the better fixed codec there, delta on flatter signals).
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: From the store, column by column
items.text:
SW-64. A batch kept in a SeriesStore can be written without rebuilding its items: write_store_series writes rows of a store column by column, straight from its arrays, the same bytes as Series::with_policy(items, policy). ww_stream's batchers do it on their own. It needs every enum and Option in the rows to keep one variant (a ww_si prefix, a NumericValue type), so that no column restarts; otherwise, and for strings, byte lists and UN / IN leaves, write_store_series writes nothing and says so, and the items are walked as before.

let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf);
if !write_store_series::<Ampere, _, 32>(&mut wr, &store, 0..32, &DeltaPacked)? {
    // a prefix changed in the batch: rebuild the items and write `Series::with_policy(&items, DeltaPacked)`
}

One FOC level batch of the motor demo (21 quantities and the clock, n = 32: 21 x Series<T> + Series<Second>, examples_mcu/mcu_qemu's qemu-store-columns and usb_stm32h725ig's shared_clock_cycles):

bytes Cortex-M3 instructions STM32H725 cycles, opt-level z / 3 DeltaPacked, item walk 1 251 118 283 264 900 / 96 800 DeltaPacked, from the store 1 251 46 665 53 200 / 36 800 RawPlain, from the store 2 882 78 873 89 700 / 76 800

Before the word-wide bit writer (SW-68, see the Nomicon of the Series article) these were 143 463, 74 898 and 115 063 instructions.

At opt-level z the cycles move by up to 15 % between builds with the code layout. A firmware that writes series in a hot path gains more from opt-level = 3 than from any codec: the series code is generic and compiled into the firmware's own crate, so a [profile.release.package.shrink_wrap] override doesn't reach it.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Collecting items on a device: SeriesStore
items.text:
SW-62. A device that sends items in batches keeps them somewhere until the batch is written. SeriesStore is that place: room for N items as a struct of arrays, one array per leaf field, which #[derive_shrink_wrap(.., series)] implements next to SeriesColumns:

use shrink_wrap::series::SeriesStore;

let mut store = Timed::<Ampere>::empty_store::<32>();       // in a static or the device's state
Timed::set(&mut store, k, &Timed::new(t, Ampere::milli(i))); // item k of the batch
let item: Timed<Ampere> = Timed::get(&store, k);

Without padding between fields of different sizes it takes less RAM than the items themselves: Store<32> of Timed<Ampere> is 12 bytes per item with ww_numeric's U8, U32, I32 and F32 enabled, where [Timed<Ampere>; 32] takes 24. What each kind of type keeps:

Type Store numbers, bool, strings an array of themselves struct, tuple the stores of its fields [X; M] M stores of X Option<X> an array of flags and the store of X enum an array of discriminants (u8, u16 or u32, u32 with a #[future_version]) and the stores of every data variant's fields PhantomData nothing ww_numeric::NumericValue by hand: the variant (a byte) and one array as wide as the widest variant enabled

An enum's store takes its discriminant plus the fields of all its variants per item, so for an enum with several data variants it can be bigger than the enum itself (enum { A(u32), B(u32) }: 9 bytes against 8). series(no_store) leaves the derived store out, to write a better one by hand as NumericValue does (ww_numeric/src/store.rs): one payload array for all its variants. A type with a #[series(opaque)] field gets no store, and a type with a field of such a type needs series(no_store) too.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Cells: a store shared with an interrupt (SeriesCells)
items.text: series(cells) also implements shrink_wrap::series::SeriesCells, the same struct of arrays made of atomics (AtomicU8 / AtomicU16 / AtomicU32, two or four AtomicU32s for 64 and 128 bits): one context puts items into rows with relaxed stores (on a Cortex-M a plain str, as for a global variable), another copies rows into a SeriesStore with relaxed loads (copy_rows), without a lock and without static mut. A value of two words can mix two items only in a row copied while it is written; the code sharing the cells has to find and drop such rows (observe cells count rows, see observing.md). All-zero bytes are an empty, valid set of cells (empty_cells(), or core::mem::zeroed() in a const fn), which is why the trait is unsafe to implement. ww_numeric::NumericValue has its cells by hand, ww_si's quantities and Timed derive them. Opt-in, because a type with a hand-written store inside would need cells of its own; strings, byte lists and opaque fields have none.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Size bounds
items.text:
The batch has to fit into the message it goes out in, so a device needs to know how big a Series of n items can get without writing it. SeriesColumns::MAX_ITEM_BITS and MAX_FIXED_BITS are the worst case of a type's group, per item and per series: every column at its longest code under any CodecPolicy (not only the one SMALLEST picks), every run changing at every item. Series::<T>::max_bytes(n) puts them together with the count and the padding. Strings, byte lists and opaque fields have no bound (None).

The bound is far from what real data takes: 32 samples of Timed<Volt> at a regular clock are 22 bytes, against a bound of 570 with the number types up to 32 bits and 1272 with every one enabled (NumericValue is bounded by its widest variant). It tells when a batch is safely below a budget, and a measurement (BitCounter) is needed only close to it.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Introspection and dynamic clients
items.text:
A Series<T> in an API is in its introspection data as Series<T> (ww_self::Type::Series, with T as written and #[series(opaque)] marked on the field), so clients without generated code read it too: ww and the dynamic wire_weaver_client API show it as a list of items, and Python gives the items or, with decode_columns, one numpy array per leaf field:

cols = dev.readings.decode_columns(data)   # or a property's / stream's decode_columns
cols["value"]               # array([3298, 3299, ...], dtype=int32)
cols["status"]              # variant of each item: array(['Idle', 'Busy', ...], dtype=object)
cols["status.Fault.code"]   # masked where an item is in another variant

The dynamic decoder (ww_self, ValueOwned::des_shrink_wrap_dyn for the items, des_series_columns_dyn for the columns) walks the type tree with the same rules as the code the derive generates: column by column, restarting a column after an earlier enum or Option tag changes, a newer or older T read as the typed decoder reads it (missing fields take their declared #[default]). The bytes come from a device, so they are untrusted: malformed data is an error, and since an item can take no bits at all (a constant column), the work and the memory are bounded by the decode's budget (values and bytes of memory, a repeated value counted once per copy), not by the length of the bytes.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: What's not here yet
items.text: Series<T> as a type you put in a property, method or stream today works end to end (phase 1 of SW-60). Picking the batch for you — a stream or property opting into batching (no size in the API itself: the device owns the batch size through its own config, default 32, and the host picks latency) sending Series<Timed<T>> batches instead of one item per event — is phase 2, API-41, done: see Batching for the how-to, sealing, budgets and the measured numbers. The numbers above (default batch 32, integer storage, autoranging cost) come from the simulator built for that work and hold for Series used by hand too.
path: Series<T>: compressed sequences of any derived type

items.title: Showcase
items.text:
A tour of shrink_wrap tricks, from plain bit-packing to self-referential types, illustrated with real code from wire_weaver itself and from the ww_stdlib crates (ww_version, ww_date_time, ww_client_server, ww_self). Every byte sequence shown below was produced by actually running the snippet - none of it is hand-waved.

Read ShrinkWrap, derive and size assumptions first if you haven't; this page assumes you know what Unsized/final_structure/self_describing/sized mean and how #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] decides between borrowed and owned types.

items.title: Sub-byte packing
items.text:
bool is 1-bit aligned, nib (the Nibble type) is 4-bit aligned, and u1..u64/i2..i64 (U1, U2, ..., I2, ...) are 1-bit aligned regardless of width - they just cost exactly as many bits as you ask for, packed back-to-back with no padding in between:

let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf);
wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();          // 1 bit
wr.write(&U2::new(3).unwrap()).unwrap(); // 2 bits
wr.write(&U1::new(1).unwrap()).unwrap(); // 1 bit
let bytes = wr.finish().unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, &[0b1111_0000]); // 1 + 11 + 1 = 4 bits used, rest padded with zeros

A whole tuple of 8 bools packs into a single byte, no framing at all:

let bytes = (true, false, true, false, true, true, false, false)
    .to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, &[0b1010_1100]);

This is what the ElementSize::Sized { size_bits } case (see size assumptions) is built on: a sized struct/enum's fields are just laid out bit after bit, so putting a bool field or a small enum next to another Sized field is free - they share the same byte instead of each getting its own.

items.title: Bit-sized fields and variant payloads: a 7- or 10-bit I2C address
items.text:
The same U1..U64 / I2..I64 types work as struct fields, enum variant payloads and #[ww_trait] method arguments, returns and properties. Next to a 1-bit discriminant they share its byte:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Copy, Clone), ww_repr = u1, self_describing)]
enum I2cAddress {
    Seven(U7),
    Ten(U10),
}

let seven = I2cAddress::Seven(U7::new(0x50).unwrap());
assert_eq!(seven.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x50]);       // 0 1010000: 8 bits
let ten = I2cAddress::Ten(U10::new(0x3ff).unwrap());
assert_eq!(ten.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0xff, 0xe0]);   // 1 1111111111 00000: 11 bits

With Seven(u8) instead, the byte-aligned u8 pads the discriminant to a byte and the same address takes [0x00, 0x50]. The variants are 7 and 10 bits, so the enum is self_describing, not sized (a sized enum needs variants of one size, see size assumptions). Same-sized payloads can be sized and then nest without any size information, e.g. a 32-bit frame (shrink_wrap/tests/sub_byte.rs):

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(..), ww_repr = u1, sized)]
enum Offset { Up(U7), Signed(I7) }                                  // 1 + 7 bits

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(..), ww_repr = u2, sized)]
enum Reg {                                                          // 2 + 14 bits
    Wide { addr: U10, write: bool, len: U3 },
    Narrow { addr: U12, bank: I2 },
    Idle(U14),
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(..), sized)]
struct Frame { kind: U3, offset: Offset, reg: Reg, tail: I5 }       // 3 + 8 + 16 + 5 bits

let frame = Frame {
    kind: U3::new(0b101).unwrap(),
    offset: Offset::Signed(I7::minus_one()),
    reg: Reg::Wide { addr: U10::new(0x2aa).unwrap(), write: true, len: U3::new(5).unwrap() },
    tail: I5::new(-16).unwrap(),
};
// 101 1 1111111 00 1010101010 1 101 10000
assert_eq!(frame.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0xbf, 0xe5, 0x55, 0xb0]);

U7::new(x) returns None when x does not fit, U7::try_from(x) an Error::SubtypeOutOfRange, and u8::from(addr) / addr.value() give the number back. The dynamic client (ww_self::ValueOwned) reads and writes these as the smallest standard integer (U7 as a u8, I10 as an i16) and rejects values that don't fit.

items.title: UNib32: variable-length numbers by the nibble
items.text:
UNib32 encodes a u32 as 1-or-more nibbles: 1 continuation bit + 3 value bits per nibble.

assert_eq!(UNib32(0).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x00]);   // 1 nibble
assert_eq!(UNib32(7).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x70]);   // 1 nibble, max for that size
assert_eq!(UNib32(8).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x81]);   // 2 nibbles: needs a continuation
assert_eq!(UNib32(0o777).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0xff, 0x70]); // 3 nibbles

Small numbers (the overwhelming majority in practice - lengths, indices, enum discriminants) cost a single nibble. It's self_describing: a reader always knows where it ends from the continuation bits alone, no length prefix needed. This is why ww_version::Version uses UNib32 for major/minor/patch instead of u8/u32 - most real-world version numbers are small, so Version::new(0, 1, 2) serializes to just 2 bytes:

let version = Version::new(0, 1, 2);
assert_eq!(version.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("01 20"));

UNib32 is also what a struct/enum's own reverse-length marker is built from when it's Unsized - see the FIFO-of-lengths section below.

For numbers that are usually large, UVlq32 is the byte-based alternative: standard big endian VLQ, 1 continuation bit + 7 value bits per byte, most significant group first, byte-aligned. It is also self_describing and takes 1 to 5 bytes instead of 1 to 11 nibbles:

assert_eq!(UVlq32(0).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x00]);         // 1 byte
assert_eq!(UVlq32(127).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x7f]);       // 1 byte, max for that size
assert_eq!(UVlq32(128).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x81, 0x00]); // 2 bytes
assert_eq!(UVlq32(u32::MAX).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x8f, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x7f]); // 5 bytes

UVlq64 is the same encoding widened to u64, for values that can outgrow 32 bits (byte counters, unix milliseconds): still self_describing, 1 to 10 bytes (10 groups of 7 bits cover 70 bits, with room to spare for u64::MAX):

assert_eq!(UVlq64(0).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x00]);         // 1 byte
assert_eq!(UVlq64(127).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x7f]);       // 1 byte, max for that size
assert_eq!(UVlq64(128).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x81, 0x00]); // 2 bytes
assert_eq!(UVlq64(u32::MAX as u64).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x8f, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x7f]); // 5 bytes, same as UVlq32
assert_eq!(UVlq64(u64::MAX).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x81, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x7f]); // 10 bytes

There is no UVlq64Backfill; UVlq32Backfill is the same number, but always written as the full 5 bytes, padded with empty 0x80 groups in front. That reserves room for a value that is only known after the message is serialized, like a request sequence number assigned right before sending. Once it is known, UVlq32Backfill::backfill() writes it right-justified into those 5 bytes and returns the slice starting at its shortest encoding, so it costs no more than a plain UVlq32:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed)]
struct Message<'i> {
    seq: UVlq32Backfill, // must be the first field, so that bytes in front of it can be dropped
    payload: &'i str,
}

let len = Message { seq: UVlq32Backfill(0), payload: "ab" }.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap().len();
// buf[..len] is 80 80 80 80 00 61 62 02
let bytes = UVlq32Backfill::backfill(&mut buf[..len], 300).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, hex!("82 2c 61 62 02"));

The skipped leading bytes are filled with the padded form, so the whole buffer would also read back as 300.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] rejects UVlq32Backfill anywhere other than the first field of a struct: after another field (a bool or an Option flag would be written in front of it), nested in Option, Vec, tuples or arrays, and in enums, whose discriminant always comes first. The macro recognizes the type by name and only sees one type at a time, so it can't check that the struct itself is serialized first and is not, for example, a field of another struct.

items.title: Bounding a value from the inside with TailSize
items.text:
A value read from a buffer longer than itself - a header at the start of a file, a record at a fixed offset - has no back for its FIFO of lengths to live at. TailSize<N> (see the wire format page) is a field the writer fills in with the number of bytes from the end of the field to the end of the value, as a UVlq32 right-justified in N bytes, and the reader bounds the rest of the value with:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Header<'i> {
    magic: u16,
    size: TailSize<2>, // ignored on write, filled in; up to 16 KB with 2 bytes
    name: &'i str,
    count: u32,
}

let header = Header { magic: 0xABCD, size: TailSize(0), name: "ab", count: 7 };
let mut region = [0xFFu8; 64]; // the file region: longer than the value, garbage after it
let len = header.to_ww_bytes(&mut region).unwrap().len();
assert_eq!(&region[..len], hex!("CD AB 80 07 61 62 07 00 00 00 02"));
//                                 ^^^^^ 7 bytes follow the slot: "ab", count, "ab"'s reversed length

// the whole region: the reader stops where the slot says, the 0xFF bytes are never looked at
let back = Header::from_ww_bytes(&region).unwrap();
assert_eq!(back, Header { size: TailSize(7), ..header });
// one byte short: an error, not garbage
assert!(Header::from_ww_bytes(&region[..len - 1]).is_err());

A field added after count later is skipped by this reader the same way, since it only ever reads the 7 bytes. Nested values each carry their own slot; the sizes compose the way the FIFO does:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Inner<'i> { a: u8, size: TailSize<1>, s: &'i str }

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Outer<'i> { size: TailSize, inner: Inner<'i>, after: u8 }

let outer = Outer { size: TailSize(0), inner: Inner { a: 1, size: TailSize(0), s: "xyz" }, after: 9 };
assert_eq!(outer.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("80 80 80 80 08 01 04 78 79 7A 03 09 06"));
//  outer slot, 5 bytes, 8 follow ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ inner: a, slot (4 follow), "xyz", its length
//                                         after ^^ ^^ inner's size (6) in the outer's FIFO, inside the outer's 8

This is what makes Unsized records at fixed file offsets work: serialize each into a buffer of the slot's capacity (a record that outgrows it fails to serialize instead of overflowing), read each with from_ww_bytes on its region, and evolve the record type with #[default] fields like any other. The fields before the slot must be Sized or SelfDescribing, and there is one slot per struct or enum variant, in Unsized types only; the macro checks all of that at compile time. A reader that doesn't care about the value reads the fields up to the slot and split()s past it.

items.title: Option<T> and Result<T, E>: a flag, not a tag
items.text:
Both are SelfDescribing: one bool flag followed by the payload (for Result, true picks Ok, false picks Err - both variants exist on the wire, unlike a length-prefixed encoding that would need to know the size of whichever branch to skip):

impl<T: SerializeShrinkWrap> SerializeShrinkWrap for Option<T> {
    const ELEMENT_SIZE: ElementSize = ElementSize::SelfDescribing;
    fn ser_shrink_wrap(&self, wr: &mut BufWriter) -> Result<(), Error> {
        match self {
            Some(val) => { wr.write_bool(true)?; wr.write(val) }
            None => wr.write_bool(false),
        }
    }
}

No size marker is stored for the Option/Result itself - the flag bit is the delimiter. That's why stacking several Options in a struct costs almost nothing extra: each is just one more bit plus its payload's bits, all packed contiguously:

// from docs/types.md - v1 struct, then evolved with an inserted Option<U6> field
wr.write_bool(true)?;                        // 1 bit
wr.write(&Some(U6::new(5).unwrap()))?;       // 1 (flag) + 6 (value) bits
wr.write_u8(0xAA)?;                          // byte-aligned, starts a fresh byte
// -> [0xC5, 0xAA], same total size as before the field was added

items.title: Picking an enum's discriminant width - and when Option<bool> beats it
items.text:
ww_repr = <width> sets exactly how many bits an enum's discriminant costs (see derive reference). Pick the width for the variant count you'll ever need - a 3- or 4-variant enum needs ww_repr = u2:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u2, sized)]
enum Speed3 { Slow, Medium, Fast }

assert_eq!(Speed3::Slow.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0b00_000000]);
assert_eq!(Speed3::Fast.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0b10_000000]);

A sized enum like this always costs exactly its declared width, no matter which variant. But if your "enum" is really just "a common default state, plus one bit of extra information when it isn't the default", Option<bool> can be smaller on average, because it's SelfDescribing rather than fixed-width:

assert_eq!(None::<bool>.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(),       &[0b0_0000000]); // 1 bit used
assert_eq!(Some(false).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(),        &[0b10_000000]); // 2 bits used
assert_eq!(Some(true).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(),         &[0b11_000000]); // 2 bits used

Same worst case (2 bits, tying the u2 enum), but the common/default case (None) costs only 1 bit instead of 2. ww_date_time::Timezone uses exactly this shape for the same reason - UTC is the overwhelmingly common case:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, ..), self_describing, ww_repr = u1)]
pub enum Timezone {
    UTC,              // costs 1 bit
    Other(OtherTimezone), // costs 1 bit + OtherTimezone's own bits
}

Timezone has a fixed size discriminant (ww_repr = u1, so UTC and Other(..) both cost at least 1 bit), and it is self_describing rather than sized, because its two variants are not of one size - but notice it's shaped exactly like Option<OtherTimezone> would be, and was written as an explicit enum instead so that Other's payload (OtherTimezone, itself ww_repr = u3, self_describing) could be added as a real, named variant rather than a bare tuple. Same bit-level trick, better ergonomics for a type with more than two states down the line.

items.title: Relocating presence flags with #[flag]
items.text:
By default, an Option<T>/Result<T, E> field gets its presence flag written immediately in front of it. #[flag] lets you park that flag bit somewhere else entirely - most usefully, right next to other small fields so they all land in the same byte instead of the flag re-opening a new bit run right before its Option. ww_version::Version does exactly this, grouping both presence flags together right after the three UNib32 numbers, ahead of the two Option<&str> fields they belong to:

pub struct Version<'i> {
    pub major: UNib32,
    pub minor: UNib32,
    pub patch: UNib32,
    #[flag]
    build: bool,          // presence flag for the `build` field below, relocated here
    pub pre: Option<&'i str>,
    pub build: Option<&'i str>,
}

Flags are tracked in LIFO order - #[flag] fields are pushed in declaration order and popped by the Options that consume them, so #[flag] build (pushed first) must be consumed after pre's auto-generated flag (pushed second, popped first) - the macro checks this ordering at compile time and rejects anything that isn't valid LIFO. The payoff: major/minor/patch/build-flag/pre-flag all land in the same 14 bits, so a version with no pre-release or build metadata (the common case) still fits in 2 bytes, and a fully-populated one packs its two strings back to back with no gap for their flags:

let version = Version::full(0, 1, 2, Some("pre"), Some("build"));
// major/minor/patch nibbles + 2 flag bits, then "pre" bytes, then "build" bytes,
// then (per the FIFO-of-lengths rule below) build's reverse length, then pre's.
assert_eq!(version.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("01 2C 707265 6275696C64 5 3"));

items.title: The FIFO-of-lengths: why strings can come before their length
items.text:
An Unsized value's length isn't written where the value starts - it's appended to the back of the buffer as a reversed UNib32, so the writer never needs to know a value's size before it has finished writing it (see the high-level overview). Multiple lengths stack up in reverse order, forming a FIFO read from the back:

let bytes = ("abc", "de").to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, hex!("61 62 63 64 65 23"));
//                      a  b  c  d  e  ^^ reversed nibble lengths: 2 ("de"), then 3 ("abc")

The last byte, 0x23, holds both strings' lengths as two reversed nibbles - "de" (written second, so its length is closest to where the FIFO starts) then "abc". Reading walks the same FIFO from the back to know exactly where each string ends, without ever touching a byte before it needs to.

items.title: Zero-copy vectors, strings and pre-serialized payloads
items.text:
RefVec<'i, T> is the no-alloc, zero-copy stand-in for Vec<T> - it stores a reference into the original buffer (or a native &[T] slice) and only decodes elements as you .iter() over them:

let v = RefVec::new_bytes(&[0xAA, 0xBB, 0xCC]); // RefVec<'_, u8>, zero-copy byte array

When owned(feature = "std") is requested, the exact same field becomes a Vec<T> on the owned side - see the type mapping table.

TailBytes<'i> is a more specialized trick used by ww_client_server: a byte slice that is not length-prefixed at all, because it's guaranteed to be the last thing in an already-Unsized message (the framer/transport already knows the whole message's length, so re-encoding the tail's length would be pure waste):

pub struct Request<'i> {
    pub seq: u16,
    pub path_kind: PathKind<'i>,
    pub kind: RequestKind<'i>, // eventually bottoms out in `Call { args: TailBytes<'i> }`
}

Method arguments and property values are serialized once into their own buffer, then handed to the outer message as TailBytes - one buffer, no copying to reframe it, no length to write since it's already implied.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] rejects TailBytes / TailBytesOwned anywhere other than the last field of a struct or enum variant: before another field, which it would swallow, and nested in Option, Vec, tuples or arrays. As with UVlq32Backfill, the macro only sees one type at a time: a sized or final_structure type ending in TailBytes must itself be last, up to the first Unsized type on the way up, and that is not checked.

items.title: Self-referential types with RefBox
items.text:
Rust needs a compile-time-known size for any type; a struct or enum can't directly contain itself. RefBox<'i, T> breaks the cycle the same way Box<T> does on the heap, but for no_std/no-alloc: it stores either a plain &'i T reference or an unparsed BufReader slice, and only actually deserializes T when you call .read(). Serializing a RefBox is nearly free (it forwards straight to T's own serialization, no boxing overhead on the wire), and deserializing one is a plain buffer-position save - reading the boxed value is deferred until you ask for it:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Linked<'i> {
    a: u8,
    next: Option<RefBox<'i, Linked<'i>>>,
}

let linked = Linked {
    a: 1,
    next: Some(RefBox::new(&Linked { a: 2, next: None })),
};
assert_eq!(linked.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("01 80 02 00 02"));
//                                                       a1 fl a2 fl len
// a=1, Option-flag=1, a=2, Option-flag=0 (nested Linked has no `next`), reverse length of the boxed Linked

RefBox composes with Option/Result/enum variants exactly like any other field, which is how you build actual recursive data. ww_self (the introspection/AST crate) uses this to describe types themselves recursively - Type::Vec(RefBox<'i, Type<'i>>) means "a Vec whose element type is this boxed Type", Type::Option(RefBox<..>) likewise for Option<T>, and so on all the way down. Stripped to the essentials, the same idea looks like this:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone), ww_repr = nib)]
enum Ty<'i> {
    U8,
    U32,
    Str,
    Vec(RefBox<'i, Ty<'i>>),      // Vec<T>, T described recursively
    Option(RefBox<'i, Ty<'i>>),   // Option<T>
    Tuple(RefVec<'i, Ty<'i>>),    // (T0, T1, ...) - a real collection this time, no RefBox needed
}

// describes the Rust type `Vec<Option<u8>>`
let inner = Ty::U8;
let opt = Ty::Option(RefBox::new(&inner));
let vec_of_opt = Ty::Vec(RefBox::new(&opt));
let bytes = vec_of_opt.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(); // [0x30, 0x40, 0x00, 0x01, 0x03]

let des = Ty::from_ww_bytes(bytes).unwrap();
// des == Vec(RefBox(..)); nothing past the outer variant is decoded yet
if let Ty::Vec(elem_ty) = &des {
    assert_eq!(elem_ty.read().unwrap(), opt); // .read() decodes lazily, one level at a time
}

Note RefVec<'i, Ty<'i>> needs no RefBox even though Ty is self-referential - a RefVec never holds T inline, only a reference to where its elements live in the buffer, so there's no Rust-level sizing problem to begin with. RefBox is only needed for a single recursive field (Option<T>, a boxed enum payload, etc.), never for a collection of them.

items.title: Patching a discriminant after you've already started writing its payload
items.text:
Sometimes you don't know which variant you're building until you've already started writing it - a response builder that reserves space for a result flag or an event kind before it knows whether the call will succeed, for example. discriminants (see the derive reference) generates a fieldless {Name}Discriminants enum for exactly this, and BufWriter::save_state/restore_state let you go back and patch bits you already reserved:

// ww_client_server's EventKindBuilder, trimmed
pub struct EventKindBuilder { discriminant: BufWriterState }

impl EventKindBuilder {
    pub fn new(wr: &mut BufWriter<'_>) -> Result<Self, Error> {
        let discriminant = wr.save_state();   // remember where the discriminant nibble goes
        wr.write_nib_masked(0)?;              // write a placeholder
        Ok(Self { discriminant })
    }

    pub fn finish_with_kind(self, kind: EventKindDiscriminants, wr: &mut BufWriter<'_>) {
        let after = wr.save_state();          // remember where we ended up
        wr.restore_state(self.discriminant);  // rewind to the placeholder
        _ = wr.write_nib_masked(kind.discriminant()); // patch it in
        wr.restore_state(after);              // resume from where we left off
    }
}

Between new() and finish_with_kind(), the caller writes the variant's actual payload with no idea yet which EventKindDiscriminants it'll turn out to be - ErrorBuilder in the same module does the same trick one level deeper, wrapping the whole payload in an UnsizedBuilder so its reverse-length still comes out correct even though the discriminant in front of it was written last. ww_client_server's tests confirm the builder's output is byte-for-byte identical to building the equivalent value up front and calling .to_ww_bytes() on it directly - the builder is purely a streaming-friendly way to produce the exact same bytes.

items.title: Compressed sequences of numbers: Series
items.text:
A Series<T> of plain numbers is one column: the item count, a 4-bit header naming the column's codec, the values bit by bit against the previous one, padding to the byte. Five u8 readings, as a Vec<u8> and as a Series<u8>:

let v: Vec<u8> = vec![100, 100, 101, 99, 200];
assert_eq!(v.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("64 64 65 63 c8 05"));
assert_eq!(Series::new(&[100u8, 100, 101, 99, 200]).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("54 64 40 a0 7e 50"));

The Vec ends in its count nibble 5; the Series starts with it, then the header 0100 (predictor delta, coder prefix: the smallest here). Then 01100100 (the first value, 8 bits), 0 (100 again), 10 0000010 (+1: zigzag 2 in the 7-bit bucket of the delta code), 10 0000011 (-2: zigzag 3), 11 11001010 (+101: zigzag 202 does not fit 7 bits, so the full 8 bits after 11); 29 bits padded to 4 bytes. Here the saving is small; it grows with every repeated or slowly moving value, which costs 1 or 9 bits instead of 8 to 64:

// timestamps every 10 s with a little jitter
let ts = [1_700_000_000u32, 1_700_000_010, 1_700_000_020, 1_700_000_030, 1_700_000_041, 1_700_000_050];
let delta = CodecPolicy::fixed(NumericCodec::new(Predictor::Delta, Coder::Prefix), FloatCodec::Xor);
assert_eq!(Series::with_policy(&ts, delta).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap().len(), 11); // 8 + 32 + 5 x 9 bits
assert_eq!(Series::new(&ts).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("68 65 53 f1 00 8a 10 28 18"));

The smallest is delta of delta: 6 (the count), 1000 (predictor delta of delta, coder prefix), 65 53 f1 00 is 1_700_000_000, most significant bit first; then 10 0 0010100 (the first difference, 10, as a change from 0), 0, 0 (two more steps of 10), 10 0000010 (+1: a step of 11), 10 0000011 (-2: back to 9), 69 bits in 9 bytes. A regular clock costs one bit per tick (with the constant coder, nothing at all).

let temps = [21.5f32, 21.5, 21.5, 21.75, 21.75, 22.0];
assert_eq!(Series::new(&temps).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("61 41 ac 00 00 37 02 d6 3f"));

6, then 0001 (the XOR code); 41 ac 00 00 is 21.5, then 0, 0 (repeats); 21.75 XORs to 0x0002_0000, one significant bit after 14 leading zeros: 11 01110 00000 1 (14, length 1 written as 0, the bit); 0 (repeat); 22.0 XORs with 21.75 to 0x001e_0000, four bits after 11 leading zeros, which do not fit the previous window (14 leading, 17 trailing), so again an explicit 11 01011 00011 1111. 72 bits in 9 bytes. Had the next value XORed to, say, 0x0004_0000, it would fit that window and cost 10 plus 4 bits. In a real block one Series per signal holds a minute or an hour of samples, and the block is bounded by a TailSize slot (see bounding from the inside), so it can sit at any offset of a file.

items.title: Compressed columns: Series<T>
items.text:
Series<T> (layout) writes a list column by column instead of item by item. IvSample { v: Volt, i: Ampere }, Volt/Ampere each a ww_si-shaped { prefix: Prefix, value: NumericValue } (series, final_structure), 4 readings with v around 3300 mV and i around 152 000 µA, both in their usual range:

let items: Vec<IvSample> = [3300u16, 3301, 3301, 3299]
    .into_iter()
    .zip([152_000i32, 152_002, 151_999, 152_001])
    .map(|(v, i)| IvSample {
        v: Volt { prefix: Prefix::Milli, value: NumericValue::U16(v) },
        i: Ampere { prefix: Prefix::Micro, value: NumericValue::I32(i) },
    })
    .collect();
assert_eq!(
    Series::new(&items).to_ww_bytes_owned().unwrap(),
    hex!("42 11 14 33 90 51 91 8a 00 04 a3 80 1c b0")
);

14 bytes against 33 for the smallest plain form (Vec<IvSample> as final_structure, no evolution): 4 (n = 4), 2 (IvSample's 2 fields), v's prefix run (Milli, no change, end: 0001 0), v's value tag run (U16, end), v's U16 column (header 01 01: delta + packed, first value 3300 at full width, then a packed block of 3 residuals: +1, 0, -2), then the same shape for i's prefix, tag and I32 column (delta + packed: 152000, then +2, -3, +2). The header and first-value bytes are what batches of 4 pay for; at 100 items the same IvSample shrinks to 104 bytes (7.7x smaller) because they're paid once per batch, not once per item - see sizes against Vec<T>.

The same 4 items, but i jumps from the µA range to the mA range after item 2 (Milli U16 storage once there):

let items: Vec<IvSample> = [
    (3300u16, Prefix::Micro, NumericValue::I32(480)),
    (3300, Prefix::Micro, NumericValue::I32(482)),
    (3301, Prefix::Milli, NumericValue::U16(120)),
    (3300, Prefix::Milli, NumericValue::U16(121)),
]
.into_iter()
.map(|(v, i_prefix, i_value)| IvSample {
    v: Volt { prefix: Prefix::Milli, value: NumericValue::U16(v) },
    i: Ampere { prefix: i_prefix, value: i_value },
})
.collect();
assert_eq!(
    Series::new(&items).to_ww_bytes_owned().unwrap(),
    hex!("42 11 14 33 90 44 94 44 d1 20 5e 2f 22 57 81 e2 00")
);

17 bytes against 29 plain. i's prefix run now has a change (Micro, gap 1, Milli, end) and so does its value tag run (I32, gap 1, U16, end); because the prefix is an enum field declared earlier in Ampere, i's numeric column restarts where it changes: the I32 column holds only 480, 482 (one delta), the U16 column starts fresh at 120 (not a delta of -362 against 482) and holds just 120, 121. Columns never carry a delta across a boundary the reader can't make sense of.

items.title: Sparse updates with OptionAnyVec
items.text:
A trait level with 32 f32 properties, of which 3 changed since the last update: slots 3, 17 and 30 with 1.0, 2.5 and -3.0 (12 bytes of values whatever the encoding). The OptionAnyVec header in each mode, and the alternatives:

Encoding Bytes Header / overhead OptionAnyVec, index list (picked) 16 33 3d 1c 10: mode 3, count 3, deltas 3, 13, 12, pad OptionAnyVec, two-level 17 24 b1 04 00 20: 4 groups, bits 1011, 3 group bytes OptionAnyVec, dense 18 1f 31 00 04 00 20: len 31, 31 bits EitherAnyVec of Either<(), f32> 16 4 flag bytes, in line; the slot count implied, not stored 3 StreamData events, path [slot] 24 4 bytes per event (seq, result, kind, path) 1 StreamData event, path [], the vec as data 19 3 bytes of event + 4 bytes of header 
let mut wr = OptionAnyVecWriter::new(&mut buf, [3u32, 17, 30]).unwrap();
wr.write(3, &1.0f32).unwrap();
wr.write(17, &2.5f32).unwrap();
wr.write(30, &-3.0f32).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    wr.finish_and_take().unwrap(),
    hex!("33 3d 1c 10 00 00 80 3f 00 00 20 40 00 00 40 c0")
);

The event sizes are without the link's framing, which comes once per message on top, so separate events lose more than shown. One level deeper (paths [2, slot] and [2]) it is 26 against 20 bytes.

With byte-aligned values EitherAnyVec takes as much here, but it pays a flag byte per 8 slots whatever is present, pads every group to a byte and can't be read by a side with another slot count. Where that shows:

  • Other sets of 32: slots 0, 1, 2 take 13 bytes (03: all, n = 3), slots 29, 30, 31 take 15 (24 10 70: two-level), a single slot 3 takes 6 (14 10: dense, len 4, bits 0001); EitherAnyVec takes 16, 16 and 8.
  • Few of many: slots 3, 70, 120 of 128 take 16 bytes (33 3a 81 96: the index list), dense would be 30, EitherAnyVec 28.
  • Bit-sized values: 3 bools at slots 3, 17, 30 take 4 bytes (33 3d 1c 1e: the three 1 bits share the last header byte), EitherAnyVec 7.
  • All present: 32 f32s take 130 bytes, 2 of them header (08 40: all, n = 32).

items.title: Putting it together: real wire sizes
items.text:
A few real types from ww_stdlib, each combining several of the tricks above:

  • ww_version::Version - UNib32 for major/minor/patch, final_structure (flattened into its parent, no reverse-length of its own), a relocated #[flag] for build. Result: 2 bytes for a 0.1.2 with no pre-release/build metadata, growing gracefully only when those fields are actually used.
  • ww_date_time::DateTime - self_describing, a Year newtype storing years as UNib32 shifted by 2025 (so "now" costs a handful of bits, ancient or far-future dates cost more), and a Timezone that's UTC in 1 bit for the common case. A full UTC timestamp with second-level precision packs into 4 bytes: 
    let dt = DateTime::from_ymd_hms_utc_opt(2025, 5, 30, 16, 20, 0, 0).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), hex!("05 F3 96 C0"));
  • ww_client_server::PathKind - ww_repr = nib picking between three addressing modes (Absolute, GlobalCompact, GlobalFull), each shaped so the cheapest, most common case (a short absolute path) costs a single nibble discriminant plus the path itself, while the most expensive case (routing to an arbitrary crates.io trait by name) only costs more when you actually use it.

None of these types hand-roll any bit-twiddling - they're all plain #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] structs/enums built from the pieces on this page.

items.title: ShrinkWrap
items.text:
ShrinkWrap is the wire format of WireWeaver: every method argument, return value, property and stream item goes through it. It is dense (values are packed down to single bits), it works on a microcontroller without an allocator, and it lets newer and older versions of a type read each other's data.

It lives in its own crate, shrink_wrap, with no dependency on the rest of WireWeaver. If all you need is a compact format for files, messages or flash records, you can use it on its own.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
Put #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] on a struct or enum and it gets everything it needs to go on the wire:

use wire_weaver::prelude::*; // or `use shrink_wrap::prelude::*;` for the crate on its own

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Sample<'i> {
    id: u8,
    ok: bool,
    label: &'i str,
    error: Option<u16>,
}

fn main() {
    let sample = Sample { id: 7, ok: true, label: "temp", error: None };

    // no_std, no allocator: serialize into a buffer you own
    let mut buf = [0u8; 64];
    let bytes = sample.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0x07, 0x80, 0x74, 0x65, 0x6d, 0x70, 0x04]);

    // read it back without copying: `label` points into `bytes`
    let read = Sample::from_ww_bytes(bytes).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(read, sample);

    // with std: `SampleOwned` has a `String` instead of `&str`, same bytes
    let owned = SampleOwned::from_ww_bytes_owned(bytes).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(owned.to_ww_bytes_owned().unwrap(), bytes);
}

Seven bytes for the whole value:

Bytes What 07 id 80 ok: one bit, the rest of the byte is padding before the next byte-aligned field 74 65 6d 70 "temp" 04 error's None flag (one bit), padding, and the length of "temp" (4)

Two things stand out: a bool or an Option flag costs one bit, and the string's length is not in front of the string but at the end of the buffer. Both are explained below.

items.title: What you get
items.text:
• Small. Values are packed at 1-bit, 4-bit or 1-byte alignment, lengths take a nibble when they are small, and nothing is stored that the reader already knows (no field names, no type tags).
  • no_std and no allocator, also for strings, lists and nested types, for reading and writing. On the host, the same type gets an owned twin (Sample → SampleOwned) with String and Vec, writing the same bytes.
  • Zero-copy reading. A &str or a list read from the buffer points into it.
  • Safe on untrusted data. A malformed buffer is an error, never a panic, and a recursive type nested too deep is Error::NestingTooDeep instead of a stack overflow (nesting depth).
  • Evolvable. By default a type can get new fields later; old and new code keep reading each other's data (derive: evolving types).
  • Many types out of the box: integers of any bit width, variable-length numbers, strings and lists with an optional maximum length, Option, Result, tuples, arrays, compressed time series and more (built-in types).

items.title: How it stays small
items.text:
Bits are packed. A bool takes one bit, a U3 three bits, an enum with four variants can take two. Byte-sized values (u8, u32, f32, strings) start on a fresh byte, the unused bits before them stay zero. Those zero bits are not wasted forever: a later version of a type can put a new bool or Option flag there, and old data reads as false or None.

Lengths go to the back. A string, a list or a nested type whose size isn't known in advance needs its length stored somewhere. Most formats write it in front of the value, which means knowing the size before writing it. ShrinkWrap writes the value first and puts its length at the end of the buffer, as a variable-length number of nibbles. That keeps serialization a single pass with no copying, and small lengths cost half a byte. The reader picks the lengths up from the back while it walks the data from the front.

Nothing extra by default, less if you ask. A struct is evolvable by default, which costs a length nibble or two when it is nested in another type. A type that will never change can say so (sized, final_structure, self_describing) and then costs exactly its fields (size assumptions).

For the exact bytes, bit by bit, see wire format internals.

items.title: Size assumptions: final_structure, self_describing, sized
items.text:
By default every derived type is evolvable (Unsized): its serialized size isn't known up front, so when it is nested inside another struct or enum, the parent stores a length for it (a nibble-based reverse length, like UNib32). That length is what lets fields be added later without breaking anyone (see evolving types).

Three directives opt a type out of that flexibility in exchange for a smaller wire size. They are mutually exclusive, and they are part of the type's wire contract: once released, a choice can't be undone. (Why the lengths exist at all: the FIFO of lengths.)

items.title: The options
items.text:
Directive ElementSize Meaning Trade-off (none) Unsized Size unknown, stored as a reverse length in the parent. Fully evolvable. final_structure UnsizedFinalStructure Size still unknown, but the type is flattened onto its parent: no length is stored for it; its own lists still have theirs. Can't evolve. Only the first version of a type can be final_structure, and it can't be removed later. self_describing SelfDescribing No size is stored; a reader can tell where the value ends from the encoding itself. No overhead, but only for types whose encoding ends by itself (variable-length numbers, enums of unequal variants). sized Sized { size_bits } Size is fixed and known at compile time, computed from the fields. Nothing is stored for it, ever. Can't evolve at all: adding, removing or resizing a field changes the layout for every reader. Most compact.

Free bits can still be used

A final_structure or sized type can still grow into the gaps it already has, which are zero by default. If a bool is followed by a u8, 7 bits are unused and skipped by readers; a later version can put a bool or an Option flag there, and old data reads as false / None.

items.title: What it looks like on the wire
items.text:
ww_repr alone does not make an enum compact: without one of these directives it stays Unsized, exactly like a struct.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u2)]
enum SpeedUnsized { Slow, Medium, Fast, Turbo }

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u2, sized)]
enum SpeedSized { Slow, Medium, Fast, Turbo }

// A `Sized` field: its 2 bits are known up front, so the next field packs into the same byte.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct PayloadWithSized {
    speed: SpeedSized,
    after: bool,
}

// An `Unsized` field: the struct stores a length for it, and the next field starts on a fresh byte.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct PayloadWithUnsized {
    speed: SpeedUnsized,
    after: bool,
}

fn compact_vs_not() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 4];
    // Sized, so (Slow, Turbo) packs into 2+2 = 4 bits of a single byte:
    let bytes = (SpeedSized::Slow, SpeedSized::Turbo).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0x30]);

    // Unsized, standalone: no length needed, since nothing follows it.
    let mut buf2 = [0u8; 4];
    let bytes2 = SpeedUnsized::Turbo.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf2).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes2, &[0xC0]);

    // 0b11_1_00000: Turbo (11), then `after` (1), then padding.
    let mut buf3 = [0u8; 4];
    let sized_payload = PayloadWithSized { speed: SpeedSized::Turbo, after: true };
    let bytes3 = sized_payload.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf3).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes3, &[0xE0]);

    // `speed` is padded to its own byte; `after` starts a new byte, and the length of
    // `speed` (1) shares its low bits:
    let mut buf4 = [0u8; 4];
    let unsized_payload = PayloadWithUnsized { speed: SpeedUnsized::Turbo, after: true };
    let bytes4 = unsized_payload.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf4).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes4, &[0xC0, 0x81]);
    // bool and reverse length end up in the same byte, and there are even 3 bits left
}

items.title: Enums
items.text:
Only one variant of an enum is on the wire, so its size is the discriminant (see ww_repr) plus the fields of one variant:

  • sized needs every variant to take the same number of bits (unit variants take 0), and a fixed-size discriminant (anything but unib32). ELEMENT_SIZE is then Sized { size_bits: discriminant + variant }.

  • Variants of different sizes make the enum self_describing: the discriminant tells how long the value is. Asking for sized is a compile error that names the variants and their sizes:

    sized enum Reading: variants differ in size (Short: 8 bits, Long: 32 bits); use self_describing instead of
sized, or pad the variants to one size

sized and self_describing give the same bytes, for the type and for whatever contains it, so switching between the two is not a wire change.

items.title: Checked at compile time
items.text:
Whichever assumption you pick, the macro inserts a compile-time assertion that the type's actual ELEMENT_SIZE matches the one asked for. If a field turns out to make the type Unsized after all, the build fails instead of silently producing an incompatible layout.

User types are counted wherever they appear in a field (Point, [Point; 3], (Point, u8), Option<Point>, Range<Point>): the macro can't see their size, so it emits a const expression over their ELEMENT_SIZE and the compiler folds it. Array lengths can be any const expression; a sized type's ELEMENT_SIZE carries them symbolically.

size_bits is the sum of the fields' own bits. Alignment padding between fields depends on where the value starts in the buffer and is not part of it: struct { a: bool, b: u8 } is Sized { size_bits: 9 } and takes 2 bytes on its own. How sizes combine in detail: traits and ElementSize.

items.title: Special types
items.text: Types of the shrink_wrap crate for cases the plain ones don't cover: a value that bounds itself inside a longer buffer, owned strings and lists without an allocator, compressed time series, lists written in place, and sparse sets of values. Each section starts with what the type is for and how to use it; the exact bits are in wire format internals.

items.title: TailSize<N>: the size of the rest of a value
items.text:
The FIFO of lengths puts a value's size at the back of the buffer, which is exactly right when the buffer is the value: the reader knows where the back is. It doesn't help when the value sits in a buffer longer than itself (a header at the start of a file, a record at a fixed offset of a ring file, a message with padding after it), nor when a reader wants to skip a value without parsing it.

TailSize<N> covers that from the inside. It is a field that the writer fills in, once the value is serialized, with the number of bytes to the end of the value, and that the reader uses to bound the rest of it:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Header<'i> {
    magic: u16,
    size: TailSize<2>, // filled in on write, ignored as an input
    name: &'i str,
    count: u32,
}

N is the number of bytes the slot takes (1 to 5, 5 by default), which caps the size: 127 bytes for N = 1, 16 KB for 2, 2 MB for 3, 256 MB for 4, 4 GB for 5. A bigger value fails with Error::LenTooLong.

What you get:

  • a buffer longer than the value stops at the value's end;
  • a truncated one fails with Error::OutOfBoundsSplit instead of reading garbage;
  • fields a newer writer appended after the ones this reader knows are skipped: the usual evolution rules keep working inside the bounded range;
  • nested values each get their own slot, and a value with a slot is still a plain Unsized value to whatever contains it.

The rules the macro checks:

  • one TailSize per struct or enum variant, as a plain field (not inside Option, Vec, tuples or arrays);
  • only in Unsized types: a sized, final_structure or self_describing type has no end of its own on the wire;
  • every field before it is Sized or SelfDescribing. A Vec, String or Unsized field keeps its length at the back of the buffer, which is not where the value ends when the buffer is longer than it.

The slot, its position and N are part of the layout: put it in the first version of a type. The showcase has the bytes.

items.title: ArrayString / ArrayVec: owned values without an allocator
items.text:
&str / RefVec<'i, T> borrow from the buffer they were read from, and String / Vec<T> need an allocator. Neither fits a field that must own its bytes without one: a value_on_changed field of a string or list property in a no_alloc server (which can't hold a &'static str), or a settings value kept in RAM between loads.

ArrayString<N> and ArrayVec<T, N> are the owned, no-alloc alternative: a fixed-size [u8; N] / [MaybeUninit<T>; N] plus a length. They write the same bytes as &str / String and Vec<T>, so a field can move between the borrowed, owned and array-backed forms without changing a single byte:

use shrink_wrap::prelude::*;

let mut s: ArrayString<8> = ArrayString::new();
s.push_str("abc").unwrap();
assert_eq!(s.as_str(), "abc");

let mut buf = [0u8; 16];
let bytes = s.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, "abc".to_ww_bytes(&mut [0u8; 16]).unwrap());
  • A value longer than N is never cut: it fails with Error::MaxLenExceeded, whether in push_str / push, ArrayString::try_from, serializing, or deserializing a value too long for this reader's N (the same check MaxLen makes).
  • Both have a CAPACITY const and Deref to str / [T].
  • Both set MAX_SIZE from N, so a type built out of them has a compile-time worst-case size like any other bounded type.
  • ArrayVec<T, N> drops its elements in place like a normal container; T does not need Copy.

They are Rust-side types: an API (#[ww_trait]) describes such a field as a string or a list.

items.title: Compressed sequences of numbers: Series<T>
items.text:
A list of readings taken one after another is mostly redundancy: the next value is usually the previous one or close to it. Series<'i, T> (SeriesOwned<T> with std) writes such a list bit by bit against the value before, picking per list the code that comes out smallest: for integers the difference to the previous value or the change of that difference (timestamps with a near-constant step) in a prefix code, bit-packed blocks, a constant or the plain values; for f32 / f64 the XOR with the previous value (the Gorilla code) or the plain values. It is used like RefVec<'i, T>: a field holding a slice to serialize (Series::new(&values)), decoded as you .iter() after deserializing.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Block<'i> {
    ts: u32,
    size: TailSize<2>,
    stamps: Series<'i, u64>, // timestamps with a near-constant step
    counts: Series<'i, i16>, // a counter, fixed-point readings
    temps: Series<'i, f32>,  // floats
}

It works in derived types and in every API position (arguments, returns, properties, stream items); the dynamic client and Python read and write it as a list. Series<T> also takes structs and enums, a column per field: see Series for all of it, the codecs and a fixed codec for a small MCU (Series::with_policy).

What to expect. cargo run --example time_series (in shrink_wrap/shrink_wrap) prints the encoded sizes of a minute of 1 Hz synthetic data against the raw Vec<T>: timestamps with jitter 38 B instead of 481 B, a counter 31 B instead of 241 B, a sine wave in f32 70 B instead of 241 B, a constant 13 B. Floats with full-precision noise (a CPU percentage computed from counters) XOR badly: every value changes most mantissa bits; the same values as fixed-point integers compress well. A Series has a count, a 4-bit header per column and pads to a byte, so a list of a handful of values gains little.

Malformed input. The decoder never panics: every read is bounds-checked, the item count is capped (SERIES_MAX_ITEMS) and the columns are validated in one pass before an item is decoded; inside a struct, the enclosing length slot or TailSize bounds the value and a truncation is caught there.

The codes: wire format internals; the bytes: showcase.

items.title: RefVecBuilder: lists written in place
items.text:
RefVec::Slice needs the elements in a slice first. RefVecBuilder<T> writes a list straight into a BufWriter instead, one element at a time, from an iterator or a loop reading a sensor, with no memory for the elements:

  • RefVecBuilder::<T>::new(&mut wr) at the place of the list: the whole buffer, a field of a struct written by hand, an element of another list (a RefVec stores no size of its own, so it is the same call everywhere);
  • then push(&mut wr, &value) per element, extend(&mut wr, items) for an iterator, or push_with(&mut wr, |wr| ..) to write an element by other means, e.g. with a nested builder;
  • then finish(&mut wr), which writes the element count.

The bytes are those of the same RefVec::Slice, so a reader can't tell. Three 12-bit samples between a byte and a flag:

let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf);
wr.write_u8(7).unwrap();
let mut samples = RefVecBuilder::<U12>::new(&mut wr).unwrap();
for ch in 0..3 {
    samples.push(&mut wr, &adc_read(ch)).unwrap(); // 0x023, 0x123, 0x223
}
samples.finish(&mut wr).unwrap();
wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();
assert_eq!(wr.finish_and_take().unwrap(), hex!("07 02 31 23 22 38 03"));

The samples are bit-packed as in any list (023 123 223), the flag follows in the next bit (3 1 and padding), and the count 3 is at the back. A list of lists takes a nested builder per element:

let groups: [&[&str]; 2] = [&["a", "bc"], &["d"]];
let mut outer = RefVecBuilder::<RefVec<&str>>::new(&mut wr).unwrap();
for group in groups {
    outer.push_with(&mut wr, |wr| {
        let mut inner = RefVecBuilder::<&str>::new(wr)?;
        inner.extend(wr, group)?;
        inner.finish(wr)
    }).unwrap();
}
outer.finish(&mut wr).unwrap();
assert_eq!(wr.finish_and_take().unwrap(), hex!("61 62 63 64 11 21 22"));

push_with writes the element as its type's ser_shrink_wrap would; for an evolvable element the builder adds its size around it, as wr.write does.

  • A push that fails (out of buffer space, an element that fails to serialize) returns the error and undoes what the element wrote: the list holds the elements pushed before and can still be finished, the count is never off.
  • finish must be called. Until then the count is 0 while the elements are already in the buffer, and a reader sees garbage. The builder is #[must_use], but that only catches one that is never used at all.
  • MaxLen<RefVec<'i, T>, N>: start it with RefVecBuilder::with_max_len(&mut wr, N), push N + 1 fails with Error::MaxLenExceeded and writes nothing. A BufWriter keeps lengths as u16 until they are encoded, so the 65 536th push fails with Error::LenTooLong.

RefVecBuilderOwned<T> is the same builder for a BufWriterOwned and SerializeShrinkWrapOwned elements, with the same bytes.

A list of bytes, RefVecBuilder<u8>, has two more ways to add elements, both mixing freely with push:

  • extend_from_slice(&mut wr, &bytes) copies a whole slice at once, one element per byte;
  • write_bytes_with(&mut wr, |wr| ..) counts every byte the closure writes, by any means: write_raw_slice, write_u8, or other values, making the list a byte blob that holds them.
