It aligns to a byte first, encodes the lengths the values inside pushed (so they are part of the blob) and aligns again; a closure that writes nothing adds nothing, not even the alignment. On an error the writer is back where it was, as for a push.
let mut bytes = RefVecBuilder::<u8>::new(&mut wr).unwrap();
bytes.write_bytes_with(&mut wr, |wr| {
    wr.write(&"hi")?;
    wr.write_u8(0x42)
}).unwrap();
bytes.finish(&mut wr).unwrap();
wr.write_u8(0x99).unwrap();
assert_eq!(wr.finish_and_take().unwrap(), hex!("68 69 42 02 99 04"));

68 69 is "hi", then 42, then the length of "hi" (2 after a padding nibble), all inside the blob of 4 bytes: 99 follows it and the count 4 is at the back. Read it back as a RefVec<u8> and the blob with a BufReader of its own.

items.title: OptionAnyVec: sparse slots of any types
items.text:
shrink_wrap::option_any_vec::OptionAnyVec<'i> is an array of Option slots whose values can be of any type (numbers, structs, lists, strings, enums, another OptionAnyVec), where only the present values are written. It is made for messages that carry "some of these N things": the properties of a trait level that changed since the last update, a sparse set of readings.

It is low-level machinery: the type of each slot is known to both sides and not stored, and slot ids are u32 from 0. For a struct with a field per slot, use a sparse struct instead, which is built on it.

use shrink_wrap::option_any_vec::{OptionAnyVec, OptionAnyVecWriter};

let mut buf = [0u8; 64];
// the present slots are given up front, in increasing order
let mut wr = OptionAnyVecWriter::new(&mut buf, [0u32, 2, 3]).unwrap();
wr.write(0, &0x2Au8).unwrap();
wr.write(2, &"hi").unwrap();
wr.write(3, &true).unwrap();
let bytes = wr.finish_and_take().unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, hex!("14 b0 2a 68 69 82"));

let vec = OptionAnyVec::new(bytes).unwrap(); // checks the header
let mut slots = vec.iter();
assert_eq!(slots.next::<u8>(), Ok(Some(0x2A)));
assert_eq!(slots.next::<u16>(), Ok(None));
assert_eq!(slots.next::<&str>(), Ok(Some("hi")));
assert_eq!(slots.next::<bool>(), Ok(Some(true)));
assert_eq!(slots.next::<u8>(), Ok(None)); // and every slot after the writer's last one

The bytes: 1 4 is the header's mode (dense) and length, 1011 says slots 0, 2 and 3 are present, then 2a, 68 69, the true bit, and the length of "hi" in the last nibble. The writer picks the smallest of four header modes for the present set (header modes).

items.title: Evolution
items.text:
The header describes the writer's present set on its own, without either side's slot count, so the vec is read by older and newer code alike as long as slots are only appended:

  • a reader that knows fewer slots reads its own and stops: the values it doesn't know come after all of its slots;
  • a reader that knows more slots sees the new ones as absent: they are not in the header.

A slot's type can't change once released, as for a struct field. Since values carry no length of their own, a reader can't skip a present value it doesn't know the type of, which, with append-only slots, it never has to.

items.title: Untrusted input
items.text:
OptionAnyVec::new (and reading it as a field) parses the whole header and checks every count and length against the bytes left before looping over it:

  • a length past the data, an index list past u32::MAX, a two-level group listed without a slot in it is Error::MalformedOptionAnyVec;
  • a truncated header is an out-of-bounds error, never a panic.

Reading the values is bounds-checked like any other read. Slot ids from the header are not bounded by any slot count, so stop at the last slot you know (iter().next() does that by itself).

items.title: Writing in place
items.text:
OptionAnyVecBuilder writes into a BufWriter that holds other things too:

  • OptionAnyVecBuilder::new(&mut wr, present) for a vec that is the whole buffer, new_nested for one that is a struct field or a slot of another vec (its size is stored, as for every Unsized value);
  • then write(slot, &value, &mut wr) per present slot, or start_slot(slot) and a write of your own (e.g. a nested builder);
  • then finish(&mut wr), which fails with Error::OptionAnyVecWrongSlot if a present slot got no value.

The present set is any increasing iterator of slot ids that can be cloned; SetBits::new(&[u32]) gives one from a bitset. new_with_mode forces a header mode. A child level is one slot holding its own vec:

let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf);
let mut parent = OptionAnyVecBuilder::new(&mut wr, [0u32, 1]).unwrap();
parent.write(0, &7u8, &mut wr).unwrap();
parent.start_slot(1).unwrap();
let mut child = OptionAnyVecBuilder::new_nested(&mut wr, [2u32]).unwrap();
child.write(2, &0x1234u16, &mut wr).unwrap();
child.finish(&mut wr).unwrap();
parent.finish(&mut wr).unwrap();
assert_eq!(wr.finish_and_take().unwrap(), hex!("02 07 13 20 34 12 04"));

The bytes:

  • 0 2: mode all, slots 0 and 1;
  • 07: slot 0;
  • the child, 4 bytes: 1 3 (dense, 3 slots), 001 and padding, 34 12;
  • 04: the child's size in the parent's reverse lengths (after a padding nibble).

The same bytes come out of writing the child into a buffer of its own first and parent.write(1, &child_vec, ..). Reading: iter.next::<OptionAnyVec>() gives the child, child.iter() its slots; next_present() jumps over absent slots, present() lists the present ids without reading values. OptionAnyVecBuilderOwned is the same builder for a BufWriterOwned, the bytes are the same.

items.title: Slots with gaps
items.text: A reader that knows slots 0, 1 and 5 but not 2..=4 reads them with iter.read_slot::<T>(slot), which steps over the absent slots in between. A present slot in such a gap can't be stepped over (its type, so its size, is unknown): read_slot fails with Error::OptionAnyVecUnknownSlot. Gaps are for slots that are never present, as the methods between the properties of a trait level, never for slots a newer version might fill.

items.title: EitherAnyVec
items.text: OptionAnyVec is Unsized. EitherAnyVec is the counterpart for Either slots that are all present: each element is L or R, the flags are in-line in groups of 8, and the element count is implied. It is used to answer multi requests, one Either<Error, value> per index.

items.title: Use cases
items.text:
Where ShrinkWrap is used outside the RPC machinery, in two small programs of the vhrd.tech tool chain (tpm_mesh_dash and tpm_mesh, which watch and connect a handful of PCs). Nothing here is no_std: the point is that a dense, evolvable format with bounded values is useful on a desktop as well, for files, streams and size-capped messages. Every size and byte sequence below is asserted by shrink_wrap/shrink_wrap/tests/use_cases.rs, which holds the same types as the snippets (the shipped code names the same items, see each section).

Read ShrinkWrap and derive first, this page assumes Unsized types, the FIFO of lengths and TailSize<N> are familiar.

items.title: Ring files of a load history
items.text:
tpm_mesh_dash keeps the load history of a PC (CPU, memory, network, ... up to 64 series) in one file per resolution: a 1 s tier for an hour, 1 min for a day, 15 min for 30 days, 1 h for a year. A tier is a header followed by a fixed number of record slots, indexed by time ((ts / period) % slots), so one write_at per sample, nothing grows, and there is no cursor to lose. This is the case TailSize<N> was made for: a value that lives at a fixed file offset, in a region longer than itself.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct TierHeaderOwned {
    magic: u32,
    size: TailSize<2>,   // bounds the rest, the file region is 4096 bytes
    period: u32,
    slots: u32,
    names: Vec<String>,  // series in use, in slot order
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct FineRecordOwned {
    ts: u32,             // start of the slot, a record whose ts is not the expected one reads as empty
    size: TailSize<2>,
    values: Vec<f32>,    // a value per series in use, NaN for none
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, owned, sized, derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone, Copy, Default))]
struct Stat { min: f32, avg: f32, max: f32 }

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct CoarseRecordOwned {
    ts: u32,
    size: TailSize<2>,
    values: Vec<Stat>,   // the coarser tiers keep min / avg / max of the samples in the slot
}

Why the fields are in this order: everything before a TailSize must be Sized or SelfDescribing (a Vec keeps its length at the back of the buffer, which is not where the value ends in a longer region), so ts, magic and the like go first and the Vec after the slot.

A header with three series, written into the zero-padded 4096-byte region at the start of the file:

let header = TierHeaderOwned {
    magic: u32::from_le_bytes(*b"TMH2"),
    size: TailSize(0),                       // ignored on write, filled in
    period: 1,
    slots: 3600,
    names: vec!["cpu".into(), "mem".into(), "net".into()],
};
let bytes = header.to_ww_bytes_owned().unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, hex!("54 4D 48 32  80 13  01 00 00 00  10 0E 00 00  63 70 75 6D 65 6D 6E 65 74  33 33"));
//                     magic        slot   period       slots        "cpu" "mem" "net"             lengths
region[..bytes.len()].copy_from_slice(&bytes);
let back = TierHeaderOwned::from_ww_bytes_owned(&region).unwrap(); // all 4096 bytes, stops at the header's end
assert_eq!(back.names, header.names);
assert_eq!(back.size, TailSize(19));         // bytes after the slot: 4 + 4 + 9 + 2

The header takes 25 bytes of its 4096, and the reader needs neither to know the 25 nor to find the end of the names: the slot says 19 bytes follow. The same holds for the records, which is what lets them be sized to the series in use instead of to the worst case:

Record 3 series in use 64 series (slot capacity in the file) FineRecordOwned 19 B 264 B CoarseRecordOwned 43 B 776 B

A record is ts (4) + slot (2) + values (4 per series, 12 for a Stat) + the reversed length of the Vec (1 byte up to 63 series, 2 at 64), and the capacity is computed from that at compile time in the shipped code and checked in its tests (4 + 2 + 64 * 4 + 2). Be honest about what this buys: the file slot stays at the capacity, so the file does not get smaller (the 1 s tier is 4096 + 3600 * 264 ≈ 0.95 MB), but a write is 19 bytes instead of 264, and what matters more:

  • a series added later just makes the next records longer, a record written before it reads the new series as "no value" (a Vec that ends early), no migration of the file;
  • a field appended to a record or the header later with #[default = ..] keeps old files readable, and old readers skip it, because the slot bounds what they parse (see evolution);
  • a half-written or zeroed slot is an error (MalformedUVlq32, OutOfBoundsSplit), never garbage values;
  • no hand-packed offsets anywhere: the file format is the three structs above.

The shipped code is src/history.rs of tpm_mesh_dash; a header that does not match (magic, period, slots) means the file is recreated, as the data is telemetry and not worth a migration.

items.title: Request and reply frames over streams
items.text:
tpm_mesh lets one PC ask another PC's daemon a question next to its gossip (NET-8): a QUIC stream per question (iroh), one request frame in, one reply frame out. The payload of both is JSON the daemon never looks into, so ShrinkWrap only does the envelope:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
pub struct AskRequestOwned {
    pub service: String,   // which local program answers
    pub body: Vec<u8>,     // its request, JSON bytes
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, ww_repr = u8, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
pub enum AskReplyOwned {
    Ok(Vec<u8>),           // the provider's JSON bytes
    Err(String),           // or why there is none
}

Streams have no message boundaries, so a frame is a UVlq32 length followed by the message, and the length is checked against a cap before a byte of the body is read or allocated: 16 KiB for a request, 1 MiB for a reply.

fn frame<T: SerializeShrinkWrapOwned>(msg: &T, cap: usize) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Error> {
    let body = msg.to_ww_bytes_owned()?;
    if body.len() > cap { /* refuse: over the cap */ }
    let mut wr = BufWriterOwned::with_capacity(body.len() + 5);
    wr.write_uvlq32(body.len() as u32)?;
    wr.write_raw_slice(&body)?;
    wr.finish_and_take()
}

fn unframe<T: DeserializeShrinkWrapOwned>(bytes: &[u8], cap: usize) -> Result<T, Error> {
    let mut rd = BufReader::new(bytes);
    let len = rd.read_uvlq32()? as usize;
    if len > cap { /* refuse */ }
    let body = rd.read_raw_slice(len)?;
    if rd.bytes_left() != 0 { /* refuse: bytes after the frame */ }
    T::from_ww_bytes_owned(body)
}

The request {service: "history", body: {"range":"24h"}} is 25 bytes on the wire, 24 of them the message:

18                                     frame length, UVlq32 (24)
68 69 73 74 6F 72 79                   "history"
7B 22 72 61 6E 67 65 22 3A 22 32 34 68 22 7D   {"range":"24h"}
07 97                                  reversed lengths of the two fields (7 and 15)

and AskReplyOwned::Err("no") is 5: 04 | 01 | 6E 6F | 02, the length, the discriminant (ww_repr = u8), the text and its length. The rules a frame reader enforces, all tested in tpm_mesh: over the cap is refused (also on the way out), a truncated frame is an error, bytes after the frame are an error, and a hostile length such as 85 80 80 80 00 is refused by the cap before anything is read. The owned types allocate, which is fine on a daemon.

Note

The derive's generated code names BufReader and friends unqualified, so such types go into their own module with use shrink_wrap::prelude::*; if the program also imports another BufReader (tokio's here).

items.title: Small messages under a size cap: gossip payloads
items.text:
tpm_mesh announces each PC's state to the others over iroh-gossip, which caps a message at 4 KiB. The messages were JSON, and 7 Oct 2026 was spent finding out what a more compact encoding gains, on 67 live events. Average bytes per message:

Message JSON JSON + deflate ShrinkWrap ShrinkWrap + deflate bot 219 162 110 112 sessions 759 367 364 294 stats 809 513 536 436

Then the stats message with a schema designed for the wire instead of ported from the JSON one: percents as u8 instead of floats, counts as UVlq32, memory in MiB instead of bytes, times as offsets. It is 323 B, and deflate gains nothing on it. Two lessons:

  • Schema choice beats general compression on small messages. ShrinkWrap alone with a straight port of the JSON schema (536 B) is no better than JSON + deflate (513 B), a tight schema (323 B) beats everything including the straight port with deflate (436 B), and nothing is left for deflate to find in it. Deflate on 200 to 800 bytes has little history to learn from and pays its own header.
  • Compression pays for string-heavy messages. sessions is mostly text (working directories, titles): there ShrinkWrap + deflate (294 B) is a clear step below ShrinkWrap alone (364 B) and JSON + deflate (367 B), whereas for bot it is 2 bytes worse than ShrinkWrap alone.

A small tight schema looks like this (an illustration of the style, not the shipped type):

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct SessionOwned {
    name: String,
    busy: bool,
    cpu_percent: u8,   // not an f32
    mem_mib: UVlq32,   // 512 MiB is 2 bytes, not a u64
}
// {"name":"omarchy-m1","busy":true,"cpu_percent":42,"mem_mib":512} is 64 bytes of JSON, and:
assert_eq!(bytes, hex!("6F 6D 61 72 63 68 79 2D 6D 31  80  2A  84 00  29"));  // 15
//                     "omarchy-m1"                    busy cpu mem    length of name

The switch of the gossip payloads to ShrinkWrap is in progress in tpm_mesh as gossip-sw; this section describes its design and the measurements behind it, it has not shipped. The JSON/deflate numbers are measured on real events, the 323 B figure is the tight stats schema; the type above is only an example.

items.title: Where compression wrappers would pay: time series
items.text:
SW-28 compression-wrappers (planned: Compression<T>, delta, delta-of-delta and float XOR encodings) is the opposite case of the gossip messages. A gossip message is a snapshot: dozens of unrelated fields, once, where the only redundancy is in text, so the schema is the lever. A time series is thousands of values of one field where each is close to the previous, which is where delta-of-delta (timestamps) and float XOR (values, as in Gorilla) shrink a stream severalfold:

  • the ts of consecutive records of a tier is previous + period: the delta-of-delta is 0, a bit or a byte instead of the 4 bytes u32 per record;
  • f32 load values change slowly, so their XOR with the previous one has long runs of zero bits;
  • 15 min and 1 h tiers repeat the pattern at a smaller scale.

The ring files above would not use it per slot, though: they depend on every record being independently readable at a fixed offset (the TailSize slot and the time index), and delta chains break exactly that. Where it would fit is the data around the rings: an answer to a range question (a chart's worth of up to 720 points per series, sent through the ask protocol of the previous section), or an archive of old slots written once as a block. A snapshot message of the gossip kind gains nothing from it.

items.title: Wire format internals
items.text:
How ShrinkWrap lays values out in bytes, and the reader and writer that do it. You don't need any of this to use #[derive_shrink_wrap]; it explains why the derive macro's directives (evolvable by default, final_structure / self_describing / sized) exist and what each one trades. It is also the reference for a hand-written SerializeShrinkWrap impl or a reader in another language (see ShrinkWrap in C).

The showcase has worked byte-by-byte examples of most of what is described here.

items.title: The FIFO of lengths
items.text:
The core idea: lengths are kept at the back of the buffer, written in reverse while values are written forward from the front. This allows serialization in a single pass with no extra copying.

Consider two strings of arbitrary length in one buffer. To get both back, their lengths have to be stored too. Most formats write a value's length right before the value:

l1 abc l2 qwerty

That's fine for a string, whose length is known before its first byte is written. It falls apart for a nested struct or a Vec of them. Either you make a full pass first just to compute the serialized length (and get it exactly right), or you write a placeholder, serialize the value and patch the placeholder. But how many bytes should the placeholder take, if small lengths are to take little space?

A fixed-width length field has the same problem in another shape. One byte caps a value at 255 bytes; four bytes waste space on the overwhelming majority of values, which are small.

ShrinkWrap never writes a length where the value starts:

  1. When a value's size can't be known up front, a slot is reserved at the back of the buffer.
  2. The value is written normally from the front.
  3. The slot is filled in with the now-known size, as a variable-length UNib32 (see the showcase).

Several slots stack up back to front, forming a FIFO that a reader consumes in the same order while walking the buffer forward. The showcase has a worked byte-by-byte example.

items.title: BufWriter and BufReader
items.text: The two core types are BufWriter and BufReader. Both work on plain byte slices that may start at any address: the bit, nibble and byte alignment below is tracked as a bit and byte cursor, not imposed by the platform.

items.title: BufWriter
items.text:
use wire_weaver::shrink_wrap::prelude::*;

fn simple_wr() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 256];
    let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf);
    wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();
    wr.write_u8(0xaa).unwrap();
    let bytes = wr.finish().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0x80, 0xaa]);
}

BufWriter is created from a mutable byte slice, which does not need to be zeroed first (zeroing a large scratch buffer isn't free on no_std). It keeps one index advancing from the front for the data, and one retreating from the back for the FIFO of lengths.

  • write_bool consumes a single bit, here the top bit of the first byte.
  • write_u8 aligns to the next byte first, which is why the true sits alone in 0x80.
  • Bit-aligned writes (write_bool, the write_un* family behind U1..U64 / I2..I64) pack back to back. A new byte starts only when something byte-aligned (write_u8, write_u16, a &str, ...) or an explicit align_nibble / align_byte comes along.
  • finish() encodes the lengths still pending as reversed UNib32s at the back and returns the written bytes.

When nothing pushed a length (no string, list or nested Unsized value), finish_no_lens() returns the same bytes without linking the code that encodes the FIFO, which matters on a CPU with a few kilobytes of flash (see code size). wr.finish_for::<T>() picks one of the two at compile time by T::PUSHES_LEN, which #[derive_shrink_wrap] computes from the fields; to_ww_bytes does that for you. A hand-written impl may set const PUSHES_LEN: bool = false; when no path through its ser_shrink_wrap pushes a length. The default is true for everything that is not Sized, which is always correct.

items.title: BufReader
items.text:
use wire_weaver::shrink_wrap::prelude::*;

fn simple_rd() {
    let bytes = [0x80u8, 0xaa];
    let mut rd = BufReader::new(&bytes);
    assert_eq!(rd.read_bool().unwrap(), true);
    assert_eq!(rd.read_u8().unwrap(), 0xaa);
}

BufReader mirrors BufWriter: it walks the same slice forward with matching read methods, and can split() off a sub-reader bounded to exactly the number of bytes a length slot says a value takes.

split() is also what makes evolution work. A reader bounded to a value's byte range never reads past it, so:

  • code that doesn't know a newer field skips whatever trailing bytes it doesn't understand;
  • code reading data that lacks a field it knows runs out of bytes and falls back to that field's default.

See the evolution rules for which changes stay wire-compatible.

items.title: Nesting depth
items.text:
A type that contains itself (Box<T>, RefBox<T>, Vec<T> or RefVec<T> of a type with T in it, like a tree or the introspection Type / Value) is read by a recursion as deep as the data: 38 KB of 10 000 nested lists would overflow the stack of whoever reads them. So BufReader counts how deep it is, and a value nested deeper than it allows is Error::NestingTooDeep:

  • read::<T>() / read_owned::<T>() of a value that is neither Sized nor SelfDescribing goes one level deeper, and back up when it is done; split() gives a reader one level deeper. Every field, list element and boxed value is read that way, so every way a type can contain itself takes a level per step.
  • Values read later keep the depth they were read at: a RefBox, a RefVec, the slots of a sparse struct and the elements of an EitherAnyVec are read with a reader as deep as the one they came from.
  • BufReader::new allows BufReader::DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH = 128 levels, from_ww_bytes and from_ww_bytes_owned too. BufReader::new(buf).with_max_depth(n) sets another limit, depth_left() tells what is left.

128 is far more than real data needs: the introspection data of every API in this repository's tests reads within 20. A level costs about 3.5 KiB of stack in a debug build (far less in release), so 128 levels of the introspection Type take about 450 KiB, well within the 2 MiB of a spawned thread. Lower the limit on a small stack (an MCU) that decodes a recursive type. A hand-written des_shrink_wrap that calls T::des_shrink_wrap of a nested value directly, without read, takes no level for it: read nested values with read there too.

items.title: BufWriterOwned
items.text: BufWriterOwned writes the same bits into a growable Vec<u8> instead of a fixed slice (std only), and has no u16::MAX limit per value, which plain BufWriter currently has.

items.title: Alignment
items.text:
bool, U1..U64 and I2..I64 are bit-aligned, Nibble and UNib32 nibble-aligned, everything else byte-aligned. Byte arrays, strings and Unsized values are all byte-aligned, to keep the code and the computations small. Unused bits are set to zero and can be reclaimed when evolving a type:

fn version1() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
    let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf[..]);
    wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();
    wr.write_u8(0xAA).unwrap();
    let bytes = wr.finish_and_take().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0x80, 0xAA]);
}

A later version, while the older one is still in use, adds an Option<U6> in the free bits:

fn version1_1() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
    let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf[..]);
    wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();
    wr.write(&Some(U6::new(5).unwrap())).unwrap();
    wr.write_u8(0xAA).unwrap();
    let bytes = wr.finish_and_take().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0xC5, 0xAA]);
}

Older code reads the new data and skips the bits, newer code reads old data and gets None (the zero bits). The size didn't even change.

items.title: Traits and ElementSize
items.text:
Every serializable type implements SerializeShrinkWrap and DeserializeShrinkWrap. Both work on borrowed data, no allocator required. Types that also support std implement the ..Owned counterparts, SerializeShrinkWrapOwned / DeserializeShrinkWrapOwned, which write into a BufWriterOwned. #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] generates one pair per representation you ask for (see borrowed, owned, or both?).

Each trait carries ELEMENT_SIZE: ElementSize, the one piece of information the FIFO of lengths is built on. It tells a parent type, at compile time, whether a field needs a length slot at all:

ElementSize Meaning Unsized Size isn't known up front; a parent reserves a slot for it. The default for structs and enums: fully evolvable. UnsizedFinalStructure Also size-unknown, but flattened onto the parent instead of getting its own slot. Vec<T>, String, &str, arrays and tuples are this. SelfDescribing No size is stored; the reader tells where the value ends from the encoding itself (UNib32's continuation bits, Option's flag, ...). Sized { size_bits } Size is fixed and known at compile time; nothing is stored for it.

How a struct's or enum's own ELEMENT_SIZE is computed from its fields:

  • ElementSize::add combines fields. It is deliberately "sticky" upward: Sized + SelfDescribing = SelfDescribing, anything + Unsized = Unsized, and UnsizedFinalStructure wins over everything. A type can never claim a stronger guarantee than its fields give; a compile-time assertion checks it.
  • ElementSize::one_of combines the variants of an enum, of which only one is on the wire. Variants of the same Sized size keep it, Sized variants of different sizes give SelfDescribing (the discriminant tells the length), anything else follows add.
  • The discriminant is added on top: Sized for every ww_repr but unib32.
  • size_bits counts the bits of the value itself, without alignment padding: struct { a: bool, b: u8 } is 9 bits and takes 2 bytes.

Size assumptions covers how to pick one of these for your own types.

items.title: write / read vs ser_shrink_wrap / des_shrink_wrap
items.text:
There are two ways to put a value into a BufWriter. They are not interchangeable: each has a read-side counterpart, and mixing them up gives a reader misaligned with what was written.

  • value.ser_shrink_wrap(&mut wr) writes exactly the value's own bytes, with no length slot. The caller already knows (or doesn't need) its extent. Read back with T::des_shrink_wrap(&mut rd).
  • wr.write(&value) first reserves a slot, but only if T::ELEMENT_SIZE is Unsized, then calls ser_shrink_wrap and fills the slot in. Read back with rd.read::<T>(), which reads the length and split()s a bounded sub-reader first, again only for Unsized types.

write / read is what makes a value's size discoverable to whatever is around it: use it for a value that is a field of another one (generated code does exactly that for every field). ser_shrink_wrap / des_shrink_wrap is right when nothing needs to skip over the value from outside, most commonly the top-level value of a message, whose extent is the buffer's own length:

fn to_ww_bytes<'i>(&self, buf: &'i mut [u8]) -> Result<&'i [u8], Error> {
    let mut wr = BufWriter::new(buf);
    self.ser_shrink_wrap(&mut wr)?; // not `wr.write(self)`: no point sizing the whole message
    wr.finish_and_take()
}

items.title: to_ww_bytes / from_ww_bytes
items.text:
The traits have default methods that wrap that boilerplate for the top-level value:

let mut buf = [0u8; 64];
let bytes: &[u8] = my_value.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf)?;      // SerializeShrinkWrap::to_ww_bytes
let value = MyType::from_ww_bytes(bytes)?;               // DeserializeShrinkWrap::from_ww_bytes

// std: no scratch buffer to manage, and no u16::MAX limit per value
let bytes: Vec<u8> = my_value.to_ww_bytes_owned()?;      // SerializeShrinkWrapOwned::to_ww_bytes_owned
let value = MyType::from_ww_bytes_owned(&bytes)?;        // DeserializeShrinkWrapOwned::from_ww_bytes_owned

These are what every example on this site calls. BufWriter / BufReader and write / read only matter for a hand-written type, a streaming API on top of ShrinkWrap (see the builder pattern), or anything else that needs more control than one call.

items.title: Encodings of the special types
items.text: How the types of special types look on the wire. These codes are part of the wire format and stay as they are.

items.title: TailSize<N>
items.text:
A UVlq32 right-justified in N bytes (1 to 5, 5 by default), padded with empty 0x80 groups in front, so any UVlq32 reader decodes it. N is the capacity: 127 bytes for N = 1, 16 KB for 2, 2 MB for 3, 256 MB for 4, 4 GB for 5; serialization fails with Error::LenTooLong beyond it.

The value is the number of bytes from the end of the field to the end of the enclosing value, the value's own reverse lengths included. The derive macro generates, around the fields after the slot, what you would write by hand with BufWriter::reserve_tail_size() and backfill_tail_size():

  1. reserve the slot and write the rest of the fields;
  2. encode the reverse lengths those fields pushed, so they land inside the value's range, where they would have gone anyway;
  3. align to a byte and fill the slot in.

On read: read the slot, split() the reader to that many bytes, read the rest from the split. The showcase has the bytes.

items.title: The delta and XOR codes
items.text:
Two bit-level codes that Series columns use (they were the standalone types Delta, DeltaOfDelta and XorFloat before Series, SW-31 and SW-32). Both go through the bit cursor, most significant bit first, with no alignment in between.

  • The delta code (SW-31), the prefix coder of a numeric column: a residual z (the zigzag of a difference, wrapped at the width W of the column, so u8 0 after 255 is +1) is written as:

    Prefix Then For 0 nothing z = 0 10 7 bits z < 128 110 9 bits z < 512 1110 12 bits z < 4096 11110 20 bits z < 2^20 111110 32 bits z < 2^32

    Buckets at or above W are left out, and the last bucket is W bits after a 1 for every bucket and no 0: 11 + 8 bits for u8/i8, 1111 + 16 bits for 16-bit types, 11111 + 32 bits for 32-bit, 111111 + 64 bits for 64-bit types. A repeated value costs 1 bit, a step within -64..=63 costs 9. With the delta of delta predictor the residual is the change of the difference: a value that grows by the same step as the one before costs 1 bit (the Gorilla timestamp code).

  • The XOR code (SW-32), the XOR codec of a float column: the XOR of the bit patterns of the value and the previous one.

    • 0 when it is zero (a repeated value);
    • 10 and the bits inside the window of the previous explicitly coded XOR (its leading and trailing zero counts) when the new XOR fits in it;
    • otherwise 11, the leading zero count (5 bits for f32, 6 for f64), the number of significant bits minus one (5 / 6 bits) and those bits, which become the new window.

    Pure bit operations: NaN payloads, -0.0 and infinities round-trip exactly.

The showcase has the bytes.

items.title: OptionAnyVec
items.text:
Layout: |presence header|present values in slot order|reverse lengths|. The values are written exactly as BufWriter::write writes them anywhere else (an Unsized value with its size, lists and strings with their length at the back), one after another without padding between them: a bool takes one bit, a u8 aligns itself to a byte as always.

The header starts with a mode nibble. The writer knows the present set before writing anything and picks the mode with the fewest bits for it (on a tie, the first one in this table):

Nibble Mode Then 0 all n: UNib32: slots 0..n are present 1 dense len: UNib32 (last present slot + 1), then len bits, one per slot, MSB first 2 two-level groups: UNib32 (of 8 slots, up to the last present one), a bit per group, then 8 bits for each group whose bit is set, slot 8g in the MSB 3 index list count: UNib32, then count UNib32: the first present slot, then for each next one slot - previous - 1 4..15 reserved a reader fails with Error::EnumFutureVersionOrMalformedData

No present slot at all is written as no bytes (a reader also takes 0 0 and 3 0 as empty). The mode nibble costs nothing extra in practice: the UNib32 after it is nibble-aligned anyway. The reserved codes leave room for slots with a third state (absent / value / error, SW-56) at no cost to the two-state vec.

Header bits from a nibble boundary:

Mode Bits all 4 + 4·nibbles(n) dense 4 + 4·nibbles(len) + len two-level 4 + 4·nibbles(groups) + groups + 8·(non-empty groups) index list 4 + 4·(nibbles(count) + Σ nibbles(delta))

Dense wins for clustered sets up to a few dozen slots, the index list for a few slots among many, two-level for a few dense clusters far apart. The showcase has the numbers.

items.title: Series<T>
items.text:
SW-60. What Series<T> is for and when to reach for it is its own page; this is the bit-level layout. All bit-level codes below write most significant bit first through the bit cursor, with no alignment unless stated; nib(x) is the UNib32 code written through the bit cursor without nibble alignment.

n:          UNib32 (nibble-aligned)     number of items; 0: nothing else follows
group(T):   the columns of T over all n items
padding:    zero bits to the next byte

Series is ElementSize::Unsized: as a field it gets a length slot in the parent's FIFO like any other evolvable value, and nothing inside a Series uses the FIFO - a lazy reader walks the columns in parallel, which would consume FIFO entries out of order. At the top of a message or stream item its extent is the buffer's own.

Groups. The group of a type over a subsequence of items (all of them at the top, fewer inside an enum variant or an Option) is written by the type's own rule, recursively; an empty subsequence writes nothing (its size is already known to the reader from the tag runs above it):

Type Group integers (u8..u64, i8..i64, U1..U64, I2..I64, Nibble, UNib32, UVlq32, UVlq64) a numeric column at the type's value width u128, i128 a numeric column, predictor raw and coder plain only (other codes malformed) f32, f64 a float column bool a two-valued run unit-only enum, or enum with data a tag run (always the general form, even with 2 variants: a later version may add a third), then, for each variant that has items here, the variant's fields as a struct group over just those items Option<X> the { None, Some(X) } enum: a two-valued tag run, then group(X) over the Some items struct, final_structure / self_describing / sized the fields' groups in declaration order struct, evolvable (Unsized, the default) outermost: fields: nib (how many fields this writer's T has), then the fields' groups; nested inside another group: len: nib (bits of the group after len), then the fields' groups tuple, [X; N] like a final_structure struct of the elements &str/String, &[u8], RefVec<u8>/Vec<u8>, or any type marked #[series(opaque)] an opaque run of the bytes (to_ww_bytes for #[series(opaque)])

Columns appear in the order the groups above produce them: depth first, declaration order, an enum's tag run before its variants' columns - the order a reader needs to find every column's start in one forward pass.

Numeric column:

predictor:  2 bits   00 raw, 01 delta, 10 delta of delta, 11 escape (reserved in v1: malformed)
coder:      2 bits   00 prefix, 01 packed, 10 constant, 11 plain
values:     m values of width W

The values split into segments at restarts (below). With predictor delta or delta of delta, a segment's first value is written at the full width W; every other value is a residual: the zigzag of the difference to the previous value (delta) or of the change of that difference (delta of delta, the running difference starting at 0 at each segment start), wrapped at W. With predictor raw there are no segment starts; every value is a residual (its zigzag for signed types, itself for unsigned ones).

Coders, for the residuals:

  • prefix - each residual in the delta code at width W.
  • packed - the residuals of a segment in blocks of 8 (the last block of a segment shorter, its length known from m and the restarts): width in bits(W) bits (4 bits for W = 8, 5 for 16, 6 for 32, 7 for 64 - enough for 0..=W), then each residual of the block at exactly width bits. A block of all zeros costs only its width field.
  • constant - the first residual of the column in the prefix code; every later residual equals it and is not written. Delta + constant is t0 + period (a regular clock, a counter); raw + constant is a plain constant column.
  • plain - each residual at the full width W.

The writer may try any subset of predictor x coder combinations (or a fixed one via CodecPolicy) and keeps the smallest encoding; the reader follows whatever the 4-bit header says. Predictor 11 is reserved for a later, extended column mode (an escape, so existing codes keep their meaning and cost); a v1 reader fails on it with Error::MalformedSeries.

Float column:

codec:      4 bits   0000 plain (each value at full width), 0001 XOR (the XOR code), others reserved

XOR: the first value of a segment at full width, then the XOR code against the previous value; a segment start also resets the leading/trailing zero window.

Run (discrete leaves - enum tags, bool, Option presence, opaque bytes):

first:      value of the first item
repeat:     1, gap: nib, value      a change: gap = items since the previous change (or the start) minus 1;
                                    value left out when two-valued (a change just flips it)
end:        0

An enum's discriminant is written as nib (per its ww_repr); a bool as 1 bit; an opaque value as len: nib bytes, zero bits to the next byte, then the bytes. A change landing at or past the subsequence's end is malformed.

Restarts. A numeric or float column restarts (full value, codec state reset, packed block ended) at an item where: the item enters this enum variant (or Some) from another one, so the column only ever holds that variant's own items; an enum-typed field declared earlier in the same struct changed (Volt { prefix, value } restarts value when prefix changes, so 480 µA followed by 120 mA is a full value, not a delta of -360); or the enclosing group itself restarts (it propagates down). bool, string and opaque runs never restart anything - a flag toggling every other item would otherwise cost a full value each time. "Declared earlier" keeps one forward pass enough to decode, and keeps evolution working: a field appended later can never restart a column an older reader already knows how to read.

Evolution. Series<T> follows T's own evolution rules, same as Vec<T> does: an appended #[default = ..] field's columns go at the end of its struct's group, which an older reader skips (nested: via the group length; outermost: the Series simply ends after the columns it knows, filling the field's default into every item for a newer reader reading older data). A final_structure / self_describing / sized struct has no count or length inside a Series either, exactly as in plain form. A new enum variant an older reader doesn't know fails with Error::EnumFutureVersionOrMalformedData, as a plain decode of that item would.

The showcase has a 4-item example worked out byte by byte, including a column restart.

items.title: Device contract
items.text:
Six ww_stdlib crates that every device implements, whatever it does. Together they answer what a host, a tester's bug report or a production line asks of any unit: what firmware is this and where is its ELF, what board, which unit, what has it counted, what did it log, and why did it last reset. One host tool, ww info and ww report, asks the same questions of every device, because all of them implement the same global traits.

Question Crate Trait What ww shows What firmware, which build? ww_firmware_info FirmwareInfo name, version, git, build time, profile, build id Why did it last reset? ww_firmware_info LastReset cause, boot count, fault registers, stack, panic message Which board? ww_board_info BoardInfo name, revision and where it came from, variant, BOM, serial Which unit? ww_uid Uid chip id, MAC, ..., the first is the primary id What did the user call it? ww_user_info UserInfo label and notes, whether they survive a power cycle What has it counted? ww_counters Counters the cnt counters, decoded with the ELF What did it log? ww_log LogDefmt the stored defmt log, decoded with the ELF

items.title: Where to put them
items.text:
Implement each trait once, at any depth of the API tree. The conventional place is one Device subtree of the API root:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Device {
    ww_impl!(firmware: ww_firmware_info::FirmwareInfo);
    ww_impl!(last_reset: ww_firmware_info::LastReset);
    ww_impl!(board: ww_board_info::BoardInfo);
    ww_impl!(uid: ww_uid::Uid);
    ww_impl!(label: ww_user_info::UserInfo);
    ww_impl!(counters: ww_counters::Counters);
    ww_impl!(log: ww_log::LogDefmt);
}

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyDevice {
    ww_impl!(device: Device);
    // ... what the device does
}

Where they sit doesn't matter to ww: its calls carry a global trait path (crate, version, trait name) that the device resolves itself (addressing), so ww info works with a device whatever its own API and whatever version of it, also one flashed years ago. A device that doesn't implement a trait, or implements an incompatible version of it, is reported as such for that part; the rest is still shown.

Every item of the first four crates is a const: the device serves it from a value, without a handler (const items), and the host reads it once per connection.

items.title: Linking a firmware to its ELF: the build id
items.text:
Three of the traits need the firmware's ELF on the host: defmt logs (the format strings are in the ELF, not on the wire), cnt counters (names, types and units are in non-loaded sections of the ELF), and a crash record (addresses to name). The ELF is found by the firmware's GNU build id: the linker hashes the linked output, so it changes with every byte of code, and the device has it in flash while the ELF has it in a note.

Three lines make a firmware report it:

  1. The linker writes the note. In .cargo/config.toml (or the build's RUSTFLAGS):

    [target.thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf]
rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=--build-id=sha1"]

  2. memory.x keeps the note in flash and names its bounds:

    SECTIONS {
    .note.gnu.build-id : ALIGN(4)
    {
        __build_id_start = .;
        KEEP(*(.note.gnu.build-id));
        __build_id_end = .;
    } > FLASH
} INSERT AFTER .rodata;

  3. The firmware reads it where the traits ask for it, ww_firmware_info::build_id() (feature build-id). The same value goes into FirmwareInfo::BUILD_ID, DefmtInfo::build_id and CountersInfo::build_id, so each trait is usable alone. build.rs of the firmware calls ww_firmware_info::build::emit() for the rest of FirmwareInfo::FIRMWARE (see ww_firmware_info).

Without the note the build id is empty. ww then can't tell which ELF belongs to the device: it uses only an ELF passed with --elf, and says it couldn't check it.

items.title: Where ww looks for the ELF
items.text:
For each build id the device reports, in this order:

  1. --elf PATH: used, and refused if its build id differs from the device's (--force to use it anyway).
  2. The ELF directory: <build id>.elf in each directory of WW_ELF_PATH, then ~/.cache/ww/elf.
  3. The ELFs of the cargo project in the current directory (target/), the one with that build id.

Nothing is found by guessing: when no ELF has the device's build id, the parts that need one say so and name the places searched. --force takes the newest binary under target/ instead, with a warning.

The ELF directory is filled with ww elf add:

ww elf add target/thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf/release/usb_io_fw   # one ELF, stored as <build id>.elf
ww elf add usb_io_fw-0.5.0-elf.tar.zst                          # a whole release
ww elf id usb_io_fw                                             # its build id, and whether it is in the directory

ww elf add and cnt elf add are the same code (cnt_core::elf), they fill one directory.

items.title: The release archive
items.text:
A firmware release ships one archive of all its ELFs, not loose files: <firmware>-<version>-elf.tar.zst, with every board variant and profile of the release. A tester who got a bug report from a unit runs ww elf add on the archive of the version printed in the report, and ww report finds the right ELF by build id from then on.

# at release time, in the firmware's repo: every ELF of the release, and a plain list of build ids to read
for elf in release/*.elf; do echo "$(ww elf id $elf) $(basename $elf)"; done > index.txt
tar --zstd -cf usb_io_fw-0.5.0-elf.tar.zst index.txt release/*.elf

ww elf add reads each ELF's build id from the ELF itself, so a file in the archive that is not an ELF (the index, notes) is ignored and an ELF without a build id is listed as skipped. The version a unit runs is in its report (FirmwareInfo::FIRMWARE), which says which archive to fetch.

items.title: ww info
items.text:
$ ww info --serial 4B333720
API        usb_io_api@0.5.0
Firmware   b200_usb_io 0.5.0 (a1b2c3d-dirty, built 2026-10-03 18:20), release
Build id   28a4e144e867138da2cccccd14e3e6baa2c78fbc
Board      rePort rev B (strap 2), BOM std, serial RP-0042
Ids        chip e6613871235b1c2d (internal, primary)
Label      "bench 2", notes "DUT of the CAN test" (kept over power cycles)
Last reset Panic, boot 3 since cleared, ran 2.5 s
            message: index out of bounds

The same data as JSON with --format json (each part is {"status": "value" | "not_implemented" | "error", ...}). It needs no ELF and no user API.

items.title: ww report
items.text:
ww report is ww info plus the counters, the stored log and the last reset's addresses named with the ELF, in one file a tester sends along with a bug report:

ww report --serial 4B333720 -o report.md

It has the sections of the output above, then:

  • Last reset: the fault's pc and lr and the stack words named by function (fn+0x1c) from the ELF of the firmware that crashed (the record carries its build id: it may be older than an update since).
  • Counters: every cnt counter of RAM and backup with its value and unit, decoded with the ELF.
  • Log: what the device's log store holds, from the first message since boot, decoded with defmt; gaps are shown where the device dropped messages. Reading it does not empty the store.

Each part that needs an ELF it couldn't get says why and the rest of the report is still complete, so a tester without the archive still sends something useful. --elf, --force and --format json behave as for ww counters.

The log is a stream, which is opened on the trait's absolute path in the device's API (the host reads the device's introspection data for it, it needs no API of its own): that is the one part where ww report is more than global trait calls.

items.title: On the host (Rust)
items.text:
ww_report is the library behind both commands:

let device = DynClient::from_config(config).connect().await?;
let contract = ww_report::clients::Contract::new(&device);   // keep it: dropping it disconnects the device
let report = ww_report::report::collect_report(&contract, &ReportOptions::default()).await;
println!("{}", ww_report::report::render_report(&report));

tests/device_report runs it against a mock device implementing every trait of the contract.

items.title: IO trait family
items.text: A set of global WireWeaver trait crates for devices that expose IO over the wire: a dev board bridging its pins to a host, a USB adapter (an FTDI-like dongle, a Bus Pirate-like probe), a motor controller, a sensor node, a lab instrument. A device picks the traits it implements and puts each one once into its API tree (ww_impl!); nothing here assumes a particular kind of device.

items.title: Crates
items.text:
Crate Traits What it's for ww_gpio Bank, Pin Logical-pin GPIO: read, drive, reconfigure, watch edges ww_uart Uart Bridge a serial port; watch both lines of a link without driving them (optional) ww_can_bus Can, CanGroup, CanTimeTriggered, CanXl CAN / CAN FD controllers: frames, error state, optional filters, TX events, bus errors, buffers, debugger items; groups sharing a clock; TTCAN; CAN XL ww_i2c I2c, I2cWatch, I2cMonitor Master transfers and bus recovery; autonomous polling; bus sniffing ww_spi Spi Master transfers with CS held across operations; bus sniffing (optional) ww_adc Adc, AdcStream, AdcCapture One calibrated reading; continuous streaming; triggered block capture ww_pwm Pwm, PwmCapture PWM channel outputs; pulse/frequency measurement on capture-capable channels ww_onewire OneWire Reset, ROM search, addressed transactions, strong pull-up ww_timebase Clock Device time, clock sync (master/slave), time-of-day for a master ww_logic_analyzer LogicAnalyzer, LogicStream Timestamped capture of many digital channels, triggered or streamed ww_signal_generator PatternGenerator, WaveformGenerator Digital pattern playback (replays a capture); DAC waveforms

ww_si and ww_numeric underpin all of them: every physical value on the wire is a typed ww_si quantity, not a raw integer with an implied unit.

What only some devices have is never a method that answers "not supported" on most implementers. A function with state, configuration and several items of its own is its own trait: AdcStream and AdcCapture are separate from Adc, I2cMonitor and I2cWatch from I2c, PwmCapture from Pwm. A thermometer implements Adc only; a data logger adds AdcStream; an I2C sniffer may implement only I2cMonitor with no master at all. A function that is one stream is an optional item of the main trait instead (Uart::monitor, Spi::monitor), so an array of ports (ww_impl!(uart[]: Uart)) carries it without a second array or trait to keep in step, and a device without the hardware leaves it out (omit = ["uart.monitor"]). A host finds out what a device actually has through introspection (global trait paths, left-out items) and, within a trait, through its capabilities() method.

items.title: Shared conventions
items.text:
Capabilities are queried, never assumed. Every core trait has a capabilities()-shaped method (Bank::capabilities, Pin::capabilities, I2c::i2c_capabilities, Spi::capabilities, Adc::capabilities / AdcStream::stream_capabilities / AdcCapture::capture_capabilities, Pwm::capabilities, OneWire::capabilities, Clock::info, LogicAnalyzer::capabilities / LogicStream::stream_capabilities, PatternGenerator::capabilities, WaveformGenerator::capabilities) describing ranges, rates, formats and which optional behaviors work, so a host doesn't have to special-case devices by name.

One configuration, answered with what was set. A bus or bank is configured in one call with one struct, not a property per setting: Uart::configure(UartConfig), I2c::i2c_configure(I2cConfig), Spi::configure(SpiConfig), Can::configure(CanConfig), Bank::configure(BankConfig), OneWire::configure(OneWireConfig). Each answers with the same struct as actually set (the baud rate or clock the divider settled on, the IO level in effect), so a host sees the rounding and a port never runs with half a configuration. Stream functions that configure what they watch do the same (Uart::monitor answers its MonitorConfig).

IO level in the configuration. On adapters with level translators the IO level is a field of that configuration, io_level: Option<Volt> (None leaves it as it is, and is the answer of a device without level control), and the capabilities list what it can be set to in the same three fields everywhere: io_levels (discrete levels), io_level_min / io_level_max (an adjustable supply). PWM, ADC, logic analyzer and signal generator channels sit on pins of a GPIO bank or bus and use its level; the logic analyzer sets its own input threshold per capture.

Common errors. Each crate has its own error enum (ww_gpio::GpioError, ww_uart::UartError, ww_i2c::I2cError, ww_spi::SpiError, ww_can_bus::CanError, ww_adc::AdcError, ww_pwm::PwmError, ww_onewire::OneWireError, ww_timebase::ClockError, ww_logic_analyzer::LaError, ww_signal_generator::PgError / WgError), and every one of them starts with ww_error::CommonError as its #[common] Common variant for the situations every device shares: Unsupported (this device doesn't have the mode, level or feature asked for), InvalidArgument, InUse (the pins or peripheral already serve another function), Busy, WrongState, NoPower (the level translators or output buffers have no supply), Refused (a safety rule of the device declines the request), Timeout. Only what a caller acts on specifically stays crate-specific: Nack and Arbitration for I2C, NoPresence for 1-Wire, NoSuchChannel, SharedTimer. Host code handles the common part of any of them the same way (e.common()), and each method lists the variants it can return with #[errors(..)].

Typed values through ww_si. Voltages, frequencies, baud rates and durations are ww_si quantities (Volt, Hertz, Baud, Second), never a bare integer with an implied unit. The device reports in whatever storage and prefix are convenient for it (a u32 of µs, an f32 of volts); the host reads any of them. Timestamps, in method results and in stream heads alike, are ww_si::Second: time since the device's own clock started, in the prefix and number type the device picks. A fixed-width value wraps (a u32 of µs wraps after about 71.6 minutes); a host that needs the full value reads Clock::now() and unwraps around it. Devices with several timed traits (a logic analyzer, an ADC capture, an I2C monitor) share one clock, so their timestamps line up against each other.

Arrays of channels. A bank, bus or generator with several identical resources (ww_gpio::Bank::pin, ww_pwm::Pwm::channel, ww_signal_generator::WaveformGenerator::channel) exposes them as ww_impl!(name[]: Trait), a WireWeaver array of sub-traits. Every other method that addresses one of them takes a plain index into that same array, in the order its crate's *Info / *Capabilities type lists them — no bitmasks, no names on the wire.

Monitors. Watching a bus without taking part in it is a counted stream function: Uart::monitor and Spi::monitor, optional items of the bus trait, and I2cMonitor::records, a trait of its own because I2C monitoring also exists without a master (I2cMode::MonitorOnly) and next to the master's own traffic. A monitor reports one record per transaction/frame; a master that also wants to see its own traffic sets the matching monitor flag where the trait offers one (e.g. I2cMode::Master { monitor: true, .. }). On CAN, monitoring is a mode of the controller (ww_can_bus::Mode::ListenOnly) on its one rx stream, no separate item.

Streams are opened with their configuration. A stream that needs a configuration is a stream function: the host opens it with the configuration as its arguments and gets back what the device actually set, or an error, and closing the stream stops sampling or monitoring (AdcStream::samples, LogicStream::data, Pin::event, PwmCaptureChannel::capture, Spi::monitor, I2cMonitor::records, Uart::monitor). Opening it again starts a new session with the new configuration, so there is no separate configure / start / stop to keep in sync.

let (actual, mut samples) = adc.adc_stream().samples(config).call().await??;

Counted streams: positions, losses and time in the head. Every device → host stream of the family with measured or received data is counted (stream delivery): each event's head carries its position in the stream's unit (a sample set, a byte, a frame, an edge, as the stream's rustdoc says), how many units the device dropped right before it, and the device time of its first unit. Item types carry no positions or losses, and only the time that is their own: an RxChunk is bytes, line flags and, if the device measures it, when its last byte arrived, an I2cRecord / SpiFrame when the transaction ended, a SampleBlock raw samples. A host sees exactly what it missed and where (StreamEvent::Gap), whether the device dropped it (no host, a full buffer) or the link lost it.

Credit sinks for bulk host → device data. Where the host sends more than fits one reply — a UART's tx bytes, a PatternGenerator's pattern, a WaveformChannel's arbitrary table — the method is a #[credit] sink!(..) rather than a plain one: the device's free buffer is the credit, so the host can never overrun it, and Open / Close mark where one logical write begins and ends.

items.title: Composing a device API
items.text:
A device picks whichever traits it supports and puts each one into its API tree once, outside any trait array, so generic tooling can find it by global trait path:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyBridge {
    ww_impl!(gpio: ww_gpio::Bank);
    ww_impl!(uart: ww_uart::Uart);
    ww_impl!(i2c: ww_i2c::I2c);
    ww_impl!(i2c_monitor: ww_i2c::I2cMonitor);
    ww_impl!(la: ww_logic_analyzer::LogicAnalyzer);
}

Channels of different crates that happen to be the same physical pin cross-reference each other by gpio_pin: Option<u8> (an index into that device's ww_gpio::Bank::pin), e.g. ww_logic_analyzer::ChannelInfo::gpio_pin or ww_signal_generator::PgChannelInfo::gpio_pin, so a tool can show "logic analyzer channel 3 = PA5 = GPIO pin 5" without guessing from names.

See each crate's own page — linked in the table above — for its traits, types and a worked example.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
ww_stdlib is a set of crates with ready-made WireWeaver traits and data types: GPIO, UART, I2C, CAN, logging, firmware info, firmware updates, physical units and more. Instead of designing its own GPIO or logging API, a device picks the crates it needs and puts their traits into its API, and a host (driver, CLI, GUI) gets a matching typed client from the same codegen.

[dependencies]
ww_gpio = "0.1"
ww_firmware_info = { version = "0.1", default-features = false }

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyBoard {
    ww_impl!(firmware: ww_firmware_info::FirmwareInfo);
    ww_impl!(gpio: ww_gpio::Bank);
    fn my_own_method(value: u8);
}

A crate's name and version are part of the wire contract (see folder structure), so using ww_gpio on both ends is what lets tools of unrelated projects recognize "this is a GPIO bank" without agreeing on anything else: ww info reads the firmware info of any device that has it, wherever it sits in the API.

All crates are no_std by default; the std feature adds owned types (..Owned, String instead of &str) for host code. Most of them live under ww_stdlib/ in this repo (canonical home: vhrdtech/ww_stdlib); the framework crates ww_self and ww_global live in the wire_weaver repo root, versioned the same way.

items.title: Picking crates
items.text:
Start from what the device has:

  • Every device implements the device contract: which firmware and board it is, which unit, its log and counters, so ww info and a support case have one place to look whatever the device does.
  • Add the I/O traits for the hardware the device exposes over the wire (a GPIO bank, a UART bridge, an I2C master, ...). Pick only what is bridged: a thermometer implements Adc, not AdcStream as well.
  • Use the data types in your own methods and types: a physical value is a ww_si quantity, not a raw integer with an implied unit, and an API's error enum nests ww_error::CommonError first.
  • The framework crates are used by the codegen and introspection; an API crate rarely depends on them directly.

items.title: I/O
items.text:
Traits for devices that expose IO over the wire: a dev board bridging its pins to a host, a USB adapter, a motor controller, a sensor node. The IO trait family page has the conventions they share (capabilities queried at runtime, one configure() call per bus, common errors, typed ww_si values, counted streams).

  • ww_gpio — Bank, Pin: read, drive and reconfigure pins, edge events as a stream
  • ww_uart — Uart: bridge a serial port, optionally watch a link without driving it
  • ww_can_bus — Can, CanGroup, CanTimeTriggered, CanXl: CAN, CAN FD and CAN XL controllers, from simple bridges to bus debuggers
  • ww_i2c — I2c, I2cWatch, I2cMonitor: master transfers and bus recovery, autonomous polling, bus sniffing
  • ww_spi — Spi: transfers with CS held across operations, optional bus sniffing
  • ww_adc — Adc, AdcStream, AdcCapture: one calibrated reading, continuous streaming, triggered block capture
  • ww_pwm — Pwm, PwmCapture: PWM outputs, pulse and frequency measurement
  • ww_onewire — OneWire: reset, ROM search, addressed transactions, strong pull-up
  • ww_timebase — Clock: device time, clock sync (master/slave), time of day
  • ww_logic_analyzer — LogicAnalyzer, LogicStream: timestamped capture of many digital channels
  • ww_signal_generator — PatternGenerator, WaveformGenerator: digital pattern playback, DAC waveforms
  • ww_memory — Memory8, Memory32: read and write words at addresses, optional watches, for register maps and raw memory access
  • ww_pin_diag — PinDiag: raw access to a board's digital points for bring-up and production tests (shorts, pulls, connectivity), the board's rules kept in the firmware; with ww_interned names as ids
  • ww_block — BlockDevice: read, CRC, erase and write an SD card, eMMC or flash by block; writes under a lease that stops the card's own user, optional bulk sink and read stream
  • ww_sd — SdCard: an SD card's state, raw registers, init with a per-step report, raw commands with response, status bits and timing

items.title: Device contract
items.text:
The crates every device implements, whatever it does, so generic tools have one place to look. The device contract page shows where to put them and how a host finds the firmware's ELF.

  • ww_firmware_info — FirmwareInfo (name, version, git, build time, build id), LastReset (why the device last reset: fault record, stack words, boot count)
  • ww_board_info — BoardInfo: PCB series, revision and how the revision was determined
  • ww_uid — Uid: the unit's unique ids (chip id, MAC, EUI-64, ...)
  • ww_user_info — UserInfo: a name and notes the user gives a unit
  • ww_log — LogDefmt, LogText: device logging over a reliable stream, raw defmt frames or text; ww_defmt_logger (repo root) is the device side
  • ww_counters — Counters: the device's cnt counters, decoded on the host with the firmware's ELF (ww counters)
  • ww_recorder — Recorder, Track: control a logger that writes tracks to an SD card or flash: status, card facts, two-step format, recordings, markers, flush settings, counters
  • ww_indication — Indication: LED and buzzer mode, brightness, identify
  • ww_dfu — UpdateNode, BootControl, Inventory, Stage, StageBulk: firmware updates, A/B or in place, step by step or bulk

items.title: Data types
items.text:
Types other crates and your own API build on.

  • ww_si — Volt, Hertz, Second, ...: physical values with their unit, in whatever number type the device picks
  • ww_error — CommonError, HasCommon: the errors every API can return (Unsupported, InUse, Busy, ...), nested first in a crate's own error enum
  • ww_date_time — DateTime (ISO 8601, optional time zone and nanoseconds, 32 bits minimum), NaiveDate, NaiveTime
  • ww_numeric — NumericValue, NumericBaseType, NumericAnyType: the number types ww_si quantities are stored as

items.title: Framework
items.text:
Used by the codegen and introspection; an API crate rarely depends on these directly.

  • ww_version — Version, FullVersion (SemVer, with pre and build strings), CompactVersion (a global type id and the version numbers): how an API is identified on the wire
  • ww_client_server — Request, Event, Error: the protocol every generated server and client speaks underneath a device's own API
  • ww_self — ApiBundle, ApiLevel, Type, Value: WireWeaver's model of an API and its types, for introspection and dynamic access (repo root, not ww_stdlib/)

ww_global (the global type id registry, see addressing) is the other framework crate in the wire_weaver repo root; it has no page of its own.

items.title: Host-side _hl crates
items.text:
Crates with a more ergonomic client on top of a generated one, for drivers, CLIs and GUIs rather than firmware.

  • ww_gpio_hl — async, blocking and promise wrappers over ww_gpio's generated client

items.title: ww_adc
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_adc is a global WireWeaver trait family for analog inputs: a single calibrated reading, continuous sampling streamed to the host, and lossless triggered block capture into device RAM. It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver, ww_numeric and ww_si (for Volt/Hertz/Second and NumericValue).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_adc = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
items.text: A thermometer or a battery monitor implements Adc only; a data logger adds AdcStream; a device that samples faster than its link (e.g. 500 kS/s over USB full speed) adds AdcCapture. A trait a device doesn't put into its API tree costs it nothing.

items.title: Adc
items.text:
The channels, their units and ranges, and one calibrated reading on demand:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Adc {
    fn read(channel: u8) -> Result<Reading, AdcError>;
    fn capabilities() -> AdcCapabilities<'i>;
}
  • read - one calibrated reading of channel, in the channel's unit (NoSuchChannel, Common(Busy) if a stream or capture can't be interrupted, Common(NoPower), Common(Timeout)).
  • capabilities - the channels, their units, ranges and calibration, see AdcCapabilities under Types below.

Channels are numbered 0..n in the order AdcCapabilities::channels lists them; every other method addresses a channel by that same index. Several Adc::reads, even in one multi-call, are taken one after the other — a capture of one sample set (AdcCapture::capture with sets: 1, Trigger::Now) is how several channels are read at the same instant, if CaptureCapabilities::simultaneous says the hardware supports it.

items.title: AdcStream
items.text:
Continuous sampling of chosen channels, streamed while the link keeps up:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait AdcStream {
    #[stream(SampleBlock<'i>, counted)]
    fn samples(config: StreamConfig<'i>) -> Result<StreamActual, AdcError>;
    fn stream_capabilities() -> StreamCapabilities<'i>;
}
  • samples - a counted stream function: the host opens it with the channels, rate and format to sample and gets back what was actually set (the nearest rate the hardware can do), or an AdcError. Each SampleBlock holds whole sample sets interleaved in the order of StreamConfig::channels, packed as StreamConfig::format. Closing the stream stops sampling (blocks already sampled are still sent); opening it again restarts it with the new configuration. Only one stream runs at a time.
  • stream_capabilities - rates, channel counts and formats the stream supports.

The stream's unit is a sample set (one sample of every configured channel). Positions, sets the device dropped and the device time of a block's first set travel in the event head the framework adds (stream delivery), so a block is pure sample data:

// host
let (actual, mut samples) = adc.adc_stream().samples(config).call().await??;
while let Ok(ev) = samples.recv_event().await {
    match ev {
        StreamEvent::Item { pos, units, t, value, .. } => { /* `units` sets from set `pos`, the first at `t` */ }
        StreamEvent::Gap { at, units, cause, .. } => { /* `units` sets missing from `at` */ }
        _ => {}
    }
}

// device, in the event loop: two sets just sampled, the first at `t`
api_impl::stream_data_ser().adc_stream().samples_send_blocking(&mut server.samples, &block, 2, Some(t), &mut server.sink())?;

items.title: AdcCapture
items.text:
Lossless capture: samples go into device RAM at any rate the hardware can do, the host reads them out after:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait AdcCapture {
    fn capture_capabilities() -> CaptureCapabilities<'i>;
    fn capture(config: CaptureConfig<'i>) -> Result<CaptureActual, AdcError>;
    fn capture_status() -> CaptureStatus;
    fn capture_read(offset: u32, len: u16) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_CAPTURE_READ_LEN>, AdcError>;
    fn capture_abort();
}
  • capture_capabilities - rates, memory depth, which triggers work, and formats.
  • capture - arms a capture. With Trigger::Now it starts at once; otherwise it samples pre_trigger sets continuously and keeps them, waits for the trigger, then takes the rest. Replaces a previous capture and its data.
  • capture_status - where the capture stands: Idle, Armed, Triggered { t }, or Done { t_first, t_trigger, sets } once the data is ready — a host polls this until Done.
  • capture_read - reads len bytes of the captured data from offset; raw samples, interleaved in the order of CaptureConfig::channels, CaptureActual::bytes long, with the first pre_trigger sets before the trigger (Common(WrongState) before a capture is done, Common(InvalidArgument) outside the data).
  • capture_abort - stops an armed or running capture and drops its data.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• Reading - value: NumericValue (in the channel's unit/prefix), raw: u32 (the converter's raw code, for checking calibration), t: Second.
  • AdcCapabilities<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, ChannelInfo<'i>>, MAX_CHANNELS>.
  • ChannelInfo<'i> - name, unit: SIExpr<'i> (a unit of ww_si or the device's own, see run-time units), prefix: Prefix, min / max: NumericValue, bits (converter resolution), calibrated: bool, raw_to_value: Option<Linear> (how raw stream/capture samples turn into values; None if they don't linearly).
  • Linear - scale: f32, offset: f32; value = raw * scale + offset.
  • SampleFormat - U8, U16, Packed12 (two 12-bit samples in three bytes), I16, I24; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • StreamCapabilities<'i> - max_total_rate: Hertz (all channels together), max_channels: u8, formats: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SampleFormat>, MAX_FORMATS>.
  • StreamConfig<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_CHANNELS> (interleave order), rate: Hertz, format: SampleFormat, flush_interval: Option<Second> (send a partial block at least this often; None lets the device choose, around 10 ms).
  • StreamActual - rate: Hertz, what opening samples actually set.
  • SampleBlock<'i> - data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_BLOCK_LEN>, the stream's raw bytes.
  • CaptureCapabilities<'i> - max_total_rate: Hertz, max_bytes: u32, simultaneous: bool (channels of one sample set taken at the same instant), level_trigger / external_trigger: bool, formats: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SampleFormat>, MAX_FORMATS>.
  • CaptureConfig<'i> - channels, rate: Hertz, sets: u32 (total, pre_trigger included), pre_trigger: u32, trigger: Trigger, format: SampleFormat.
  • Trigger - Now, Rising { channel, level: NumericValue }, Falling { channel, level }, External; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • CaptureActual - rate: Hertz, bytes: u32 (size of the data once done).
  • CaptureStatus - Idle, Armed, Triggered { t: Second }, Done { t_first: Second, t_trigger: Option<Second>, sets: u32 }; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • AdcError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), NoSuchChannel; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, shared by every trait in the crate.

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std") and cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)), so owned (*Owned) variants (ChannelInfoOwned, AdcCapabilitiesOwned, StreamConfigOwned, CaptureConfigOwned, ...) and defmt::Format are available by enabling the crate's std / defmt features. Types without a lifetime (Reading, Hertz, Second, StreamActual, CaptureActual, CaptureStatus, AdcError, ...) are used as is on both sides.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device exposes whichever traits it supports directly on its API root (or nested under a group), see tests/io_adc_api:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait IoAdcTest {
    ww_impl!(adc: ww_adc::Adc);
    ww_impl!(adc_stream: ww_adc::AdcStream);
    ww_impl!(adc_capture: ww_adc::AdcCapture);
}

items.title: Worked example (tests/io_adc)
items.text:
tests/io_adc runs a mock server implementing all three traits against the real host event loop, through tests_common::start_device (an in-process ww_device::Server and a generated client, see tests/credit_sink for another worked example of the pattern). It is a convenient reference for wiring the traits up on the server side:

  • capabilities_and_read - queries Adc::capabilities, reads a calibrated and an uncalibrated channel, and checks AdcError::NoSuchChannel for an out-of-range index.
  • stream_open_receive_close - opens AdcStream::samples with an unsupported format (AdcError::Unsupported, nothing opened), then with a good configuration (the mock caps the requested rate at 500 kHz, like real hardware would), receives a block with its position, set count and time, and closes it; Adc::read answers AdcError::Busy while the stream runs.
  • capture_now_trigger_and_read - AdcCapture::capture with Trigger::Now completes immediately (CaptureStatus::Done), capture_read returns the data with bounds checking (Common(InvalidArgument) past the end), and capture_abort drops it (Common(WrongState) after).
  • capture_polled_trigger_progresses_to_done - a non-Now trigger (Trigger::Rising) arms the capture; the mock advances Armed -> Triggered -> Done one step per capture_status poll, standing in for the real wait on the trigger, the same way a host would poll a real device.

items.title: ww_block
items.text:
ww_block (STD-39) serves a block device over WireWeaver: an SD card, eMMC, or a NOR or NAND flash, read, checked, written and erased in whole blocks by their address (LBA). It is a thin layer over the driver a firmware has anyway, and it lets a host do almost everything else: read a live card with a PC tool as if it were in a card reader, lay out a filesystem on the PC and write it out, image a card over the link, or test a card with writes, CRCs and timings. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver and ww_error.

[dependencies]
ww_block = "0.1"

Raw SD commands and the card's registers are ww_sd, served next to it for the same card. Word-addressed register access, with side-effect flags and watches, is ww_memory: a block device has a different contract (geometry and erase units, a write lease, CRCs, bulk transfers), so the two are separate crates.

pub const MAX_TRANSFER: usize = 4096;

#[ww_trait]
pub trait BlockDevice {
    fn geometry() -> Result<Geometry<'i>, BlockError<'i>>;
    fn read(lba: u64, count: u16) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_TRANSFER>, BlockError<'i>>;
    fn crc(lba: u64, count: u32) -> Result<u32, BlockError<'i>>;

    fn claim(lease_s: u16) -> Result<u32, BlockError<'i>>;
    fn release(lease: u32) -> Result<(), BlockError<'i>>;
    fn write(lease: u32, lba: u64, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_TRANSFER>, crc: u32)
        -> Result<(), BlockError<'i>>;
    fn erase(lease: u32, lba: u64, count: u32) -> Result<(), BlockError<'i>>;

    #[optional(bulk)]
    #[credit]
    sink!(write_runs: WriteRun<'i>);
    #[optional(bulk)]
    #[counted]
    stream!(written: RunAck);
    #[optional(bulk)]
    #[stream(ReadRun<'i>, counted)]
    fn read_runs(lba: u64, count: u64) -> Result<(), BlockError<'i>>;
}

items.title: Geometry
items.text:
geometry() answers the medium's Geometry, NoMedium without a card:

Field Meaning kind SdCard, Emmc, NorFlash, NandFlash, Other block_size, block_count bytes per block (512 for SD and eMMC) and blocks on the medium max_blocks most blocks one read, write or bulk run carries on this device, at most MAX_TRANSFER bytes: what fits its message size and buffers erase_blocks blocks in an erase unit: the SD card's allocation unit (AU), a NOR flash's sector best_write_blocks the write size that measured fastest, if measured erased what erased blocks read as: Zeros, Ones or Unspecified erase_before_write NOR flash: a block must be erased before it is written again read_only write-protected: claim answers ReadOnly medium_id changes when another medium is inserted, so a host notices a swap between calls name product name (the card's CID, a flash's part), may be empty

max_blocks is what a host sizes its calls by. A device with 1 KiB messages takes one 512-byte block per call, one with 4 KiB messages and buffers eight.

items.title: Reads are free
items.text: read, crc and the bulk read_runs work at any time, also while the device writes the card itself (it serialises the bus). crc(lba, count) is the CRC-32 of a range computed on the device, so a host checks what it wrote without reading it back over a slow link. The CRC is CRC-32/ISO-HDLC, the one of zip and Ethernet; ww_block::crc32 and crc32_update compute it on either side, and an STM32 CRC unit gives the same with reflected input and output.

items.title: Writes need a lease
items.text:
A write can destroy what the card's own user (a recorder logging to it) keeps there, so writes are only done under a lease:

  1. claim(lease_s) stops the card's user first (a recorder syncs and unmounts its log) and returns the lease, a u32. It may take a while to answer. One lease at a time: Common(Busy) while another is held.
  2. write(lease, lba, data, crc) writes whole blocks, erase(lease, lba, count) erases a range (CMD38 on an SD card, a sector erase on flash, a discard on eMMC). write checks crc (the CRC-32 of data) before anything is written and answers BadCrc otherwise; it answers once the blocks are on the medium.
  3. release(lease) gives the card back, and its user mounts it again and finds what the host wrote.

Every call carrying the lease renews it. After lease_s seconds without one, or when the medium is removed, the lease lapses and the card goes back to its user; a call with it then answers BadLease. A host that crashed mid-job leaves the device working again after lease_s.

There is no writing beside a running user (e.g. outside the extent a recorder uses): a PC that wants to change files on a live card does it through the card's USB mass storage view, if the device has one.

items.title: Who may write
items.text: Who may claim the card is the firmware's choice per link: for example USB and RTT yes, a remote UDP link no. A link that may not answers claim with Common(Refused), and without a lease nothing else writes. ww_block has no access rules of its own; the firmware's handler of claim knows which link a request came on from cx.medium() (see Methods).

items.title: Bulk
items.text:
The bulk group is for long jobs and slow links: writing a prepared filesystem, imaging a card. A device without it leaves it out with omit = ["card.bulk"] (the path from your API root, see Optional items), and a host calling it gets Unimplemented.

  • write_runs is a credit sink of WriteRun { lease, lba, crc, data }: the host never sends more than the device has room for.
