Each run is written as write would, and its outcome comes on written as RunAck { lba, count, status }, in the order the runs came. RunStatus is Written or the reason it was not (BadLength, OutOfRange, BadLease, BadCrc, WriteFailed, NoMedium). written is a counted stream, unit: run, so a host learns about lost acknowledgements and checks those ranges with crc.
  • read_runs(lba, count) opens a counted stream of ReadRun { lba, data }, unit: block: the whole range at the link's full speed instead of one call per run. Opening it again starts another range.

A host preparing a card on the PC does, for example: geometry(), lay out the filesystem, claim, the sectors over write_runs, a crc per region, release. The device needs no format code for that.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
BlockError nests CommonError first (see ww_error), then its own variants; each call lists those it returns (#[errors]):

Variant When NoMedium no card in the slot, or the medium doesn't answer OutOfRange a block past the last one BadLease the lease lapsed, was released, or is not the current one BadCrc write's CRC doesn't match the data: nothing was written ReadOnly the medium is write-protected ReadFailed { reason }, WriteFailed { reason } the medium reported an error Common(Busy) another lease is held (claim), or the bus is taken Common(Refused) this link may not write the card (claim) Common(InvalidArgument) more than max_blocks, or data that isn't whole blocks

items.title: Serving it
items.text: ww api scaffold <crate> prints the server struct (the SinkCredit of write_runs and the Counted states of the streams included) and every handler stub. tests/block_sd serves a mock card as a block device and an SD card, and a small read-only flash that leaves bulk out.

items.title: ww_board_info
items.text:
ww_board_info describes the PCB and its assembly in one value, so ww list and a support case need a single read. It is no_std by default and uses ww_date_time for the build date.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait BoardInfo {
    const BOARD: BoardSummary<'i>;
}

BOARD is a const item, served without a handler and read by a host once per connection. A board read from OTP or straps at boot provides it as a fn (const_model = "BOARD=fn", fn board_board(&self) -> BoardSummary<'_> for board: BoardInfo), a firmware for one fixed board as a Rust const. It never fails; what a device does not know is an empty string or None.

Field Meaning name Board series, B200 (32 bytes) revision Revision as printed on the board, B (8 bytes) revision_source Record, Strap { value } or Assumed variant, bom_variant, serial Assembly variant, BOM variant, serial number (32 bytes each) build_date Option<DateTime>

items.title: Where the revision comes from
items.text:
RevisionSource tells how the firmware knows the revision, which matters for support:

  • Record - read from a record written in production (OTP, EEPROM, flash).
  • Strap { value } - read from resistor straps or a revision pin at boot; value is the raw reading, so a host can show what was measured.
  • Assumed - neither exists: the firmware assumes the revision it was built for. A unit on an assumed revision is a different case from one that read its record.

Device-specific capability flags (a load switch present, a rail powered) stay in the device's own API: they mean nothing on other boards.

BoardSummary has no defmt::Format (its DateTime has none).

items.title: ww_can_bus
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_can_bus is the WireWeaver API of CAN controllers: a USB-CAN adapter, a gateway, a node with a CAN port, a bus analyzer or debugger. The host configures the bus, sends and receives classic, CAN FD and CAN XL frames, and watches the controllers' error state. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver and ww_si (Baud bit rates, Hertz clocks, Ohm terminators, Second timestamps).

[dependencies]
ww_can_bus = "0.1"                                    # classic and FD
ww_can_bus = { version = "0.1", features = ["xl"] }   # plus CAN XL

items.title: Traits
Sending and receiving
items.text:
let mut rx = node.can().rx().call().await?;
let mut tx = node.can().tx().await?;
tx.send_owned(TxFrameOwned { frame, marker: Some(UNib32(1)) }).await?;
while let Ok(event) = rx.recv_event().await {
    if let StreamEvent::Item { t, value, .. } = event {
        println!("{t:?} {:?} {:02x?}", value.frame.id, value.frame.data);
    }
}

rx is a counted stream: every event head carries the frame's position, the frames the device lost right before it (a full receive FIFO, a full link buffer) and the time it was received. tx is a credit sink in bytes of serialized frames; a frame the controller can't send as configured (FD with FD off, anything in a mode that doesn't send) is dropped and reported as TxOutcome::Rejected on tx_events.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
pub struct CanConfig {
    pub mode: Mode,                       // Off, Config, Normal, Restricted, ListenOnly, Internal/ExternalLoopback, Test, Sleep
    pub nominal: Timing,                  // arbitration phase
    pub fd: Option<FdConfig>,             // data phase timing, TDC, ISO / non-ISO; None: classic only
    pub options: Options,                 // one_shot, presume_ack, triple_sample, tx_pause, tx_order, rx_overflow,
                                          // edge_filtering, protocol_exception, wake_on_bus
    pub bus_off_recovery: Option<Second>, // recover by itself after this long; None: wait for `recover`
}

pub enum Timing {
    Rate { rate: Baud, sample_point: u16 }, // sample point in tenths of a percent
    Segments(BitTiming),                    // prescaler, seg1, seg2, sjw in time quanta
}

A host asks for a bit rate and sample point, or for exact segments; configure always answers with segments, so the host sees what the controller runs at. BitTiming counts like SocketCAN and the M_CAN NBTP register: a bit is 1 + seg1 + seg2 quanta of prescaler clock periods, sampled after 1 + seg1, so BitTiming::bit_rate(clock_hz) and BitTiming::sample_point() follow from the answer and Capabilities::clock. Capabilities::nominal / data give the segment limits (as SocketCAN's can_bittiming_const), for a host that computes timings itself.

Tdc::Auto leaves the transceiver delay compensation to the device (offset at the data sample point), and the answer says the offset it set. A setting the controller doesn't have is Common(Unsupported), a bit rate it can't reach Common(InvalidArgument). configure takes the controller off the bus and back as its hardware needs (frames queued for sending stay queued) and ends in CanConfig::mode.

let actual = node
    .can()
    .configure(CanConfig {
        mode: Mode::Normal,
        nominal: Timing::Rate { rate: Baud::kilo(500u16), sample_point: 875 },
        fd: Some(FdConfig {
            data: Timing::Rate { rate: Baud::mega(2u8), sample_point: 750 },
            tdc: Tdc::Auto,
            iso: true,
        }),
        options,
        bus_off_recovery: Some(Second::milli(100u8)),
    })
    .call()
    .await?;
let nominal = actual.nominal.segments().unwrap(); // e.g. prescaler 1, seg1 139, seg2 20 at 80 MHz

items.title: Frames
items.text:
pub struct Frame<'i> {
    pub id: CanId,                                  // Standard(U11) or Extended(U29)
    pub kind: FrameKind,                            // Data, Remote { len }, Fd { brs, esi }, DataLongDlc { dlc }
    pub data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_DATA_LEN>, // up to 64 bytes
}

CanId::standard(0x123) and CanId::extended(0x18FF_0001) build an ID (None when out of range). FrameKind::DataLongDlc is a classic frame with 8 bytes and a DLC of 9-15 on the wire, for bus debuggers.

A received frame is an RxFrame { frame, filter }, filter being the index of the filter element that accepted it (None without filters or for non-matching frames). A frame to send is a TxFrame { frame, marker }: the marker comes back in the frame's TxEvent, so a host matches events to what it sent (M_CAN's message marker, MCP2518FD's sequence number, gs_usb's echo ID). On the wire a classic standard frame with 8 bytes takes 12 bytes as an RxFrame or TxFrame, a 64-byte FD frame with a marker 69.

A device with CAN XL carries those frames on a trait of its own, see CAN XL.

items.title: Time
items.text: Received frames, TX events and bus errors carry their time in the event head: a Second of the device's one clock (ww_timebase::Clock), in the prefix and number type the device picks (usually a u32 of µs, which wraps every 71.6 minutes; the host unwraps it around Clock::now()). Capabilities::timestamps says how fine it is and where in the frame it was taken: start of frame (M_CAN, bxCAN in TTCM, MCP2518FD), end of frame (gs_usb), or by software when the frame was read out (no hardware timestamps); None, and heads without a time, on devices without a clock.

items.title: Status and errors
items.text:
status is an observable read-only property: Status { state, tec, rec, last_error, last_data_error }, state being Stopped, Active, Warning, Passive, BusOff or Sleeping. The device sends it to observers when the state changes:

let mut status = node.can().observe_status().await?;
while let Ok(s) = status.recv().await {
    if s.state == ErrorState::BusOff { node.can().recover().call().await?; }
}

Methods return CanError: CommonError as Common (unsupported, invalid argument, in use, wrong state, ...), plus OutOfFilters { max } (fall back to fewer or wider filters), OutOfMemory { available } (a smaller layout or schedule) and BusOff (recover first). Each method lists what it returns with #[errors(..)]. Errors on the bus are not errors of a call: they are counted in Status and reported one by one on bus_errors.

items.title: Tests
items.text: tests/io_can runs two mock nodes end to end through the real host event loop: a full node with every optional item (internal loopback through the filters, TX events with markers and queue times, bus-off and recovery, explicit modes and configuration steps, raw protocol status, timing detection, bus load, sleep and wake-up, transceiver, buffers, terminator, test pins) and a minimal node with all of them left out. tests/io_can_group runs a group of two controllers (clock selection, enable / disable, independent interfaces), time-triggered operation and CAN XL frames.

items.title: More
items.text: The ww_can_bus reference has every item of Can and which controllers have what, controller groups (CanGroup), CAN XL, the debugger items, what the device measures, sleep and the transceiver, filters and message memory, and time-triggered CAN.

items.title: ww_can_bus reference
items.text: Everything of ww_can_bus beyond the common case: every item of Can, controller groups, CAN XL, the items for bus debuggers, filters and message memory, and time-triggered CAN.

items.title: Can
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Can {
    fn capabilities() -> Capabilities<'i>;
    fn configure(config: CanConfig) -> Result<CanConfig, CanError<'i>>;
    fn config() -> CanConfig;
    property!(ro status: Status);
    #[counted]
    stream!(rx: RxFrame<'i>);
    #[credit]
    sink!(tx: TxFrame<'i>);

    #[optional] fn set_mode(mode: Mode) -> Result<Mode, CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional] fn recover() -> Result<(), CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional] fn tx_abort() -> u32;
    #[optional] #[counted] stream!(tx_events: TxEvent);
    #[optional] #[counted] stream!(bus_errors: BusError);
    #[optional] fn protocol_status() -> ProtocolStatus;
    #[optional] property!(ro bus_load: BusLoad);
    #[optional] fn detect_timing(candidates: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Timing>, 16>, per_candidate: Second)
        -> Result<Option<CanConfig>, CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional(filters)] fn set_filters(filters: FilterConfig<'i>) -> Result<(), CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional] fn set_layout(layout: MemoryLayout) -> Result<MemoryLayout, CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional(rx_buffers)] fn rx_buffer(index: u16) -> Result<Option<BufferedFrame<'i>>, CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional(tx_buffers)] fn tx_buffer(index: u16, frame: Option<TxFrame<'i>>, period: Option<Second>)
        -> Result<(), CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional(transceiver)] fn set_transceiver(mode: TransceiverMode) -> Result<TransceiverMode, CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional(transceiver)] property!(ro transceiver_state: TransceiverState);
    #[optional(terminator)] fn set_termination(termination: Termination) -> Result<Termination, CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional(terminator)] property!(ro termination: Termination);
    #[optional] fn test_pins(tx: TxPin) -> Result<BusLevel, CanError<'i>>;
}
Item Required What it is for capabilities() ✓ Controller clock, bit timing limits, FD and TDC, modes and options, FIFO / buffer / filter counts, memory, timestamps, transceiver modes, terminator values configure(CanConfig) ✓ Mode, nominal and data bit timing, TDC, options and bus-off recovery in one call, answered with what was set config() ✓ The configuration in effect, for a host attaching to a running node status ✓ Error state, TEC / REC and the last protocol errors; observable, so a bus-off or a wake-up reaches the host without polling rx ✓ Received frames, a counted stream (unit: frame) with the receive time in the head tx ✓ Frames to send, a credit sink: the host never overruns the device's TX queue set_mode Switch the mode alone, keeping timing, filters and layout (see Debuggers) recover() Start the bus-off recovery on request tx_abort() Drop every frame queued and not on the bus yet tx_events When each sent frame went on the bus, with its marker and how long it waited, or why it didn't bus_errors Every error detected on the bus: kind, phase, direction protocol_status() The controller's raw protocol state bus_load Bus load the device measures, sent once per window detect_timing Find the bit timing of a running bus set_filters (filters) Acceptance filters: exact ID, mask or range, into a FIFO (optionally high priority), a dedicated buffer, or rejected set_layout Divide the message memory between filters, FIFOs, buffers and TX events rx_buffer (rx_buffers) The latest frame of a dedicated RX buffer, without streaming every frame tx_buffer (tx_buffers) A dedicated TX buffer: send once, or cyclically every period by the device set_transceiver, transceiver_state (transceiver) Transceiver standby / silent / sleep, bus wiring faults set_termination, termination (terminator) A switchable terminator (relay, MOSFET) test_pins Production test: drive TX, read RX

Which controllers have what:

bxCAN M_CAN (STM32 FDCAN) MCP2518FD ESP32 TWAI SocketCAN gs_usb / candleLight CAN FD – ✓ ✓ – ✓ ✓ tx_events – TX event FIFO TEF – own-message echo echo frames bus_errors LEC PEA / PED, LEC diagnostics error capture error frames BERR protocol_status ESR PSR, ECR TREC, BDIAG status, error capture state, berr-counter GET_STATE set_filters filter banks std / ext elements 32 filters one mask socket filters – set_layout – message RAM (full M_CAN) FIFO RAM – – – rx_buffer – dedicated RX buffers (full M_CAN) FIFO of depth 1 – – – tx_buffer mailboxes dedicated TX buffers FIFOs – BCM – recover without ABOM INIT – initiate_recovery restart reset Mode::Sleep sleep clock stop sleep – – – transceiver, terminator board board board board termination TERMINATION CanTimeTriggered TTCM (timestamps only) TTCAN (FDCAN1 of an H7) – – – –

items.title: CanGroup
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait CanGroup {
    ww_impl!(interface[]: Can);
    fn group_capabilities() -> GroupCapabilities<'i>;
    fn enable() -> Result<GroupClock, CanError<'i>>;
    fn disable() -> Result<(), CanError<'i>>;
    property!(ro group_state: GroupState);
    #[optional(clock)] fn set_clock(clock: GroupClock) -> Result<GroupClock, CanError<'i>>;
    #[optional] fn performance() -> Performance;
}

On STM32 every FDCAN instance hangs off one kernel clock and one message RAM: none can be clocked, powered down or re-laid out alone. CanGroup is that hardware. The group starts disabled (clock off, its lowest power state); enable() clocks it with the source and frequency set last (or the device's default) and answers the clock in effect, then each interface[i] is configured on its own. disable() needs every controller in Mode::Off.

Advanced nodes pick the clock to hit an exact bit timing: set_clock(GroupClock { source, frequency }) while disabled, from GroupCapabilities::clock_sources (name and frequency range of each), answered with the nearest frequency the dividers reach. The controllers then report that clock in Capabilities::clock and count their time quanta in it. A bridge leaves set_clock out and runs on the default. A standalone controller with its own oscillator choice (MCP2518FD) is a group of one.

performance() is what the group guarantees together (frames and bytes per second passed on without loss): a device whose controllers share a CPU or a link to the host knows it, the host can't.

A device that mirrors its hardware puts a group into its API instead of single controllers, with the time-triggered and XL parts next to it as arrays indexed like the controllers (valid only at indices that have the hardware):

#[ww_api_root]
trait Analyzer {
    ww_impl!(can: ww_can_bus::CanGroup);                 // can.interface[i]
    ww_impl!(can_tt[]: ww_can_bus::CanTimeTriggered);    // can_tt[i] is controller i
    ww_impl!(can_xl[]: ww_can_bus::CanXl);               // can_xl[i] is controller i
}

items.title: CAN XL
items.text:
CAN XL frames carry up to 2048 bytes, and a credit sink sizes the device's buffer for its largest item. So they are not part of Frame but of CanXl, behind the xl cargo feature: devices without XL neither reserve 2 KiB buffers nor carry the types.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait CanXl {
    fn configure_xl(config: Option<XlConfig>) -> Result<Option<XlConfig>, CanError<'i>>;
    #[counted] stream!(rx_xl: XlFrame<'i>);
    #[credit] sink!(tx_xl: XlTxFrame<'i>);
}

XlFrame has the 11-bit priority ID, VCID, SDU type, SEC, acceptance field and 1-2048 data bytes. XlConfig sets the XL data phase timing, TDC, PWM symbols for transceiver mode switching (CAN SIC XL) and data phase error signalling; it needs CAN FD configured on the controller. A device sending full-size XL frames takes WireWeaver messages of at least 2.1 KiB.

items.title: Debuggers
items.text:
configure sets a node up in one call. A bus debugger keeps every step in hand:

  • set_mode switches the mode alone, keeping bit timing, filters and layout: Mode::Config to stay off the bus (TX recessive) for configuration-only steps, then Restricted, ListenOnly, a loopback, Test, Sleep or back to Normal. Items that need configuration mode (set_layout, set_filters on most controllers, CanTimeTriggered::configure_tt) switch through it and back by themselves, and stay in it when called there.
  • protocol_status() reads the controller's raw protocol state: activity (synchronizing, idle, receiving, transmitting), the counters, its error logging counter, last error codes of both phases, flags of the last received FD frame, protocol exceptions, the measured transceiver delay and message memory ECC errors. Reading resets what the controller resets on a read.
  • bus_errors reports every error with kind, phase and direction; test_pins drives TX and reads RX.
  • Raw register access is not part of this crate: a device that offers it implements ww_memory next to it.
let can = dev.can().interface(0);
can.set_mode(Mode::Config).call().await?;
can.set_layout(MemoryLayout { standard_filters: 64, ..layout }).call().await?;
can.set_filters(filters).call().await?;
can.set_mode(Mode::ListenOnly).call().await?;
let ps = can.protocol_status().call().await?;

items.title: Measured on the device
items.text:
What the device sees better than the host is measured there:

  • receive, TX event and bus error times (stream heads, see Time);
  • TxEvent::queued: how long a frame waited from the device accepting it to its start of frame (queue, arbitration, retransmissions);
  • bus_load: busy time of the bus per window, frames and error frames, sent to observers once per window;
  • ProtocolStatus::tdc_value: the transceiver loop delay the controller measured;
  • detect_timing(candidates, per_candidate): listens without acknowledging at each candidate timing and answers the first one a frame came in at without errors, leaving the controller configured with it in ListenOnly.

items.title: Sleep and the transceiver
items.text: Mode::Sleep puts the controller to sleep; with Options::wake_on_bus bus activity wakes it, back in the mode it was in, and status goes from Sleeping to Active. The transceiver is switched separately (set_transceiver: Standby, Silent, Sleep); its transceiver_state property reports wiring faults (CAN_H / CAN_L open or shorted, dominant timeout, over temperature) as they appear.

items.title: Filters, memory and dedicated buffers
items.text:
node.can().set_filters(FilterConfigOwned {
    filters: MaxLen::new(vec![
        Filter { matching: FilterMatch::Exact(CanId::standard(0x100).unwrap()), action: FilterAction::Buffer(2) },
        Filter {
            matching: FilterMatch::Range { from: CanId::standard(0x200).unwrap(), to: CanId::standard(0x20F).unwrap() },
            action: FilterAction::Fifo { fifo: 0, high_priority: false },
        },
    ])?,
    non_matching_standard: NonMatching::Reject,
    non_matching_extended: NonMatching::Accept { fifo: 1 },
    reject_remote: false,
}).call().await?;
let latest = node.can().rx_buffer(2).call().await?; // the last 0x100 frame, if one came

The first matching filter wins. A device maps the list to its hardware (filter banks, elements, masks) and answers OutOfFilters or Unsupported (a range on a mask-only controller) when it can't. On controllers with a configurable message memory (Capabilities::memory, in 32-bit words), set_layout sets how many filters, FIFO and buffer elements and TX events it holds and how many data bytes an element takes; controllers of a group share the memory, so a layout that doesn't fit next to the others is OutOfMemory. tx_buffer(index, Some(frame), Some(period)) makes the device send a frame cyclically (a heartbeat) until the buffer is written again or cleared with None.

items.title: Time-triggered CAN
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait CanTimeTriggered {
    fn configure_tt(config: Option<TtConfig>) -> Result<Option<TtConfig>, CanError<'i>>;
    fn set_schedule(triggers: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Trigger>, MAX_TRIGGERS>) -> Result<(), CanError<'i>>;
    property!(ro tt_status: TtStatus);
}

TtConfig sets the ISO 11898-4 level, the role (slave, or potential time master with a priority), the reference message ID, the matrix cycle length and the network time unit; the controller must be in Mode::Config or Mode::Off. The schedule is a sorted list of triggers (time mark, cycle repeat and offset, and what to do: send the reference message, send a TX buffer exclusively or in a merged arbitrating window, check a reception, watch, end of list), bounded by the trigger memory (OutOfMemory). tt_status reports synchronization, master role, the basic cycle and the error level.

items.title: ww_client_server
items.text:
ww_client_server is the wire protocol every generated server and client speaks underneath a device's own API - "an API for an API", or a meta-API: a Request/Event pair that addresses a resource (by path or by trait), carries a method's serialized arguments or return value as opaque bytes, and leaves what those bytes mean to the API-specific codegen built on top. It is no_std by default (std is the crate default; disable it on firmware with default-features = false) and is mostly consumed by ww_codegen!-generated code rather than directly, though some types (StreamCursor, SinkCredit, the max_len helpers) are meant for user code too. Add it with:

[dependencies]
ww_client_server = { version = "0.2", default-features = false }

items.title: Request and Event
items.text:
• Request<'i> - seq: UVlq32Backfill (request id, 0 = no answer expected), path_kind: PathKind<'i>, kind: RequestKind<'i>. Request::set_seq/peek_seq fill in or read seq in an already-serialized buffer without touching the rest, since a client picks the id only right before sending.
  • PathKind<'i> - how a resource is addressed, one of three ways: Absolute { path } (a plain index path, smallest on the wire), GlobalCompact { gid: CompactVersion, path_from_trait } (a global trait id, for traits used often enough to have one assigned), GlobalFull { gid: FullVersion, trait_name, path_from_trait } (any crates.io trait, by crate name and version - biggest, since it carries the name as a string). A server honors a global path wherever the matching trait sits in its API tree (API-20), after checking its own version is protocol-compatible (FullVersion::is_protocol_compatible) - what makes a global path work across API versions, e.g. for firmware update or device info calls.
  • RequestKind<'i> - the operation: Call { args } / MultiCall (same method over an array or several methods at once), Read / MultiRead, Write { data } / MultiWrite, StreamSideband { sideband }, Introspect (send the ww_self::ApiBundle of the addressed resource), StreamOpen { resume, args } (open a counted or reliable stream, optionally resuming a StreamCursor), Observe { cfg } (how a trait level's properties are sent, see below and Observing properties). Arguments and written values travel as TailBytes<'i> - already ShrinkWrap-serialized by the generated code on either end, opaque to this crate.
  • MultiIndex<'i> / MultiArgs<'i> - which resources a multi-request covers (Range, List, or Mask32) and whether every one gets the same serialized arguments (MultiArgs::Same) or each its own (MultiArgs::Different) - see Multi requests for the full request/reply shape.
  • Event<'i> - seq: UVlq32 (echoes the request's, 0 for unsolicited stream/property updates), result: Result<EventKind<'i>, Error<'i>>.
  • EventKind<'i> - Value { data } (a call's or read's return value), Written, StreamData { path, data } (plain stream/property update), StreamSideband { path, sideband }, StreamItem { path, head: StreamHead, data } (one event of a counted/reliable stream, see below), PropertyUpdate { path, t, missed, data } (observed properties of one trait level, see below).
  • Error<'i> / ErrorKind<'i> - err_seq (the site in the generated server that raised it, numbered the same in every server: see err_seq and where an error came from) plus a kind: path/argument/property deserialization failures, Unimplemented (an optional item the device leaves out), TraitNotFound (a global path to a trait the device doesn't implement in a compatible version), UserBytes/UserStr (an API's own error, forwarded verbatim), stream session errors, and more.

A Request is as small as 3 bytes (seq ≤ 127, an empty Absolute path - a root call with no arguments) once set_seq has filled in the real seq; a GlobalCompact call adds about 2 bytes for its CompactVersion when every number in it is ≤ 7.

items.title: Building an Event/Error while writing its payload
items.text: Generated server code often doesn't know yet which EventKind/ErrorKind variant it's building until the payload is already (partly) written - a call might succeed or fail partway through serializing its answer. EventBuilder, EventKindBuilder and ErrorBuilder (builder module) use BufWriter::save_state/ restore_state to reserve space for a result flag / discriminant up front and patch it in afterwards, the same discriminant-patching trick used elsewhere in the wire format - the crate's own tests check the result is byte-for-byte identical to building the value up front and calling .to_ww_bytes().

items.title: Counted and reliable streams
items.text:
• StreamHead - per-event head of an EventKind::StreamItem: pos/units (where the event's units sit in the stream, up to MAX_POS = 2⁵⁷-1), lost (units the device dropped right before it), t: Option<Second> (device time), ext: Option<HeadExt> (rare markers, evolvable). end()/after_previous()/lost_units() are small helpers over these positions. See stream protocol for how a host turns a sequence of heads into "what did I just lose".
  • StreamCursor - session / pos: a point in a stream session, kept by the host and passed back in RequestKind::StreamOpen to resume after a reconnect.
  • StreamOpened<'i> - the answer to StreamOpen: the (possibly new) session, oldest position the device still has, live_from (where the live run starts), resume_from (where backfill starts, None without one), and result (the stream function's own serialized return value).

items.title: Observing properties
items.text:
The observe module (API-38) is the protocol for sending a trait level's properties at the rates a host asks for, any subset of them in one event. A level is one trait (the root API or a ww_impl! trait), addressed by its path; its properties are named by their resource index within the level, as in the introspection data. Only properties declared with +observe can be observed. See Observing properties for the device/host APIs built on this protocol and the full wire-format picture; this section is the raw types.

  • ObserveRequest<'i> - body of RequestKind::Observe: entries (an ObserveEntry { index, mode } per property), patch (true: properties not listed keep their setting; false: they are Off) and budget (bytes per second the level's updates may take on the link, None leaves it to the device).
  • ObserveMode - Off, OnChange { min_us } (on a change, at most every min_us), Periodic { every_us }, OnChangeOrBeat { min_us, max_us } (on a change, and at least every max_us). Periods are in microseconds. Evolvable: a mode from a newer host reads as Unknown(_) and is refused.
  • ObserveGranted<'i> - the answer, in an EventKind::Value: every property observed now with its mode as clamped by the device, the refused entries with an ObserveRefusal (NoSuchIndex, NotObservable, ModeNotSupported, Duplicate), and the granted budget.
  • EventKind::PropertyUpdate { path, t, missed, data } - one level's update: device time t, missed (sends that were due but didn't fit the budget since the previous update) and data, one slot per resource index with the properties sent this time present. ser_property_update_event writes it with the data in place. Without t and missed, the event costs 4 bytes plus its data for a level one deep.

Old hosts never send Observe, so they never receive a PropertyUpdate. A device without observe support answers Observe with OperationNotSupported.

items.title: Credit sinks
items.text: A #[credit] sink!(..) (credit sinks) uses the messages of reliable streams the other way round: the host opens its session with RequestKind::StreamOpen { resume: Some(cursor) } (answered with stream::StreamOpened, whose capacity is the sink's buffer), writes with RequestKind::SinkWrite { pos, data } (one unit) or SinkWriteUnits { units, pos, data } (build both with RequestKind::sink_write(units, pos, data), read them with as_sink_write()), and the device answers with StreamSideband::Ack, Resend and Query. A read of the sink returns its stream::StreamStatus. The state machines, SinkCredit on the device and SinkTx on the host, are in ww_stream::sink (stream protocol).

items.title: Worst-case message sizes (max_len module)
items.text: call_request/call_request_compact/value_event compute the upper bound in bytes of a Request/Event for a given resource path and argument/return MaxSize (SW-19) - None when something in them is unbounded. This is what backs the generated <METHOD>_REQUEST_MAX_LEN/<METHOD>_RESPONSE_MAX_LEN consts (API-18), used to size fixed buffers ahead of time.

items.title: On the wire
items.text: PathKind, RequestKind and EventKind are all final_structure with a ww_repr = nib discriminant - one nibble to say what kind of request or event this is, no reverse-length for the enum itself since it's always the outermost or last-written thing. StreamSideband and ErrorKind similarly pick discriminant widths (nib, u8) sized to how many variants they have and how often each is used. FULL_VERSION/COMPACT_VERSION (the protocol's own version, built with wire_weaver::full_version!() the same way every #[ww_trait] is) are exchanged and checked during link setup with a remote device, independently of any user API's own version.

items.title: ww_counters
items.text:
ww_counters carries a device's cnt counters over WireWeaver: the same counters cnt read and cnt tui show through a debug probe, now over USB, UDP or any other link, with the same views (ww counters).

cnt counts into two buffers of 32-bit words: RAM (zeroed at boot) and backup (in memory that survives a reset). A u64 counter is two words, low first. A counter's word index is assigned by the linker, and what each word is (name, group, type, unit, severity, source location) is in symbol names of the firmware's ELF only: it exists after the link, so it can't be compiled into the same image. So the device sends raw words and the host decodes them with the ELF (cnt_core), exactly as over a probe. The ELF is found by the firmware's build id.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Counters {
    const INFO: CountersInfo<'i>;
    #[errors(Common(InvalidArgument, Unsupported))]
    fn read(buffer: CounterBuffer, offset: u16) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, UVlq32>, 64>, CountersError<'i>>;
    #[errors(Common(Unsupported))]
    fn reset(buffer: CounterBuffer) -> Result<(), CountersError<'i>>;
    #[optional]
    #[stream(CounterChanges<'i>, counted)]
    fn watch(period: Second) -> Result<Second, CountersError<'i>>;
}
  • INFO - a const item: the cnt format version (cnt::SIGNATURE_VERSION, 2 today), ram and backup (None without one) as BufferInfo { used_words, capacity_words }, and the build_id (the same as FirmwareInfo::BUILD_ID, empty without the note). All are fixed at link time, so a server provides it as a fn (const_model = "INFO=fn").
  • read(buffer, offset) - words of Ram or Backup from word offset, at most 64, never past the used words (empty at the end). Words are UVlq32: a counter at 0 costs one byte, so a 64-word buffer of mostly small counters is one call of about 80 bytes. Common(Unsupported) for the backup buffer of a device without one, Common(InvalidArgument) for an offset past the used words.
  • reset(buffer) - zero a buffer.
  • watch(period) - optional and not served by anything yet: changed words every period, for slow links where polling read costs too much. Leave it out with omit = ["counters.watch"].

items.title: Serving the counters
items.text:
The helpers in ww_counters serve read and reset from cnt's buffers. read_words copies one page of atomics into a 64-word scratch in the server struct (256 bytes) at once, so a page is one snapshot. For counters: ww_counters::Counters in the API root Device:

pub struct Server {
    scratch: [UVlq32; ww_counters::MAX_WORDS],
    // ..
}

impl api_impl::DeviceConsts for Server {
    fn counters_info(&self) -> CountersInfo<'_> {
        CountersInfo {
            format: cnt::SIGNATURE_VERSION,
            ram: BufferInfo::new(cnt::ram_used_words(), cnt::counters_ram_buffer()),
            backup: None, // Some(BufferInfo::new(cnt::bkp_used_words(), cnt::counters_bkp_buffer()))
            build_id: MaxLen::new_unchecked(RefVec::new_bytes(ww_firmware_info::build_id())),
        }
    }
}

impl Server {
    fn counters_read(
        &mut self,
        _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
        buffer: CounterBuffer,
        offset: u16,
    ) -> RpcResult<Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'_, UVlq32>, 64>, CountersError<'_>>> {
        RpcResult::Ready(match buffer {
            CounterBuffer::Ram => {
                read_words(cnt::counters_ram_buffer(), cnt::ram_used_words(), offset, &mut self.scratch)
            }
            CounterBuffer::Backup => Err(CountersError::unsupported()),
        })
    }

    fn counters_reset(
        &mut self,
        _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
        buffer: CounterBuffer,
    ) -> RpcResult<Result<(), CountersError<'_>>> {
        match buffer {
            CounterBuffer::Ram => reset_words(cnt::counters_ram_buffer()),
            CounterBuffer::Backup => return RpcResult::Ready(Err(CountersError::unsupported())),
        }
        RpcResult::Ready(Ok(()))
    }
}

mod api_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        device_api :: Device for super::Server,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = false,
        const_model = "INFO=fn",
        omit = ["counters.watch"],
    );
}

cnt::ram_used_words(), cnt::bkp_used_words() and cnt::SIGNATURE_VERSION are new in cnt 0.5. The build id needs the note in flash, see build id; tests/counters has a complete server.

items.title: On the host
items.text:
$ ww counters tui --serial 4B333720
Using ELF target/thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf/release/usb_io_fw

ww counters reads INFO, finds the ELF with the device's build id and shows the counters with the views of cnt (crate cnt_view): read (default), watch, tui, reset, info, --format json|jsonl. It works with any device implementing Counters anywhere in its API, through a global trait path.

The ELF is looked up in this order (cnt_core::elf):

  1. --elf PATH: used, and refused if its build id differs from the device's (--force to use it anyway);
  2. <build id>.elf in the directories of WW_ELF_PATH, then in the ELF directory ~/.cache/ww/elf;
  3. the binaries under the cargo project's target/ (when run inside the firmware's project).

cnt elf add <ELF or release archive> fills the ELF directory: a single ELF, or a firmware release's <firmware>-<version>-elf.tar.zst with every ELF of the release, each stored under its build id. A device without a build id gets the newest ELF under target/, with a warning that it can't be checked. INFO's used words are checked against the ELF as well: an ELF that needs more words than the device uses is other firmware.

A u64 counter can tear between its two words (a carry between reading them). The host reads a u64 counter again when its high word changed or its value went down since the last read, until its high word reads the same twice.

cnt over a probe does the same check: it reads the build id note from the target's flash and refuses an ELF of other firmware, so neither path decodes words with the wrong names any more.

From code, ww_counters::host::WwSource (feature host) is a cnt_core::Source over a CountersDevice, the two calls on a generated client; cnt_core::Counters::read / read_changes decode, cnt_view shows.

items.title: Evolution
items.text: CounterBuffer is no_future_version (cnt has these two buffers); CountersInfo, BufferInfo and CounterChanges are evolvable structs, CountersError an evolvable enum with the Common errors. A new cnt buffer layout bumps cnt::SIGNATURE_VERSION, which INFO.format carries: the host refuses a format it doesn't read.

items.title: ww_date_time
items.text:
ww_date_time gives device APIs a compact ISO 8601 date and time, nibble-packed instead of a fixed-width timestamp: DateTime, built from a NaiveDate, a NaiveTime, and an optional Timezone. It is no_std by default and depends only on shrink_wrap; an optional chrono feature adds conversions to and from the chrono crate's own date/time types for host-side code.

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_date_time = "0.1"

items.title: Types
items.text:
• DateTime - date: NaiveDate, time: NaiveTime, timezone: Timezone; self_describing.
  • NaiveDate - an ISO 8601 calendar date without timezone: year: Year, month: U4 (1-12), day: U5 (1-31); self_describing.
  • Year - a signed year, -262_142..=262_141, stored as a UNib32 shifted by 2025 so that years close to now take the fewest nibbles; a year before 2025 is masked into the low 19 bits instead, so it always costs the same extra nibbles regardless of how far back it is (see sizes below). Year::new constructs one (bounds-checked), Year::year() reads it back as i32.
  • NaiveTime - an ISO 8601 time without timezone: secs: U17 (seconds since midnight, 0-86399), frac: Option<U31> (sub-second part in nanoseconds, omitted entirely when zero); self_describing.
  • Timezone - UTC (preferred, costs only 1 bit) or Other(OtherTimezone); self_describing, ww_repr = u1.
  • OtherTimezone - Naive (no timezone information at all) or FixedOffset { secs: I18 } (offset from UTC in seconds); self_describing, ww_repr = u3 leaves room to add up to 6 more kinds later without breaking compatibility.

All of the above derive Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash (Timezone/OtherTimezone also Debug), and get owned (*Owned) counterparts when the std feature is enabled.

items.title: Sizes on the wire
items.text:
DateTime's size depends on how far the year is from 2025 and on which fields are present, since Year, the Option<U31> fraction and the Timezone enum are all self-describing rather than fixed-width:

Year range UTC, no nanoseconds naive/fixed-offset, no nanoseconds UTC, with nanoseconds naive/fixed-offset, with nanoseconds 2025-2032 32 bits (minimum) 53 bits 63 bits 84 bits (maximum) 2033-2088 and so on +4 bits per range +4 bits per range +4 bits per range +4 bits per range before 2025 +24 bits +24 bits +24 bits +24 bits

NaiveDate alone is 13 bits minimum (2025-2032), 17 bits for 2033-2088, and up to 37 bits for the widest years. NaiveTime alone is 18 bits without a fractional part, 49 bits with one.

A real DateTime for 2025-05-30 16:20:00 UTC (no fractional seconds) serializes to exactly 4 bytes (05 F3 96 C0), matching the 32-bit minimum above - ww_date_time's own test suite checks this against a real ser_shrink_wrap() call.

items.title: Construction
items.text:
use ww_date_time::{DateTime, Timezone};

let utc = DateTime::from_ymd_hms_utc_opt(2025, 5, 30, 14, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();
assert_eq!(utc.timezone, Timezone::UTC);

let naive = DateTime::from_ymd_hms_naive_opt(2025, 5, 30, 14, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();

from_ymd_hms_utc_opt is a const fn (so it can build a DateTime in a const item, e.g. a compile-time build timestamp), from_ymd_hms_naive_opt is not, since it always picks Timezone::Other(OtherTimezone::Naive). Both return None on an out-of-range month, day, hour, minute, second or nanosecond, same as NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt and NaiveTime::from_hms_opt they build on.

Debug is implemented by hand for compact, human-readable output rather than deriving it: a NaiveDate prints as 2025-M5-D30, a NaiveTime as 14:0:0 (.123 appended when a fractional part is present), and DateTime as the two joined with the timezone.

items.title: chrono interop
items.text: With the chrono feature (on by default), ww_date_time re-exports the chrono crate and adds From/Into conversions in both directions: chrono::NaiveDate ↔ NaiveDate, chrono::NaiveTime ↔ NaiveTime, chrono::NaiveDateTime ↔ DateTime (as Timezone::Other(OtherTimezone::Naive)), and chrono::DateTime<Utc> / chrono::DateTime<FixedOffset> → DateTime. This is what lets host-side code build a DateTime from chrono::Utc::now() without touching the wire representation directly.

items.title: Features
items.text: Feature What std (default) owned (*Owned) type variants, via shrink_wrap/std chrono (default) the chrono interop above defmt defmt::Format on the borrowed types, via shrink_wrap/defmt

items.title: ww_dfu: firmware updates
items.text: ww_dfu is the firmware update API every WireWeaver device shares: a handful of small traits a node picks from, and eight ways to put them together, depending on how much flash the device has, who receives the update and how fast the link is. The docs are organized by those eight scenarios. Read the overview on this page, pick your scenario with the questions below, then read only its section, on the A/B or the one-slot page: each one is complete on its own, with the flash layout, the flow, what happens on a power cut, and the real exchange recorded from its test.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
An update is a plan: a header (which image it produces, for which flash geometry, signed) and a list of steps that turn what the device holds into the new image:

  • ERASE an erase block,
  • COPY a chunk the device already has (a delta: unchanged code is not sent again),
  • WRITE a chunk whose data comes with the step.

A plain full image is a plan made only of ERASE and WRITE, so a node that doesn't do deltas implements the same traits and simply never sees a COPY. The plan, manifest and descriptor are records of the chunky protocol, defined in octets by its SPEC.md (a draft) and implemented by chunky_format; ww_dfu only carries them, as raw bytes. See the other side: chunky.

Trait What it is for Implemented by UpdateNode Who this node is, its versions and state, and which of the other traits it offers. every node BootControl Boot state, confirm, revert, reboot into the app or the updater. every node Inventory What the node holds now, chunk by chunk (the manifest the host plans against). the node that receives the plan Stage Receive a plan step by step, apply or store it, finish it; session control. the node that receives the plan StageBulk Receive a whole plan as one stream on a credit sink, one acknowledgement at the end. the node that receives the plan on a slow link

A host always starts with UpdateNode::node: one call tells it the profile, versions, boot state, the manifest digest and which traits are there (Offers). On a slow link that is often the only call before the update.

items.title: The scenarios
items.text:
Each scenario has a code, <slots><switch>-<receiver>-<delivery>, and a two-word name:

  • slots and switch: 2C two slots, the bootloader copies the new image into place; 2R two slots, the hardware remaps the boot address; 1S one slot, the plan is stored and applied by the bootloader; 1L one slot, applied live by an updater.
  • receiver: APP the running application receives the plan; UPD an updater does (a bootloader with a transport, or a recovery app).
  • delivery: STEP one call per step (Stage); BULK the whole plan as one stream (StageBulk).
  • name: the mode (Swap, Flip, Parcel, Pit stop) and the delivery (Shuttle: back and forth for every step; Freight: one load, one receipt).
Code Name Flash Receives Delivery Bootloader transport Downtime Revert Test link 2C-APP-STEP Swap Shuttle A/B, bootloader copies app step by step none one slot copy at reboot yes USB 64 B 2C-APP-BULK Swap Freight A/B, bootloader copies app bulk none one slot copy at reboot yes UDP 2R-APP-STEP Flip Shuttle A/B, hardware remap app step by step none a reboot yes WebSocket 2R-APP-BULK Flip Freight A/B, hardware remap app bulk none a reboot yes USB 512 B 1S-APP-STEP Parcel Shuttle one slot + plan area app step by step none applying the plan no USB 64 B 1S-APP-BULK Parcel Freight one slot + plan area app bulk none applying the plan no UDP 1L-UPD-STEP Pit-stop Shuttle one slot updater step by step yes (or recovery app) download and apply no USB 64 B 1L-UPD-BULK Pit-stop Freight one slot updater bulk yes (or recovery app) download and apply no WebSocket

The other combinations make no sense, which is why they have no code:

  • A/B with a stored plan (2x + Stored): the inactive slot already is the place to put the update; storing a plan to apply it in place later costs a plan area and gives up the revert. An A/B node answers Error::Unsupported (StageLimits::stored is false).
  • A/B received by an updater (2x-UPD): the app can write the inactive slot while it runs; rebooting into an updater only adds downtime and a second transport.
  • One slot, live, received by the app (1L-APP): the app would overwrite the code it runs from. An app that copies itself to RAM to do this is an updater.
  • One slot, stored, received by an updater (1S-UPD): an updater with a transport can apply live, and resumes after a power cut just as well; storing first only costs the plan area.
  • Full image is not a scenario of its own: a plan of ERASE and WRITE steps works in all eight. Use it when the host has no manifest for the device (a development build) or the delta isn't smaller. 2R-APP-STEP shows one.
  • Bootloader or recovery app as the updater is not a scenario either: the flow is the same, only NodeInfo::role differs (Bootloader or Recovery).

items.title: Picking yours
items.text:
1. Does the flash hold two images?
    • Yes, and the chip or its boot ROM maps either bank to the boot address (dual-bank flash with bank swap on STM32 H7, G4, L4; RP2350 partition tables; ESP32 OTA partitions; nRF dual bank): 2R (Flip).
    • Yes, but the image always runs from the same address (single-bank parts with embassy-boot, STM32 F1, G0): 2C (Swap).
    • No: go on.
  2. One slot. Must the device keep working during the download, or can't the bootloader have a transport? (A download over LoRa can take hours; a bootloader in 8 KB has no room for USB.)
    • Yes, and there is flash for a plan area as large as the largest plan: 1S (Parcel).
    • No, the bootloader (or a write-protected recovery app) has a transport: 1L (Pit stop).
  3. How long is a round trip?
    • Short (USB, Ethernet, WebSocket on a LAN, RTT): STEP (Shuttle). Errors are named per step, up to StageLimits::in_flight calls can be outstanding.
    • Long or metered (LoRa, LTE-M, satellite, a gateway that stores and forwards): BULK (Freight). The plan flows on a credit sink, never more than the device has room for, one acknowledgement at the end.

items.title: What every scenario shares
items.text:
• The device trusts nothing it receives. It checks every index and offset against its own layout before touching flash (Error::OutOfRange), every COPY source and every WRITE against the hash in its step (Error::SourceMismatch, Error::HashMismatch), the plan header against its geometry, its version floor and the release signature before the first step (Error::WrongGeometry, Error::BelowFloor, Error::BadSignature), and the finished image against the signed descriptor before it is staged (Error::VerifyFailed). Per-chunk hashes are not a trust boundary on their own; the signed descriptor over the whole image is. Chunky's device core refuses what needs no key (magic, format, signature scheme, reserved bytes, image length) on the raw bytes before it verifies the signature, so a junk plan never costs a signature check.
  • A session is identified by its plan header. Stage::begin (or StageBulk::begin_bulk) with the header of an unfinished session does not start over: it answers Session { resumed: true, resume_from } and the host continues from there.
  • Step order. A step ahead of its turn is Error::OutOfOrder(expected); a step the node already has is accepted again and skipped (its reply was lost), so resending is always harmless.
  • Reboots. BootControl::reboot answers before the reset; the host then reconnects to the same device (USB serial number, IP address) and finds whatever firmware answers there. When the updater is a boot ROM that doesn't speak WireWeaver (RP2350 BOOTSEL), see Following a reboot.

items.title: More
items.text:
• A/B scenarios: 2C (Swap) and 2R (Flip), step by step and bulk.
  • One-slot scenarios: 1S (Parcel) and 1L (Pit stop), step by step and bulk.
  • Transcripts and chunky: how the recorded exchanges are made and checked, and the chunky records (descriptor, plan, manifest) ww_dfu carries.
  • The code of the API itself: ww_stdlib/ww_dfu/src/lib.rs.

items.title: ww_dfu: A/B scenarios
items.text: The four ww_dfu scenarios for a flash that holds two images: the update goes into the inactive slot while the app keeps running, and an image that doesn't confirm itself is reverted at the next reset. 2C (Swap) when the bootloader copies the new image into place, 2R (Flip) when the hardware or boot ROM remaps the boot address. Picking yours says which one fits; each section below is complete on its own.

items.title: 2C-APP-STEP: Swap Shuttle
items.text:
A/B with a copying bootloader; the running app receives the plan one call per step over a fast link.

Setup. Two slots of the same size; the image always runs from the active one, and the bootloader copies the new image into place at the next reset, page by page through a swap page, so a cut during the copy resumes (embassy-boot on STM32 F1, G0 and other single-bank parts).

| bootloader (no transport) | ACTIVE slot: runs here | DFU slot: the update goes here | swap / state pages |

The app implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Inventory and Stage (Profile::AB(SlotSwitch::Copy)). The bootloader has no transport.

Choose it when the flash holds two images, the part can't remap banks, and the link answers within milliseconds (USB, Ethernet, a LAN). The device keeps running during the whole download.

Flow.

  1. UpdateNode::node: profile, version, boot state, manifest digest. A known digest means the host knows every chunk and can plan a delta; otherwise it reads Inventory::chunks.
  2. Stage::limits: max_piece (chunks larger than this come in pieces), in_flight.
  3. Stage::begin(Target::Live, header): every check that can be made before writing (format, geometry, version floor, signature, boot state).
  4. Stage::erase / copy / write for every step, into the DFU slot; nothing the app runs from is touched.
  5. Stage::finish: the image in the DFU slot is checked against the signed descriptor and marked Staged.
  6. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the bootloader swaps the slots and starts the new image on trial.
  7. The host reconnects; the new image checks what matters to it and calls BootControl::confirm. Without a confirm, the next reset swaps back (BootState::Reverted).

Failures and power cuts. A lost link or a cut during the download costs only time: the DFU slot is scratch. A cut during the swap is resumed by the bootloader from its swap state. A refused step changes nothing and names why.

Resume. After a lost link, begin with the same header answers resumed: true, resume_from: <next step>. After a reset during the download the session is gone (it lives in RAM); the host starts over.

What the device checks in this scenario: a COPY source hash before copying, each WRITE's chunk hash once all its pieces are in, every index against the slot, and the whole image against the descriptor in finish.

items.title: Transcript
items.text:

items.title: 2C-APP-BULK: Swap Freight
items.text:
A/B with a copying bootloader; the running app receives the whole plan as one stream over a slow link.

Setup. Two slots of the same size; the image always runs from the active one, and the bootloader copies the new image into place at the next reset, page by page through a swap page, so a cut during the copy resumes (embassy-boot on single-bank parts).

| bootloader (no transport) | ACTIVE slot: runs here | DFU slot: the update goes here | swap / state pages |

The app implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Stage and StageBulk (Inventory too if hosts may not know its manifest). The bootloader has no transport.

Choose it when the flash holds two images, the part can't remap banks, and a round trip takes long (LoRa, LTE-M, satellite, a store-and-forward gateway): a call per step would cost more than the delta saves.

Flow.

  1. UpdateNode::node (and Stage::limits for max_piece, unless the host knows the device type).
  2. StageBulk::begin_bulk(Target::Live, header, total_len, ack_every): the checks of Stage::begin; ack_every: 0 asks for one acknowledgement at the end.
  3. The host opens the plan credit sink and sends the plan after its header as PlanSegment { offset, data }. The device grants credit in bytes as it frees its buffer, so the host never sends more than fits; lost segments are sent again from the device's position (go-back-N). The device applies the steps into the DFU slot as they arrive.
  4. When all bytes are in, the device sends PlanAck { have: total_len, status: Complete } on plan_ack.
  5. Stage::finish: checked against the descriptor, Staged.
  6. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the bootloader swaps the slots and starts the new image on trial; the host reconnects and calls BootControl::confirm.

Failures and power cuts. A lost link or a cut during the download costs only time: the DFU slot is scratch. A step that fails ends the session with PlanAck { status: Failed(error) }; a segment that doesn't continue what the device has is answered with BulkStatus::Gap and the position to resend from. A cut during the swap is resumed by the bootloader.

Resume. begin_bulk with the same header answers resumed: true and resume_from in bytes after the header; the host sends from there. The plan sink continues its own session too: a host that saved Sink::cursor() opens it again with plan_resume(cursor), which answers how many segments the device has in it (one unit per segment), so nothing the device already took is sent again and a device that lost the session (a reset) is reported as StreamError::SinkSessionLost: the host starts over. See credit sinks. The transcript shows a host that restarts half way.

What the device checks: each segment's offset against what it has, each step as it completes (COPY source hash, WRITE hash, index ranges), the image against the descriptor in finish.

items.title: 2R-APP-STEP: Flip Shuttle
items.text:
A/B with a hardware remap; the running app receives the plan one call per step over a fast link.

Setup. Two banks or partitions; the hardware or boot ROM maps the chosen one to the address the image runs from, so nothing is copied and the switch is instant (STM32 H7, G4, L4 bank swap; RP2350 partition table with an A/B pair and try-before-you-buy; ESP32 OTA partitions; nRF dual bank).

bank 1: | image A: runs (mapped to the boot address) |
bank 2: | image B: the update goes here              |      boot ROM / option bytes choose the bank

The app implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Inventory and Stage (Profile::AB(SlotSwitch::Remap)).

Choose it when the part can remap its banks and the link answers within milliseconds. The first boot of the new image takes no longer than any other boot, and so does a revert.

Flow.

  1. UpdateNode::node, Stage::limits.
  2. Stage::begin(Target::Live, header).
  3. Stage::erase / copy / write for every step, into the inactive bank.
  4. Stage::finish: checked against the descriptor, Staged.
  5. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the bootloader (or boot ROM) maps the other bank and starts it on trial.
  6. The host reconnects, BootControl::boot_state is Trial; the image calls BootControl::confirm.

Failures and power cuts. Nothing the app runs from is touched until the switch, and the switch is a single write (an option byte, a partition flag), so a cut or a lost link at any point costs nothing but time. An image that doesn't confirm is mapped out again at the next reset.

Resume. After a lost link, begin with the same header continues at resume_from; after a reset the host starts over.

What the device checks: COPY source hashes, WRITE chunk hashes, every index against the bank, the image against the descriptor in finish.

items.title: 2R-APP-BULK: Flip Freight
items.text:
A/B with a hardware remap; the running app receives the whole plan as one stream.

Setup. Two banks or partitions; the hardware or boot ROM maps the chosen one to the boot address, nothing is copied, the switch is instant (dual-bank STM32, RP2350 partitions, ESP32 OTA, nRF dual bank).

bank 1: | image A: runs (mapped to the boot address) |
bank 2: | image B: the update goes here              |      boot ROM / option bytes choose the bank

The app implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Stage and StageBulk (Profile::AB(SlotSwitch::Remap)).

Choose it when the part can remap its banks and round trips are long or metered, or simply when the whole plan should go in one stream (a high-speed link where the host wants to keep the pipe full).

Flow.

  1. UpdateNode::node, Stage::limits.
  2. StageBulk::begin_bulk(Target::Live, header, total_len, ack_every: 0).
  3. The plan after its header on the plan credit sink; the device applies steps into the inactive bank as they complete.
  4. PlanAck { status: Complete } on plan_ack, then Stage::finish: Staged.
  5. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the other bank starts on trial.
  6. The new image confirms with BootControl::confirm, or gives up with BootControl::revert (or never confirms): the next reset maps the previous bank back, BootState::Reverted, LastResult { outcome: Reverted }.

Failures and power cuts. As for any A/B: nothing the app runs from is touched until the switch, a cut costs only time. A failed step ends the session with PlanAck { status: Failed(error) }.

Resume. begin_bulk with the same header answers the byte to continue from.

What the device checks: segment offsets, each completed step (COPY source hash, WRITE hash, ranges), the image against the descriptor in finish.

items.title: ww_dfu: transcripts and chunky
items.text: How the exchanges on the scenario pages are recorded and checked, and the chunky records ww_dfu carries as raw bytes.

items.title: About the transcripts and their tests
items.text:
Every transcript on the scenario pages (A/B, one slot) is recorded by its test in tests/dfu_scenarios (src/scenarios.rs) and checked against the file included there: a test fails when the exchange changes, until just dfu-transcripts writes the new one and the change is looked at. So the bytes here are the bytes the current code sends.

  • Two views. The readable one decodes each ww_link message with the API model of the firmware that runs: method, arguments, result, sink writes (⇐) and stream items (⇒), credit and sideband events, with each message's size and first bytes. The wire view shows every unit of the medium: USB packets, UDP datagrams or WebSocket frames. Both are taken on the device side.
  • Left out: link setup (Nop, GetDeviceInfo, LinkSetup, LinkReady, the WebSocket upgrade), which is the same on every connection and carries crate versions that change with every release, and pings. WebSocket frames from the host are masked with a random key; they are shown unmasked with the key zeroed.
  • The device is a simulation with real firmware logic on a simulated flash: two banks with NOR semantics (programming only clears bits), 8 chunks of 64 bytes, erase blocks of 128 bytes, a plan area, an apply journal, and power cuts injected at a given step. It runs as a task next to the host on one single-threaded runtime, as firmware runs on one core, so every run of a scenario interleaves host and device the same way (over the simulated USB the clock is paused as well, timeouts don't depend on the machine's load). A reset restarts the device task on the same link endpoint, running the bootloader logic first; the host reconnects as it would to a real device. The firmwares are generated ww_dfu servers (tests/dfu_app_api, tests/dfu_lean_app_api, tests/dfu_updater_api).
  • The plan format is a small stand-in for chunky's (a 35-byte header with a toy signature; steps 01 block, 02 dst src hash, 03 dst hash len data), so the step bytes in the transcripts are readable. Hashes are SHA-256 truncated to 8 bytes, as in chunky's format 2. The real records are in The other side: chunky.
  • The links are the real ones from ww_device up: WebSocket and UDP on localhost through wire_weaver_client's ws and udp transports; USB is simulated by wire_weaver_client::in_process::usb_device, which runs the real USB framing on both ends with full-speed (64 B) or high-speed (512 B) packets, but not USB itself (enumeration, data toggles, NAKs). RTT is not used: with a debug probe attached a device is flashed directly, without a bootloader.
  • Changing a scenario's link is one line, const LINK: Link = ... in its test (UART and CAN will join Link).

items.title: The other side: chunky
items.text:
ww_dfu is the transport half of an update. What it carries, and the code that checks and applies it on the device, is chunky (chunky_mcu_updater, public).

  • SPEC.md is the protocol in octets (a draft): the records, the receiver's checks in order, delivery modes, resume and segmentation, with annotated vectors. Its §10 describes this carrier.
  • chunky_format/src/lib.rs defines the records. They are shrink_wrap types with a fixed little endian layout, and the same bytes are read by Rust (with or without BufReader) and by a generated C reader:
    • Descriptor (CKY2): a 64-byte body (product, version, security counter, image length, geometry, SHA-256 of the image) and a 64-byte seal over a domain string and exactly the body's bytes. The scheme is Ed25519, or SHA-256 only for an unsigned build, which a signed device refuses.
    • Plan (CKP2): a 145-byte header (geometry, step count, body length, the descriptor), then the steps. A step is a head_tail enum read through Step::view: ERASE is 3 bytes, COPY 13, WRITE 13 plus one chunk.
    • Manifest (CKM2): a 13-byte header and one entry per chunk, a hash (8 bytes of SHA-256), blank or unreadable.
  • chunky/src/apply.rs is the apply engine: it runs an untrusted plan against the DFU slot over embedded_storage, one step per call, checking the descriptor first, then every COPY source and WRITE hash, then the whole image.

The raw octets are these records: Stage::begin and StageBulk::begin_bulk take the 145 header bytes, Stage::write carries one step's data, and the StageBulk::plan sink carries the body as segments. What a node answers with Error::BadSignature, BelowFloor, WrongGeometry or VerifyFailed is what chunky decides; WrongGeometry is what chunky and the spec call GeometryMismatch.

Status. Chunky does not implement the ww_dfu traits yet (chunky NET-1 is open): it is the device core and the record format that ww_dfu carries, and the server side that exposes them as UpdateNode, Stage and the rest is to come. Until then the exchanges on the scenario pages are recorded with the stand-in plan above.

items.title: ww_dfu: one-slot scenarios
items.text: The four ww_dfu scenarios for a flash that holds only one image: the app is rewritten in place and there is no revert. 1S (Parcel) stores the plan in a plan area while the app runs and lets the bootloader apply it; 1L (Pit stop) reboots into an updater that applies the plan live as it arrives. Picking yours says which one fits; each section below is complete on its own.

items.title: 1S-APP-STEP: Parcel Shuttle
items.text:
One app slot and a plan area; the running app stores the plan, step by step, and the bootloader applies it in place after a reset.

Setup. One app slot, updated in place, and a plan area big enough for the largest plan with its WRITE data. The bootloader has no transport; it applies a stored plan offline and keeps an apply journal (a bit per step, cleared without an erase) so a cut while applying resumes.

| bootloader (no transport, applies plans) | APP slot: runs here, rewritten in place | plan area (≥ largest plan) |

The app implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Inventory and Stage (Profile::InPlace, StageLimits { stored: true, plan_area }).

Choose it when the flash can't hold a second image but has room for a plan area, the bootloader can't have a transport, and the downtime may be the apply time only (no revert: the old image is gone once applied).

Flow.

  1. UpdateNode::node. If the host doesn't know the manifest digest (a development build, an image changed by an interrupted update), it reads Inventory::layout and Inventory::chunks and plans against that.
  2. Stage::limits: stored: true and plan_area.
  3. Stage::begin(Target::Stored, header): also checks that the plan fits the plan area (Error::PlanTooBig).
  4. Stage::erase / copy / write: stored in the plan area in the plan's byte form, nothing in the app slot changes.
  5. Stage::finish: the stored plan is checked before anything is touched: complete, header signature, every COPY source still has its hash, every WRITE's data its hash. The state is PlanStored.
  6. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the bootloader applies the plan in place, checks the image against the descriptor and starts it. The update is confirmed as applied (LastResult { outcome: Confirmed }), there is no trial.

Failures and power cuts. During the download nothing but the plan area changes; the app keeps running. During the apply, the bootloader journals every finished step; after a cut it redoes the step in flight and continues (every step's result is checked by its hash, the WRITE data is still in the plan area). A plan that fails while applying leaves the app slot unbootable; the device needs an updater then (Outcome::Recovery), so keep a recovery path for this case.

Resume. After a lost link or an app reset during the download, begin with the same header continues where the plan area ends (resume_from: the next step). After a cut while applying, the journal resumes; the host sees nothing but a longer reboot.

What the device checks: COPY source hashes and WRITE chunk hashes as the steps arrive and again in finish, the plan area size, the header signature; the applied image against the descriptor.

items.title: 1S-APP-BULK: Parcel Freight
items.text:
One app slot and a plan area; the running app receives the whole plan in one stream into the plan area, keeps doing its job, and the bootloader applies the plan after a reset.

Setup. One app slot, updated in place, and a plan area big enough for the largest plan. The bootloader has no transport; it applies a stored plan offline, with an apply journal.

| bootloader (no transport, applies plans) | APP slot: runs here, rewritten in place | plan area (≥ largest plan) |

The app implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Stage and StageBulk (Profile::InPlace, StageLimits { stored: true, plan_area }).

Choose it when the link is slow or metered and the device must keep working while the download takes hours (a sensor on LoRa), the flash can't hold a second image, and the bootloader has no transport. This is the scenario that ww_dfu's bulk path was made for: the bytes after the header are the plan area's content, unchanged.

Flow.

  1. UpdateNode::node (and Stage::limits, unless the host knows the device type).
  2. StageBulk::begin_bulk(Target::Stored, header, total_len, ack_every): checks the header and that the plan fits.
  3. The plan after its header on the plan credit sink, written to the plan area as it arrives. The app answers anything else meanwhile.
  4. PlanAck { status: Complete } on plan_ack.
  5. Stage::finish: the stored plan is checked before anything is touched (complete, signature, COPY sources, WRITE hashes); PlanStored.
  6. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the bootloader applies the plan in place and starts the new image.

Failures and power cuts. A cut during the download loses nothing stored: after the reboot, begin_bulk with the same header resumes after the bytes in the plan area. A cut during the apply is resumed from the journal. No revert once applied.

Resume. begin_bulk with the same header: resume_from is the number of plan bytes already in the plan area. With ack_every the device also reports its position every so many bytes, for very long downloads.

What the device checks: segment offsets and the plan area size as bytes arrive; in finish the whole stored plan (complete, signature, COPY source hashes, WRITE hashes); while applying, every step's result by its hash and the image against the descriptor.

items.title: 1L-UPD-STEP: Pit-stop Shuttle
items.text:
One app slot; the app reboots into an updater (a bootloader with a transport, or a recovery app), which receives the plan one call per step and applies it in place as it arrives.

Setup. One app slot, no extra flash. The updater is either the bootloader with its own transport (USB, CAN) or a small write-protected recovery app at its own address; it must come back up after any cut and finish the job.

| bootloader + transport = updater | APP slot: rewritten in place |
| bootloader | recovery app (updater, write-protected) | APP slot: rewritten in place |

The app implements UpdateNode and BootControl only (often just reboot(BootTarget::Updater) matters). The updater implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Inventory and Stage (NodeInfo::role is Bootloader or Recovery).

Choose it when the flash has no room for a second image or a plan area, and the bootloader (or a recovery app) can have a transport. It is the fastest end to end and needs no extra flash, but the device does nothing else from the reboot into the updater until the new app starts.

Flow.

  1. To the app: UpdateNode::node: offers has no stage, so the host calls BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::Updater).
  2. The host reconnects to the same device; the updater answers, with a different API.
  3. UpdateNode::node, Stage::limits: an updater usually has a small buffer, chunks come in pieces of max_piece.
  4. Stage::begin(Target::Live, header): from here on the app slot is not bootable until the session finishes (BootState::Updating); the updater records the session in flash.
  5. Stage::erase / copy / write applied in place as they arrive; the planner never copies from a chunk an earlier step has overwritten.
  6. Stage::finish: the new image is checked against the descriptor and marked bootable (Confirmed).
  7. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the new app runs.

Failures and power cuts. A cut leaves no bootable app: the bootloader sees that and starts the updater again (BootState::Updating, app_version: None), and the host continues. A lost link the same. The updater must be able to resume any session it started, which is why it keeps its session record (header and next step) in flash.

Resume. begin with the same header: resumed: true, resume_from the step after the last one that finished; the step in flight is redone from its first piece (Stage::progress shows the piece offset while the link is up).

What the device checks: the header (format, geometry, floor, signature) before erasing anything, every index against the app slot, COPY source hashes, WRITE chunk hashes after the last piece, the image against the descriptor.

items.title: 1L-UPD-BULK: Pit-stop Freight
items.text:
One app slot; the app reboots into an updater, which receives the whole plan as one stream and applies it in place as the steps complete.

Setup. One app slot, no extra flash; the updater is the bootloader with a transport or a recovery app.

| bootloader + transport = updater | APP slot: rewritten in place |
| bootloader | recovery app (updater, write-protected) | APP slot: rewritten in place |

The app implements UpdateNode and BootControl. The updater implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Stage and StageBulk.

Choose it when there is no room for a second image or a plan area, the updater has a transport, and round trips are long, or the link is fast and the host just wants to stream the plan without waiting on every step.

Flow.

  1. To the app: UpdateNode::node, then BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::Updater).
  2. The host reconnects; the updater answers. UpdateNode::node, Stage::limits.
  3. StageBulk::begin_bulk(Target::Live, header, total_len, ack_every: 0): the app slot stops being bootable.
  4. The plan after its header on the plan credit sink, in segments of at most max_piece; the updater parses the steps from the stream and applies each in place as soon as it is complete.
  5. PlanAck { status: Complete } on plan_ack, then Stage::finish: checked, Confirmed.
  6. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the new app runs.

Failures and power cuts. A cut leaves no bootable app; the bootloader starts the updater again and the host resumes. A step that fails ends the session with PlanAck { status: Failed(error) }; the device stays in the updater until a session finishes.

Resume. begin_bulk with the same header answers the byte after the last applied step (the updater keeps it in its session record); bytes of a step that was not complete are sent again.

What the device checks: segment offsets, the header before erasing anything, each completed step (ranges, COPY source hash, WRITE hash), the image against the descriptor.

items.title: ww_error
items.text:
Errors every API can return (STD-16): Unsupported, InUse, Busy, ... look the same in every crate, generic host code handles them without knowing the crate, and tools recognise them by their type. An API crate nests them as one #[common] Common(CommonError) variant of its own error enum (see below and Errors).

wire_weaver re-exports the crate: wire_weaver::prelude has CommonError, CommonErrorOwned (with std) and HasCommon, so an API crate needs no dependency of its own.

items.title: CommonError
items.text:
Variant Message (its doc line) When Unsupported Not supported by this device (a mode, a range, a feature of the call). The device knows the call, and can't do what was asked. InvalidArgument { arg: u8, reason } Argument number {arg} is invalid: {reason}. arg counts from 0. InUse { by } In use by {by}. A resource another function holds ("USART2"). Busy Busy with another operation, try again later. WrongState { reason } Not possible in the current state: {reason}. NoPower { rail } No power on {rail}. A missing supply or IO level ("VIO"). Refused { reason } Refused: {reason}. Possible, but the device won't (locked, a policy). Timeout Timed out. Fault { code: u32 } Hardware fault {code:#x}. Device-specific code.

Strings are bounded (reason 64 bytes, by 32, rail 16) and may be empty: a device that saves flash sends "", and the message leaves the part out (Refused). CommonError is an Unsized enum, so it ends in Unknown(u32) (SW-47): a variant added in a newer ww_error reaches an older host as Unknown(n), not as a decode error.

Unsupported is not the framework's Unimplemented: that one means the device has no implementation at all (a handler returning Unimplemented, an item left out), and stays a framework error.

Display and core::error::Error are implemented for both types, the message is the variant's doc line with its fields filled in, without the final period: In use by USART2.

items.title: In an API's error enum
items.text:
Put CommonError first, marked #[common], and keep the crate's own variants for what a tool or a caller should act on specifically (Nack, UnsupportedSpeed with the range):

use wire_weaver::prelude::*;

#[ww_trait]
trait Sensor {
    fn read() -> Result<u16, SensorError<'i>>;
    /// An error enum of its own isn't needed when only common errors can happen.
    fn calibrate() -> Result<(), CommonError<'i>>;
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone), ww_repr = unib32)]
pub enum SensorError<'i> {
    #[common]
    Common(CommonError<'i>),
    /// The sensor did not answer.
    Nack,
}

#[common] makes #[derive_shrink_wrap] add, for the borrowed and the owned type:

  • From<CommonError<'i>> for SensorError<'i> (From<CommonErrorOwned> for SensorErrorOwned): a helper returns CommonError and is ?-ed into the error of any crate.
  • HasCommon with fn common(&self) -> Option<&CommonError>: generic code gets the common part of any crate's error.

One variant per enum can be #[common], and it has exactly one unnamed field. On the wire a common error takes two discriminants (Common, then the CommonError variant), 4 bits more than a variant of the crate's own.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
fn claim(&mut self) -> Result<(), CommonError<'static>> {
    if self.uart_active {
        return Err(CommonError::InUse { by: MaxLen::new_unchecked("USART2") });
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn sample(&mut self) -> Result<u16, SensorError<'static>> {
    self.claim()?; // CommonError into SensorError
    Ok(self.adc.read())
}

fn read(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) -> RpcResult<Result<u16, SensorError<'_>>> {
    Ready(self.sample())
}

items.title: Host side
items.text:
fn is_retryable<E: HasCommon<Common = CommonErrorOwned>>(e: &E) -> bool {
    matches!(e.common(), Some(CommonErrorOwned::Busy | CommonErrorOwned::Timeout))
}

tests/common_error runs these through a generated server, the generated client and the dynamic client.
