A track is one stream declared in some trait of the device's own API — a stream!(..) such as can[1].rx — identified by its numeric resource path (see Settings and tracks). The recorder logs that stream's items as they come, and a host reads them back through the same stream's own reliable protocol (backfill from the store, see streams): the data itself never goes through Recorder, only through the stream it names. A PC tool decodes a card from the API bundle stored on it. Recorder is what you call to see the state of the card, format it, label spans and moments, and tune how it writes.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Recorder {
    ww_impl!(track[]: Track);
    fn status() -> Status<'i>;
    fn card() -> Option<CardFacts<'i>>;
    fn prepare_format(action: FormatAction) -> Result<FormatOffer<'i>, RecorderError<'i>>;
    fn format(token: u32, rw_mb: Option<u32>) -> Result<(), RecorderError<'i>>;
    fn recording_start(trigger: Trigger, pre_trigger_s: u16) -> Result<u32, RecorderError<'i>>;
    fn recording_stop() -> Result<u32, RecorderError<'i>>;
    fn recordings(after: u32) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, RecordingInfo>, 8>, RecorderError<'i>>;
    fn marker(kind: MarkerKind, label: MaxLen<&'i str, 64>, value: Option<i64>) -> Result<(), RecorderError<'i>>;
    fn sync() -> Result<(), RecorderError<'i>>;
    property!(rw settings: Settings, RecorderError<'i>);
    fn counters() -> RecorderCounters;
    #[optional]
    fn refresh_usb() -> Result<(), RecorderError<'i>>;
}

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Track {
    fn info() -> TrackInfo<'i>;
    property!(rw enabled: bool, RecorderError<'i>);
    property!(rw durability: Durability, RecorderError<'i>);
    #[optional]
    property!(rw compression: Compression, RecorderError<'i>);
    fn counters() -> TrackCounters;
}

items.title: Status
items.text:
status() answers what the recorder is doing:

State Meaning What a UI offers NoCard nothing in the slot "insert a card" NeedsFormat a card without a log (new, or from another system) "format?" with prepare_format Unbound { reason } the card has a ring file, but it is not where the device put it (moved, deleted, replaced by a PC, other card); logging stays off and nothing is overwritten re-create the ring file (keeps the read-write files) or format Formatting { percent } a card check or format is running progress Logging everything works Full the ring is full and the full policy is DropNewest: new items are refused and counted download, then format or switch the policy Failed { reason } a write error, or the card was removed while logging check the card

Status also has the session of this boot (counts up for the life of the card), the running recording, the device time of the newest record, and how much of the ring holds data. State is an Unsized enum, a later version can add a state without breaking older hosts.

card() is None without a card, else CardFacts: kind (SD, eMMC, NOR), capacity, product name, manufacturer and serial from the CID, and what the card reports about its own geometry: allocation unit, the recording unit of its speed class, speed class, UHS grade and video class (0 where the card reports nothing). It also says what is on the card (CardContent: unrecognised, other files, a ring, an unbound ring) and the result of the last card check (CardCheck).

items.title: Formatting
items.text:
A format erases a card, so it takes two steps and the second needs what the first returned:

  1. prepare_format(action) reads the card and writes nothing. It answers a FormatOffer: a one-use token, how long it stays valid, the card, how many bytes would be erased, whether the card holds ring data or files in its read-write region (a UI warns on these), the default and the limits of the read-write region in MB, and the ring size that gives. action is Format (everything) or RecreateRing (after Unbound, keeps the read-write files).
  2. format(token, rw_mb) carries it out. The token works once, for the card the offer was made for, and expires. rw_mb of None is the offer's default and is ignored for RecreateRing. The call stops logging, runs the card check, then writes the layout; progress is State::Formatting in status().

The card check is why the second step is separate: it overwrites the card. It tests that the card really has the capacity it claims (a fake card wraps around when written past its true size), measures sustained sequential write speed and the longest stall, and sweeps write sizes to find the best flush size for this card. The result is CardCheck { aliasing_ok, write_kib_s, worst_stall_ms, best_flush_bytes, rating } where the Rating compares the card with the configured data rate: Good, Marginal (keeps up on average, but its worst stall is longer than the RAM buffer holds: drops are possible), TooSlow or Unchecked. A card that fails the aliasing test is refused with CardFailed before anything is formatted.

A device with no UI can start the same flow from a button (long press) and call the same handlers itself.

items.title: Recordings and markers
items.text:
A recording is a labelled span of the log with an id that counts up for the life of the card. It is started by a Trigger (Api: this call; Button; more kinds are planned) and stopped by a call, the button or a duration. recording_start(trigger, pre_trigger_s) returns the id. In the default RecordingMode::Continuous everything is logged all the time, so a recording only labels a span and pre_trigger_s moves its start back by that many seconds for free; in Triggered mode tracks are written only inside recordings, and a pre-trigger needs a RAM ring per track (Unsupported on a device that has none). recordings(after) lists them oldest first, eight per page, with their trigger, device-time start and length, how they ended (StopReason) and how many bytes of the ring they cover. Recordings whose data the ring already overwrote are not listed. A recording survives a reboot; a power cut in the middle continues it.

A marker is a moment to find again: marker(kind, label, value) writes a record into the system track (track 0) at once, not with the next flush. MarkerKind is Api, Button, Trigger or User { code } (the application's own, stored as a byte >= 3, see MarkerKind::code).

sync() writes what is in RAM to the card now and answers when it is there: before a planned power-off, or from a brown-out warning.

items.title: Settings and tracks
items.text:
settings is one property, Settings:

Field Default Takes effect flush_bytes 64 KB, or the card check's best at once; a multiple of 512 and of the card's recording unit, at most a segment flush_interval_ms 1000 at once; the most a power cut takes when data comes slowly full DropOldest (a logger); DropNewest stops when full next boot mode Continuous; or Triggered next boot usb_view split by recording; by_time, by_track, csv add folders and files next refresh or mount

A write outside the limits answers Common(InvalidArgument). Larger flushes are faster on most cards and lose more in a power cut: nothing written before the last completed flush is lost, and the next mount counts what was in RAM.

track[] is the array of the session's tracks, indexed by track number: 0 is the system track (markers, recordings, drops, card events), the data tracks follow from 1. valid_indices_root_track returns those, and they change only on a boot. Each Track has:

  • info(): the track's identity, numbers only: the stream's resource path in the device API as resource ids with array indices (the form requests use, addressing; empty for the system track), the item type as its ww_self signature and ww_global id, a stable 64-bit key (the same track across sessions and firmware that keeps the path, made from numbers only) and the nominal rate. The device has no resource or type names at hand: a host makes can[1].rx and ww_can_bus::Frame from the device's API, and what a position counts (bytes, frames) from the item type;
  • enabled (a disabled track keeps its place and position and counts its items as dropped; track 0 can't be disabled), durability (Normal: with the next flush; Immediate: written right after each item, for events and errors) and the optional compression (None, Lz4, Heatshrink);
  • counters(): records and item bytes stored this boot, where the stream continues (next, counts across boots), up to where the track is on the card (durable), up to where the host released it, and units dropped.

items.title: Counters
items.text: counters() is for a status screen and for deciding whether a card is good enough: bytes written since the format, data segments reused and ring size (their ratio is the overwritten span), torn blocks and records found by mounts, units dropped in all tracks, card stalls over the threshold with the longest, card write errors, the number of sessions, and the device time of the oldest data still in the ring. A card that falls behind shows as counted drops and card events in track 0, never as silent loss. Numbers are variable length: the counters of an idle track fit in 8 bytes (a test checks it).

items.title: USB view
items.text: refresh_usb() (optional) tells the USB mass storage view to show the log as it is now. The view is a snapshot taken when the host mounts the virtual volume, so new data shows only after a re-mount; this raises a media change instead. A device without a USB view leaves the call out.

items.title: Optional groups
items.text:
A small firmware doesn't need every tier of this API: formatting a card from the host, labelled recordings, markers, per-track durability, counters and the USB view can each be left out whole, not just refresh_usb and track[].compression one call at a time. Optional groups name them so omit / omit_if in ww_codegen! can drop a whole group with one entry.

The minimum every device keeps, whatever it leaves out: status, card, sync, the settings property, and track[].info / track[].enabled.

Group Leaves out A device without it formatting prepare_format, format can't erase or lay out its own card (formatted elsewhere, or fixed at the factory) recording recording_start, recording_stop, recordings logs one continuous span, nothing to label markers marker has no button or application event worth finding again track_settings track[].durability flushes every track the same way, no per-track timing counting counters, track[].counters has no status screen and doesn't judge the card by its wear usb refresh_usb has no USB mass storage view

track[].compression keeps its own plain #[optional] (not a group of its own): a device without a codec leaves only that one property out, same as before.

A build that leaves every group out (tests/recorder_groups compiles and round-trips one end to end):

ww_codegen!(
    my_api::Device for Server,
    server = true,
    omit_if(not(feature = "recorder-full")) = [
        "recorder.formatting",
        "recorder.recording",
        "recorder.markers",
        "recorder.track.track_settings",
        "recorder.counting",
        "recorder.track.counting",
        "recorder.usb",
    ],
);

Without recorder-full, the dispatch arms and handlers of every group above are compiled out; with it, nothing is left out. A device picks any subset the same way, one omit_if(..) entry (or plain omit = [..]) per group.

items.title: Serving it
items.text:
Generate handler stubs with ww api scaffold (AGENTS.md describes the flow) for the same options as your ww_codegen! call:

cargo ww api scaffold ww_stdlib/ww_recorder --name Recorder

It prints the server struct, a stub for every handler (status, card, prepare_format, ..., track_info, track_counters, valid_indices_root_track, the settings getter and setter) and the matching ww_codegen!; the output compiles as it is. --omit formatting,recording,markers,track.track_settings,counting,track.counting,usb leaves the same groups' stubs out.

items.title: Evolution
items.text: No type uses sized or final_structure, so fields can be appended with #[default = ..] and variants added without breaking older hosts; an enum reads a newer variant as Unknown(u32). Adding a method or an optional item is wire compatible. ww_recorder is versioned like any API crate (its version is its identity, see crate layers).

items.title: ww_sd
items.text:
ww_sd (STD-40) gives a host raw access to an SD card: its state, its registers as the card sent them, the init sequence with what each step answered, and single raw commands with their response, status bits and timing. It is for bring-up, card checks and odd cards; on the device it is a passthrough to the SDMMC (or SPI) driver. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver and ww_error.

[dependencies]
ww_sd = "0.1"

Reading and writing data is ww_block's BlockDevice, served for the same card: it holds the write lease that ww_sd's changing commands need.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait SdCard {
    fn capabilities() -> Capabilities;
    fn state() -> CardState;
    stream!(detect: bool);
    fn registers() -> Result<SdRegisters<'i>, SdError<'i>>;
    fn reinit(lease: u32, max_clock_khz: u32, bus_width: BusWidth) -> Result<InitReport<'i>, SdError<'i>>;
    fn command(lease: Option<u32>, cmd: RawCommand<'i>) -> Result<RawResponse<'i>, SdError<'i>>;
}

items.title: State and registers
items.text:
• capabilities(): the host controller's Interface (Sd or Spi), widest bus, highest clock, UHS (1.8 V), and unrestricted, whether this build lets restricted commands through.
  • state(): CardState with present, the capacity class (Sdsc, Sdhc, Sdxc, Sduc), the bus after the last init (BusState: width, clock in kHz, SpeedMode, 1.8 V or not) and leased, whether a ww_block lease holds the card.
  • detect: card inserted (true) or removed (false).
  • registers(): SdRegisters with CID, CSD, OCR, RCA, SCR and SD Status (ACMD13) as raw bytes, MSB first, as the card sent them. Decoding is the host's: the device keeps no parser for fields it doesn't use itself. Read at init and cached, so safe at any time; Common(WrongState) before the card is initialised.

items.title: Init with a report
items.text: reinit(lease, max_clock_khz, bus_width) runs the init sequence again (CMD0, CMD8, ACMD41, CMD2, CMD3, ..., then bus width and speed up to the limits given) and answers an InitReport: each step's command, argument, the first 32 bits of its response, its Outcome, how often it was sent (ACMD41 polls while the card is busy) and how long it took, then the state it ended in and the total time. A card that doesn't come up is not an error: the report says where it stopped. It needs the lease, since the card's user loses the card meanwhile.

items.title: Raw commands
items.text:
command(lease, cmd) sends one RawCommand: the index (0..=63), the argument, whether it is an application command (CMD55 goes first), the ResponseType the controller should expect (None, R1, R1b, R2, R3, R6, R7), an optional DataPhase (Read { block_len, blocks } or Write { block_len, data }, at most MAX_DATA = 4096 bytes) and an optional timeout.

The answer RawResponse has:

  • outcome: Ok, ResponseTimeout, ResponseCrc, DataTimeout, DataCrc, BusyTimeout or Other { code }. What the card did is data, not an error of the call, so the bytes and the timing come back on a failure too (R3 has no CRC: a controller that checks it anyway reports ResponseCrc with good bytes).
  • response: the response bytes, MSB first, without start bit, index and CRC (4 bytes, 16 for R2).
  • status: the card status bits of an R1 or R1b response as CardStatus, with the bits as constants (CardStatus::ILLEGAL_COMMAND, ...), current_state() and is_error().
  • data: what the data phase read.
  • timing: microseconds from sending the command to the end of the response, of the data phase and of busy. This is what makes raw commands worth having for bring-up and for judging cards.

An error of the call means the command wasn't sent: NoCard, BadLease, Restricted, Common(Unsupported) for a command the interface doesn't have (SPI mode), Common(InvalidArgument).

items.title: What a command needs
items.text:
ww_sd::access(index, arg, app) (also RawCommand::access() and RawCommandOwned::access(), so a host can tell before sending) sorts commands into three Access classes:

Access Commands Needs Free reads and status queries: CMD9, CMD10, CMD13, CMD17, CMD18, CMD19, CMD30, CMD55, CMD6 in check mode, CMD56 read, ACMD13, ACMD22, ACMD51, and CMD58/CMD59 of SPI mode nothing Lease everything else: writes, CMD38 erase, CMD6 switch (changes the speed under the driver), CMD0, bus width, ... the current lease of ww_block::BlockDevice::claim Restricted CMD42 (lock, unlock, passwords, force erase) and CMD27 (program CSD, whose permanent write-protect bit can't be cleared) refused: they can lock a card or damage it for good

It is an allow-list: a command not known to only read needs the lease. A firmware built with the feature raw-sd-unrestricted of ww_sd lets restricted commands through with the lease, for bring-up builds only, and says so in Capabilities::unrestricted. ww_sd::check_access(&cmd, lease_ok) is the whole rule for the device's command handler.

fn sd_command(
    &mut self,
    _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
    lease: Option<u32>,
    cmd: ww_sd::RawCommand<'_>,
) -> RpcResult<Result<ww_sd::RawResponse<'_>, ww_sd::SdError<'_>>> {
    let lease_ok = lease.is_some_and(|l| self.lease_ok(l));
    if let Err(e) = ww_sd::check_access(&cmd, lease_ok) {
        return Ready(Err(e));
    }
    // hand the command to the driver
}

Who may call the lease commands at all is the firmware's choice per link, made where it hands out the lease (ww_block answers claim with Common(Refused), see Who may write); ww_sd has no access rules of its own.

items.title: Errors
items.text: SdError nests CommonError first (see ww_error), then NoCard, BadLease (the command changes the card and the call has no current lease) and Restricted { index }. Each call lists those it returns (#[errors]).

items.title: Serving it
items.text: ww api scaffold <crate> prints the server struct and every handler stub. The device needs a raw-command hook in its SD driver. tests/block_sd serves a mock card through SdCard and BlockDevice with one shared lease.

items.title: ww_self
items.text:
ww_self is WireWeaver's own AST: a self-describing model of an API (its traits, methods, properties, streams) and of the data types it uses, serializable with shrink_wrap like any other wire type. The codegen builds one from a #[ww_trait]/#[ww_api_root] definition at compile time, a device can send its own as introspection data, and tools (the dynamic client, the ww CLI, the Python bindings) walk it to call methods, decode values and show an API without any generated code for it. It lives in the wire_weaver repo root, not ww_stdlib/, but is versioned and published the same way; add it with:

[dependencies]
ww_self = "0.2"

items.title: The API model
items.text:
• ApiBundle<'i> - one API as serialized/introspected: magic (ww_self::MAGIC), ww_self_version (the ww_self version the bundle was built with, so a reader knows which format it's in), root: ApiLevel<'i> (the entry point), a deduplicated types: RefVec<TypeLocation<'i>> and traits: RefVec<ApiLevelLocation<'i>> (referred to by index from elsewhere in the model), ext_crates: RefVec<FullVersion<'i>> (every external crate a type or trait in the bundle comes from), and root_omitted (ids of the root's optional items this device leaves out).
  • ApiLevel<'i> - one trait's worth of API: docs, crate_idx (into ext_crates), trait_name, and items: RefVec<ApiItem<'i>>.
  • ApiItem<'i> - one item of a level: id, kind: ApiItemKind<'i>, multiplicity (Flat or Array { index_type_idx } for a ww_impl!(x[]: ..) array), since (the version it was added in), ident, docs, and optional (#[optional]/#[optional(group)], see optional items).
  • ApiItemKind<'i> - what kind of item: Method { args, return_ty, errors }, Property { ty, access, write_err_ty }, Stream { ty, is_up }, Trait { trait_idx, omitted } (a nested level), FlowSink { ty, flow } (a credit sink), or StreamFn { ty, delivery, args, return_ty } (a stream opened by calling it, with its own arguments and Delivery: Plain, Counted or Reliable).
  • TypeLocation<'i> / ApiLevelLocation<'i> - either InLine (the actual Type/ApiLevel, plus which ext_crates entry it's from) or Skipped{FullVersion,CompactVersion} (name/id and version only, plus a signature hash) - how a device leaves out a definition the host is expected to already know (from a published crate), to save flash, while still letting the host check it's the exact same definition.

items.title: The type and value model
items.text:
• Type<'i> - every shape a value on the wire can have: Bool, NumericAny (any ww_numeric number type), String, Vec, Array { len, ty }, Tuple, Struct(ItemStruct), Enum(ItemEnum), Option { some_ty }, Result { ok_ty, err_ty }, Box (self-referential types), Range/RangeInclusive, MaxLen { max_len, ty }, Series (a list written column by column, SW-60), OutOfLine { type_idx } (a reference into ApiBundle::types, how recursive and shared types stay out of the inline tree), and Flag (a relocated Option/Result presence bit, #[flag] - marks a named field, never appears in a value).
  • Value<'i> - a value matching some Type: Bool, Numeric(NumericValue), String, Vec/Array/Tuple (of Values), Struct { fields: FieldsValue }, Enum { variant, fields }, Option, Result, Range/ RangeInclusive (of NumericValue). This is what a dynamic client builds from wire bytes plus a Type, without generated Rust types for the API at hand.
  • ItemStruct<'i> / ItemEnum<'i> - a struct's/enum's own size: ElementSize (the same size assumption #[derive_shrink_wrap] picks), crate_idx, docs, ident, and fields/(repr: Repr, variants: RefVec<Variant>).
  • Field<'i> / Variant<'i> - ident, ty, docs, since; a Field also carries its default: Option<Value> (for a #[default = ..] field) and relocates its own presence flags with #[flag] the same way ww_version::Version does.

Every enum in this model is no_future_version (SW-47): rather than tolerating an unknown future variant the usual ShrinkWrap way, a bundle names its own ww_self_version and a reader is expected to walk the whole model, so a newer kind of item or type can't silently be skipped - that tolerance is handled one layer up instead (introspection version negotiation, INT-8).

items.title: Dynamic access helpers
items.text:
With the std feature, owned types (TypeOwned, ValueOwned, ApiBundleOwned, ...) get methods for walking the model without generated code:

  • ApiBundleOwned::get_item(id_chain) / get_trait / get_ty / crate_name / crate_version - resolve an item path, a nested trait, an out-of-line type, or an ext_crates entry by index.
  • TypeOwned::get_in_line(bundle) - follows an OutOfLine reference to the actual Type.
  • TypeOwned::human_name / human_definition - a Rust-like name ("Option<Vec<u8>>") or full definition, with or without the owning crate's name, for display in a tool.
  • TypeOwned::is_lifetime / is_unsized / is_byte_slice / max_len - what the type needs structurally (does it borrow, is its size written to the FIFO, is it Vec<u8>/MaxLen<Vec<u8>, N>, what bound a MaxLen carries).
  • TypeOwned::is_common_error / ValueOwned::common_error / doc_message - recognise ww_error::CommonError (by crate and type name, any version, even when its definition was left out) inside an API's own error enum, and turn an error variant's first doc line into a message with its fields filled in (doc_message, used for Display on generated error types; fill in ww_self::common does the {field} substitution).
  • ww_self::errors - per-method #[errors(..)] lists (API-32): ApiItemKindOwned::error_list, error_list_docs (one doc line per entry, "any CommonError" for a bare Common), error_list_contains (whether a returned error value matches the list), error_value_name.
  • ApiItemKindOwned::as_stream_fn / as_stream - see any device-to-host stream (a plain stream!, a #[stream] method, or a StreamFn) uniformly as a StreamFnRef (item type, Delivery, arguments, return type), or as a stream/sink with its direction and flow control.

items.title: Signatures, and putting skipped definitions back
items.text:
ww_self::signature computes a signature for a trait or type: a truncated SHA-256 (SIGNATURE_LEN, 8 bytes) of a canonical bundle holding just that definition and everything it refers to, in-line, with indices renumbered in the order of first use - so the signature depends only on the definition, not on where it sat in the original bundle or what else was alongside it. trait_signature/type_signature take a Resolve callback to look up Skipped* definitions (e.g. from a crate's published snapshot) along the way.

ww_self::inline::inline_skipped uses the same signatures to put Skipped* locations back: it resolves each one, checks its signature matches what was stored, and replaces it in place (appending whatever the restored definition itself refers to). Anything not found, or found with a different signature, comes back as a NotInlined (kind, crate/version if known, name, reason) instead of being substituted silently.

A signature is an honest description of the definition a device was built with, docs included: a crate version that is not published yet changes under the same version, and so does a signature when the ww_self model gets a field. A device built from another revision than the host then sends a signature the host's snapshot doesn't have.

items.title: The definition cache
items.text:
For that case, codegen keeps every definition it leaves out of a device's introspection data in ~/.wire_weaver/definitions/ on the machine it builds on: the canonical bundle's bytes as they were hashed, in a file named after crate, version, kind, name and signature (ww_si-0_1_0-type-Volt-049a2a94f6d68bb5.ww). A host (wire_weaver_client, the ww CLI, Python's connect()) that doesn't find a skipped definition in its snapshots under its signature looks it up there with ww_self::inline::inline_skipped_or_cached, which checks the bytes against the signature before using them, so an entry written by an older ww_self still reads. The definition is put back in-line and the API check then compares it with the host's by the evolution rules, with a warning that the device has another revision of it:

Device API has type ww_si::Volt 0.1.0 with signature 049a2a94f6d68bb5 (this host's is 0af8195a2e0069fe): likely a
build from another revision of an unpublished crate, its definition is from the definition cache and is compared by
the evolution rules

Only when no definition with that signature is found anywhere does a resource that uses it fail the check, with both signatures, the likely cause and the fix: rebuild (reflash) both sides from one revision, or build the device's firmware once on the host's machine so that its definitions get into the cache. Entries are a few hundred bytes each and are never changed; deleting the directory only loses the ability to talk to such devices.

items.title: Visiting the model
items.text: ww_self::visit::Visit (read-only) and ww_self::visit_mut::VisitMut (mutable) are exhaustive visitor traits over every node kind above, generated from one define_visitor! macro definition: each has a default per-node method (visit_type, visit_api_item_kind, ...) that recurses into its children, plus leaf methods (visit_ident, visit_docs) that do nothing by default - override just the node kinds you care about and call the matching free function (visit::visit_api_bundle, ...) to keep recursing into the rest. Canonical (behind signature) and the remapping pass in inline are both built this way, overriding only visit_type/ visit_api_item_kind/etc. to rewrite the handful of index fields (type_idx, trait_idx, crate_idx) that need remapping.

items.title: How it relates to the rest
items.text: wire_weaver_core's codegen (transform/codegen) builds an ApiBundle from the trait source it parses and hands it to both the server (introspection data a device can send) and client codegen; wire_weaver_client uses it for the dynamic client, compatibility/evolution checks against a cached bundle, and the generated client's own layout; wire_weaver_cli and wire_weaver_py walk it to print an API tree, introspect a live device, and expose it to Python. wire_weaver_snapshots stores published crates' bundles so devices can skip their definitions and hosts can still resolve and verify them via the signatures above.

items.title: ww_si
items.text:
ww_si gives device APIs typed physical values: a quantity is an SI prefix plus a ww_numeric NumericValue in whatever number type the device picks, with the unit in the type. The API says "this is a voltage", each device decides whether that is a u16 of mV or an f32 of V, and the host reads them all.

use ww_si::{Ampere, Prefix, Volt, Watt};

let v = Volt::milli(3300u16);          // prefix Milli, value U16(3300)
let w = Volt::from_f32(3.3);           // prefix Unit, value F32(3.3)
assert_eq!(Volt::milli(1500u16), Volt::base(1.5f32)); // compares values, not representations
assert_eq!(v.to_f64(), 3.3);           // in V
assert_eq!(w.to_i32_in(Prefix::Milli), Some(3300));
assert_eq!(v.to_string(), "3300 mV");
let p: Watt = v * Ampere::milli(500u16);              // the compiler checks the units

Volt::milli(3300u16) is 3 bytes on the wire, 12 e4 0c: the prefix and number type nibbles, then the u16.

items.title: One type for every quantity
items.text:
Every quantity is the same generic struct, and every unit a zero-size marker type in ww_si::units:

pub struct Quantity<U: Unit> {
    pub prefix: Prefix,
    pub value: NumericValue,
    _unit: PhantomData<U>,      // no bits on the wire, no bytes in RAM
}

pub type Volt = Quantity<units::Volt>;
pub type Ampere = Quantity<units::Ampere>;
// .. one alias per unit

APIs and code write the aliases (property!(ro vbus: Volt), Timed<Ampere>). Everything below is written once for all quantities, so Hertz::kilo(400u32) works the same way as Volt::milli(3300u16).

A marker knows its unit through the Unit trait: its SI dimension (Dim, exponents of s, m, kg, A, K, mol, cd), its name and symbol, and how a value becomes coherent SI (Scale: coherent, a power of ten, a factor, or a factor and an offset for °C). Volt::unit() returns it; ww_si::units::by_name("Volt") finds it by the marker's name, which is what a client that only sees introspection data uses.

items.title: Features
items.text:
Everything is a cargo feature, so a firmware compiles only what it uses. std (the default) enables all of them.

Feature What time Second, Hertz, HertzPerSecond, Baud, Timed<T> electrical Ampere, Volt, Ohm, Farad, Siemens, Henry, Coulomb, Watt, Weber, Tesla mechanical Meter, Gram, Newton, Pascal, Joule, Torque, Litre, VolumetricFlow, Speed .. Yank angle Radian, Degree, Steradian, AngularVelocity, AngularAcceleration thermal Kelvin, DegreeCelsius chemical Mole, Katal photometric Candela, Lumen, Lux radiation Becquerel, Gray, Sievert, ElectronVolt logarithmic DeciBel, DeciBelmW (plain structs without a prefix) dimensionless Ratio: duty, probability, scale (a group of its own, as it is used next to any other) quantities all of the groups above host host helpers: Unwrapper u16, f32, .. all number types of NumericValue, passed on to ww_numeric (see ww_numeric) 
# firmware with voltages and timestamps, stored as u16, u32 and f32
ww_si = { version = "0.2", default-features = false, features = ["time", "electrical", "u16", "u32", "f32"] }

The bytes on the wire are the same for every feature set.

items.title: Constructors
items.text:
Constructor Value new(prefix, value) any enabled number type: u16, f32, UVlq32, .. base, milli, micro, nano, pico Volt::base(3u8) is 3 V, Second::micro(100u32) 100 µs centi, kilo, mega, giga Hertz::kilo(400u32) is 400 kHz, Gram::kilo(5u8) 5 kg from_f32(x) f32 in the unit itself, const from_parts(prefix, value) const, for statics and tables quantize(x, prefix, storage) an f32 put into the representation an API documents Ratio::percent, per_mille, ppm Centi, Milli, Micro

Mass is in grams, so a prefix works on it like on any other unit: 5 kg is Gram::kilo(5u8).

quantize is what a device does with a value it computed as a float: Ampere::quantize(0.1523, Prefix::Milli, NumericBaseType::I32) is 152 mA, rounded to the nearest integer and saturated at the storage's range (a float storage takes the value as is). It computes in f32, no f64 code on a device.

items.title: Conversions and comparisons
items.text:
• to_f64() / to_f32(): the value in the unit itself (V, A, Hz, s, °, g);
  • to_f64_in(prefix): in another prefix, Volt::from_f32(3.3).to_f64_in(Prefix::Milli) is about 3300.0;
  • to_i32_in(prefix) / to_u32_in(prefix): as an integer, exact for integer storage (truncated toward zero when going to a bigger prefix), rounded for floats; None when it doesn't fit. Second::milli(5u16).to_u32_in(Prefix::Micro) is Some(5000);
  • to_u32_wrapping_in(prefix): the same modulo 2^32, what a wrapping 32-bit counter of that unit shows, to compare a timestamp with a device clock;
  • to_i128_in(prefix): like to_i32_in up to i128, only with a 64- or 128-bit number type enabled (std has them);
  • to_si_f64(): in coherent SI through the unit's scale: 90 ° is 1.5708 (rad), 20 °C is 293.15 (K), 5 g is 0.005 (kg);
  • with_prefix(prefix): the same value in another prefix and the same number type, if that is exact (Volt::milli(3000u16) to Unit is 3 V; 3300 mV is None), for autoranging before sending;
  • same_repr(&other): same prefix and the same number in the same type, a cheap "did it change since I sent it".

PartialEq and PartialOrd compare values across prefixes and number types: Volt::milli(1000u16) == Volt::base(1u8). Two integers are compared exactly, even 60 orders of magnitude apart; through f64 when one is a float.

On a small MCU the integer conversions, comparisons and the exact arithmetic below take no wider arithmetic than the enabled number types need: with types up to 32 bits (u32, i32, ..) everything is u32 code, nothing of 64 or 128 bits is linked, and ww_numeric::Integer (sign and magnitude) does the work. The same prefix compares the stored numbers; across prefixes the value with the bigger prefix is scaled by powers of ten with an overflow check, and an overflow means it is the bigger one. On a Cortex-M0+ (Donguru, opt-level z) this took 6 KiB of flash off what widening to i128 cost.

Display writes the number as stored with its prefix, {:#} in the unit itself; Debug adds the unit's name and the number type, defmt::Format is like Display:

Value {} {:#} {:?} Volt::milli(3300u16) 3300 mV 3.3 V Volt(3300 mV U16) Torque::milli(250i32) 250 mN·m 0.25 N·m Gram::kilo(5u8) 5 kg 5000 g Ratio::percent(50u8) 50 % 0.5

Baud is a symbol rate, the baud rate of a UART or a protocol decoder, kept apart from Hertz so a baud rate is never taken for a clock frequency (and a tool shows 115200 Bd, not 115.2 kHz). Torque (N·m) has the dimension of Joule but is kept apart the same way. Ratio is a plain fraction (0.5 is half; percent is Centi), for a duty cycle, a probability or a scale factor; DeciBel is the logarithmic one.

items.title: Unit algebra
items.text:
* and / between quantities are checked by the compiler: only the products in the table below build, and the result has the right type. + and - take two values of the same unit, a Ratio keeps the unit, and * f32 / / f32 scale a value.

use ww_si::{Ampere, AngularVelocity, Ratio, Torque, Volt, Watt};

let p: Watt = Volt::milli(3300u16) * Ampere::milli(500u16);   // 1.65 W
let p_mech: Watt = Torque::base(2u8) * AngularVelocity::base(100u8);
let i: Ampere = p / Volt::base(3.3f32);
let v_applied: Volt = Volt::base(48u8) * Ratio::percent(50u8); // 24 V

Volt::base(1u8) * AngularVelocity::base(1u8) and Volt::base(1u8) + Ampere::base(1u8) don't compile (the first names the missing UnitMul<AngularVelocity> impl of Volt).

A * B = C (also B * A, C / A, C / B) Volt * Ampere = Watt Torque * AngularVelocity = Watt Ampere * Ohm = Volt Watt * Second = Joule Ampere * Second = Coulomb Farad * Volt = Coulomb Volt * Second = Weber Henry * Ampere = Weber AngularVelocity * Second = Radian Speed * Second = Meter Acceleration * Second = Speed Gram * Acceleration = Newton Newton * Meter = Joule Hertz * Second = Ratio HertzPerSecond * Second = Hertz

Each line is checked against the SI exponents of its units when ww_si compiles, so the table can't be wrong; a unit with an offset scale (°C) can't be in it. Newton * Meter is a Joule (work), a torque comes from Torque values.

The numbers are computed in f32 (in f64 when an operand is stored as F64) through each unit's scale (Gram::kilo(2u8) * Acceleration::base(3u8) is 6 N), and the result is stored as F32 / F64 without a prefix: operators are for host and FPU math, the representation on the wire stays the device's choice through quantize. They need the f32 feature.

items.title: Exact integer arithmetic
items.text:
For values of the same unit in integer storage, timestamps and durations above all, there are exact methods that keep integer storage and never round:

Method Result a.checked_add(&b) a + b in the finer prefix of the two and a's number type a.checked_sub(&b) a - b, the same way a.checked_mul_int(n) a * n (any integer up to the widest enabled type) in a's prefix and number type a.wrapping_add(&b) a + b in a's prefix and number type, wrapping at its width like a device clock a.wrapping_sub(&b) a - b, the same way t0.steps(&dt) t0, t0 + dt, t0 + 2·dt, .. without end, each as wrapping_add computes it

The checked_* ones give None when the result doesn't fit the number type; all of them give None for floats (their operators are +, -, *) and the wrapping_* ones and steps when b is not a whole number of a's prefix (40 µs added to a time in ms), or when b in a's prefix is beyond the widest enabled integer type.

use ww_si::Second;

assert_eq!(Second::milli(5u32).checked_add(&Second::micro(40u16)), Some(Second::micro(5040u32)));
assert_eq!(Second::micro(u32::MAX).checked_add(&Second::micro(1u8)), None);
assert_eq!(Second::micro(u32::MAX).wrapping_add(&Second::micro(2u8)), Some(Second::micro(1u32)));
// the times of 32 samples at 40 µs, the first one taken at t0
let t0 = Second::micro(4_294_967_000u32);
let times: Vec<Second> = t0.steps(&Second::micro(40u8)).unwrap().take(32).collect();

A batched stream's generated <name>_push_many(state, t0, dt, values) stamps a block of samples this way.

items.title: Compound units and your own
items.text:
A unit outside the list is written with Per<A, B> and Times<A, B> of markers. They are not normalized: Per<Meter, Second> is not Speed, it is shown as m/s and has the same dimension.

use ww_si::Quantity;
use ww_si::units::{AngularVelocity, Per, Times, Torque};

/// Torque = b·ω.
let b = Quantity::<Per<Torque, AngularVelocity>>::from_f32(1.2e-4);
assert_eq!(b.to_string(), "0.00012 N·m/(rad/s)");
/// Propeller: torque = k·ω·|ω|.
let k = Quantity::<Per<Torque, Times<AngularVelocity, AngularVelocity>>>::base(2u8);
assert_eq!(k.to_string(), "2 N·m/((rad/s)·(rad/s))");

An API crate can declare its own marker: a field-less struct deriving Copy, Clone, Debug, Default and an impl Unit with its dimension and UnitExpr (see the Unit rustdoc, a revolutions-per-minute example). It works with every method above; it has no products, and clients that don't know it show it by name. Its UnitExpr can be a power too, UnitExpr::Pow(&METER, 2) is shown as m²; a marker whose UnitExpr is not a named one writes its run-time form SI_EXPR as well.

items.title: Second as a timestamp
items.text:
A Second that marks when something happened (an ADC sample, the start and end of an I2C transaction) is the device's time since its clock started. A device has one clock, so the timestamps of all its traits line up, and ww_timebase::Clock::now() reads it in full. The device picks the prefix and the storage, and keeps them the same for a given stream or method.

Fixed-width unsigned storage holds the time modulo 2^bits, so it wraps:

Storage Wraps after (µs) Wraps after (ms) U16 65.5 ms 65.5 s U32, UVlq32 71.6 min 49.7 days U64, UVlq64 584 000 years never

Timestamps are never signed or floats. On the host, Unwrapper (feature host) gets the full time back. It is anchored on a full-width reading of the same clock, then takes each timestamp as the value with the same low bits closest to the previous one:

use ww_si::{Second, Unwrapper};

let mut unwrapper = Unwrapper::new(Second::micro(5_000_000_123u64)).unwrap(); // Clock::now()
let full = unwrapper.unwrap(Second::micro(705_032_827u32)).unwrap();        // U32 µs from a stream
assert_eq!(full, Second::micro(5_000_000_123u64));

That works while consecutive timestamps are less than half a wrap period apart; re-anchor with anchor(now) after a longer pause. Use one Unwrapper per stream. U64 and signed values pass through unchanged. The anchor and the timestamps can be in different prefixes, and the timestamps can change prefix and storage from one to the next.

Without a full reading of the clock, Unwrapper::default() takes the first timestamp as is (the earliest time it can be) and counts on from there; restart() starts over, for a device whose clock restarted. This is what wire_weaver_client does for every time a device sends (timestamps).

items.title: Timed values
items.text:
Timed<T> { t: Second, value: T } is a value with the time it was taken, t a device timestamp as above: a sample of a property, an item of a stream (Timed<Ampere>). It is a final_structure struct of t and then value, the same bytes a #[derive_shrink_wrap(final_structure)] struct of those two fields has, so no fields can be added to it later. In an API it is used with its argument, property!(ro current: Timed<Ampere>); its definition is in the ww_si snapshot, so devices leave it out of their introspection data (see generic types in an API).

use ww_si::{Ampere, Second, Timed};

let sample = Timed::new(Second::micro(1_000_000u32), Ampere::milli(-1200i32));

In a Series (see series) t is a column like any other: 32 Timed<Volt> samples at a 40 µs clock are 22 bytes.

items.title: On the wire and in introspection
items.text:
A quantity is a final_structure struct of its prefix and its value; the unit takes no bits. The bytes are the same as in ww_si 0.1, where each quantity was a struct of its own, so recorded data and Series blobs still decode:

Value Bytes Volt::milli(3300u16) 12 e4 0c Ampere::micro(-152000i32) 26 40 ae fd ff Volt::from_f32(3.3) 07 33 33 53 40

In the API model a use of Volt is an instance of the generic Quantity with the marker units::Volt as its argument (an alias is not a definition of its own). Both are in the ww_si snapshot, so a device sends a reference to them, not their definitions.

items.title: In ww, Python and dynamic clients
items.text:
A client that only has a device's introspection data still knows a quantity for what it is: ww introspect and ww observe print 3300 mV, Python gets a ww.Quantity. The unit comes from the marker: a marker of ww_si::units by its name through units::by_name (symbol, dimension and scale), Per<A, B> and Times<A, B> as a tree of their parts (0.00012 N·m/(rad/s)), and a marker of your own API crate (struct Rpm;) by its name and docs, without a dimension or a conversion to SI. This works for ww_si 0.2 and later.

q = dev.supply.read()        # Quantity(3300 mV U16)
str(q), float(q)             # "3300 mV", 3.3
q.symbol, q.dim              # "V", {"kg": 1, "m": 2, "s": -3, "A": -1}
q.to_si()                    # 3.3
dev.supply.write(1.5)        # 1.5 V

In Rust, wire_weaver_client::quantity::DynQuantity::from_value(&value, &ty, &bundle) gives the prefix, the number and a DynUnit; its Display is the same text as the typed Quantity's, to_si_f64() converts through the unit's scale and to_value() makes a value to write. See wire_weaver_py/README.md for the Python side.

An AnyQuantity goes the same way: DynQuantity::from_value reads its unit from the value, a named unit of ww_si becomes the same DynUnit as the typed quantity's (so 3300 mV either way), a device's own unit keeps the dimension and scale it sent, and ww, Python and to_value() treat it like any other quantity. DynUnit is shown and converted by ww_si::tree, the code behind the typed Display: a client with its own unit model implements ww_si::tree::Tree for it and gets the same text.

items.title: Units known only at run time
items.text:
Some units are not known when the API is written: an ADC input whose unit is set by configuration, a generic sensor channel, a calibration that turns volts into bar. For those the unit goes on the wire as an SIExpr, and a value with one is an AnyQuantity { prefix, value, unit }:

use ww_si::units::{self, AngularVelocity, Per, Torque};
use ww_si::{AnyQuantity, Dim, Prefix, SIExpr, Scale, Volt};

// a ww_si unit, or a typed quantity turned into one
let v = AnyQuantity::from(Volt::milli(3300u16));
assert_eq!(v.to_string(), "3300 mV");
assert_eq!(format!("{v:#}"), "3.3 V");
assert_eq!(v.to_quantity::<units::Volt>(), Some(Volt::milli(3300u16)));
let unit = SIExpr::of::<Per<Torque, AngularVelocity>>();
assert_eq!(unit.to_string(), "N·m/(rad/s)");

// a device's own unit: its dimension and scale make it convertible to SI anyway
let rpm = SIExpr::Named {
    name: "Rpm",
    symbol: "rpm",
    dim: Dim::new(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
    scale: Scale::Factor(core::f64::consts::TAU / 60.0),
};
let speed = AnyQuantity::new(Prefix::Kilo, 3u8, rpm);
assert_eq!(speed.to_string(), "3 krpm");

SIExpr is the same model as the markers, put on the wire: Named { name, symbol, dim, scale }, Mul, Div and Pow of other SIExprs (through RefBox, so decoding one reads only its top node). A marker's UnitExpr maps one to one onto an SIExpr (Unit::SI_EXPR, SIExpr::of::<U>(); SIExprOwned::from(&UnitExpr) on a host), and back SIExpr == UnitExpr compares the trees and known() finds the ww_si unit of a named one. Symbol, name, dimension and factor are computed by the same code for both, so a run-time unit is shown exactly like the typed one. A tree that comes from another device is walked at most MAX_UNIT_DEPTH (32) levels deep: a deeper part has no dimension and is shown as …, it can't overflow the stack.

Dim is seven 4-bit signed exponents in the order s, m, kg, A, K, mol, cd (each -8..=7, 28 bits, sized). Dim::new is const and refuses an exponent out of range at compile time; checked_mul, checked_div and checked_pow give None for a run-time tree whose exponents leave the range. Scale is a nibble and then its numbers. These are the bytes:

Value Bytes Dim of Volt (s⁻³ m² kg A⁻¹) d2 1f 00 0 Scale::Coherent 0 Scale::Pow10(-3) 1 fd Scale::Factor(0.5) 2 and the f64, 8 bytes SIExpr::of::<units::Volt>() 00 56 6f 6c 74 56 d2 1f 00 00 00 01 14, 13 B SIExpr::of::<Per<Torque, AngularVelocity>>() 49 B AnyQuantity::from(Volt::milli(3300u16)) 12 e4 0c, the 13 B of the unit, 59: 17 B

The unit costs bytes on every value (17 bytes instead of 3 for 3300 mV), so a value whose unit is known when the API is written stays a typed quantity, and a channel's unit is better sent once in its description than with every reading: ww_adc has ChannelInfo::unit: SIExpr<'i> and plain numbers in its readings.

items.title: Prefixes
items.text: Prefix covers every SI prefix from Quecto (10⁻³⁰) to Quetta (10³⁰), From<Prefix> for i8 gives the power of ten and symbol() its symbol (m, µ, k). The most used ones (Unit, Milli, Micro, Nano, Pico, Kilo, Mega, Giga) take one nibble on the wire.

items.title: ww_signal_generator
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_signal_generator is a global WireWeaver trait family for driving outputs: digital patterns on many pins at a fixed rate, and analog waveforms on DACs. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver, ww_si (Hertz/Second/Volt), ww_logic_analyzer (reuses its chunk encodings and Edge) and ww_adc (reuses SampleFormat and Linear for DAC tables).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_signal_generator = "0.1"

It is the reverse of ww_logic_analyzer: that crate samples many digital channels on one clock, this one drives them. A square wave from a timer pin is ww_pwm, not this crate; WaveformGenerator is for actual DACs (an MCU's DAC with a DMA table, a DDS chip, a lab function generator).

items.title: Traits
items.text: A device with a pattern generator (DMA-to-GPIO, a PIO program) implements PatternGenerator; one with analog outputs implements WaveformGenerator. A device can have both, neither, or only one.

items.title: PatternGenerator
items.text:
Digital channels driven from a pattern at a fixed rate, all switching on the same tick:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait PatternGenerator {
    fn capabilities() -> PgCapabilities<'i>;
    fn configure(config: PgConfig<'i>) -> Result<PgActual, PgError>;
    #[credit]
    sink!(pattern: StreamChunk<'i>);
    fn start() -> Result<(), PgError>;
    fn stop();
    fn status() -> PgStatus;
}
  • capabilities - channels, rates, pattern memory, which encodings it accepts (raw / transitions), and which start conditions work (external_start, analyzer_start).
  • configure - sets channels, rate, repetition (Repeat::Once / Times(n) / Forever), idle levels and the start condition, and returns what was actually set; drops a pattern already loaded.
  • pattern - the pattern data, appended in order; Open starts a new pattern, Close marks it complete. The sink's credit is the device's free pattern memory, so a host can never overrun it.
  • start - starts output now, or arms it to wait for PgConfig::start. Started before the pattern is complete, it plays what it has while the sink keeps filling, and stops with PgStatus::Underrun if the host falls behind.
  • stop - stops output; channels go to their idle levels.
  • status - Idle, Loading { samples }, Ready, Running { repeat, t_start }, Done { t_start }, Underrun.

Replaying a capture. The pattern sink takes ww_logic_analyzer::StreamChunk — Raw words or per-channel Transitions — the very item type LogicAnalyzer::read_raw / read_transitions and LogicStream produce. A host replays a capture by reading it out in an encoding the generator accepts (PgCapabilities::raw / ::transitions) and feeding the chunks to the sink unchanged, with the capture's rate and channel mapping carried over into PgConfig.

Start conditions (Start): Now (on start()), External { edge } (the external trigger input), or AnalyzerTrigger (this device's own LogicAnalyzer triggering) — a stimulus and its response sharing one time base. PgCapabilities::external_start / analyzer_start say which work.

Pins. While a pattern plays, its channels belong to the generator: ww_gpio::Pin::set_mode / set_output_level on the same pin answer PgError::InUse; reading the level still works.

items.title: WaveformGenerator
items.text:
DAC outputs, one sub-trait per channel:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait WaveformGenerator {
    ww_impl!(channel[]: WaveformChannel);
    fn capabilities() -> WgCapabilities<'i>;
    fn start_together(channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_CHANNELS>) -> Result<(), WgError>;
}

#[ww_trait]
pub trait WaveformChannel {
    fn set(waveform: Waveform) -> Result<WaveformActual, WgError>;
    fn stop(level: Volt) -> Result<Volt, WgError>;
    fn state() -> WaveformState;
    #[credit]
    sink!(table: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_TABLE_CHUNK>);
}
  • capabilities - the channels and their ranges, rates, resolution and table formats (WgChannelInfo).
  • start_together - starts every already-set channel in the list on the same sample clock tick, so their phases line up against each other (WgError::Unsupported if the channels don't share a clock).
  • WaveformChannel::set - starts or changes one output's waveform and returns what the DAC actually does (clamped levels, the frequency its sample clock divides to).
  • stop - stops and holds a level, returning the level actually held.
  • state - Stopped { level }, Held { waveform } (set, waiting for start_together), or Running { waveform, actual }.
  • table - raw DAC codes of a Shape::Arbitrary waveform, appended in order (Open / Close bracket one table); the credit is the channel's free table memory.

Shapes (Waveform { shape, freq, amplitude, offset, phase }, amplitude peak-to-peak, phase against the other channels in start_together): Sine, Square { duty }, Triangle, Sawtooth { rising }, Dc (offset only), and Arbitrary { format, once } — the table sink's codes played once per period, or once and held with once; fed faster than it plays, a once table is a streamed DAC output. Table codes are raw, converted to volts by WgChannelInfo::code_to_volt (a Linear, the same pair ww_adc uses the other way round).

items.title: Types
items.text:
• PgCapabilities<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, PgChannelInfo<'i>>, MAX_CHANNELS>, rates: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, RateLimit>, MAX_RATE_LIMITS>, memory: u32, raw / transitions: bool, external_start / analyzer_start: bool.
  • PgChannelInfo<'i> - name, gpio_pin: Option<u8> (the same pin's index in the device's ww_gpio::Bank).
  • PgConfig<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_CHANNELS>, rate: Hertz, repeat: Repeat, idle: u32 (bit i is the idle level of channels[i]), start: Start.
  • Repeat - Once, Times(u32), Forever.
  • Start - Now, External { edge: Edge }, AnalyzerTrigger.
  • PgActual - rate: Hertz, width: u8 (the raw word width the generator expects).
  • PgStatus - Idle, Loading { samples: u32 }, Ready, Running { repeat: u32, t_start: Second }, Done { t_start: Second }, Underrun; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • PgError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), NoSuchChannel; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, used by PatternGenerator.
  • WgCapabilities<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, WgChannelInfo<'i>>, MAX_CHANNELS>.
  • WgChannelInfo<'i> - name, min / max: Volt, max_freq: Hertz, max_sample_rate: Hertz, bits: u8, table_len: u32, code_to_volt: Linear, formats: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SampleFormat>, MAX_FORMATS>.
  • Waveform - shape: Shape, freq: Hertz, amplitude: Volt, offset: Volt, phase: u16 (0..=65535 = 0..360°).
  • Shape - Sine, Square { duty: u16 } (0..=65535 = 0..100%), Triangle, Sawtooth { rising: bool }, Dc, Arbitrary { format: SampleFormat, once: bool }.
  • WaveformActual - freq: Hertz, amplitude: Volt, offset: Volt.
  • WaveformState - Stopped { level: Volt }, Held { waveform: Waveform }, Running { waveform: Waveform, actual: WaveformActual }; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • WgError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), NoSuchChannel; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, shared by WaveformGenerator and WaveformChannel.

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std") and cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)), so owned (*Owned) variants and defmt::Format are available by enabling the crate's std / defmt features.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyBench {
    ww_impl!(la: ww_logic_analyzer::LogicAnalyzer);
    ww_impl!(pattern: ww_signal_generator::PatternGenerator);
    ww_impl!(dac: ww_signal_generator::WaveformGenerator);
}

A device with both ww_logic_analyzer and PatternGenerator can replay what it just captured: read the capture out in a shared encoding and feed it straight to the pattern sink, see ww_logic_analyzer.

items.title: ww_spi
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_spi is a global WireWeaver trait for talking to the SPI devices on a bus remotely: full-duplex transfers, transactions with CS held across several operations, plain writes, watching a bus without taking part, and standing in for a chip on another master's bus (slave mode). It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver and ww_si (for the Hertz, Second and Volt quantity types).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_spi = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
items.text:
Spi is one bus: configure it, full-duplex transfers, transactions with CS held, writes, and, on adapters with the hardware for it, every frame on the bus on the optional monitor stream. A device with several buses nests it as an array, ww_impl!(spi[]: ww_spi::Spi), monitoring included:

#[ww_api_root]
trait MyAdapter {
    ww_impl!(spi: ww_spi::Spi);
}

// an adapter without monitoring hardware
ww_codegen!(my_adapter_api::MyAdapter for Server, server = true, omit = ["spi.monitor"]);

items.title: Spi
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Spi {
    fn transfer(data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>, SpiError>;

    fn transaction(ops: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SpiOp<'i>>, MAX_OPS>) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>, SpiError>;

    fn write(data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>) -> Result<(), SpiError>;

    fn capabilities() -> SpiCapabilities<'i>;

    fn configure(config: SpiConfig) -> Result<SpiConfig, SpiError>;

    fn set_cs(active: bool) -> Result<(), SpiError>;

    #[optional]
    #[stream(SpiFrame<'i>, counted)]
    fn monitor(config: SpiMonitorConfig) -> Result<(), SpiError>;
}
  • transfer - full duplex: writes data, returns as many bytes as were read. CS is asserted for the call and released after (CsMode::Auto); with CsMode::Manual the bus must already be selected through set_cs.
  • transaction - CS asserted once for every op of ops, released at the end; returns the bytes of every SpiOp::Read and SpiOp::Transfer, concatenated in order. This is how a command-then-response exchange (write a register address, then read it) stays under one CS assertion instead of two separate transfer calls.
  • write - like transfer, ignoring what comes back.
  • capabilities - frequency range, word sizes, master support, IO levels; see Types below. Slave mode is in the device's introspection (the slave group) and slave_capabilities.
  • configure - sets the bus (role, frequency, mode 0-3, bit order, word size, CS mode, IO level) in one SpiConfig and answers with what was actually set: the frequency the hardware settled on, never above what was asked, and the IO level in effect (io_level: None leaves it as it is). SpiRole::Disabled releases the pins.
  • set_cs - asserts or releases CS, only meaningful with CsMode::Manual.
  • monitor - #[optional], a counted stream function: the host opens it with the bus settings needed to decode frames (mode, bit order, word size, IO level) and receives one SpiFrame per CS assertion seen on the bus, in order, until it closes the stream. The monitor doesn't drive CS or the clock itself, it only listens. Its unit is a frame: the event head carries when CS was asserted and how many frames the device dropped (stream delivery). A device without monitoring hardware leaves it out, and a host sees that in the device's introspection.

items.title: Slave mode
items.text:
A device with the slave group of Spi (optional, left out with omit = ["spi.slave"]) answers another master on its bus:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Spi {
    // ...
    #[optional(slave)]
    fn slave_capabilities() -> SpiSlaveCapabilities;
    #[optional(slave)]
    #[stream(SpiSlaveFrame<'i>, counted)]
    fn slave_frames(config: SpiSlaveConfig) -> Result<(), SpiError<'i>>;
    #[optional(slave)]
    fn slave_map_write(offset: u32, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>) -> Result<(), SpiError<'i>>;
    #[optional(slave)]
    fn slave_map_read(offset: u32, len: u16) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>, SpiError<'i>>;
    #[optional(slave)]
    #[credit]
    sink!(slave_answers: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>);
    #[optional(slave)]
    fn slave_clear_answers() -> u32;
}

Opening slave_frames with a SpiSlaveConfig (mode, bit order, word size, IO level, answers) starts it, closing the stream stops it (MISO released); transfer, transaction and write answer WrongState meanwhile. Every frame comes back as a SpiSlaveFrame with what the master sent and what the device answered.

SPI has no clock stretching: the master clocks whenever it likes, so what the device sends has to be ready before CS goes active. answers picks where it comes from:

  • SpiSlaveAnswers::Queue { idle, repeat_last } - answers the host sends on the slave_answers credit sink, one per frame (CS assertion). A shorter frame leaves the rest unsent, a longer one gets idle for the rest. With none queued when CS goes active (the host was too slow), the frame sends idle, or the last answer again with repeat_last (a status the master polls), and SpiSlaveFrame::underrun says so; an answer that comes during a frame waits for the next one. A device with a TX FIFO loads a frame's first bytes before CS goes active, so "queued in time" means there by the time it loads them. This fits protocols where the master sends a command, waits, and reads the answer in a frame of its own, or polls until it is there.
  • SpiSlaveAnswers::Registers(SpiRegisters { addr_bytes, rw, dummy_bytes, idle, len }) - a register map on the device, filled and read back with slave_map_write / slave_map_read. The first addr_bytes bytes of a frame are the address (big-endian), rw (ReadOnly, SetIsRead { bit }, ClearIsRead { bit }) says from a bit of the first byte whether the frame reads or writes, dummy_bytes are clocked between address and data of a read frame (a write frame has none). The device has to turn the address around into data within a bit time or the dummy bytes, so this works up to SpiSlaveCapabilities::map_max_freq without dummy bytes, and each dummy byte gives it 8 more bit times. A host update takes effect between two frames.

SpiSlaveCapabilities tells the fastest SCK with the queue (max_freq), the queue depth, the map size, the widest address and map_max_freq (None: no register map).

items.title: Types
items.text:
• SpiConfig - role: SpiRole, freq: Hertz, mode: SpiMode, bit_order: BitOrder, word_bits: u8, cs: CsMode, io_level: Option<Volt>; the argument and the answer of Spi::configure.
  • SpiMonitorConfig - mode, bit_order, word_bits, io_level: the subset of SpiConfig a monitor needs to decode frames, the argument of Spi::monitor.
  • SpiRole - Disabled, Master. Slave mode is slave_frames, not a role.
  • SpiSlaveConfig - mode, bit_order, word_bits, io_level, answers: SpiSlaveAnswers.
  • SpiSlaveAnswers - Queue { idle: u8, repeat_last: bool } or Registers(SpiRegisters), see slave mode.
  • SpiRegisters - addr_bytes: u8, rw: SpiRwBit, dummy_bytes: u8, idle: u8, len: u32.
  • SpiRwBit - ReadOnly, SetIsRead { bit: u8 }, ClearIsRead { bit: u8 }.
  • SpiSlaveFrame<'i> - end: Second, truncated, overrun (the device lost MOSI bytes), underrun (no answer was queued), addr: Option<u32>, mosi / miso.
  • SpiSlaveCapabilities - max_freq: Hertz, queue_len, map_len, max_addr_bytes, map_max_freq: Option<Hertz>.
  • SpiMode - Mode0..Mode3, the usual CPOL/CPHA numbering; sized, 2 bits.
  • BitOrder - MsbFirst, LsbFirst; sized, 1 bit.
  • CsMode - Auto (asserted per transfer/transaction, released after), Manual (only Spi::set_cs), None (not driven by this device).
  • SpiOp<'i> - one operation of a Spi::transaction: Write, Read(u16), Transfer, Delay(Second).
  • SpiFrame<'i> - one frame seen by Spi::monitor: end: Second (CS released; asserted is the head's time), truncated, mosi / miso: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>.
  • SpiCapabilities<'i> - min_freq / max_freq: Hertz, min_word_bits / max_word_bits: u8, master: bool, io_levels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Volt>, MAX_IO_LEVELS>, io_level_min / io_level_max: Option<Volt> (an adjustable supply), max_len: u32 (largest transfer this device does, at most SPI_MAX).
  • SpiError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), BufferTooBig; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable. Each method lists the variants it returns (#[errors]).

SPI_MAX (512 bytes) bounds every transfer, write and the reads of one transaction concatenated; MAX_OPS (16) bounds the operations of one Spi::transaction. Both are compatible to raise later, not to lower.

items.title: ww_timebase
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_timebase is a global WireWeaver trait for a device's clock: reading device time, and synchronising it with other devices over a sync line (IRIG-B, PPS, ...). It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver, ww_si (for the Second timestamp type) and ww_date_time (for set_time_of_day).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_timebase = "0.1"

items.title: Device time (D6)
items.text: Every device has exactly one free-running clock. Every timestamp it reports elsewhere in its API (captures, stream items) is a ww_si::Second since that clock started, in whatever fixed width fits the field, so it wraps (a U32 of microseconds wraps every 71.6 minutes). There is no separate Ticks type and no unbounded UVlq64: the width is picked per field, and Clock::now() always returns the full-width value so a host can unwrap a truncated timestamp and correlate device time with its own.

items.title: Clock
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Clock {
    fn now() -> Second;

    fn info() -> ClockInfo<'i>;

    stream!(time_map: TimeMapPoint);

    fn configure_sync(config: SyncConfig) -> Result<(), ClockError>;

    fn sync_config() -> SyncConfig;

    fn sync_status() -> SyncStatus;

    fn set_time_of_day(t: DateTime) -> Result<(), ClockError>;
}
  • now() - device time now, full width.
  • info() - static description of this clock: its resolution, what it calls itself, and which SyncFormats it supports.
  • time_map - local time mapped to the shared sync time, sent about once a second while synced and on every SyncState change, so a host can line up this device's timeline with others and see the unsynced spans.
  • configure_sync / sync_config - switch sync off, or make this device the master on the sync line, or a slave locking to one, in a given SyncFormat; sync_config() reads back the last accepted configuration.
  • sync_status() - current sync state, with the offset and local time of the last lock, when known.
  • set_time_of_day - time of day a sync master sends on the sync line, set from its host; has no effect on a slave or while sync is off.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• ClockInfo<'i> - resolution: Second, source: MaxLen<&'i str, 32> (e.g. "RP2350 TIMER0"), sync_formats: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SyncFormat>, 8> (empty without a sync line).
  • SyncConfig - Off, Master { format: SyncFormat }, Slave { format: SyncFormat }; unib32 discriminant, evolvable.
  • SyncFormat - IrigB, Pps; unib32 discriminant, evolvable.
  • SyncStatus - state: SyncState, offset: Option<Second> (local minus shared time at the last lock), last_lock: Option<Second>.
  • SyncState - Free, Acquiring, Locked, Holdover; unib32 discriminant, evolvable.
  • TimeMapPoint - one time_map item: local: Second, shared: Second, state: SyncState.
  • ClockError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors); unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable.

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std"), so owned (*Owned) variants are available by enabling the crate's std feature.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device exposes its clock once at the root (or nested, if grouped with other traits):

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait DeviceApi {
    ww_impl!(clock: ww_timebase::Clock);
    // ... other traits
}

items.title: Server and client usage (tests/io_timebase)
items.text:
There is no dedicated example crate yet (no device in this repo has a sync line); tests/io_timebase is the reference mock server and client, driven through tests_common::start_device like a real device over USB. A sync master, locking immediately, then publishing a time_map point:

client
    .clock()
    .configure_sync(SyncConfig::Master { format: SyncFormat::IrigB })
    .call()
    .await?; // one `?`: a `ClockError` arrives as `CallError::Device`

let mut time_map = client.clock().time_map().call().await?;
let point = time_map.recv().await?;
assert_eq!(point.state, SyncState::Locked);

On the server side, a handler sends a time_map update at any point it decides the sync state changed, same as any other stream item:

fn clock_configure_sync(
    &mut self,
    cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
    config: SyncConfig,
) -> RpcResult<Result<(), ClockError>> {
    // ... update state ...
    api_impl::stream_data_ser()
        .clock()
        .time_map_send_blocking(&point, cx)
        .unwrap();
    Ready(Ok(()))
}

See tests/io_timebase/src/lib.rs for the full mock (a real Instant-backed clock, an IrigB-only sync line to exercise ClockError::Unsupported, and a slave that locks right away instead of staying Acquiring).

items.title: ww_uart
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_uart is a WireWeaver trait for bridging a UART (serial port) to the host, and for watching both lines of a serial link without driving them. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver and ww_si (for Baud rates, the Volt reference-voltage type and Second timestamps).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_uart = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
items.text: Uart is one port: configure it, receive on rx, send on the tx credit sink, and, on ports with the hardware for it, watch both lines of a link between two other devices on the optional monitor stream. It composes with the rest of the API using ww_impl! and is nested as an array when a device has more than one UART (ww_impl!(uart[]: ww_uart::Uart), as examples/uart_api does); monitoring comes with each element, no second array or trait to keep in step.

items.title: Uart
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Uart {
    #[counted]
    stream!(rx: RxChunk<'i>);

    #[credit]
    sink!(tx: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, UART_TX_MAX>);

    fn capabilities() -> Capabilities<'i>;

    fn configure(config: UartConfig) -> Result<UartConfig, Error>;

    fn set_pin_level(pin: Pin, is_high: bool) -> Result<(), Error>;
    fn send_break(duration: Second) -> Result<(), Error>;
    fn tx_pending() -> u32;

    #[optional]
    #[stream(MonitorChunk<'i>, counted)]
    fn monitor(config: MonitorConfig) -> Result<MonitorConfig, Error>;
}
  • rx - received bytes, chunked as they arrive (see RxChunk below). A chunk ends when the line stays idle for more than UartConfig::idle_chars character times, when it is full, or on a line error, so each chunk is one burst of back-to-back characters (a frame of most protocols, or the part of it that fit). A counted stream, opened by calling it: its unit is a byte, so the event head carries each chunk's byte position, the device time of its first byte, and exactly how many bytes the device dropped before it (stream delivery); the chunk itself says when its last byte arrived, if the device measures it (Time below).
  • tx - bytes to send, a credit sink (API-28): the host tracks the device's TX buffer (Capabilities::tx_buffer) and never sends more than it holds, so a large write (e.g. a file piped to the UART) can't overrun it. Its positions count bytes of the payload (API-34), so the device's position is the bytes taken for the line, and credit_progress() on the host says how many.
  • capabilities() - what this device supports: baud rate range, flow control modes, IO levels, buffer sizes.
  • configure - the whole line configuration in one UartConfig (baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits, mode, back-feed detector, IO level, the idle time that ends a chunk), answered with what was actually set: the hardware rounds the baud rate to what its divider can do and the idle time to what its receiver can time, and io_level: None keeps the level and is answered with the level in effect. One call instead of a property per setting, so a port never runs with half a configuration.
  • set_pin_level - manual control of a pin, only in Mode::Test; every other mode answers Common(WrongState).
  • send_break - holds TX low for duration (a break condition), after the bytes already queued.
  • tx_pending() - bytes queued for sending and not sent yet.
  • monitor - #[optional], a counted stream function: the host opens it with the line settings of the watched link (baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits, IO level) and gets back what was actually set (as Uart::configure does), then both directions of the link (rePort: RX and CTS/RX2) in one stream, in the order they arrived: each MonitorChunk says which MonitorLine it came from, so a request and its answer stay in order. Closing the stream stops receiving. The unit is a byte of either line. Most bridges can't sniff a link they aren't part of: such a device leaves it out with omit = ["uart.monitor"] in its ww_codegen!, and a host sees that in the device's introspection.

items.title: Time
items.text:
Every received chunk, on rx and on monitor, says when it arrived, on the device's one clock (ww_timebase::Clock) that also timestamps everything else the device captures:

What Where first byte arrived (end of its stop bit) the event head's t always set last byte arrived RxChunk::end: Option<Second> set by devices that measure it

The bytes of a chunk came back to back, so the time of each one follows from the first. Byte i (from 0) of a chunk of n bytes arrived at:

  • first + i * (end - first) / (n - 1) when end is set. This takes up the sender's baud rate error: UARTs accept 2-3 % off the nominal rate, which adds up to milliseconds over a long burst, so a device that can time the last byte does.
  • first + i * frame_bits / baud when it isn't: frame_bits is start + data + parity + stop bits (UartConfig::frame_bits(), 10 for 8N1) and baud the rate configure answered. The last byte is then at first + (n - 1) * frame_bits / baud.

All are ww_si::Seconds since the device's clock started, in the prefix and number type the device picks (usually a u32 of microseconds, which wraps every 71.6 minutes; the host unwraps it around Clock::now()). With them a host:

  • lines up serial traffic with the device's other data: a GPIO edge, an ADC sample, an I2C transaction;
  • tells a request and its answer apart in time on a monitor link, and measures the turnaround between them;
  • sees the gaps on the line: a chunk ends on a silence of more than idle_chars character times, so the next chunk's first byte comes at least that much after the previous chunk's last one.

On the client the head's time is the t of StreamEvent::Item (rx.recv_event()), next to the chunk:

let actual = client.uart().configure(config).call().await??;
let char_time = actual.frame_bits().unwrap() as f64 / actual.baud_rate.to_f64();
let mut rx = client.uart().rx().call().await?;
loop {
    match rx.recv_event().await? {
        StreamEvent::Item { t: Some(first), value, .. } => {
            let n = value.bytes.len();
            // measured, or one character time per byte after the first
            let last = value.end.map(|end| end.to_f64())
                .unwrap_or(first.to_f64() + (n - 1) as f64 * char_time);
            println!("{n} bytes from {:.6} s to {last:.6} s", first.to_f64());
        }
        StreamEvent::Gap { units, .. } => println!("{units} bytes lost"),
        _ => {}
    }
}

A device that can't time each byte (a DMA that hands over a block when the line goes idle) times the block's end from the idle interrupt, sends it as end, and takes the first byte a character time per byte earlier at the configured baud rate, as examples_mcu/usb_stm32h725ig does.

idle_chars defaults to IDLE_CHARS_DEFAULT (2): a gap of one character time would split the output of senders that pause briefly between characters (a CPU feeding its UART byte by byte, a USB-serial bridge between its USB packets), more would merge the frames of protocols that keep only a short gap between them (Modbus RTU separates frames by 3.5 character times, which 2 still splits). A protocol with its own rule sets it in UartConfig.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• ww_si::Baud - a baud rate (Baud::base(115_200u32)), in the number type and prefix the caller picks, like every other ww_si quantity.
  • Mode - Asynchronous (no flow control), HardwareFlowControl (RTS/CTS), SoftwareFlowControl (XON/XOFF), HighZ (all pins High-Z), Test (manual pin control through set_pin_level).
  • Pin - Tx, Rx, Rts, Cts, used by set_pin_level.
  • StopBits - Stop1, Stop2.
  • Parity - None, Odd, Even.
  • DataBits - Eight, Seven, Nine, Six, Five.
  • UartError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors); unsized, evolvable. Each method lists the variants it returns (#[errors]); line errors of received data are RxFlags of the chunk, not errors.
  • RxChunk<'i> - end: Option<Second> (when the last byte arrived, if the device measures it), flags: Option<RxFlags>, bytes: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, UART_CHUNK_MAX>; when the first byte arrived is the time in the event head, see Time.
  • MonitorChunk<'i> - line: MonitorLine (A or B, 1 bit), chunk: RxChunk<'i>.
  • RxFlags - parity_error, framing_error, overrun, break_detected, seen while receiving a chunk.
  • UartConfig - baud_rate: Baud, data_bits, parity, stop_bits, mode, prevent_back_feed: bool, io_level: Option<Volt>, idle_chars: u8 (idle character times that end a chunk); the argument and the answer of configure. frame_bits() is the bits of one character on the line (start + data + parity + stop).
  • MonitorConfig - baud_rate, data_bits, parity, stop_bits, io_level, idle_chars of the link Uart::monitor watches; the argument and the answer of monitor.
  • Capabilities<'i> - min_baud_rate / max_baud_rate: Baud, io_levels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Volt>, MAX_IO_LEVELS>, io_level_min / io_level_max: Option<Volt> (an adjustable supply), hw_flow_control / sw_flow_control / high_z_mode / test_mode / back_feed_detector: bool, rx_buffer / tx_buffer: u32 (device receive and transmit buffer sizes, in bytes).

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std"), so owned (*Owned) variants are available by enabling the crate's std feature; the plain configuration enums (Mode, Pin, StopBits, Parity, DataBits) also derive PartialEq/Eq.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device exposes a UART by implementing Uart on its API root:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyDeviceApi {
    ww_impl!(uart: ww_uart::Uart);
}

// a port without monitoring hardware
ww_codegen!(my_device_api::MyDeviceApi for Server, server = true, omit = ["uart.monitor"]);

tests/io_uart_api is exactly this shape (used by tests/io_uart's mock server and in-process tests); a device with more than one UART nests it as an array instead (ww_impl!(uart[]: ww_uart::Uart), see examples/uart_api).

items.title: Client usage (examples/uart)
items.text:
The generated client wraps wire_weaver_client::Commander; see examples/uart/src/lib.rs for the small UartBridge wrapper type (connecting over USB with a fixed VID/PID). Sending bytes through the tx credit sink (examples/uart/examples/simple.rs):

let device = UartBridge::new().connect().await?;
let mut tx = device.uart(0).tx().await?;
tx.send_bytes(b"abc000def").await?;

Receiving chunks from rx and configuring the port look the same as any other nested trait, method and stream (see streams); for a non-array uart resource (as in tests/io_uart_api) the same calls drop the index: client.uart().rx(), client.uart().configure(config).

items.title: ww_uid
items.text:
ww_uid lists the unique ids of a unit: a chip's factory id, a MAC address, an EUI-64. One trait implemented once can carry several, which one-trait-per-id could not (a trait cannot be implemented twice on one server).

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Uid {
    const IDS: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, UniqueId<'i>>, 4>;
}

IDS is a const item, served without a handler and read by a host once per connection. Ids are read from the chip at boot, so a server provides them as a fn (const_model = "IDS=fn", fn uid_ids(&self) -> MaxLen<RefVec<'_, UniqueId<'_>>, 4> for uid: Uid). At most 4 ids.

items.title: The primary id
items.text: The first id is the primary id. A device puts its hex (lower case, no separators) into the USB serial number string and a host shows it in ww list.
